name: Pileated woodpecker
blurb: A crow-sized black woodpecker with a flaming red crest. It chisels rectangular holes into dead trees to hunt the ants living inside them.
size: About 1.5 ft (45 cm) from bill to tail, about the length of your forearm.

facts.text: Up to 19 in (49 cm) from bill-tip to tail-tip, with a wingspan reaching 30 in (75 cm) — about the width of a doorway. A crow with a chisel on the front.
Most woodpeckers drill neat round holes. This one gouges rectangles — long squared-off trenches down the trunk, sometimes deep enough to snap a small tree clean in half.
facts.more: The rectangular hole is a signature. Find one in the woods and you can name the bird that made it without ever seeing the bird. Fresh chips at the base of the tree, pale and sharp-edged, mean it was working there recently.

facts.text: It isn't eating the wood. It's mining. Carpenter ants tunnel galleries inside dead trees, and the woodpecker follows those tunnels like a map to the nest.
facts.more: Carpenter ants are the largest part of what a pileated woodpecker eats. Wood-boring beetle grubs come close behind. It also takes berries and nuts, including poison ivy berries, which do it no harm at all.

facts.text: Its tongue is too long to fit in its head the ordinary way. The bones supporting it curl up around the back of the skull and anchor near the nostril.
facts.more: That looping structure is the hyoid apparatus. When the bird pushes its tongue out, the whole apparatus slides forward and the tongue shoots far past the bill tip. It is barbed at the end and coated in sticky saliva, made for hooking ants out of a tunnel it cannot see into.

facts.text: A split second before every strike, a third eyelid sweeps sideways across the eye. Sawdust flying, eye shut, bill still swinging.
Two toes forward, two toes back, and a tail of stiff spiny feathers braced hard against the bark. Feet and tail make a tripod, so the bird is its own ladder.
facts.more: Watch one closely and you will see the tail doing real work. It is shoved against the trunk like a third leg, taking the push-back from every blow. The central tail feathers are noticeably stiffer and stronger than the rest, for exactly this job.

facts.text: It doesn't sing to claim its patch of woods. It drums — a deep rolling burst lasting about three seconds — and it picks a hollow dead tree. Hollow wood carries further, which is the best read of the choice.
It carves a fresh nest cavity nearly every year and almost never reuses the old one. Owls, wood ducks, swifts, squirrels and bats move into the leftovers.
facts.more: This makes the pileated woodpecker a kind of landlord for the whole forest. Plenty of animals need a hole in a tree and have no way of making one. Take the woodpecker out of a woodland and you quietly take the housing supply with it.

facts.text: Both parents take turns sitting on the eggs through the day. But the male takes every single night shift, alone in the dark of the cavity, for about two weeks.
It sleeps standing up inside a hollow tree. Roost trees often have several entrance holes, which reads as more than one way out if something comes in.
Pairs hold the same territory all year and stay together on it. They hammer away within earshot of each other through winter. Most other birds have long since left.

wonder: Feet, tail, tongue, eyelid and skull all doing one job together — a bird made whole for the work it was given.

name: Sociable weaver
blurb: A small brown desert sparrow of southern Africa. It builds the biggest nest of any bird on earth. The nest is a giant grass haystack shared by a hundred families at once.
size: About 5.5 in (14 cm) long, about the length of your hand, and only about 1 oz (28 g).

facts.text: The bird itself is nothing much: 5.5 in (14 cm) long and around 1 oz (28 g). Then you look up at what it built.
Sociable weavers build the largest nest of any bird in the world — a shaggy grass haystack draped over a camelthorn tree. The biggest could shade a parked car.
facts.more: It looks less like a nest than like a haystack that fell out of the sky and got stuck. From below you can see dozens of dark round doorways in the underside. The birds never stop working on it; they add grass their whole lives.

facts.text: Some of these nests grow so heavy that the branch holding them tears loose, or the whole tree comes down under the weight.
Each pair gets a private room off its own entrance tunnel. The room runs up to 10 in (25 cm) long and about 3 in (7 cm) wide. It is lined with soft fur and plant fluff.
facts.more: The birds jab sharp straw spikes downward around each doorway, points facing out. A snake climbing up into a chamber has to push past a mouthful of them. Over a hundred pairs may live in one nest mass, which can mean several hundred birds under a single roof.

facts.text: The Kalahari swings from near-freezing nights to scorching afternoons. Outside air ran from 16°C to 33.5°C (61°F to 92°F). Inside the occupied chambers, temperatures moved only 7-8°C.
facts.more: Thick packed grass is a superb insulator, the same reason a straw bale holds heat in. In a place with no shade and no shelter, the birds are carrying their own weather around with them, built out of dead grass.

facts.text: The chambers deep in the middle of the mass stay warmest, so those become the night bedrooms. The outer rooms stay cooler, so those are where birds wait out the worst of the afternoon.
A nest is not built and abandoned. Some have been lived in without a break for more than a hundred years, handed down from parents to chicks to grandchicks.
facts.more: No single bird lives anything like that long. The building outlasts everyone in it, each generation repairing and extending what it inherited. It is the closest thing in the bird world to a family home.

facts.text: Grown-up birds who aren't raising their own chicks that year help feed somebody else's. Older brothers and sisters often stay on as helpers at the nest.

African pygmy falcons are actual birds of prey. They move into spare chambers and live inside the weaver colony. Nobody has found the southern birds nesting anywhere else. Almost the whole population there depends on weaver nests for somewhere to sleep.
facts.more: It is an uneasy arrangement. The falcons mostly hunt lizards and insects rather than their landlords, but nestling weavers are taken often enough that the birds squabble with them. The weavers put up with it anyway.

facts.text: They eat insects and seeds, and get all the water they need straight out of their food. In a desert with no drinking water for miles, that is the whole trick.
Cape cobras and boomslangs climb the tree and work through the chambers one at a time, emptying them. In one study, 70% of all the clutches laid were eaten.

wonder: A bird weighing about 1 oz (28 g), raising the only apartment block in the desert.

name: Satin bowerbird
blurb: An Australian forest bird. The males build a decorated stage out of sticks. They spend their lives collecting blue objects to put in front of it.
size: About 12 in (30 cm) bill to tail, the length of a school ruler.

facts.text: About 12 in (30 cm) long — a school ruler, beak to tail. The adult male is glossy blue-black with violet eyes; the female is olive-green and scaly-patterned, with the same startling blue stare.
The male builds an avenue. Two parallel walls of upright sticks are pushed into the ground about a hand's width apart. A cleared court sits at each end.
facts.more: He lines the avenue up roughly north to south, so the sun falls along the court rather than into it. He weeds the court bare, then arranges his collection on the ground so the female — standing inside the avenue — looks straight at it.

facts.text: The bower is not a nest. No egg is ever laid in it, no chick is ever raised in it. It is a stage, built purely to be looked at.
facts.more: This confused the first naturalists who found bowers and went hunting for eggs inside them. They aren't houses. They're closer to an art gallery, and the male is both the artist and the gallery owner.

facts.text: The female does the actual nesting alone. She builds a shallow cup of twigs high in a tree, well away from the bower, and raises the chicks with no help at all.
He collects blue above all. Blue parrot feathers, flowers and berries. Near towns, blue bottle caps, straws, clothes pegs and pen lids. Yellow leaves and anything shiny go on the pile too.
facts.more: Young males start with a jumble of colors and shift steadily toward blue as they mature. Blue is genuinely uncommon on an Australian forest floor. A male holding a big pile of it has been searching a long time and guarding it hard.

facts.text: He chews leaves and fruit into a pulp. Then he picks up a wad of bark and holds it in his bill like a paintbrush. He paints the inner walls of his avenue with it.
facts.more: That wad of bark is a tool — an object picked up and used to do a job the beak alone can't do well. Very few animals use tools at all, and fewer still make one for decorating something.

facts.text: A male needs seven or eight years to finish turning blue-black. Until then he looks like a female, and spends those years building clumsy practice bowers that impress nobody.
Mid-display he throws in impressions of other birds: kookaburras, currawongs, whipbirds. He mixes them into a strange mechanical buzzing. It sounds nothing like a songbird.
Males raid each other. Given ten seconds alone at a rival's bower, a male will wreck the walls and make off with the best blue pieces.
He watches the female constantly and dials his display up or down depending on how she reacts. Push too hard and she leaves; the males who read her best do best.
facts.more: Researchers tested this with robotic female bowerbirds that could be made to crouch or not crouch. Males who kept the intensity high when the female was not crouching startled her away. The successful males were the ones paying attention.

facts.text: Mostly fruit, with leaves, seeds and insects on the side. Chicks get a diet of beetles, grasshoppers and cicadas until they leave the nest.
One wild satin bowerbird was marked with a leg band. It was still alive twenty-six years later. That is the greatest age ever recorded for a banded songbird.

wonder: Nothing about the bower feeds him or shelters him. He builds it because beauty is worth the trouble.

name: Magnificent frigatebird
blurb: A huge black seabird with an eight-foot wingspan and a scarlet throat balloon. It cannot swim and cannot walk well. So it almost never stops flying.
size: Wingspan wider than a doorway is tall, but weighs less than a house cat

facts.text: The wings span up to 8 ft (2.44 m) — wider than a doorway is tall. The whole bird weighs about 3 lb (1.4 kg), roughly a big bottle of water.
facts.more: That ratio is the entire story of this animal. Enormous wing, almost no body. No other bird alive has more wing for its weight. That is why it can hang in the air for hours without a single flap.

facts.text: Its skeleton makes up only about a twentieth of its body weight. Every bone it owns, put together, weighs less than its feathers do.
A seabird that must never touch the sea. Its feathers aren't properly waterproof and its legs are tiny, so a frigatebird that lands on water may not get off it again.
facts.more: So it feeds without stopping. It dips down at speed and plucks a fish off the surface with the hooked tip of its bill. Or it snatches flying fish out of the air as they burst clear of the waves. Everything happens on the wing.

facts.text: It also robs. It chases boobies and terns until they give up their catch, then twists round and takes the falling fish out of mid-air before it hits the water.
facts.more: Sailors named the bird after the frigate, a fast warship built for chasing other ships down. Stealing is only part of its diet, not all of it. But it is very good at it. It will pull a booby by the tail to make its point.

facts.text: The male has a bare red throat pouch he blows up like a scarlet balloon under his chin. Filling it can take him around twenty minutes, and he then sits holding it for hours.
A tree full of displaying males rattles. They clatter their bills, drum on the inflated pouch and call as females circle overhead, deciding.
Frigatebirds fitted with trackers have stayed airborne for weeks at a stretch — no land, no water, no rest at all. They feed, travel and sleep on the wing.
facts.more: They ride thermals, the invisible columns of warm rising air. They spiral upward as high as 8,200 ft (2,500 m) without flapping. Then they glide slowly back down over the ocean until they find the next one. It costs them almost nothing.

facts.text: Tracked frigatebirds sleep on the wing in brief scraps. Often only one half of the brain shuts down at a time. It all adds up to well under an hour a day at sea.
A frigatebird chick is fed by its mother for close to a year after it has learned to fly. That is one of the longest childhoods of any bird.
facts.more: The chick takes so long that a female usually cannot raise another one the next year. She is still feeding the last one. Frigatebirds breed slowly. That is exactly why a colony that gets wiped out takes so long to come back.

facts.text: They nest in colonies in low mangroves and scrub on tropical islands, packed close together. The warm waters they use run from the southern United States down to Brazil and out to the Galápagos.

They can barely walk. Those tiny legs are almost useless on the ground, and a frigatebird nests where it can drop off the edge straight into open air. Nobody has watched one weigh it up; the legs are the obvious reason.

wonder: Bones lighter than feathers, wings like sails — built to live where nothing else can stay.

name: Brown pelican
blurb: A big gray-brown coastal seabird. It hunts by folding its wings and smashing head-first into the ocean from sixty feet up.
size: Wingspan wider than a car, and a bill longer than your forearm

facts.text: Wings spanning up to 7.5 ft (2.28 m) — wider than a car — and a bill reaching nearly 14 in (35 cm), which is longer than most people's forearms.
The stretchy pouch slung under that bill can hold around 3 gallons (11 liters) of water. That is two or three times what the pelican's own stomach holds.
facts.more: The pouch is a net, not a lunchbox. It scoops, then it drains. Cartoons show pelicans carrying fish around in there. They do not. The fish goes down the throat within seconds, and the pouch goes flat again.

facts.text: It hunts by falling. From 59-69 ft (18-21 m) (60-70 ft) it half-folds its wings and drops bill-first, hitting the water hard enough to stun small fish just under the surface.
facts.more: Of the world's eight pelican species, only the brown pelican and its close relative the Peruvian pelican hunt this way. All the others feed sitting on the water, swimming and scooping together. The dive is this bird's signature.

facts.text: Air sacs sit under the skin of its chest and neck. Nobody has been inside a diving pelican to watch them work. But they are the best explanation for two things. The bird takes the smack of the dive. Then it pops back up to the surface like a cork.
Surfacing, it points the bill down and lets the water pour out of the sides of the pouch before tipping its head back to swallow. Eleven liters of seawater is heavy.
facts.more: Those few seconds of draining are the pelican's weakest moment. Laughing gulls know it. They shadow feeding pelicans and snatch fish straight out of the open pouch. Sometimes they stand on the pelican's head to do it.

facts.text: It flies 65 ft (20 m) above the water and picks out one fish. The surface below is heaving, full of glare and chop. The target is only a few centimeters long.

Pelicans fly in single file just above the waves, wingtips almost brushing the water. A wing that low gets extra lift out of the air squeezed underneath it — worked out from the physics, and it makes the travel close to free.
facts.more: Air squeezed between a wing and the surface just below it gives extra lift for no extra effort. Aircraft do the same thing on landing. Watch a pelican line skim a swell and you'll see them rise and fall to stay in that cushion.

facts.text: Chicks feed by shoving their whole head down inside the parent's throat to reach the fish. A big chick can vanish to the shoulders doing it.
Brown pelicans nearly disappeared. A pesticide called DDT worked up the food chain into the fish. It thinned pelican eggshells. Parents settled onto their nests and crushed their own eggs.
facts.more: In some places every single nest failed, year after year. Then the chemical was banned, the fish cleaned up, and the eggshells thickened again. The pelicans came back — off the endangered list entirely. It is one of the plainest proofs anywhere that damage done can be undone.

facts.text: To cool off on a hot day it flutters the bare skin of its pouch rapidly, like a dog panting. The moving air carries heat away through the thin skin.
Adults are nearly silent — the odd low croak and nothing more. The nesting colonies are still deafening, because the chicks scream constantly.
They nest in noisy crowds on islands and in mangroves along warm coasts. The colonies run from the United States down to Brazil and Peru. Some are out on the Galápagos.

wonder: Twenty meters up, through glare and moving water, it finds one fish in a whole ocean — then folds itself into an arrow to reach it.

name: Electric eel
blurb: A long, air-breathing river fish from South America. It can flood the water around it with the strongest electric shock any animal is known to make.
size: About 6.6 ft (2 m) long, as long as a doorway is tall, and about 44 lb (20 kg).

facts.text: A wall socket in an American house carries 120 volts. One kind of electric eel has been measured at 860 — the strongest electric shock any animal on Earth is known to produce.
facts.more: Most electric eels top out nearer 600 volts, which is still five wall sockets. What keeps it from being deadly is how brief each pulse is: thousandths of a second. It stuns rather than kills. Human deaths are very rare, and usually from drowning after a shock rather than from the shock itself.

facts.text: Everything an electric eel needs to stay alive is crammed into the front fifth of its body. Heart, gills, guts — all up front. The whole long tail behind it is electric organ.
facts.more: The organ is built from flat cells called electrocytes, stacked like coins in a roll. There are about 6,000 in a row. Roughly 35 of those rows sit side by side along each flank. Each cell adds its own tiny voltage to the total. Batteries stack in a flashlight exactly the same way.

facts.text: It has a much weaker setting too. A soft pulse of around ten volts goes out constantly, and the eel reads it back. That maps muddy water it cannot see through. This is electrolocation.
facts.more: Amazon backwater is the color of strong tea, and eyes are nearly useless in it. The weak field wraps around rocks, roots and fish, and sensors in the eel's skin feel exactly where that field bends. It is hunting by electricity, not by sight.

facts.text: When a fish hides in the leaves, the eel fires a pair of high-voltage pulses. The shock seizes the hidden fish's own muscles and makes it twitch — and the twitch gives it away.
facts.more: The eel is not zapping at random. Those paired pulses reach the nerves that control a fish's muscles and fire them all at once, the way a doctor's little hammer makes your knee jerk. The hidden fish cannot help moving. Then the eel unloads a full volley.

facts.text: Struggling prey gets the curl. The eel bends into a horseshoe so head and tail press the same fish from both sides, and the shock running between them roughly doubles in strength.
facts.more: Water carries a shock away in every direction. So most of the eel's output is normally wasted on empty river. Folding the body puts both ends of the battery against one animal. That is the difference between a warning and a takedown.

facts.text: An electric eel will leap clear of the water and press its chin against whatever is threatening it. That runs the shock straight into the animal instead of losing it in the river.
facts.more: The higher it climbs, the more of the jolt goes into the target instead of leaking away into the river. One researcher measured this by letting a small eel leap at his own arm: 40 to 50 milliamps went through him, and his hand came back fast.

facts.text: An electric eel can drown. It breathes air through the roof of its mouth, surfacing about every two minutes, and the folded, blood-rich lining in there works like a lung.
facts.more: Its gills are small and barely used. Warm, still Amazon water holds very little oxygen. Gulping air at the surface solves that neatly. But an eel pinned underwater by a net or a fallen log runs out of breath the way you would.

facts.text: It is not an eel at all. Scientists file it with the knifefish, and it swims by rippling one long fin that runs the entire underside of its body — forwards or backwards, whichever it prefers.
facts.more: That single ribbon fin has hundreds of rays. It can send its wave in either direction, so the eel reverses out of a tangle of roots without turning around. Its back carries no fin at all. The whole body is smooth as a rope.

facts.text: Look for it in the slowest, muddiest water in the Amazon and Orinoco. That means flooded forest, swamps and creeks. They are so warm and still that most fish would struggle to get a breath there.
The male whips up a nest of foam out of his own saliva. The female lays around 1,200 eggs into it, and he stands guard over the froth until they hatch.
facts.more: He builds it in the dry season, in a shallow pool cut off from the main river. It looks like nothing much — a patch of bubbles under a bank — which is rather the point.

facts.text: A big one is as long as a doorway is tall — 6 ft 7 in (2 m). It weighs about 44 lb (20 kg), all of it stretched into the shape of a rope.
The very first battery was built to copy a fish. Alessandro Volta stacked metal discs in a pile. He was imitating the stacked cells of an electric fish's organ. The volt is named after him.
facts.more: Engineers are still borrowing. Soft, bendable power sources have been built from stacked gel cells modeled on electrocytes. They are aimed at devices that could one day run inside a human body. No hard metal battery needed.

wonder: That long tail is a living battery — wired, stacked and finished before the eel ever hunts once.

name: Anglerfish
blurb: A deep-sea fish that hunts in total darkness. It dangles a glowing lure in front of its own mouth and waits for something to come and look.
size: Most are hand-sized; the largest females grow longer than your arm

facts.text: The glowing bulb over an anglerfish's mouth hangs from a spine on its back that works as a fishing rod. Scientists call the rod the illicium and the lit bait the esca.
facts.more: In one species the rod stretches nearly five times the length of the fish's own body. In others it is barely there at all. Every species carries a differently shaped esca — some fringed like seaweed, some branched like a tiny antler, each one its own advertisement.

facts.text: The anglerfish does not make its own light. Billions of bioluminescent bacteria live inside the lure and glow on its behalf, and the fish gives them a safe home and food in return.
facts.more: The fish is not the source of the light, but it still works the lamp. It flashes it, dims it, and tucks the whole rod away. Sunlight has never once reached down there. A small blue-green glow is the most interesting thing for miles. Hungry animals swim straight at it.

facts.text: An anglerfish can swallow prey up to twice its own size. The jaw opens far past what looks possible, the stomach stretches to take it, and the whole meal goes down at once.
facts.more: Food is desperately scarce down there — you might not meet another meal for weeks — so the rule is simply never refuse. Long, thin teeth angle inwards, letting prey slide in easily and giving it nothing to push back against.

facts.text: In some species the male is a fraction of the female's size. He bites onto her and never lets go — their tissues join together, and he spends the rest of his life attached to her body.
facts.more: He is built for one job. His nostrils are huge, for tracking her scent through the dark. He has no lure of his own, and a gut too small to feed himself with. Once fused, he draws food from her blood. In return he supplies what she needs to fertilize her eggs.

facts.text: In one species the female reaches 30 in (77 cm) (2 ft 6 in) and the male stops at 6 in (16 cm). In another the male is 0.28 in (7 mm) — a grain of rice beside a female seven times longer.
Deep-sea anglerfish live far below the last of the sunlight, often more than half a mile down. The water there is black, close to freezing, and pressing in from every side.
Some anglerfish have ultra-black skin that absorbs more than 99.5% of the light hitting it. In the beam of a submarine's lamp they show up as a fish-shaped hole in the water.
facts.more: Their skin is packed with pigment granules, arranged so tightly that light cannot get back out. It bounces around inside until it is used up. That matters because the lure is a beacon. The animal holding it needs to stay completely invisible right beside it.

facts.text: Its eyes are small and weak, and there is almost nothing down there to see with them. The best read is that it hunts by its lateral line — a row of sensors along its flank that feels water shifting when something swims near.
facts.more: In deep-sea anglerfish those sensors sit out on little stalks. Held clear of the body, they are not drowned out by the fish's own movements. A shrimp kicking half a meter away makes a pressure ripple. The anglerfish reads it like a footprint.

facts.text: Forget the monster from the films. A humpback anglerfish female is about as long as your hand, 7 in (18 cm), and plenty of deep-sea anglerfish are smaller than that.

An anglerfish is a poor swimmer. Its muscle is soft and watery, and its flesh is loose. That is the argument for why weak swimming suits it. Cheap flesh costs almost nothing to carry. So it can hang motionless in the dark for days.
Not all anglerfish live deep. The same group includes frogfish that walk across coral on their fins, and the goosefish, a flat wide-mouthed thing that lies half-buried on the seabed.
facts.more: Frogfish have arm-like fins with a bend partway along and a proper grip at the end. They stroll rather than swim. They carry the rod and lure too. A frogfish can suck in prey in about six thousandths of a second. That is one of the fastest gulps ever measured.

wonder: A fish that cannot make light, carrying a lamp made of living things that can — two lives fitted together, and neither one works alone.

name: Seahorse
blurb: A small upright fish with a horse-shaped head, a curling tail and bony armor instead of scales. And it is the male who gets pregnant.
size: From shorter than your thumb to about the length of your forearm, depending on the species

facts.text: The male gets pregnant. The female places her eggs into a pouch on his belly, he fertilises them in there, and he carries them for anywhere from 9 to 45 days before giving birth.
facts.more: The pouch is not just a bag. It bathes the eggs in fluid, feeds them, and slowly shifts the saltiness inside until it matches the open sea, so the babies are ready for it. When labor comes he grips a stem with his tail and pumps until the young shoot out.

facts.text: One father can release between 100 and 1,000 babies in a single birth — and the best estimate is that fewer than five in a thousand survive to grow up. That is still far better odds than most fish ever get.
A seahorse has no stomach at all. Food rushes straight through, so it has to eat almost without stopping — a dwarf seahorse can put away up to 3,000 tiny shrimp in a day.
Its snout is a spring-loaded trap. Muscles wind up like a bow being drawn, then let go, snapping the head upwards and sucking prey in faster than you can blink.
facts.more: Biologists call it pivot feeding. It runs on elastic recoil: energy stored in stretched tissue and released all at once. A catapult uses the same trick. A seahorse has no teeth and no way to chew. Whatever it catches goes down whole.

facts.text: Each eye swivels on its own. One can track a passing shrimp while the other scans behind for a crab, so a seahorse never has to choose between eating and not being eaten.
The dwarf seahorse is the slowest fish in the world: about 5 ft (1.5 m) per hour. Crossing your bedroom would take it over three hours. It would take you four seconds.
facts.more: Being slow is not really a problem for it, because it was never built to chase or to flee. It hides, it holds on, and it lets the food come within snout range. Speed would cost energy it would rather spend on eating.

facts.text: Cut across a seahorse's tail and you get a square, not a circle. Square segments grip better and survive being crushed — which is why engineers have copied the shape for robot arms.
facts.more: Researchers 3D-printed one tail with round segments and one with square, then squashed both. The square tail sprang back and kept its grip; the round one buckled and stayed bent. Grippers built on the design are aimed at medical tools and at robots that reach into rubble.

facts.text: Seahorses have no scales. Bony plates ring the body instead, like a suit of armor, which is why a dried seahorse holds its shape and feels like a small carving.
A seahorse winds its tail around seagrass or coral and stays put. It swims so weakly that a strong current can carry it away and wear it out — so the tail reads as a holdfast, not a paddle.
facts.more: In a storm, seagrass beds thrash and the anchors tear loose. Seahorses are sometimes found exhausted after rough weather. They have spent everything they had trying to hold position in water that would not stay still.

facts.text: Seahorses click. They grind two bones in the skull against each other to make a sharp snap. It happens while feeding and while courting. Some growl when handled, a low buzz you feel more than hear.
Many seahorse pairs meet every single morning. They change color, spiral around the same stem of grass and hold tails for a few minutes, then part for the rest of the day.
facts.more: Biologists call it the greeting dance. It keeps the two of them in step, so the female's eggs come ready on the very day the male's pouch is empty again. Miss that window and a whole batch of eggs is wasted.

facts.text: Pygmy seahorses grow bumps on their skin matching the coral they live on, color and all. Some are under 0.59 in (15 mm) — about as wide as your thumb — and one kind was only found when someone collected the coral and looked closer.

wonder: The father carries them, feeds them, and slowly tunes the water in his pouch to match the sea outside — a nursery that gets them ready for the world before they ever see it.

name: Clownfish
blurb: A small orange-and-white reef fish that lives its whole life inside a stinging sea anemone. It is the one address on the reef that nothing else dares approach.
size: About as long as your finger

facts.text: A clownfish lives inside an animal that stings. Anemone tentacles fire venom-loaded harpoons at anything that brushes them. The clownfish sleeps in there.
facts.more: The tentacles are covered in stinging cells called nematocysts. Each one is a coiled dart set to fire on contact. The clownfish wears a thick coat of mucus that does not trigger them. So the anemone treats it roughly the way it treats its own tentacles.

facts.text: The anemone gives the clownfish a fortress nothing will enter. The clownfish drives off anemone-eating fish, clears away scraps, and fans fresh water through the tentacles all night. Add it up and both sides gain.
facts.more: The fanning matters more than it sounds. A clownfish wriggling among the tentacles pushes oxygen-rich water past them. Its droppings feed the anemone as well. Anemones with a clownfish in residence grow faster than anemones without one.

facts.text: A clownfish does not hatch male or female. It grows up male first — then the largest fish in the anemone turns female, the second largest becomes her mate, and the rest queue up behind without breeding.
facts.more: The word for this is protandry, meaning male first. If the female dies, her mate physically changes sex and takes her place — a permanent change, not a costume — and every fish below shuffles up one rung. The whole household reorganises itself in a matter of weeks.

facts.text: The father does the childcare. He scrubs a bare patch of rock beside the anemone for the eggs. Then he fans them with his fins and picks out any that go moldy. He keeps that up for six or seven days, until they hatch.
Newly hatched clownfish drift in the open ocean for up to twelve days. Then they find their way back to a reef. They steer by smell, and by the sound of the reef itself.
facts.more: A healthy reef is loud: snapping shrimp, breaking waves, fish. Tiny larvae swim toward that noise, and toward the chemical signature of anemones and even of leaves from trees on reef islands. Most never make it. The ones that do choose an anemone and rarely leave it again.

facts.text: Rank is measured in millimeters. Each fish in the queue keeps itself to about 80% of the size of the one above it, staying small enough not to look like a challenge.
facts.more: Being thrown out of an anemone on a coral reef is usually a death sentence. So the smaller fish deliberately eat less and stay stunted, holding their place in line rather than risking a fight they would lose. When a rank above them opens up, they grow into it.

facts.text: Clownfish talk with their teeth. Snapping the jaw shut makes pops and chirps, boomed out through the swim bladder, and the female uses them to tell the others to stay in their place.
A fish this small ought to live a couple of years. Wild orange clownfish have been estimated at twenty to thirty — extraordinary for an animal the length of your finger.
facts.more: The anemone is why. In a safe home, an old clownfish is not a lucky clownfish. It is simply an established one. Holding the top spot in a good anemone is worth more than gambling on a new one.

facts.text: Out of roughly a thousand anemone species in the sea, only ten will host clownfish. Each kind of clownfish settles in certain ones. It tests the tentacles carefully before moving in.
facts.more: A young clownfish acclimates: a brief touch, then a longer one, building its mucus coat a little at a time until it can bury itself in the tentacles. Wash that mucus off and the very same anemone will sting it.

facts.text: Most clownfish are finger-length, about 3 in (8 cm). The biggest, the maroon clownfish, reaches 6 in (16 cm) — and in every species the female is the largest fish in the anemone.
A clownfish is a poor swimmer and behaves like one. Most spend their entire lives within a meter or two of their anemone and never cross open sand, where a bright orange fish is simply a snack.
Count the white bars and you can name the species. Orange clownfish have three; an adult tomato clownfish has just one, behind the eye — young ones start with more and lose them as they grow.

wonder: Of all the thousands of fish on the reef, one can live inside the stinging tentacles — and the anemone ends up better off for it.

name: Archerfish
blurb: A mangrove fish that hunts insects in the air above it by shooting them down with a jet of water fired from its mouth.
size: Most are about the length of your hand; the biggest reach 16 in (40 cm)

facts.text: It shoots its dinner down. An archerfish spots an insect on a leaf above the water and lines up underneath. It fires a jet that knocks the insect clean off. Then it eats the insect as it falls.
facts.more: It presses its tongue up against a groove in the roof of its mouth to make a barrel. Then it slams its gill covers shut to force water down the barrel. A large archerfish can bring down prey 6.6 to 9.8 ft (2 to 3 m) (6 to 10 ft) above the surface.

facts.text: The jet is not a steady stream. The archerfish makes the back of it travel faster than the front, so the water bunches into one heavy blob at exactly the moment it arrives.
facts.more: That timing is the whole trick. A spread-out stream would only splash. All the water has to land at once. That delivers a punch far harder than the mouth muscles could manage on their own. The fish retunes the timing for how far away the target is.

facts.text: Look at a straw in a glass of water: it appears bent where it enters. Light bends the same way coming the other direction, so an insect is never quite where the archerfish sees it — and it corrects for that anyway.
facts.more: The bending is called refraction. Archerfish shoot accurately at angles anywhere from 45 to 110 degrees off the horizontal. One fixed correction would never cover that. Somewhere in that small head, the aim is being recalculated for every single shot.

facts.text: The fish starts swimming before the insect lands. Within about a tenth of a second of the hit, it has worked out where the prey will come down and is already turning that way.
facts.more: A tenth of a second is roughly one blink. In that time the archerfish reads which way the insect is tumbling, how fast, and from what height, picks a landing spot and goes. Everything else in the pool wants that insect too.

facts.text: Shooting is the easy part. Archerfish feed in crowds. A fish that never fired a drop can still reach the falling insect first. The shooter often watches its dinner vanish into someone else.
Young archerfish are terrible shots. They start spitting when they are about 1 in (2.5 cm) long, fire short sloppy jets and miss constantly — the accuracy has to be practiced into them.

An archerfish can learn to shoot by watching another fish do it. Some only ever spectated and never fired at that kind of target themselves. They still hit moving prey accurately on their first attempt.
facts.more: In the experiment, one fish was trained while others watched from the side. The watchers had never aimed at a moving target, yet their first tries matched the trained fish's. Learning from someone else's practice rather than your own is rare enough in animals that the result made news.

facts.text: Archerfish can learn to tell human faces apart. Shown two photographs and rewarded for spitting at one of them, they picked the right face about four times in five — even in black and white.
facts.more: Mammals recognize faces using the neocortex, a layer of brain that fish do not have at all. The archerfish manages the same job without one. Spitting is what made the test possible: the fish points straight at its answer, so there is no guessing what it chose.

facts.text: It does not always shoot. If an insect is sitting low enough, an archerfish launches its whole body clear of the water. It takes the insect off the leaf. That is a jump of roughly twice its own length.
facts.more: Jumping is costlier than spitting and it puts the fish in the air, where a bird could take it, so it is a short-range option only. High-speed film shows the archerfish lines the jump up from below the surface, the same way it lines up a shot.

facts.text: Archerfish hold the edges — mangrove creeks and estuaries where river water meets the sea, and rivers well inland. Overhanging leaves are the whole point, because that is where the insects sit.
Most archerfish are about the length of your hand, 4.7 to 7.1 in (12 to 18 cm) (5 to 7 in). The largest kind stretches to 16 in (40 cm) — longer than a school ruler.

wonder: It must aim through the bending surface of its own world, and it hits anyway.

name: Wood frog
blurb: A small brown forest frog with a dark robber's mask across its eyes. It survives northern winters by letting its own body freeze solid.
size: About 1.5 to 3 in (4 to 7 cm) long — small enough to sit in your cupped palm.

facts.text: In winter this frog freezes. Not nearly — actually. Ice fills the spaces around its organs, its heart stops, and its brain goes quiet.
facts.more: A frozen wood frog has no heartbeat, no breathing, no blood flow and no measurable brain activity. Well over half the water in its body has turned to ice. Warm it up and within hours the heart restarts, a leg twitches, and the frog hops away.

facts.text: Before the freeze its liver floods the body with glucose — sugar. The sugar works as antifreeze inside every cell, so ice can only form around cells, never in them.
facts.more: Ice crystals growing inside a cell would slice it apart. Wood frogs pack their cells with glucose and urea, which lower the freezing point and hold water in place. Ice is allowed to form only in the gaps between muscles and just under the skin.

facts.text: It lives farther north than any other frog in North America. Its range crosses the Arctic Circle, into country where winter runs most of the year.
facts.more: Alaskan wood frogs have been recorded frozen solid for about 193 days straight. That is over six months, at average temperatures near minus 6°C (21°F). Then spring arrives and they thaw. Within days they are calling from the nearest pond.

facts.text: A pond full of wood frogs in early spring does not sound like frogs. It sounds like ducks — a low clucking quack rolling across the water.
facts.more: Males call for only a week or two, sometimes just a few days. Biologists call this explosive breeding. The whole population arrives, pairs up, lays eggs and leaves. The ice has not finished melting off the edges of the pond.

facts.text: It breeds in vernal pools — woodland puddles that fill with snowmelt and vanish by summer. No fish can survive there, and the best read is that this is exactly the point.
facts.more: Fish eat tadpoles. A pool that dries out every year never holds fish, so wood frog tadpoles grow up with far fewer things hunting them. The catch: they must finish growing legs before the water disappears.

facts.text: One female lays a jelly ball about the size of your fist. It holds a thousand eggs or more. Dozens of females pile theirs into the same sunny corner.
facts.more: Massed together in the top few inches of water, the egg rafts sit slightly warmer than eggs laid alone. Warmer eggs develop faster, which matters a great deal when the pool may be dry mud by July.

facts.text: Look at the eyes. That dark patch running back from each one is why people call it the masked frog — a bandit's mask on a body the color of wet leaf litter.
Grab one and it screams — a short, piercing cry, startlingly loud for something you could hold in a cupped hand.
Adults hunt the forest floor for beetles, spiders, moth larvae, slugs and snails. Tadpoles are grazers instead, scraping algae off sunken leaves and stones.
Wood frogs spend most of the year in forest, not water. Some walk a few hundred meters (several hundred yards) back to their home pool, crossing roads and leaf litter in one wet night.
Nose to rump, 1.5 to 3 inches (4 to 7 cm). Females run noticeably bigger than males.

wonder: Everything it needs to come back from frozen is already packed inside it before the first frost arrives.

name: Surinam toad
blurb: A flat brown tongueless frog that looks exactly like a dead leaf. It lies on the bottom of muddy South American ponds. It raises its babies inside the skin of its own back.
size: About 7 in (18 cm) long, close to a dollar bill in length — and nearly as flat as one.

facts.text: The babies grow inside the mother's back. After mating, her skin swells up over the fertilised eggs and seals each one into its own pocket with a lid on top.
facts.more: For three to five months she carries them, her back a honeycomb of bumps. Then the lids open and tiny toads push their way out, one at a time. Afterwards she sheds that used layer of skin and starts over.

facts.text: There is no tadpole stage at all. What crawls out of her back is a finished toad about the size of your thumbnail — flat and brown, a miniature of its mother.
It has no tongue. None. It cannot flick prey into its mouth, so instead it inhales — snapping its jaws open and sucking prey in with a rush of water.
facts.more: Every frog in its family is tongueless. The Surinam toad feeds by suction. The mouth and throat expand so suddenly that water rushes in. Whatever was drifting in front of the toad comes with it and goes down whole.

facts.text: The tips of its front fingers end in tiny stars. They are feelers, sweeping the mud for food in water far too dark to see through.
facts.more: Its eyes are tiny lidless black beads, close to useless in a black-water swamp. The star-tipped fingers do the searching instead, then shovel whatever they find toward the mouth. Some books call it the star-fingered toad for exactly this reason.

facts.text: Mating is a slow series of underwater somersaults. The pair loops upward together, flips upside down at the top of the arc, and releases eggs while both are on their backs.
facts.more: As they roll, the eggs drop onto the female's back and the male presses them down into her skin. They repeat the loop again and again, a few eggs at a time, until roughly a hundred are in place.

facts.text: Males call underwater without pushing out any air at all. Hard parts inside the voice box snap together, and the sharp metallic click carries away through the water.
facts.more: Most frogs balloon out a throat sac and push air across vocal cords. A Surinam toad does neither. The clicking is made entirely inside the larynx, and sound carries much further through water than it ever would through air.

facts.text: Lying still on the bottom, it is not a toad. It is a dead leaf — brown, ragged-edged, flat, and completely uninteresting to anything hunting.
A lateral line runs along its flanks. It is a row of pressure sensors. A fish uses the same equipment to feel movement in the water around it.
Everything about it is built for water and nothing for land. Out of the pond it is close to helpless, barely able to drag itself along.
Worms, insects, small crustaceans and little fish — anything that drifts close enough to be sucked in whole. There is no chewing involved.
Females reach about 6.5 inches (17 cm) nose to rump, bigger than males. The whole animal is squashed almost flat. It looks as though something heavy stood on it.

wonder: A nursery, a hiding place, and a mother's own skin — all the same thing.

name: Red-eyed tree frog
blurb: A small neon-green rainforest frog with enormous red eyes, orange feet and blue-and-yellow striped sides. It keeps all of that hidden until the second it needs it.
size: About as long as your thumb.

facts.text: Asleep, it is a green leaf. Touch it and the eyes snap open — two red discs — while orange feet and blue-and-yellow flanks flash out. Then it is gone.
facts.more: Biologists call this a deimatic display: a sudden burst of color meant to startle rather than fight. The predator stalls for a fraction of a second working out what just happened, and that fraction is all the frog needs.

facts.text: Its eggs decide when to hatch. If a snake starts eating the clutch, the embryos still inside burst out early and drop into the water below.
facts.more: Left alone they hatch at six or seven days. Under attack they can go at four or five, and the hatching itself takes only seconds. They read the specific shudder of a snake chewing through jelly — rain shaking the leaf does not fool them.

facts.text: When it sleeps it vanishes. Legs folded tight under the body, feet tucked away, eyelids down — every scrap of color covered, leaving green on green.
facts.more: Its lower eyelids are not solid curtains. Each is a fine mesh veined with gold, drawn up over the eye like a net. Light still gets through, so a sleeping frog can keep watching, dimly, without opening its eyes and giving itself away.

facts.text: Look at those feet. Every toe ends in a sticky disc, and the frog can hold its whole weight on a wet, smooth leaf that anything else would slide straight off.
facts.more: The pads work by wet adhesion, not suction. Their surface is a mosaic of tiny six-sided cells holding a thin film of mucus. That film grips smooth surfaces the way a wet sheet of paper clings to glass.

facts.text: The clutch is glued to the underside of a leaf hanging over water, so hatchlings fall straight into the pond below. Nothing has to carry them anywhere.
facts.more: About forty eggs go into a clear pad of jelly on the shaded underside of the leaf, where they will not dry out. Wasps hunt them there as well — and a wasp attack triggers the same early escape a snake does.

facts.text: Males call after dark with a short dry chack. They also shake the branch they stand on, so a rival a few feet (about a meter) away feels the tremor through the plant.
facts.more: This is called tremulation. Two males will trade quivers back and forth from separate leaves, and if neither backs down they close in and wrestle, gripping the stem with their toe pads.

facts.text: All that color stays hidden. A poisonous frog advertises constantly; this one keeps its reds and blues folded away and spends them only in the instant it needs to escape.
It is strictly nocturnal. The whole day is spent flattened against the underside of a leaf, motionless, waiting for dark.
Crickets, moths, flies, grasshoppers — anything moving and small enough to swallow. Newly changed froglets start on fruit flies and other tiny insects.
About 2 inches (5 cm) for a male, up to 3 inches (7.5 cm) for a female — half again his size. She carries him on her back to the egg leaf.
It lives from southern Mexico down through the rainforests of Central America. Most of its time is spent up in the leaves. It comes down toward ponds and pools mainly to breed.

wonder: Color kept folded away until the exact half-second it is needed.

name: Hellbender
blurb: A giant, flat-headed, wrinkled salamander that spends its whole life under rocks in cold fast rivers. The largest salamander in North America.
size: About as long as two school rulers laid end to end.

facts.text: Two school rulers end to end — up to 2 feet (60 cm). The largest ever measured reached 29 inches (74 cm). Nothing else in North America comes close.
It breathes through its skin. Those loose ragged folds down each side are surface area, packed with blood vessels pulling oxygen straight out of the river.
facts.more: Hellbenders have lungs but barely use them for breathing. Nearly all their oxygen crosses the skin. That is why they need cold, fast, tumbling water. Cold moving water holds far more dissolved oxygen than warm still water does.

facts.text: When the water goes still, the hellbender rocks. A slow sway, side to side, pushing fresh water past those skin folds — breathing by moving instead of by inhaling.
It senses light through its skin, and the cells on its tail are the most sensitive of the lot. It can tell light from dark without using its eyes at all.
facts.more: Its eyes are small and its water is often cloudy. So most of what it knows comes from elsewhere. A line down its body feels movement in the current, and a sharp sense of smell tracks crayfish in the dark.

facts.text: Crayfish, mostly. Look inside a hellbender's stomach and more often than not it is crayfish and very little else.
facts.more: It hunts at night, walking along the riverbed rather than swimming. It takes prey with a fast sideways snap of the head. That pulls in water and crayfish together. It will also eat small fish, worms, insects, tadpoles and smaller salamanders.

facts.text: The father does the childcare. He digs the nest under a rock, guards the eggs for weeks, and fans oxygen-rich water over them with his own body.
facts.more: A nest usually holds 150 to 450 eggs, sometimes from more than one female, and nests of well over a thousand have been counted. He drives off anything that comes near, then stays on with the hatchlings.

facts.text: It will use the same rock for years. A hellbender picks one big flat stone with a gap beneath it and defends that address against every other hellbender.
It is a living water-quality test. It breathes through its skin, so everything in the river passes across it. Hellbenders vanish from water that turns warm, silty or polluted.
facts.more: Silt is the quiet killer. When soil washes off bare ground into a river, it fills the gaps between stones where hellbenders shelter and where their eggs sit. Find a healthy hellbender population and you have found genuinely clean, cold, fast water.

facts.text: People call it a snot otter. Also mud devil, devil dog, Allegheny alligator, and lasagna lizard — that last one for the rippled, layered folds of skin.
Despite every one of those names, it is not venomous and not dangerous to people. It would far rather be left alone under its rock.
It stays put. Most of a hellbender's life is spent lying motionless beneath one flat stone, waiting for something edible to walk past in the dark.

Nobody has followed one hellbender from egg to the end. Marked animals keep turning up under the same rocks year after year. The best read on a wild lifespan is 25 to 30 years. That is long enough to outlast your entire childhood.

wonder: Two feet of animal that breathes without lungs, tucked under a single stone in a cold river, seen by almost nobody.

name: Olm
blurb: A pale, blind, eel-shaped salamander from the flooded limestone caves of southeastern Europe. People once took it for a baby dragon.
size: About 12 in (30 cm) long, the length of a school ruler.

facts.text: It can go ten years without eating. Not ten days — ten years, longer than you have been alive, with nothing at all going into its stomach.
facts.more: Food is scarce in a cave, so the olm is built to wait. It slows its whole body down. It lives off fat and glycogen banked in its liver. Under extreme starvation it will even reabsorb some of its own tissue. Then it rebuilds when a meal finally turns up.

facts.text: Nobody has watched one olm's whole life. The numbers come from a marked cave population. The average adult lives around 68 years, and the maximum runs past 100. You could meet this salamander as a child and visit it again as a grandparent.
It is blind. The eyes are there, but tiny, buried beneath the skin, and they never finish developing. In black water there is nothing for an eye to do.
facts.more: It still avoids light. The skin itself is light-sensitive, carrying a pigment called melanopsin, so an olm moves away from a flashlight beam it cannot actually see. Shine a light on a cave pool and the pale bodies slide back under the stones.

facts.text: It hunts using electricity. Ampullary organs in its head pick up the faint electric fields every living animal gives off. There is no light whatsoever in that water.
facts.more: It also smells, feels water movement through a lateral line, hears, and lines itself up with the Earth's magnetic field. Five different ways of knowing where things are — and not one of them is sight.

facts.text: Those pink feathery fans behind its head are gills, and it keeps them for life. An olm holds its larval shape forever and never leaves the water.
facts.more: This is called neoteny. A typical salamander begins as a gilled swimmer, then absorbs the gills and walks onto land. The olm simply stops halfway and stays there, growing to full size and breeding while still shaped like a baby.

facts.text: Its skin holds almost no pigment — pale enough to see blood moving underneath. Leave an olm in the light and it slowly darkens, then fades pale again in the dark.
Floodwater used to wash olms out of the caves into daylight. People who found these pale wriggling things decided they were baby dragons, flushed out from under the mountain.
facts.more: The story stuck, and so did the name. In Slovenian the olm is still called the human fish, for skin the color of pale human skin. It remains the emblem of the caves it came wriggling out of.

facts.text: In a cave there is almost nothing to eat, so an olm does almost nothing. It lies still, drops its heart rate and its whole metabolism, and waits.
A female lays around 35 eggs beneath a stone and guards them, and they take months to hatch. The young then need roughly fourteen years to grow up.
facts.more: Fourteen years just to reach breeding age, and a female may lay only about once a decade. In a place with hardly any food, everything runs slow — including growing up.

facts.text: It lives in flooded limestone caves under the Dinaric mountains. The water there is black and far below the surface. That country is now Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and a corner of Italy.
Cave shrimp, snails and insects, swallowed whole, because it cannot chew. When food is plentiful it eats enormously and banks the surplus as fat in its liver.
About 8 to 12 inches (20 to 30 cm) long, the length of a school ruler. It is no thicker than your finger. The legs are tiny: three toes in front, two behind.

wonder: Fitted out for a place with no light at all — and thriving there.

name: Atlantic puffin
blurb: A small black-and-white seabird with a striped, brightly colored bill. It spends most of its life far out on the open ocean.
size: Stands about 8 inches (20 cm) high on land — roughly the length of a brand-new pencil.

facts.text: A puffin can hold more than a dozen small fish crosswise in its bill at once. It still opens its mouth to catch the next one. Nothing falls out.
facts.more: The trick is inside the mouth. A puffin's tongue and the roof of its mouth are lined with backward-pointing spines. It pins each fish against the roof with its tongue, then reaches for another. Fish can slide in. They cannot slide out.

facts.text: A puffin flies underwater, rowing with half-folded wings while its feet steer behind it like a rudder. Nobody can ask a bird what its wings are for — but the best read is that they are shaped for water first and air second.
facts.more: Wings small enough to work against water are almost too small for air. Watch a puffin leave the sea and you will see it sprint across the surface first, feet slapping, because it cannot simply lift off.

facts.text: In the air it reaches 50 mph (80 km/h). It pays for that by beating its wings up to about 400 times a minute. They blur into a smudge.
facts.more: Four hundred beats a minute is nearly seven every second. Your eyes cannot separate wingbeats that fast. So a flying puffin does not look much like a bird. It looks like a football with a beak going past.

facts.text: That famous orange-and-blue bill is temporary. The colored outer plates fall off after breeding season. The puffin spends the winter with a smaller, duller, gray-brown beak.
facts.more: The bright bill is breeding gear, worn in spring and summer when puffins are ashore choosing partners, then shed in a partial moult. A winter puffin at sea looks so different that people once took it for a completely different bird.

facts.text: For most of the year there is no land in a puffin's life at all. It rides the open Atlantic, sleeping on the water, far from the nearest rock.
facts.more: Puffins come ashore only to breed. The rest of the year they are pelagic — creatures of the open sea — feeding, moulting and resting on the waves. Some winter so far out that for months nobody knows exactly where they are.

facts.text: One egg. That is the whole year's effort — a single white egg, laid at the end of a burrow the parents dig themselves with beak and feet.
facts.more: Both parents take turns sitting on it for about six weeks, then both feed the chick, which is called a puffling. When it is ready it leaves the burrow alone, at night, and walks or flutters straight out to sea without its parents.

facts.text: Puffins drink seawater. They can, because a gland above each eye strips the salt out of their blood and drips it back out through their nostrils as brine.
A puffin can spend a whole winter out on the ocean. In spring it returns to the same burrow on the same clifftop. Often it returns to the same partner too.
facts.more: Colonies honeycomb the soil with burrows three to seven feet (1 to 2 m) long. Birds wearing leg rings come back to the same hole year after year. Puffins are long-lived for their size. Twenty years is ordinary, and some have passed thirty.

facts.text: Puffins nest on cliffs and offshore islands, where no fox can reach them — and the best read is that this is exactly why. The danger arrives from above instead.
facts.more: Great black-backed gulls and skuas hunt puffins in the air, and gulls will mug a returning parent in mid-flight for its beakful of fish. That is partly why puffins come in low, fast and straight, and wheel around the colony in big flocks before landing.

facts.text: For all the fame, a puffin is small. It weighs 350 to 500 grams, about a full can of soup. It would sit comfortably in your two cupped hands.
Look closely at the eye. Those aren't feathers: in breeding season a puffin grows small horny plates above and below it, which make a round eye look triangular.

wonder: One egg, one burrow, one partner — and a bird you could hold in two hands, carried safely all winter across an ocean with no landmarks on it.

name: King cobra
blurb: The longest venomous snake in the world — a tall, sharp-eyed forest snake that hunts and eats other snakes.
size: Big ones pass 13 feet (4 m), and the longest ever recorded reached 19 feet (5.85 m).

facts.text: The longest venomous snake there is. Most adults run 10 to 13 feet (3.2 to 4 m) — about three times your own height — and the record reached 19 feet (5.85 m).
King cobras hunt rat snakes, pythons, kraits and other cobras. They will even eat other king cobras. Their scientific name, Ophiophagus, means snake-eater. That is exactly the job.
facts.more: A snake is an awkward meal for most predators and an easy one for a king cobra: long, smooth, and swallowed head-first like a strand of spaghetti. It will take venomous species as readily as harmless ones.

facts.text: The king cobra is the only snake in the world that builds a nest. She rakes dead leaves into a mound with her own coils and lays her eggs inside it.
facts.more: The mound can stand nearly two feet (55 cm) tall and spread four and a half feet (140 cm) across, with a chamber hollowed out for the eggs. Damp packed leaves hold warmth in, and she coils on top of it and guards, for weeks.

facts.text: A king cobra does not hiss like other snakes. It growls — a low, dog-like sound that comes out well below the pitch of an ordinary snake's hiss.
facts.more: The sound comes from pouches branching off the windpipe, called tracheal diverticula. They work as resonating chambers. A guitar's hollow body does the same thing to a plucked string, making it louder and deeper. A king cobra's growl peaks near 600 Hz. An ordinary snake's hiss peaks near 7,500.

facts.text: Threatened, a king cobra lifts the front third of its body straight off the ground. A big one can look a grown adult in the eye. Then it moves forward at that height.
facts.more: The hood is not loose skin alone. Long ribs in the neck swing outward and stretch the skin flat, turning a narrow snake into a broad warning sign. It is a display first: the entire point is to be seen and given room.

facts.text: One bite can deliver 400 to 600 mg of venom — among the largest doses any snake gives. Antivenom for it exists, and it works.
facts.more: The venom is neurotoxic. It jams the signals traveling from nerve to muscle. That is why breathing is the thing that fails first. Hospitals treat the bite with antivenom. If needed, a ventilator breathes for the patient until the venom clears.

facts.text: No heat pits. A python or a rattlesnake has face holes that sense warmth. A king cobra has none of them. It finds other snakes by scent, and by unusually good eyesight.
facts.more: The forked tongue does the smelling, carrying scent particles back to the Jacobson's organ in the roof of the mouth. But a king cobra also watches. It will follow a moving snake with its eyes across open ground, which most snakes barely bother to do.

facts.text: Its fangs are short and fixed — they do not fold. The best read is that it does not need long ones: a king cobra bites and hangs on, chewing the venom in rather than letting go.
facts.more: Cobras are elapids, with short permanently erect fangs at the front of the mouth. Vipers are built the other way round: long hinged fangs that fold flat when the mouth shuts. An elapid trades fang length for grip.

facts.text: Look up. King cobras climb well and swim well. A snake this long can be draped along a branch high above the forest floor. It can also be out crossing a river.
She guards that nest for weeks, which almost no other snake does. Then, shortly before the eggs hatch, she leaves — and the hatchlings are on their own from the first minute.
facts.more: A clutch runs from 7 to 43 eggs and takes two to three months to develop. Hatchlings emerge around 20 inches (50 cm) long, banded black and pale, and fully venomous immediately. Nobody teaches them how to hunt.

wonder: Of all the thousands of snakes in the world, one builds a house for its eggs and sits on it. Just the one.

name: Reticulated python
blurb: The longest snake in the world. It is a heavy, net-patterned constrictor from the forests and rivers of Southeast Asia.
size: Longer than a car. The longest wild one ever properly measured, 22 feet 10 inches (6.95 m), would stretch right across a classroom.

facts.text: The longest snake on Earth. A wild one caught in Borneo and measured properly, with a tape, came to 22 feet 10 inches (6.95 m) — long enough to stretch across a classroom.
facts.more: The captive record-holder, a python named Medusa in Missouri, was verified at 25 feet 2 inches (7.67 m) and 350 pounds (158.8 kg). Far longer claims turn up online constantly. Almost none of them survive an actual tape measure.

facts.text: Reticulated means net-like. That gold-and-black web looks impossible to miss on a page. In dappled forest light it disappears completely.
facts.more: The pattern breaks up the snake's outline instead of matching a background. Sunlight coming through leaves falls in exactly that kind of broken patchwork. So an enormous animal lying still on the forest floor reads as leaf shadow. Then it moves.

facts.text: Along its lips, top and bottom, runs a row of deep pits. They are not nostrils. Each one reads heat, so the python can find a warm rat in total darkness.
facts.more: These labial pits are lined with heat-sensitive tissue. Several of them are spread along both jaws, so the snake gets a direction as well as a signal. That is enough to aim a strike at an animal it has never seen.

facts.text: A python does not crush bones and it does not smother. It squeezes hard enough to stop the blood moving, and its prey goes unconscious in seconds.
facts.more: Researchers measured what happens inside constricted prey. Blood pressure collapses almost at once. The heart cannot pump against the squeeze. The brain loses its supply long before the animal could run out of air. Every time the prey breathes out, the coils take up the slack.

facts.text: A python does not unhinge its jaw — that would break it. The two halves of its lower jaw simply are not joined at the front, and a stretchy ligament lets them spread apart.
facts.more: Add a quadrate bone at the back that swings like a double hinge, plus skin that stretches, and the mouth opens far wider than the head. The snake then walks its jaws forward over the meal, one side at a time, dragging it in.

facts.text: Swallowing something large takes hours. So the python shoves its windpipe forward out of the floor of its mouth, like a snorkel, and breathes around its dinner the whole time.
facts.more: The opening is called the glottis. In snakes it sits far forward and can be pushed out to one side of the prey. Without that, anything that took more than a few minutes to swallow would suffocate the snake doing the swallowing.

facts.text: She lays somewhere between 15 and 80 eggs. Then she wraps herself around the whole pile and stays. She barely moves and does not feed until they hatch.
facts.more: Guarding is the entire job, and it costs her a great deal of body weight over the three months or so the eggs need. The hatchlings break out around two feet (60 cm) long and are completely independent from that moment.

facts.text: Reticulated pythons are strong swimmers. They cross rivers, they swim in the sea, and they have turned up on small islands a long way offshore.
facts.more: A big snake is close to weightless in water. Swimming costs it far less effort than hauling its own bulk over the ground. That is why the species turns up on so many islands of Indonesia and the Philippines.

facts.text: It can go months between meals. The record-length wild python had eaten nothing for nearly three months when researchers measured it — and still weighed 130 pounds (59 kg).
facts.more: Pythons run on remarkably little. Between meals the gut actually shrinks down; when food finally arrives, the digestive organs ramp back up within a day or two. A meal that would last you an afternoon can last a python weeks.

facts.text: Every tooth curves backwards, like the barb on a fishing hook. They are not for chewing — a python swallows everything whole. The best read is that they are there to make sure nothing reverses out.
A big reticulated python can top 165 pounds (75 kg) — as heavy as a grown man — and be thicker through the middle than your own thigh.

wonder: Heat pits, a jaw in two halves, backward teeth, a windpipe that slides aside — four separate pieces of equipment, all built for one job: swallowing something wider than your own head.

name: Gaboon viper
blurb: A huge, heavy African viper that lies motionless in dead leaves. It wears the best camouflage of any snake in the world.
size: About 4.6 ft (1.4 m) long, and as thick through the middle as your forearm.

facts.text: The longest fangs of any snake alive — up to 2 inches (5 cm). That is the length of your thumb, folded away inside a closed mouth.
facts.more: They lie flat against the roof of the mouth and swing forward like a switchblade as it opens. A viper this size has no choice but to fold them: a fixed fang two inches long would punch straight through its own lower jaw.

facts.text: Lying in leaf litter, a gaboon viper is not there. The pale and dark geometry down its back matches dead leaves so exactly that people walk over one without ever seeing it.
facts.more: Then add stillness. Gaboon vipers hunt by ambush. An ambush hunter can hold the same position for hours or days. It waits for a rat or a ground bird to wander into range. The camouflage works because the snake refuses to move.

facts.text: Drop for drop its venom is not the strongest. It does not need to be — a gaboon viper injects more venom in a single bite than any other snake.
facts.more: A single bite has been measured at 5 to 7 milliliters, more than a teaspoonful. The largest recorded milking was close to 10 milliliters. Antivenom exists and works well. Even so, every bite is a genuine emergency and belongs in a hospital immediately.

facts.text: Most vipers strike, release, and track the prey down afterwards. A gaboon viper does the opposite: it bites and hangs on, fangs in, until the animal stops moving.
facts.more: Holding on lets it keep pumping venom in, and it means the meal never gets away to die somewhere it cannot be found. This snake is heavy and slow — chasing anything is off the table — so the first bite has to finish the argument.

facts.text: One of the heaviest venomous snakes alive. One just under six feet (1.8 m) long was weighed at 25 pounds (11.3 kg) on an empty stomach — about what a car tire weighs.
facts.more: The head alone can be almost 5 inches (12 cm) across: broad, flat and triangular, sitting on a neck a third that width. Lifted, a big gaboon viper feels less like a snake and more like a fire hose full of wet sand.

facts.text: Watch it move and something looks wrong. It travels in a straight line — no S-curves at all — creeping forward on its belly scales like an enormous caterpillar.
facts.more: This is called rectilinear locomotion. Muscles pull groups of belly scales forward, plant them, and haul the body over the top. Very heavy snakes use it — gaboon vipers, big pythons, boas — and the great advantage is that it is almost silent.

facts.text: She does not lay eggs. She gives birth to live young — as many as fifty or sixty at once — each one already patterned and already fully venomous.
facts.more: Fifty or sixty is the top of the range; smaller broods are more usual. The newborns arrive ready for work: marked exactly like the adults, fanged, and carrying working venom from the first minute. Nothing is taught to them afterwards.

facts.text: There is a pair of tiny horns on its snout, right between the raised nostrils. On the gaboon viper they are small bumps; on its close relative the rhinoceros viper, they are unmistakable.
For something this dangerous it is astonishingly reluctant. A gaboon viper will usually flatten its head and hiss like a kettle rather than strike at all.
facts.more: Reluctant is not the same as safe. The strike, when it finally comes, is over before you have registered that it started, and the snake was invisible right up to that moment. In gaboon viper country, people watch the ground.

facts.text: It eats whatever walks past: rats, ground birds, hares, and occasionally something as large as a small antelope. No stalking, no chase — just whatever chose the wrong path.
Gaboon vipers live on the floor of African rainforests. They also use thicker patches of savanna. It is always somewhere with deep leaf litter to vanish into.

wonder: That pattern is beautiful, and almost nobody was ever meant to see it — beauty laid down where only the leaves would notice.

name: Western diamondback rattlesnake
blurb: A thick-bodied American desert snake with diamonds down its back and a warning rattle on the end of its tail.
size: Usually around 4 feet (1.2 m) long.

facts.text: The rattle is not really a threat. Nobody can ask a snake what it means by it. The best read is that it is an announcement to anything big enough to tread on a snake: I am here, and I would rather you went around.
facts.more: The muscles that shake it are among the fastest known in any animal. They fire about 50 times a second. A rattlesnake can keep that up for as long as three hours. Nothing inside actually rattles. The hollow segments simply knock together.

facts.text: Every time it sheds its skin, a rattlesnake adds one new segment to the rattle. But you cannot count the segments to find its age — that part is a myth.
facts.more: A snake may shed several times in a good year and hardly at all in a lean one, so the segments count meals more than birthdays. Worse, the end ones snap off constantly against rock. A long rattle mostly means a careful snake.

facts.text: Between each eye and each nostril is a small hole. It is a heat detector, and it can register a temperature change of three thousandths of a degree.
facts.more: The pit is a thin membrane stretched across a chamber. It is wired into the same part of the brain that handles vision. So a rattlesnake does not merely detect warmth. It gets a heat picture laid over the ordinary one. That is how it strikes accurately in complete darkness.

facts.text: A rattlesnake bites a rat and immediately lets go. Then it waits, tongue flicking, and follows the trail of that one animal to wherever it finally fell.
facts.more: Hanging on to a struggling rodent is a good way to get bitten back, so the snake gets clear and lets the venom do the work. Remarkably, it can pick the trail of the rat it bit out from every other rat trail crossing it.

facts.text: Rattlesnakes do not lay eggs. The young are born alive, about a dozen at a time, each one up to a foot (30 cm) long and already venomous.
facts.more: A newborn has just one hard button on its tail — a single segment with nothing to knock against, so it cannot rattle at all. It has to shed at least once before it can make a sound. Until then it defends itself in silence.

facts.text: The fangs are hollow, hinged, and disposable. A rattlesnake swaps them for a fresh pair every six to ten weeks, with at least three spare pairs already waiting in line behind them.
facts.more: They fold flat against the roof of the mouth and swing forward as the jaws open. Because they are hollow, like a hypodermic needle, venom travels down the inside of the tooth instead of running along a groove on the outside.

facts.text: The flicking forked tongue is not smelling the air. It is collecting it — the tips carry scent particles back to two pits in the roof of the mouth called the Jacobson's organ.
facts.more: Two tips means two samples at once, from slightly different places. If the left tip brings back more of a scent than the right, the snake knows which way to turn. It is smelling in stereo, the way two ears let you hear which direction a sound came from.

facts.text: Its venom is hemotoxic — it works on blood and tissue rather than on nerves. An average bite delivers 250 to 350 mg, and the antivenom for it is effective.
facts.more: Western diamondbacks are behind a large share of serious snakebites in the American southwest. They live where people live. They also stand their ground rather than retreating. Nearly everyone who is bitten and reaches a hospital recovers.

facts.text: In winter they gather. Diamondbacks pack into rock crevices and abandoned burrows to sit out the cold. A single den can hold dozens of snakes, and other species share it too.
facts.more: It is called brumation, and it is not quite hibernation. The snake is cold and barely moving, but it will still drink. On a warm winter afternoon it may come to the mouth of the den to lie in the sun. The same dens get used year after year.

facts.text: Look at the tail just above the rattle: four to six crisp black and white rings, like a raccoon's. That banded tail is one of the marks people use to name this snake in the field.
Most are about 4 feet (1.2 m) long — roughly your own height — and weigh 3 to 6 pounds (1.2 to 2.7 kg), about a house brick. The largest reliable measurement was 7 feet (2.1 m).

wonder: A hunter that announces itself before it strikes — a warning built into the end of the tail, so that most meetings end with nobody hurt.

name: Peregrine falcon
blurb: A crow-sized falcon that hunts other birds in mid-air. It dives faster than any other animal on Earth.
size: About 1.5 ft (45 cm) from bill to tail, and about 2 lb (1 kg).

facts.text: A peregrine folds its wings and drops. In that dive — a stoop — it passes 200 mph (320 km/h), faster than any other animal alive.
facts.more: Level flight is a different story. Flapping along, a peregrine is no quicker than plenty of ordinary birds. All of that speed comes from falling: wings tucked, body stiffened, dropping like a thrown stone with a target at the bottom.

facts.text: A hunting peregrine can spot a pigeon a mile (1.6 km) away — a speck you would need binoculars to find at all.
facts.more: Deep in each eye is a pit called the fovea, packed with light-detecting cells far more tightly than anything in your eye. It works like a built-in telephoto lens. A third eyelid, clear as glass, sweeps across during the dive to keep the eye wet and clean without blinding the bird.
