facts.text: Peregrines hunt other birds, almost always in the air. Worldwide they have been recorded catching 1,500 to 2,000 different bird species — about a fifth of all the kinds there are.
facts.more: A peregrine usually strikes with a clenched foot rather than grabbing — a punch delivered at full dive speed. It then wheels around and catches the falling bird out of the air before it ever reaches the ground.

facts.text: Look at the beak. There is a notch on each side near the tip, called the tomial tooth, and the falcon uses it to sever its prey's spine with one bite.
facts.more: Hawks and eagles kill mostly by crushing with their feet. A falcon catches with the feet and finishes with the beak, and that notch fits between two neck bones like a key into a lock.

facts.text: Peregrine pairs sometimes hunt as a team. One flies low to panic a flock up into the open; the other is already waiting above it, ready to drop.
Peregrines nest on skyscraper ledges, bridges and cathedral towers. To a falcon, a high-rise is just a cliff that happens to have people inside it.
facts.more: Cities suit them: tall perches, warm updrafts rising off the streets, and enormous flocks of pigeons. Many city pairs are watched on live nest cameras, so you can follow the chicks — called eyases — from a school computer.

facts.text: The name peregrine means wanderer. Some nest on Arctic tundra and spend the winter in South America, crossing the length of two continents twice every year.
Peregrines build no nest at all. The female scrapes a shallow dish into gravel or dirt with her chest and feet, and lays her eggs straight into it.
facts.more: The dish is called a scrape, and a pair will use the same ledge over and over. Chicks hatch covered in white down and are flying about six weeks later. Young birds make their first migration with no parent to follow.

facts.text: The female is the bigger one — up to about 30% larger than the male. Falconers call the male a tiercel, from an old word meaning a third.
A peregrine pair will fly straight at an eagle, a fox or a person that comes too near the nest, screaming, and strike from behind.
Peregrines once vanished from the entire eastern United States. A pesticide called DDT made their eggshells so thin that the eggs cracked. The weight of the parent sitting on them was enough.
facts.more: The chemical built up in the small birds peregrines ate, growing stronger at every step. Once it was banned, people raised chicks by hand and released them from cliffs and city rooftops. The falcons came back, and now nest in cities that had lost them completely.

wonder: Eyes that can find a pigeon a mile off, and a body made to get there faster than anything else alive.

name: Bald eagle
blurb: A huge fish-hunting sea eagle with a snow-white head, found only in North America.
size: Wings up to 7 feet 7 inches (2.3 m) across — wider than a tall man is high.

facts.text: Stretch a bald eagle's wings out and they span up to 7 feet 7 inches (2.3 m) — wider than a tall man standing up.
facts.more: The female is the bigger one, averaging about 12 pounds (5.5 kg). That sounds heavy until you weigh the parts. One bald eagle was taken apart and weighed piece by piece. Its feathers came to more than twice the weight of the whole skeleton. The bones are hollow, braced inside with tiny struts.

facts.text: Bald eagles build the largest tree nest of any bird. The biggest ever measured was 9 and a half feet (2.9 m) across and 20 feet (6.1 m) deep.
facts.more: A pair adds sticks to the same nest year after year until it becomes a tower. A big nest grows so heavy that the branch holding it sometimes snaps under the load.

facts.text: More than half of what a bald eagle eats is fish. It skims the surface and snatches one out with its feet, never getting more than its legs wet.
facts.more: The soles of its toes are covered in rough spikes called spicules. They hold a wet, thrashing fish the way sandpaper holds wood. Eagles also take ducks, gulls and rabbits, and a great deal of carrion. An eagle is perfectly content with a dead salmon on a riverbank.

facts.text: Bald eagles are champion thieves. An eagle will chase an osprey through the air until the smaller bird drops its fish, then catch the fish before it hits the water.
facts.more: There is a word for stealing a meal somebody else caught: kleptoparasitism. Benjamin Franklin disliked the eagle partly for this habit. He wrote that it is "a Bird of bad moral Character."

facts.text: A bald eagle's head is not white until its fifth year. Young ones are blotchy brown all over and get mistaken for golden eagles constantly.
facts.more: Each year the brown fades and more white comes through, so you can roughly age a young eagle by how patchy its head and tail still look. The beak shifts from dark gray to bright yellow over the same stretch.

facts.text: That fierce scream you hear in films is not an eagle. A bald eagle's real voice is a thin, chirping whistle, a bit like a squeaky gull.
facts.more: Film-makers almost always dub in the cry of a red-tailed hawk instead, because the eagle's own call sounds too weak for the way the bird looks. Once you know this, you will catch the swap in nearly every movie.

facts.text: An eagle's eyesight is about four times sharper than yours. It can pick out a fish just under the surface from high above a lake.
facts.more: Each eye has two foveas — the tiny pits where vision is sharpest — while you have one. That gives an eagle a straight-ahead view and a sideways view, both in full detail, at the same moment.

facts.text: Its rear talon is about 2 inches (5 cm) long, longer than your thumb, and it lands with the whole weight of the bird driving it in.
The name has nothing to do with baldness. Bald here comes from an old word meaning white-headed — the same sense that hides inside the word piebald.
Courting pairs lock talons high in the air. They cartwheel toward the ground together, spinning. They let go only at the last second.
Bald eagles live in North America and nowhere else on Earth. Nobody has counted them all; surveys put Alaska alone at around 30,000.
Bald eagles nearly disappeared from the United States. The pesticide DDT thinned their eggshells until eggs broke under the parent sitting on them.
facts.more: The chemical washed off fields into rivers. It built up in fish. It concentrated in the eagles that ate those fish. DDT was banned and nests were given legal protection. Eagles returned so strongly that they were taken off the endangered species list.

wonder: Eyes to find the fish, feet to hold it, wings to carry it home — every piece of the eagle is fitted to the same job.

name: Barn owl
blurb: A pale, heart-faced owl that catches mice in total darkness using nothing but its hearing.
size: A yard (0.9 m) of wing from tip to tip, yet it weighs only about 1 lb (0.5 kg).

facts.text: Put a barn owl in a room with no light at all — none whatsoever — and it will still catch a mouse. It does it on hearing alone.
facts.more: This was tested in a completely light-proof room, and the owl struck accurately every time. When the mouse dragged a rustling scrap of paper behind it, the owl aimed at the paper. It was hunting the sound, not the animal.

facts.text: One of a barn owl's ear openings sits higher on its head than the other. That tiny mismatch tells it whether a sound came from above or below.
facts.more: Your two ears sit level, so you judge left and right easily but up and down badly. The barn owl's lopsided ears give it height as well as direction. It hears in three dimensions, and can place a mouse under grass or snow it has never laid eyes on.

facts.text: That heart-shaped face is not decoration. It is a dish of stiff feathers that funnels sound into the ears, and the owl can change its shape to focus.
facts.more: Take those stiff face feathers away and the owl can still tell left from right but loses up and down completely. Try cupping both hands behind your ears and turning your head slowly — quiet sounds jump forward. That is roughly what a barn owl wears on its face all the time.

facts.text: A barn owl flies without making a sound. Comb-like teeth along the leading edge of its flight feathers break the rushing air apart before it can turn into noise.
facts.more: The back edge of the wing is fringed like a soft brush, and the whole surface is velvety, soaking up sound. Engineers have copied that comb onto fan blades and wind turbines to quieten them. The mouse never hears it coming — and neither does the owl, so its own wings never drown out the sound it is listening for.

facts.text: A barn owl swallows a mouse whole and head first — fur, bones and all. One owl eats three or four small mammals in a night.
facts.more: Over a year that comes to roughly a thousand rodents from a single owl, and far more from a pair feeding hungry chicks. Farmers put up nest boxes for exactly this reason. A barn owl family beats any trap ever built.

facts.text: It cannot digest fur and bone. Once or twice a day it coughs up a neat gray pellet. The pellet is packed with the skeletons of everything it ate.
facts.more: Pull one apart with tweezers and you can rebuild whole mouse skulls, jaws with the teeth still seated in them, and the hair-thin leg bones of shrews. Scientists count pellet bones to work out what lives in a field without setting a single trap.

facts.text: Barn owls do not hoot. They make a long, ragged scream — the sound most people think belongs in a horror film, which is really a bird calling for its mate.
facts.more: The classic twit-twoo hooting belongs to tawny owls, not barn owls. A barn owl also hisses and clicks its tongue. A hungry chick makes a snoring noise loud enough to hear from outside the barn.

facts.text: An owl's eyes are not balls. They are tubes, locked in place by rings of bone, so it cannot swivel them at all — to look sideways it must turn its whole head.
facts.more: That is why an owl has 14 bones in its neck when you have 7. It can turn its head about 270 degrees, three quarters of a full circle, without shifting its body. The bony channels its neck arteries run through are roughly ten times wider than the arteries. There is slack to spare, so the twisting never cuts off blood to the head.

facts.text: Barn owls live on every continent except Antarctica. Almost no other land bird is found across so much of the world.
facts.more: They roost in barns, church towers, hollow trees and cliff holes — anywhere dark, dry and high up. They build nothing. The female lays her eggs straight onto a bed of her own old pellets, trodden flat.

facts.text: Barn owl chicks hatch days apart, so one nest holds a big fluffy chick beside one still tiny and pink. When food runs short, the older ones survive.
facts.more: The female starts sitting on the first egg immediately instead of waiting for the whole clutch. The eggs hatch in order rather than together. Researchers have watched older chicks pass food down to their smaller siblings. Very few birds have ever been recorded doing that.

facts.text: Pick one up and the weight is a shock. A bird a yard (0.9 m) across the wings weighs only about 1 lb (0.5 kg).
facts.more: Light bones and enormous soft feathers make a big, slow wing that costs almost nothing to carry. It lets a barn owl drift over a field at walking pace, listening, instead of having to keep its speed up just to stay in the air.

wonder: A face shaped like a dish, ears set crooked on purpose, wings that make no sound — every part of a barn owl is tuned to one job: hearing a mouse in the dark.

name: Snowy owl
blurb: A huge white owl of the Arctic that hunts in broad daylight and nests on bare ground.
size: Wings about 5 feet (1.5 m) across — wider than you are tall.

facts.text: This is the heaviest owl in North America. A big female weighs around 4 and a half pounds (2 kg) — like carrying a large bottle of water on your arm.
facts.more: A lot of that weight is insulation. Snowy owls are among the most thickly feathered of all owls, covered right down over the toes. They sit out cold that would finish an unprotected animal in minutes.

facts.text: Its toes are buried under feathers averaging an inch and a third (33 mm) long. The next-best owl, the great horned, manages barely half an inch. It walks on snow in built-in boots.
Most owls hunt at night. In an Arctic summer the sun never sets, so a snowy owl hunts in full daylight — and keeps the habit all year round.
facts.more: Above the Arctic Circle there is no darkness at all for weeks, so a night hunter would simply starve. Snowy owls perch on a hummock or a fence post in bright sun, sitting perfectly still for hours, and watch.

facts.text: A snowy owl eats mostly lemmings, small round Arctic rodents. An adult swallows three to five in a day, and in a hard freeze may need seven just to stay warm.
facts.more: Over a year that runs well past a thousand lemmings for one owl. Small ones go down whole and the bones come back up later as a pellet. When lemmings are scarce, the owls switch to ptarmigan, hares, ducks, and even other birds of prey.

facts.text: How many eggs a snowy owl lays depends on how many lemmings there are. In a lean year, five. In a lemming boom, eleven.
facts.more: Very few birds size their family to the food supply like this. In the worst years a pair may not nest at all. The eggs hatch days apart, so one nest can hold a chick the size of your fist next to one nearly ready to fly.

facts.text: There are no trees on the tundra, so a snowy owl nests on the ground. The female scrapes a hollow on a low rise where she can see anything coming.
facts.more: The rise matters twice over — it drains meltwater away from the eggs and gives her a clear view in every direction. She sits so tightly that snow can drift across her back without moving her.

facts.text: Both parents attack anything that approaches the nest, including Arctic foxes. The male dive-bombs from above while the female screams and lunges from the ground.
Geese and other tundra birds nest close to a snowy owl. The owl drives every fox off the hill. Their eggs sit safe inside its bad temper. The geese pick the spot for exactly that reason.
Males grow paler as they age; females keep dark brown flecks and bars. On open snow, an old male can be almost impossible to see until he moves.
facts.more: A female on the nest is barred brown and gray, which hides her against rock and lichen rather than snow. The palest old males end up looking nearly pure white from a distance.

facts.text: A snowy owl will sit on one low mound for hours without twitching, watching an empty white plain. The instant a lemming shows itself, it drops in one silent glide.
Some winters, snowy owls pour south in enormous numbers and turn up on farm fields, beaches and airport runways far from home. These sudden arrivals are called irruptions.
facts.more: An airport runway is flat, open and treeless. For hundreds of miles it is the closest thing to tundra, so the owls settle there. Bird crews trap them and move them safely away from the planes. Irruptions have carried snowy owls as far south as Texas and Georgia.

facts.text: Snowy owls do not always spend winter on land. Some sit out on floating sea ice for months, hunting ducks and seabirds over open ocean.
facts.more: Tracking has followed birds far out on the northern seas, well away from any shore. They perch at the edges of leads — long cracks of open water in the ice — where sea ducks come up to breathe, and take them there.

wonder: Boots made of feather, eyes built for daylight, and a family size that rises and falls with the lemmings — the snowy owl is fitted for a place almost nothing else can live.

name: Wandering albatross
blurb: A giant seabird of the Southern Ocean with the longest wings of any living bird. It can spend years at sea without touching land.
size: The longest wings of any bird alive — up to 11 feet (3.5 m) tip to tip.

facts.text: No living bird has longer wings. A wandering albatross measures up to 11 feet (3.5 m) from tip to tip — lie down twice, head to toe, and you would still fall short.
facts.more: The longest wing ever properly measured on one was about 12 feet (3.7 m). Longer spans get reported from time to time, but not one has ever been verified. An ordinary bird, around 10 feet (3 m), still spans more than most doorways are wide, twice over.

facts.text: An albatross can cover 600 miles (1,000 km) in a day without flapping once. It does not really fly — it falls forwards through the wind, over and over.
facts.more: The trick is called dynamic soaring. Wind moves slower right at the water's surface than it does higher up. The bird climbs into the fast air, turns, and dives back down into the slow air. Every swap steals it a little speed. It can keep this going for hours.

facts.text: A sheet of tendon locks its shoulder when the wing is fully out, so the wing stays open with no muscle working at all. Gliding costs it almost nothing.
facts.more: Heart rates measured on gliding albatrosses sit barely above resting. Holding those enormous wings open is the hard part, and the lock does it for free. Crossing an entire ocean is closer, in effort, to sitting still than to flying.

facts.text: It drinks seawater. A gland above each eye strains the salt out and dribbles it down grooves in the beak, so you can watch brine drip off an albatross's nose.
facts.more: The liquid it sheds is saltier than the sea it drank. Albatrosses are tubenoses, named for the two tubes running along the top of the bill. Petrels, shearwaters and fulmars share the same tube-nosed build.

facts.text: An albatross finds its food by smell rather than sight. It can pick up a dead squid floating on the water from several miles downwind.
facts.more: The scent it follows is dimethyl sulfide, a gas released wherever tiny sea creatures are being eaten. It is the smell of the sea itself. Where that gas rises, food is happening, and the albatross flies the trail upwind until it arrives.

facts.text: Squid is the main meal, with fish and crustaceans besides. An albatross takes most of it right at the surface, often at night, sitting on the water and seizing what floats up.
facts.more: It cannot dive deep. So it feeds off the top few feet of an ocean that runs miles down. The whole problem is finding the exact patch of sea where food has come up, which is why the nose matters more than the eyes.

facts.text: A parent flying home from a thousand miles out does not carry a fish. It carries a rich orange oil in its own stomach, and pours it straight into the chick.
facts.more: Tubenoses turn what they eat into concentrated stomach oil. That is far more energy for far less weight. It is the only way a meal survives a journey that long. The chick gets a few enormous deliveries instead of many small ones, and can wait days between them.

facts.text: A pair raises one chick, and only one. It takes so long — the chick sits on the nest for close to nine months — that the parents cannot breed again the following year.
facts.more: The egg alone takes about 11 weeks to hatch. Then the chick sits alone on a windswept island right through the Antarctic winter. Both parents range thousands of miles for food. They come back every few days to fill it up.

facts.text: A well-fed albatross chick can end up heavier than either of its parents — then it thins back down before it can fly.
facts.more: Chicks have been weighed at over 35 pounds (16 kg), heavier than any adult. The extra is stored fat that keeps it alive when a parent is late back. It burns that off while its flight feathers finish growing in.

facts.text: A young albatross leaves its island and does not touch land again for years. It lives entirely on the wing and the water until it returns to find a mate.
facts.more: Wandering albatrosses do not begin breeding until they are somewhere between eleven and fifteen years old. Many live past 50. A bird soaring over the Southern Ocean right now may have been at sea since before you were born.

facts.text: Pairs stay together for life. Meeting again after months apart, they dance — bills clacking, wings thrown wide, heads tipped back, screaming at the sky.
facts.more: Young birds spend years practising this dance with different partners before settling on one. The routine has set moves, and each pair works out its own version. Once they choose, they may raise chicks together for decades.

facts.text: Tracking tags have followed single albatrosses right around Antarctica. Some circle the whole Southern Ocean three times in one year — over 75,000 miles (120,000 km).
facts.more: One tracked bird covered 3,700 miles (6,000 km) in twelve days, wider than the Atlantic Ocean, without once setting foot on anything solid. The wind down there blows the same way around the whole globe, and the albatross simply leans on it.

wonder: God set the albatross in the emptiest place on earth and gave it wings that lock open, so the wind does nearly all the work.

name: Frilled-neck lizard
blurb: An Australian tree lizard, slim and gray and almost invisible on bark. A huge collar of skin sits folded around its neck. It snaps open when the lizard is frightened.
size: About 3 ft (90 cm) long — and more than half of that is tail.

facts.text: Corner it and the show starts. A collar of skin snaps open around its head, over 12 in (30 cm) across — wider than a dinner plate — while the mouth gapes bright pink and it hisses.
facts.more: None of it is a weapon. The frill makes the lizard look several times bigger than it is, and most of the time that is enough. Whatever was hunting it backs off before anything has to be settled with teeth.

facts.text: The frill has no muscles of its own. Rods of bone and cartilage in the throat swing it wide open, so the frill flies out at the same instant the jaws drop.
facts.more: The rods run off the hyoid — the same set of throat bones that works your tongue when you swallow. Shut the mouth and the whole frill folds flat along the shoulders like a closed umbrella, and the lizard is a plain gray stick again.

facts.text: When bluffing fails, it runs — on two legs. The front feet lift clear of the ground, the tail swings out as a counterweight, and it sprints flat out for the nearest tree.
facts.more: It doesn't stop at the trunk. It goes straight up, then shuffles round to the far side and freezes with the wood between itself and whatever was chasing. Walk around the tree and it walks too, staying exactly opposite you.

facts.text: Open, the frill is wider across than the lizard is long from nose to hips. All of that folds away into a neck you could close one hand around.
It spends more than nine-tenths of the day up a tree, pressed flat against the bark, gray on gray, not moving. Most people walk straight past one.
Termites, by the thousand. Ants and centipedes too, and in the wet season fat moth caterpillars. Almost everything it eats is smaller than your thumbnail.
Through the long dry season it nearly switches off. It sits in one tree for weeks, barely eating and slowly losing weight. It is waiting for the rain.
facts.more: In northern Australia the dry season can run half the year. Researchers tracking frilled lizards found individuals that shifted only a few trees in months. When the monsoon finally breaks, they come back on, feeding hard and putting the weight straight back.

facts.text: The frill is not only for enemies. Males flare it at each other over territory, heads bobbing. The argument usually ends right there. It is loud, but nobody gets bitten.
She digs a burrow in warm sandy soil, drops in anywhere from four to twenty-odd eggs, fills it in and walks away. No parent ever comes back to check.
Most of its teeth are fused straight onto the top edge of the jawbone. They do not sit in sockets. Once they wear down, an adult grows no replacements.
facts.more: Biologists call this acrodont dentition. It makes a jaw that grips hard and doesn't lose teeth in a struggle, but there is no spare set coming along behind. An old frilled lizard is chewing termites with worn-down stumps.

facts.text: Australia liked it enough to put it on money. The frilled lizard, frill up, sat on the country's two-cent coin for twenty-five years.
facts.more: Then Australia stopped making one- and two-cent pieces altogether, and the coin was retired. Millions of them are still sitting in drawers and jars around the country. Each one has a small furious lizard on the back.

wonder: Folded away it is nothing at all — a small gray lizard on a gray branch. God tucked a whole umbrella into that neck and left no seam showing.

name: Galápagos tortoise
blurb: The largest tortoise on Earth. It is a slow, plant-eating giant. It lives on a scatter of volcanic islands in the Pacific Ocean.
size: Shell about 4.3 ft (1.3 m) long, and the biggest ones weigh around 551 lb (250 kg).

facts.text: The heaviest one ever weighed came in at 919 lb (417 kg) — heavier than five grown men, walking about on four legs like tree stumps.
Passing a hundred years old is ordinary here. The oldest well-documented tortoise was kept in captivity and lived past 170. It was alive before cars, planes or electric light.
facts.more: A hatchling breaking out of its egg this morning could still be grazing that same hillside when the children alive today are grandparents. And be out there again, chewing the same grass, when their grandchildren are old.

facts.text: Look at the front of the shell. On the wet green islands it curves down like a helmet. On the dry islands it lifts at the front like a saddle.
facts.more: The saddle-shaped ones have long necks and long legs. They live where the food grows high, on cactus pads well above the ground. The helmet-shaped ones live in the humid highlands. Thick low plants grow underfoot there, so they never need to reach for anything.

facts.text: A Galápagos tortoise can go more than six months without a drink, and up to a whole year with no food and no water at all.
facts.more: It carries its own supply. Water is stored in the bladder and around the base of the neck, and fat under the shell is the fuel. On islands where the rain sometimes simply doesn't come, that is the difference between a hard year and a dead one.

facts.text: A tortoise stands up tall, stretches its neck right out and holds still, and small finches hop over and pick ticks off the skin it just exposed. Nobody can ask the tortoise what it means by the pose; the best read is that it is an invitation.
facts.more: Both sides win. The birds get a meal, and the tortoise gets cleaned in the folds it could never possibly reach. The pose is deliberate: the tortoise strikes it, and the finches come because they know exactly what it means.

facts.text: Top speed is roughly 0.2 mph (0.3 km/h). Just strolling to the kitchen, you are moving more than ten times faster than a Galápagos tortoise can run.
It sleeps up to sixteen hours a day. After dawn it lies in the sun for an hour or two, doing nothing whatsoever. A cold body cannot digest breakfast.
Some walk the same route up a volcano and back down every single year, climbing to the green highlands when the lowlands dry out. The paths are worn into the ground.
facts.more: Researchers fitted tortoises with GPS tags and watched them climb hundreds of meters, the biggest adults making the trip while smaller ones stayed put. Nobody teaches them the route. The same animals walk the same lines, season after season.

facts.text: She digs a hole with her back feet, drops in a clutch of round eggs — often fewer than a dozen — seals it over with mud and leaves. Warm nests hatch female; cooler nests hatch male.
facts.more: The hatchlings dig their way up months later, each about the size of your fist, and are on their own from the first minute. Nearly everything on the island is bigger than they are, so they hide, and they grow slowly, and they wait.

facts.text: Threatened, it pulls head and legs in and lets the shell do the work. That shell isn't luggage it carries — it is skeleton, ribs and backbone grown into plates of solid bone.
Cactus pads, grass, leaves, lichens and fallen fruit. A young tortoise can work through around a sixth of its own body weight in dry plant food in one day.

wonder: An animal that can go a year with no food and no water, on islands where the rain sometimes just doesn't come. Provided for, long before it ever needed it.

name: Leatherback sea turtle
blurb: The biggest sea turtle in the world, and the only one with no hard shell. Its back is thick rubbery skin stretched over a mosaic of tiny bones.
size: About 6.6 ft (2 m) long and up to 882 lb (400 kg).

facts.text: Grown leatherbacks run 5.9–7.2 ft (1.8–2.2 m) (6–7 ft) nose to tail and weigh 551–1,543 lb (250–700 kg) (550–1,500 lb). One would not fit through your front door.
Every other sea turtle wears a hard shell of plates. This one doesn't. Its back is leathery skin over thousands of tiny bones, ridged with seven long keels like the hull of a boat.
facts.more: The little bones are called osteoderms. Because they sit packed together instead of fused into one rigid plate, the whole back can flex. A stiff shell would be crushed at the depths this animal swims to. A flexible one simply gives.

facts.text: One leatherback was recorded diving to 4,200 ft (1,280 m). That is nearly three Empire State Buildings stacked end to end, straight down into black water.
facts.more: Deeper than most whales go. Dives of up to 70 minutes have been recorded, in cold and total darkness. Down there the pressure is more than a hundred times what you feel standing on the beach. Then the turtle surfaces and breathes like nothing happened.

facts.text: It eats jellyfish, and almost nothing else. A big leatherback can get through around three-quarters of its own body weight in jellyfish in a single day.
facts.more: Jellyfish are mostly water. That is an enormous volume of food carrying very little energy. The leatherback answers the problem by hardly ever stopping. It is also big enough to hold everything it swallows.

facts.text: Its throat is lined with hundreds of stiff spines, every one pointing backwards, running from the mouth all the way down to the stomach. A jellyfish goes down and cannot come back up.
facts.more: The spines are called papillae. Seawater comes in along with the prey and gets pushed back out through the mouth. The spines pin the jellyfish in place while that happens. It is a built-in strainer, for food with no bones and nothing to grip.

facts.text: It is a reptile that does not go cold. Leatherbacks have been measured with body temperatures up to 18°C (32°F) warmer than the sea around them.
facts.more: Biologists call it gigantothermy. A very large body loses heat slowly. Working muscles make heat constantly, and a layer of oily fat holds it in. That is how a turtle feeds off Norway and Canada, in water cold enough to hurt your hands.

facts.text: Some cross entire oceans. One tracked leatherback swam over 12,000 miles (20,000 km) between the beach where it nested and the far side of the Pacific.
facts.more: That journey took 647 days — the turtle was not racing. It fed as it went, drifting through cold water where jellyfish swarm, then turned for the tropical sand it started from.

facts.text: In a short burst a leatherback has been clocked at about 22 mph (35 km/h) — faster than you can pedal a bike. Cruising, it moves at roughly walking pace.
She comes ashore at night and digs with her back flippers. She lays around a hundred eggs the size of billiard balls. She covers them over and is back in the sea before dawn.
facts.more: On top of the real eggs she lays a batch of smaller ones with no yolk inside. They never hatch. Every leatherback nest has them sitting in the upper layer, and no other sea turtle lays them in anything like these numbers.

facts.text: Each leatherback has a pale pink patch on the top of its head, and no two are shaped the same. Researchers photograph the patch to tell individual turtles apart.
It nests on tropical beaches hot enough to burn your feet and feeds in water cold enough to ache. No other reptile lives across a range like that.

wonder: Skin where the others have armor — and it still dives deeper than the whales. God does not build every strength to look like one.

name: Saltwater crocodile
blurb: The largest living reptile. It is an armored ambush hunter of river mouths and coastlines. Fresh water and the open sea suit it equally.
size: A big male is about 14.8 ft (4.5 m) long and can weigh 1,102 lb (500 kg).

facts.text: The largest one ever caught and measured was 20 ft 3 in (6.17 m) long. It weighed 2,370 lb (1,075 kg).
facts.more: Males average about 13.1 to 14.8 ft (4 to 4.5 m). Females are far smaller, usually around 9.8 ft (3 m), so a big male and a grown female barely look like the same animal. The largest males hold the best stretches of river against all comers.

facts.text: Scientists clamped a force meter between the jaws of a 15.1 ft (4.6 m) saltwater crocodile. It bit down with 16,414 newtons, about 3,700 pounds of force. No living animal has been measured biting harder.
facts.more: The team tested every crocodilian species they could get hold of, one after another. The pattern was simple. The bigger the animal, the harder the bite. The saltwater crocodile is the biggest, so it tops the list.

facts.text: Those black speckles across its jaws are pressure sensors. In total darkness, in water like brown soup, a crocodile can feel a fish move nearby from the ripple it makes.
facts.more: They are called integumentary sense organs, and on a saltwater crocodile they are not just on the head — they are scattered right across the body. An alligator has them on the face only. This animal feels the water with its back.

facts.text: On its tongue sit salt glands, small pores that pump salt back out of the body. That is why this crocodile can live in the sea and an alligator cannot.
It doesn't swim across open ocean so much as surf it. Tracked crocodiles wait for the current to turn their way, ride it, then stop and rest when it turns against them.
facts.more: One tracked animal covered 370 miles (590 km) of coastline in 25 days this way. It barely swam at all. This is how crocodiles turn up on islands hundreds of kilometers from anywhere. They do not battle the sea. They time it.

facts.text: It waits. Sometimes for hours, with only eyes and nostrils breaking the surface. Then a lunge, a grip, and a spin — the death roll twists off a piece too big to swallow.
She heaps up a mound of mud and rotting plants, buries 40 to 60 eggs inside it, and guards it for months. Rotting plants give off heat, so the heap keeps the eggs warm.
facts.more: The temperature inside that mound decides what hatches. Around 31 to 32°C produces mostly males; warmer or cooler produces females. A couple of degrees, in a pile of leaves, settles the whole clutch one way or the other.

facts.text: The babies call before they hatch. From inside their eggs, buried under the mound, they chirp — and the mother digs them out and carries them down to the water in her mouth.
facts.more: The calling does two jobs at once. It tells the mother it is time to open the nest, and it keeps the clutch together so they all emerge as one group. She may carry a dozen at a time, in jaws that bite harder than any other animal's, without leaving a scratch.

facts.text: Those ridged lumps down its back are not just thick skin. Each one has a plate of bone inside it, called an osteoderm — armor with a skeleton of its own.
It never runs out of teeth. A replacement is always growing in underneath each one, ready to push up the moment the old tooth goes, and it happens all its life.
A resting crocodile can stay under about an hour, and voluntary dives of up to two hours have been reported. It drops its heartbeat to a couple of beats a minute to manage it.

wonder: Eyes, ears and nostrils set in one straight line along the top of the skull — the whole animal vanishes and still sees, hears and breathes. Someone thought that through.

name: American alligator
blurb: A broad-snouted, freshwater cousin of the crocodile. It rules the swamps, rivers and marshes of the southeastern United States.
size: About 11.2 ft (3.4 m) long and up to 507 lb (230 kg).

facts.text: A grown male runs 11.2 to 15.1 ft (3.4 to 4.6 m) (11 to 15 ft), females rather smaller. The heaviest males reach roughly 1,000 lb (450 kg) — half a tonne lying in a meter of water.
Broad, rounded snout, and when the mouth shuts every tooth vanishes inside. On a crocodile the big fourth tooth juts up outside the closed lip. That is how you tell them apart in a photo.
A large American alligator has been measured biting at about 13,000 newtons. That is nearly 3,000 pounds of force pressing down through its back teeth.
The muscles that slam an alligator's jaws shut are enormous. The muscles that open them are feeble — researchers hold a mid-sized one's mouth closed with a few wraps of tape.
facts.more: It is all one-way power. The same animal that can crush a turtle shell cannot shove a hand off its own snout. Handlers rely on that gap every working day of their lives, and it never stops being strange.

facts.text: A bellowing male makes a sound so low you feel it in your chest before you hear it. Below the roar is infrasound, and it makes the water on his back leap into dancing droplets.
facts.more: The droplets jump in a ring above his ribs while he holds head and tail up clear of the surface. Other alligators answer from across the marsh, and in spring a whole swamp can go off at once, one after another.

facts.text: She heaps up a mound of mud and plants, buries twenty to fifty eggs in it, and guards it. Cool nests hatch females. Hot nests hatch females too — only the middle makes males.
facts.more: A narrow band around 32.5 to 33.5°C produces males. Cooler than that or hotter than that, and the whole clutch comes out female. When the babies grunt from inside the mound, she opens it up. She carries them to the water in her mouth. She stays with them for a year or more.

facts.text: In a hard freeze, alligators tip their snouts up through the surface. They let the pond ice over around them. Each one breathes through its own hole in the ice until the thaw comes.
facts.more: They can hold that position for days. The rest of the body sits still and cold below, running so slowly it barely needs anything at all — a state called brumation. When the ice breaks up they slide out and carry on.

facts.text: It digs. Snout, feet and tail scoop out a deep pool that still holds water when the marsh dries. In a drought, every fish, frog, turtle and wading bird for miles crowds into it.
facts.more: These are called gator holes, and the biggest are wider than a house. The alligator that dug it eats well, of course. But the best read is bigger than that. Without those holes, a dry summer would empty the marsh completely. A great deal of the swamp survives because one animal was hungry and had claws.

facts.text: Fish, turtles, snakes, birds, whatever fits. And fruit — alligators have been found with wild grapes and elderberries in their stomachs, taken off low branches over the water.
Shine a flashlight across a swamp at night and pairs of red coals stare back. A mirror layer behind each eye, the tapetum lucidum, bounces light back through so it gets used twice.
It carries 74 to 80 teeth at once and replaces each one as it wears out. Count the replacements up over a long life and the total works out at more than 2,000.

wonder: The hole it digs to save itself in a drought ends up saving the whole swamp along with it.

name: Komodo dragon
blurb: The biggest, heaviest lizard alive. It is a slow-walking hunter from a handful of Indonesian islands. It brings down animals as large as deer.
size: Longer than a canoe and heavier than a grown man — up to 10 feet (3 m) from nose to tail tip.

facts.text: The largest one ever properly measured stretched 10 feet 3 inches (3.13 m). It weighed 366 pounds (166 kg), and that was with a full stomach.
facts.more: That record weight included a whole undigested meal, so the dragon itself was lighter. Ordinary adults run about 8 feet (2.5 m) and 175 pounds (80 kg). Even the ordinary ones are enormous — nothing else with scales and four legs comes close on land.

facts.text: Heaviest lizard on Earth, with no real rival. A few monitor lizards grow nearly as long, but they are slim and light. None of them carry this much bulk.
It smells with its tongue. That yellow fork flicks out, catches scent particles from the air, and wipes them onto the roof of its mouth — the vomeronasal organ.
facts.more: Because the tongue is forked, each tip samples a slightly different patch of air. More scent on the left tip than the right, and the dragon turns left. It is smelling in stereo, the way you hear in stereo. Downwind, a dead animal can be picked up from about 2.5 miles (4 km) away.

facts.text: One meal can be 80 percent of its own body weight. Imagine eating a lunch that weighs almost as much as you do — then not needing another for weeks.
About sixty curved teeth, every one edged like a steak knife. The tips are reinforced with iron — and the best read is that this is what keeps the serrations from wearing blunt.
facts.more: You can actually see it. The cutting edge carries a faint orange stain. Researchers checked museum specimens and tested the enamel. Iron really is concentrated right along the serrated edge. The teeth are also replaced over and over throughout the dragon's life. A worn one is never a problem for long.

facts.text: A Komodo dragon's bite does more than cut. Glands in its lower jaw release an anticoagulant — a chemical that stops blood clotting, so the wound keeps bleeding.
facts.more: For years people said the dragon's mouth was simply filthy, and that infection did the work. Then researchers scanned the jaw and found real venom glands. The venom also drops the victim's blood pressure, which is why bitten prey grows weak and slow.

facts.text: Under its skin, a full-grown dragon wears chain mail. Thousands of small bones called osteoderms are set into the head, neck and body, in shapes like flowers and branches.
facts.more: A scan of an adult found the bony armor nearly everywhere except around the eyes, nostrils and mouth. Hatchlings have none of it at all — it builds up as the animal grows. The only thing that seriously threatens a big Komodo dragon is another big Komodo dragon.

facts.text: Some female Komodo dragons have laid eggs that hatched without any male involved at all. Every hatchling was a son.
facts.more: Two English zoos recorded it. The process is called parthenogenesis. In Komodo dragons the chromosomes pair up a particular way. An egg produced like this can only ever become a male.

facts.text: Young dragons roll in dung and in the emptied guts of a carcass. Nobody has watched an adult turn one down over the smell. The best read is that it makes a youngster unappetizing. Grown dragons would otherwise eat it.
Hatchlings head straight up a tree and stay there. On the ground the adults treat them as food, so young dragons spend their first years in branches, hunting insects and geckos.
They swim well but they hardly go anywhere. Radio tracking showed most adults spend their whole lives inside a single valley just a few miles across.
facts.more: Researchers moved some dragons to other valleys to see what would happen. The dragons walked home. Several crossed miles of rough ground and steep ridges to get back to the exact valley they started in.

facts.text: For a heavyweight it is quick — short bursts of 13 mph (20 km/h), roughly a bicycle's pace. But it cannot hold that for long, so it prefers to wait in cover and ambush.

wonder: Chain mail under the skin, iron along the teeth, a tongue that smells in stereo — nothing here was left half-finished.

name: Veiled chameleon
blurb: A tall-helmeted tree lizard from the mountains of Yemen. Its eyes swivel independently, and its tongue fires like a spear.
size: A big male is about 2 feet (60 cm) long, and about half of that is tail.

facts.text: That tall ridge on its head is called a casque. Water that settles on it in the night fog runs down the grooves toward the corners of the chameleon's mouth.
facts.more: Veiled chameleons come from the dry mountains of Yemen and Saudi Arabia, where rain is rare but night fog is not. On a big male the casque stands about 2 inches (5 cm) tall. It does other jobs too — males use it in displays — but a lizard that can drink off its own head is doing well in a dry place.

facts.text: Each eye moves on its own. One can track a wasp behind while the other watches a branch in front — very nearly a full circle of vision from one still head.
facts.more: The eyelid is fused into a cone with a single pinhole for the pupil, so the whole turret swivels as one piece. The instant the chameleon finds something worth eating, both eyes swing forward onto the same target. That tells it exactly how far away the meal is, and how hard to fire.

facts.text: The tongue launches from a standstill and lands on the target in roughly the time it takes you to blink. It reaches out to about twice the chameleon's own body length.
facts.more: It is not thrown like a rope. A tube of muscle squeezes down over a stiff spike of bone and cartilage. Think of pinching a wet watermelon seed between two fingers. At the same moment, elastic tissue that has been stretched tight lets go. Every bit of stored energy leaves at once.

facts.text: The tongue tip is coated in mucus around 400 times thicker and stickier than your spit. Once it touches a cricket, the cricket is coming back with it.
facts.more: Researchers measured the viscosity directly. Viscosity means how much a liquid resists flowing. Water is thin and honey is thick. Chameleon tongue mucus sits closer to the honey end. The tip also folds around the prey as it lands. A struggling insect has nothing to push against.

facts.text: Chameleons do not match the wallpaper. They change color to signal mood and temperature — a calm veiled chameleon is green and banded, an angry male goes bright and blotchy.
facts.more: Color is a language first and camouflage second. A male facing a rival flares yellow and turquoise. A female carrying eggs turns dark with pale spots, which tells males to keep away. Cold chameleons darken to soak up sun; overheated ones go pale to reflect it.

facts.text: The colors are not paint. Under the skin sits a lattice of tiny guanine crystals, and the chameleon shifts color by changing the spacing between them.
facts.more: Spread the crystals further apart and the skin throws back yellow and red; squeeze them closer and it throws back blue. Green is blue crystal-light shining up through a yellow pigment layer above. Chameleons studied closely also have a second, deeper crystal layer that bounces away infrared — heat — like a built-in sunshade.

facts.text: Its feet are zygodactyl — five toes bundled into two opposing groups, two on one side and three on the other, so every foot is a pair of pliers. The tail grips too.
facts.more: The tail coils and holds like a monkey's, which makes it a fifth limb. Unlike most lizards, a chameleon cannot shed its tail to escape and grow a new one, so it takes care of the one it has.

facts.text: One female can lay up to 85 eggs in a single clutch. She digs a tunnel, lays them at the bottom, fills it in — and never sees them hatch.
facts.more: The eggs sit underground for months. A hatchling comes out barely longer than your thumb and gets no help whatsoever. It walks off into the branches and starts hunting insects on its first day.

facts.text: Watch it walk and it rocks forward and back, one slow step at a time, like a leaf shivering in wind. Predators hunting for movement often slide straight past it.
Mostly insects: crickets, grasshoppers, flies. Veiled chameleons also eat leaves and flowers, which is unusual among chameleons. The likely reason is the water locked inside them.
It has no ear opening and no eardrum. A chameleon is not deaf, but it hears poorly and in a narrow range — those eyes are doing nearly all the work.
For all that reach and drama, a big male weighs only 5 ounces (150 g). He would sit on one of your hands with room to spare.

wonder: Turret eyes, an elastic tongue, crystal skin — a hunter that never needs to hurry and never needs to chase.

name: Thorny devil
blurb: A small, spiky, ant-eating lizard of the Australian desert. It drinks by pulling water across its own skin.
size: About 8 inches (21 cm) nose to tail, about the length of a pencil, and light enough to sit in your open palm.

facts.text: It drinks with its feet. Water touching any part of a thorny devil is pulled right across the body. Microscopic grooves between the scales deliver it to the corners of its mouth.
facts.more: The grooves work by capillary action — the same force that pulls water up a paper towel dipped in a puddle. Stand the lizard in a shallow puddle and the water climbs its legs, crosses its back and reaches its mouth, traveling uphill the whole way. Then it works its jaws to swallow.

facts.text: It shovels damp sand onto its own back. The sand sits there, the skin channels wick the moisture out of it, and the lizard drinks the sand dry.
It eats one thing: ants. A thorny devil parks beside an ant trail and picks them off one at a time — well over a thousand in a single day.
facts.more: It works at up to 45 ants a minute, flicking them up with a sticky tongue without breaking the line or panicking the colony. Small black ants are the favourites. A diet of nothing but ants sounds thin, but it never runs out.

facts.text: On the back of its neck sits a spiny knob shaped like a head. When something threatens, the devil tucks its real head down between its front legs. That leaves the knob showing. Nobody has watched a predator bite the wrong one. The shape and the posture are the argument that it is a spare head.

Every one of those cones is a spine. They point in every direction at once. The best read is that this is what they are for. A snake or a bird trying to swallow a thorny devil finds no good angle to do it from.
facts.more: It can also puff itself up with air when something threatens, which makes it wider and rounder and harder still to fit into a mouth. The spines are not a weapon — the lizard never attacks with them. They simply make it an awkward parcel to swallow.

facts.text: Its browns and tans match the sand exactly. When something approaches, it freezes flat. Most predators walk past a motionless thorny devil without ever registering it.
It moves in a strange stop-start rock — a step, a pause, a sway back and forth, another step. Nothing about it moves the way an animal moves, and the best read is that this is exactly the point.
It changes color with the weather. Pale through the heat of the day, darker when the desert turns cold, because dark skin soaks up more sun.
The female digs a burrow about a foot (30 cm) deep, lays three to ten eggs at the bottom, fills it back in and walks away. The young dig themselves out months later.
It looks ferocious and it is tiny. A full-grown thorny devil is shorter than a school ruler and sits comfortably in two cupped hands. The spines are armor and bluff — not a weapon.
Engineers study that skin. It moves water sideways and uphill with no pump and no power. Dry countries need exactly that. This lizard has been doing it all along.
facts.more: The channels between the scales are shaped like tiny half-pipes. Once it is wet, the surface turns superhydrophilic. That means water spreads flat across it instead of beading up. Labs have copied the pattern to move liquid around without a motor.

facts.text: It lives in the dry interior of Australia, in spinifex grass and sandy scrub. A year there can pass with almost no rain. It is the hardest place on the continent to find a drink.

wonder: In a country where it may not rain for a year, this lizard was given skin that finds water and carries it home.

name: Tokay gecko
blurb: A loud, blue-and-orange-spotted gecko from Southeast Asia. It walks up glass and across ceilings, and it shouts its own name at night.
size: About as long as your forearm, elbow to fingertips — up to 14 inches (35 cm) counting the tail.

facts.text: There is no glue and no suction cup anywhere on a gecko. Each foot carries roughly half a million hairs called setae, and every hair splits at the tip into hundreds of finer pads.
facts.more: A single seta is about a tenth of a millimeter long — you would need a microscope to see one. Its split ends are finer still, around 200 nanometres across, smaller than the wavelength of visible light. The gecko's grip lives at a scale nobody could even look at until fairly recently.

facts.text: The grip comes from van der Waals attraction — the faint pull between any two things whose molecules get close enough. One hair is nothing. Half a million at once, and the gecko hangs off glass.
facts.more: It is not stickiness in any ordinary sense. Nothing wet, no residue left behind, nothing that wears out or gets used up. A gecko's foot works in a vacuum, and on a pane so smooth and clean that sticky tape would slide right off it.

facts.text: Measured in a lab, two front feet gripped hard enough to hold 20 newtons. That is about the pull of a full 2-liter bottle hanging off them. It is many times what the gecko itself weighs.
facts.more: A climbing gecko uses only a fraction of what its feet can actually do. That huge margin to spare is why it can sprint straight up a vertical sheet of glass without ever pausing to test its footing.

facts.text: The hard part is not sticking. It is letting go. The gecko peels each toe backwards from the tip, which breaks the contact in about 15 thousandths of a second — faster than you can notice.
facts.more: That is why gecko toes curl upward and away as the foot lifts, which looks very odd if you slow the film down. Pull straight off and the hairs would fight you the whole way. Peel from the tip and they release instantly.

facts.text: Engineers copy those hairs. Pads covered in tiny synthetic wedges have carried climbing robots up glass walls and let a person haul themselves up a sheer pane.
facts.more: The grip leaves no residue and needs no power. So the same idea is being tested for catching satellites and space junk, where ordinary glue would freeze solid, boil away, or drift off.

facts.text: It is named after the noise it makes. Males bark a loud, rasping 'to-KAY! to-KAY!' from a wall after dark, over and over, and it carries a long way.
facts.more: The call is a territory notice and an advertisement for a mate, rolled together. A gecko usually warms up with a burst of dry cackling. Then it delivers the full call several times running. Across Southeast Asia it is an ordinary night sound, like a dog barking down the street.

facts.text: It has no eyelids at all. A clear scale covers each eye like a windscreen, and the gecko keeps it clean with a swipe of its tongue.
facts.more: The eye carries three light-catching pigments. One of them is tuned to ultraviolet, a band of light your eyes cannot register at any brightness. Geckos built like this can still tell colors apart by moonlight. Your own color vision switches off in near-darkness.

facts.text: This is one of the largest geckos there is. A big male stretches from your elbow to your fingertips, and he is heavy enough that you feel him land on your hand.
Grab a tokay by the tail and it hands the tail over. The tail keeps thrashing on the ground for minutes, holding the predator's attention while the gecko walks away.
facts.more: The break happens along a weak line that is already built into the tail. Muscles clamp the blood vessels shut, so it barely bleeds. A replacement grows in around cartilage instead of bone. It usually comes back a different shape and color from the original.

facts.text: It is one of very few geckos that fights back. A cornered tokay gapes its mouth wide, hisses, and lunges — and once it has hold of something, it does not let go.
A female lays just one or two eggs at a time and glues them to a wall, a tree trunk or the underside of a roof. They set rock hard and cannot be prised off.
It hunts insects — cockroaches, crickets, moths drawn to a lamp. A big tokay will also take small lizards, including other geckos, and now and then a mouse.

wonder: Half a million hairs on every foot, and each one splits again at the tip — detail on a scale nobody could see until we had microscopes strong enough to look.

name: Common basilisk
blurb: A crested lizard of Central American riverbanks. It escapes danger by rearing up and sprinting across the surface of the water.
size: Up to 2.5 feet (76 cm) long, but three-quarters of that is tail.

facts.text: It runs on water. Not skimming, not swimming — up on its back legs, sprinting across the surface of a river. And it can do this from the day it hatches.
facts.more: In Central America people call it the Jesus lizard for exactly this reason. A basilisk crosses roughly 15 feet (4.5 m) of open water before it sinks in and swims the rest. The lightest ones — the hatchlings — stay up on top the longest.

facts.text: Every footfall is three moves: slap, stroke, recover. The slap drives the foot down and traps a pocket of air. The stroke pushes backwards against that pocket. Then the foot lifts clear.
facts.more: The whole thing depends on getting the foot out fast enough. If the water collapses around the leg first, the lizard has to drag its foot up through water instead of air. That costs far more energy than it has. Speed is not showing off here. It is the only thing keeping the animal on top.

facts.text: The three outer toes on each hind foot carry a fringe of loose scales. On land they fold flat and stay out of the way. Hit water and they spread wide, widening the foot.
A big male is longer than your arm, but you could hold him in one hand. Nearly all that length is a whip-thin tail he swings for balance while running.
Startle a basilisk and it drops. It flings itself off the branch, hits the water, and is already gone across the surface before the splash has finished.
If running fails, it goes the other way. A basilisk can stay underwater for up to half an hour. It sits motionless on the bottom until whatever was chasing it loses interest.
Males carry three crests — one on the head, one down the back, one along the tail. Females have only the head crest, so you can tell them apart at a glance.
It eats almost anything it can catch or reach: beetles, dragonflies, flowers, small snakes, birds' eggs, fish. Very few lizards are that flexible about dinner.
It never goes far from water. Basilisks live along rainforest streams and rivers, usually within a few steps of the bank. The best read on why is the water itself. It is the escape route.
facts.more: A basilisk that wanders inland loses its best trick. Out on dry ground it is just another lizard being chased by a snake. Stay near the bank and there is always somewhere to run that nothing following can follow across.

facts.text: A hatchling weighs 2 grams — two paperclips — and is barely longer than your finger. No parent sticks around, but it can already run on water, which is most of what it needs.
Across the surface it moves at about 5 feet per second (1.5 m/s). That is a brisk walking pace for you. The difference is that there is nothing underneath it but river.
facts.more: The legs are working far harder than that pace suggests. Each foot has to punch down, push back and pull clear again before the hole it made fills in, over and over, the whole way across.

facts.text: Engineers have built water-running robots by copying the basilisk's stroke. They are hunting for a machine that can cross a flooded surface without a boat.
facts.more: The hard part turned out to be the same problem the lizard already solves. The foot has to come back out of the hole it just punched. It has to happen before the water rushes in to fill it. Get that timing wrong and the robot goes straight to the bottom.

wonder: It weighs two paperclips the day it hatches, and already knows how to cross a river without swimming.

name: Texas horned lizard
blurb: A flat, spiky little desert lizard that lives almost entirely on stinging ants. When a coyote gets too close, it shoots blood out of its own eyes.
size: About as long as your hand, and flatter than a bar of soap

facts.text: Push a Texas horned lizard too far and it fires a jet of its own blood out of the corner of its eye, up to 5 feet (1.5 m). It aims for the face.
facts.more: It clamps down on the veins draining its head. Blood pressure climbs until tiny vessels around the eyelid burst. Coyotes, foxes and dogs hate the taste and back off shaking their heads. Predatory birds are not bothered at all, so the lizard saves the trick for mammals.

facts.text: About 70 percent of everything it eats is harvester ants. That makes it one of the very few animals willing to swallow an insect armed with a serious sting.
facts.more: A harvester ant stings hard enough to make a grown person yell. The horned lizard licks them up whole, one at a time, and its stomach takes up more of its body than most lizards' does. An ant is a tiny meal, so it needs a great many of them, and it needs somewhere to put them.

facts.text: A big female is about 5 inches (13 cm) from her nose to the base of her tail. She would sit comfortably in your cupped palm, if she would sit still.
It is built like a living pincushion. The two long spikes at the back of its head are true horns: solid bone, growing straight out of the skull.
facts.more: Those head spines are not scales and not claws. They are bone, grown out of the skull itself. When something leans in too close, the lizard tips its head forward and jabs, turning the widest, sharpest part of itself toward the trouble.

facts.text: Its first defense is doing absolutely nothing. Flattened against the ground and color-matched to the local dirt, it will let you walk right past and never twitch.
facts.more: Lizards from red-dirt country come out reddish; lizards from pale limestone country come out pale. It also flattens sideways to kill its own shadow. A rounded animal casts a dark giveaway blob on bright sand. A pancake does not.

facts.text: There is a third eye on top of its head. It cannot see pictures with it, but it reads light and dark, which helps the lizard track the sun through the day.
facts.more: The parietal eye is a pale spot in the middle of the skull with its own lens and light-sensing cells, wired straight to the brain. Plenty of lizards have one. It does not form an image. It registers brightness, which is enough to run a daily rhythm and time a basking session.

facts.text: In a country with almost no standing water, it drinks through its skin. Rain landing anywhere on its back runs into tiny channels between the scales and travels to its mouth.
facts.more: The channels work by capillary action, the same reason water climbs into a paper towel instead of just sitting on it. In a storm the lizard arches its back and the whole animal becomes a gutter system feeding the corners of its jaw. Then it opens and closes its mouth to pump the water in.

facts.text: Cornered, it gulps air and swells up like a spiny balloon. A lizard that was flat and easy to swallow becomes a wide, sharp shape that will not go down a throat.
The blood trick is expensive. Squirting can cost the lizard up to 6 percent of its entire body weight, which is why it holds that card back until nothing else has worked.
A female digs a burrow, lays two or three dozen eggs at the bottom, covers them over and walks away. The hatchlings emerge about the size of a quarter, spines already in place.
When the nights turn cold it digs into loose soil and shuts down for the winter. This is called brumation: months underground, not eating, barely breathing, waiting out the season.
facts.more: It is not quite the same as a bear's hibernation. A brumating reptile simply runs cold and slow because the air around it is cold and slow. Come spring, it warms back up on the surface and starts hunting ants again as though nothing happened.

facts.text: Texas made it the official state reptile, and then it started vanishing from Texas.
facts.more: Imported fire ants are a big part of it. They shove out the native harvester ants the lizard depends on, and a horned lizard cannot simply switch to another dinner. Pesticides sprayed to kill ants wipe out the food supply just as thoroughly, and plowed-up grassland leaves nowhere to dig in.

wonder: Bone horns, a skin that drinks rain, and a blood cannon behind each eye. Every part of it fitted to a hard, dry country.

name: Axolotl
blurb: A pink Mexican salamander with feathery gills sprouting from the outside of its head. It never leaves the water. It can regrow almost any part of itself.
size: About 9.5 in (24 cm) long, though a big one reaches the length of your forearm.

facts.text: Those pink feathers on its head are gills, worn on the outside where you can watch them work. Blood runs through the frills and pulls oxygen straight out of the water.
facts.more: Three stalks on each side, each branching into fine filaments. Feathery means a huge surface area for oxygen to cross, packed into a small space. When the water runs low on oxygen the axolotl fans them; when it is startled it snaps them flat against its neck.

facts.text: Most salamanders start life in the water, then grow lungs and strong legs and crawl out onto land. The axolotl skips the whole business and stays in the water for life.
facts.more: It keeps its baby gills and its baby tail fin and grows up anyway. Biologists call this neoteny: keeping juvenile features into adulthood. A full-grown axolotl can breed and hunt and live a decade while still wearing the body plan of a larva.

facts.text: Cut off an axolotl's leg and it grows a new one. Bone, muscle, nerve and skin, in the right order, in the right places, with no scar. It can do this over and over.
facts.more: It regrows far more than limbs: tail, jaw, parts of the eye and heart, even sections of its own brain and spinal cord. The wound closes without scarring, a bud of cells gathers at the stump, and the missing piece is rebuilt from scratch.

facts.text: Most axolotls are about 9.6 in (24 cm) long. A big one reaches roughly 12 inches (30 cm). Lay a school ruler beside it and the animal covers the whole thing. Larger than that is rare.
In the entire wild world there is one place axolotls live: a maze of canals and floating gardens at the edge of Mexico City. Nowhere else. Not anywhere.
facts.more: Lake Xochimilco is what remains of a much bigger lake system that was drained away as the city grew. Counts have collapsed. One survey found roughly 6,000 axolotls per square kilometer; a decade later the same water held about 100; a later four-month search turned up two.

facts.text: It does not bite its food. It opens its mouth fast and the water rushes in, dragging the meal with it. Worms, insect larvae and small fish all get inhaled whole.
facts.more: This is called suction feeding, and the axolotl finds its target by smell before it snaps. Its teeth are tiny, barely breaking the surface of the gums. They grip, they do not chew or cut. Everything goes down in one piece.

facts.text: It breathes three different ways. Those external gills are one. Oxygen also passes straight through its skin. And it rises to the surface to gulp air into a small pair of lungs.
Young axolotls crowded together bite each other's legs off. It is less of a catastrophe than it sounds, because the leg simply grows back.
facts.more: Larvae snap at anything that moves, including a brother's limb or a sister's gill frill. Anyone raising them either separates the young or accepts a lot of missing toes for a while. In a healthy tank, every one of those limbs is rebuilt.

facts.text: A female lays hundreds of eggs in one go, sticking them one by one onto water plants with her back feet, and then swims away. Nothing guards them.
Its instruction manual is enormous. The axolotl genome is roughly 32 billion letters long, about ten times the length of a human's.
facts.more: Longer does not mean more complicated. Axolotls carry around 23,000 genes, not far off our own count. The extra length is mostly vast stretches of repeated sequence sitting in between. Reading the whole thing took an international team years of work.

facts.text: Hospitals want what the axolotl has. Researchers study its healing because a human wound closes with scar tissue, while an axolotl's closes with the actual missing part.
facts.more: Human skin repairs a deep cut by laying down tough, blank collagen. That is a patch, not a rebuild, and it never becomes skin again. Axolotl tissue skips the patch entirely and reconstructs blood vessels, nerve and bone in the correct arrangement.

facts.text: The axolotl is close to gone in the wild. At the same time there are more of them alive than ever, because they are bred by the thousand in laboratories, classrooms and home tanks.

wonder: A body that answers a lost limb by quietly building another one. Nothing about that is ordinary.

name: Glass frog
blurb: A small green rainforest frog with see-through skin on its underside. Turn one over and you are looking straight in at its beating heart.
size: About as wide across as a bottle cap

facts.text: Turn a glass frog belly-up and the skin is translucent. You can watch the heart beating, the liver sitting there, and food traveling through the gut.
facts.more: Not the whole frog. The back is opaque leaf-green, and it is the underside that is clear. In some species a sheet of shiny white tissue covers part of the works. So you get the heart hidden and the intestines on display, or the other way round.

facts.text: Asleep, it does something no other animal is known to do. It pulls almost all its red blood cells out of circulation and parks them inside its liver.
facts.more: Blood is what makes a small body visible, so with the red packed away the sleeping frog turns markedly harder to see. Packing blood cells that tightly ought to cause dangerous clotting. This frog does it every day, then releases them again on waking, when it needs to move.

facts.text: It sleeps pressed against a leaf and lets the daylight come through it. Green leaf, green frog, and edges that fade out instead of ending.
facts.more: A solid frog on a sunlit leaf makes a dark blob with a hard outline, and hunting birds read outlines. Because light passes through the glass frog's legs and flanks, its edges blur into the brightness of the leaf rather than cutting a shape across it.

facts.text: Most glass frogs are about an inch (2.5 cm) long. Even the largest species in the whole family only reaches about 3 inches (7.5 cm).
The eggs are laid on a leaf hanging out over a stream. When the tadpoles hatch, they wriggle to the edge and drop into the running water below.
facts.more: It is a serious fall for something that small. They land in fast water and immediately burrow down into the leaf litter and silt on the stream bed. The leaf nursery keeps the eggs safely away from fish, and the current takes over from there.

facts.text: In many glass frogs it is the father who stays. He sits with the clutch for days, turning the eggs, and when they start drying out he urinates on them to keep them wet.
facts.more: A clutch of twenty or thirty eggs sitting on an exposed leaf can dry out in an afternoon or be found by wasps. The male crouches over them, keeps the jelly damp with his own water, and shoves off anything that comes for them.

facts.text: In many glass frogs even the bones are green. A pigment tints them. Most animals treat that pigment as waste and throw it away.
facts.more: The color comes from biliverdin, the same compound that turns a healing bruise green. Most bodies get rid of it as fast as they can. These frogs hold on to it and let it stain the skeleton, so the animal is green the whole way through.

facts.text: Males call from leaves above rushing water, a single high peep repeated all night. Each one holds his own leaf, and they space themselves out along the bank.
facts.more: Streams are loud, so the calls are pitched high and thin to cut through the roar of the water. Stand beside the right forest stream after dark and you will hear dozens of them, none of them visible, all of them somewhere just above your head.

facts.text: It hunts after dark for anything small enough to fit: flies, crickets, spiders, ants. Whatever it swallows, you can then watch making its way through it.
Glass frogs live only where fast, clean water runs through forest. No stream, no glass frogs. The whole life cycle depends on a leaf with moving water underneath it.
It has no venom, no speed and no size to fall back on. Its entire defense is a body you cannot easily pick out from the leaf it is sitting on.

wonder: A window into a working body, out walking about on a leaf, all the machinery on show and running perfectly.

name: Golden poison frog
blurb: A frog the length of your thumb, colored like a highlighter pen. Its skin carries enough poison to kill about ten grown adults.
size: About 2.4 in (6 cm) long, as long as your thumb, and about as heavy as a AA battery

facts.text: One wild golden poison frog carries roughly a milligram of batrachotoxin on its skin. That is a smear you could barely see. Nobody has tested it on people. Scaled up from lab mice, it works out at about ten adults.
facts.more: Batrachotoxin jams open the tiny gates that let sodium into nerve and muscle cells. Those gates are meant to flick open and shut to fire a signal. Held open, muscles seize and stop working, including the heart. There is no antidote for it.

facts.text: The frog does not manufacture the poison. It collects it from what it eats, which means a frog raised in a tank on crickets and fruit flies is completely harmless.
facts.more: In the forest it eats tiny insects and mites carrying the raw chemicals, and it concentrates them in glands in its skin. Remove that diet and the supply stops. Zoo-bred golden poison frogs can be safely handled, which is the only reason anyone can study them closely.

facts.text: Poisonous is not the same as venomous. Nothing about this frog injects you. No fangs, no sting. The poison sits on the outside of the skin.
facts.more: Venomous animals deliver a dose into you. Snakes, wasps and stonefish all do that. Poisonous animals are dangerous to eat or to handle. The golden poison frog is the second kind. It does its damage through a cut, a mouth or an eye, not through a wound of its own making.

facts.text: It makes no attempt whatsoever to hide. That screaming yellow, mint green or orange is called aposematic coloring. The best read is that it works as a signal rather than camouflage. The message is: leave me alone.
facts.more: Camouflage is for animals that can be eaten. This one advertises. It sits in plain sight on the forest floor in broad daylight with its color blazing. Plenty of brightly colored animals in the world are bluffing about how dangerous they are. This one is not bluffing.

facts.text: It is the giant of the poison dart frogs at about 2 inches (5 cm) long, which still means the whole animal would sit on a matchbox.
A parent carries the tadpoles up into the trees on its own back, one trip at a time. Each one gets dropped into a puddle of rainwater held in a plant.
facts.more: Bromeliads are plants whose leaves form a cup, and the cup holds water: a private pond in the canopy with no fish in it. The tadpoles wriggle onto the parent's wet back and stick there for the climb. Water-filled tree holes work just as well.

facts.text: It spends its days picking ants, termites, mites and tiny beetles off the forest floor, one flick of the tongue at a time. Its entire weapon comes out of that diet.
Every wild golden poison frog on Earth lives in one strip of rainforest. It sits on the Pacific coast of Colombia, in one of the wettest places anywhere.
facts.more: It needs heavy rain, warmth above 26°C (79°F) and thick humid air. Its whole range covers less than 5,000 square kilometers, a patch you could drive across in a morning, and it is shrinking as forest is cleared. The IUCN lists the species as Endangered.

facts.text: The Emberá people of Colombia arm blowgun darts with these frogs. They wipe the dart tip across the frog's back, and that tip stays deadly for two years or more.
facts.more: Only a handful of frog species are used this way. The golden poison frog needs no preparation at all, because the toxin is already sitting on the skin. Hunters handle the frogs with leaves, never bare hands. This is where the name poison dart frog comes from.

facts.text: Males call with a long trill, and they do it in daylight, out in the open. An animal this dangerous has no particular reason to keep quiet.
There are well over a hundred kinds of poison dart frog, in just about every color you can name. Most could not seriously hurt you. This one is in a class entirely of its own.

wonder: Bright as a warning sign and impossible to overlook. Some creatures were simply never meant to hide.

name: Goliath frog
blurb: The largest frog on Earth. This West African river frog is longer than a dinner plate is wide. It is heavy enough that you would want both hands.
size: Body about 1 ft (30 cm) long — longer still with its legs stretched out — and about 7 lb (3.2 kg)

facts.text: Body alone, a big goliath frog measures about 13 inches (32 cm), longer than a dinner plate is wide. Stretch the legs out behind it and the whole animal passes 30 inches (80 cm).
The heaviest one ever properly weighed came in at 7.3 lb (3.3 kg).
facts.more: No other frog is close. A big American bullfrog, the largest frog most people will ever meet in person, tops out at around a pound (0.5 kg). The goliath frog is in a size class entirely of its own.

facts.text: It has no vocal sac. Other frogs inflate a balloon of skin under the chin to boom across a pond. This one has nothing to inflate. So it whistles with its mouth open.
facts.more: A vocal sac works as a resonator, and it makes a frog far louder than its size suggests. The largest frog in the world does without one entirely. Its whistle is thin for such a huge animal and is easily lost under the noise of the rapids it lives beside.

facts.text: It builds nurseries. A goliath frog clears a patch of river gravel into a shallow pond about 3 feet (1 m) across, shoving stones out of the way as it works.
facts.more: Researchers watching them recorded three kinds of nest. One is a rock pool cleaned out of leaves and debris. One is an existing hollow, widened and dammed. One is a basin dug fresh into the gravel. Some of the stones they shift weigh a couple of kilograms. Very few frogs anywhere build anything at all.

facts.text: The nest gets guarded. Once the eggs are in the cleared pool, an adult stays with them through the night, which is unusual work for a frog.
facts.more: The pools sit at the edge of fast water, but out of the main current. Eggs and tadpoles are not swept downstream, and river fish cannot easily get in. The frog builds a safe pool and then stands over it all night. That is close to what a bird does with a nest.

facts.text: For all that bulk it is a serious jumper. One leap covers somewhere between 4 and 10 feet (1.2 to 3 m). It goes from a standing start, with no run-up at all.
