Adults eat crabs, insects, worms, spiders, millipedes and the occasional small snake. They hunt by sitting completely still at the water's edge and waiting.
facts.more: It does not chase anything. It waits, and whatever moves within reach and will fit in its mouth gets swallowed whole, because frogs do not chew. Crabs are a favorite, hard shell and all.

facts.text: It lives in one narrow band of forest in Cameroon and Equatorial Guinea, always beside fast rivers and waterfalls. Take away the rapids and the frog is gone.
facts.more: It needs clean, fast, oxygen-rich water running over sand and gravel. That is a very specific address, and it is disappearing. The IUCN lists the goliath frog as Endangered, hunted for food and squeezed by logging and farming.

facts.text: Its tadpoles are nothing special to look at. They are no bigger than an ordinary frog's. Everything remarkable about a goliath frog happens after it climbs out of the water.
facts.more: They are fussy eaters, though. Goliath tadpoles graze on a single kind of water plant that grows only on rocks in fast, splashing water. No plant, no tadpoles, which is one more reason the whole species is tied to the rapids.

facts.text: It is powerfully strong and, in the ways that count, defenseless. No poison, no bite worth worrying about. What it has is legs, and one jump puts it into white water.

wonder: A frog given a size no other frog gets, and forelimbs strong enough to build with, set down beside a waterfall of all places.

name: African gray parrot
blurb: A dust-gray parrot from the forests of central Africa. It has a scarlet tail and a mind that solves problems most animals cannot.
size: About as long as your forearm, and light enough to sit on your hand all afternoon without tiring it

facts.text: A gray parrot named Alex learned more than a hundred English words. He used them to answer questions he had never been asked, about objects he had never seen.
facts.more: Alex worked with the scientist Irene Pepperberg for thirty years. Shown a tray of objects, he could say how many were green, name the material a key was made of, and pick the larger of two things. Not tricks on cue. New questions, new answers.

facts.text: Parrots have no vocal cords. A gray shapes sound in its syrinx — a voice box down where the windpipe forks — then moves its thick tongue to sculpt it, exactly as you do.
facts.more: That tongue is the difference. Most birds cannot move theirs much. A parrot's is muscular and blunt. Shifting it forward or back changes the shape of the space the sound travels through. A raw buzz turns into a word.

facts.text: Nobody taught Alex a word for zero. Asked about an amount that simply was not in front of him, he borrowed a word he already had and answered: none.
facts.more: That is harder than counting. Counting means matching a word to things you can see. Saying none means naming an amount that is not there at all — and Alex was never trained to do it. He carried the word over from another task himself.

facts.text: In one experiment, a gray parrot handed metal tokens through a hole to a neighboring parrot so the neighbor could buy a walnut. The helper got nothing, and kept handing them over.
facts.more: The birds could not eat the tokens. They were only useful traded to a researcher for food. When the neighbor had no way to spend them, the helping mostly stopped. The parrots seemed to understand what the tokens were actually for.

facts.text: A gray parrot's brain is smaller than a walnut. Counted under a microscope, the neurons inside are packed far tighter than in a mammal brain the same size. That is the best answer anyone has for how so much thinking fits in so little room.

A gray parrot learns which human voice belongs to which human face, and stares longer when the wrong voice comes out of the wrong person. That stare is the whole evidence, and the best read of it is a bird tracking individuals, not just sounds.
Look at the feet: two toes forward, two toes back. That grip is called zygodactyl, and it turns a foot into a hand. Grays lift food to the bill one-footed, and most favor the same foot every time.
Fruit, nuts, seeds and oily palm fruit, plus bark, flowers and the occasional snail. That bill can crack a shell you would need a hammer for, then peel out the kernel without crushing it.
facts.more: The upper bill hinges against the skull instead of being fixed to it, so the whole tip swings. The bird can bear down hard for the crack and then work delicately with the very point — one tool, two settings.

facts.text: Three to five white eggs in a hole high in a tree. Thirty days of sitting, then about twelve weeks before the chicks leave — far longer than most birds stay home.
They roost in noisy flocks of hundreds in tall forest trees. At dawn they break into small groups. They fly out along the same routes to the same feeding trees.
Shake two closed cups in front of a gray parrot. Only one rattles, and the parrot picks it. Shake the empty one instead, and it picks the other — the silent one.
facts.more: This is called inference by exclusion, and very few animals manage it. The parrot never sees the food. It works out where the food must be from where the food is not, on sound alone, without looking inside anything.

facts.text: Nobody has followed a wild gray from hatching to death. Worked out from birds of known age, a wild life comes to around twenty-three years. Kept safe and well fed, one can reach sixty — old enough to outlive the child who first met it.
Gray parrots are Endangered. So many were trapped in the wild for the pet trade that the international wildlife treaty stepped in. It banned commercial trade in wild-caught birds altogether.

wonder: A bird that answers a question nobody taught it, and hands a token to a neighbor it gains nothing at all from helping.

name: Superb lyrebird
blurb: A chicken-sized Australian songbird. It copies the sounds of other birds so exactly you cannot hear the join.
size: About 3.3 ft (1 m) long in all; the tail alone is 28 in (70 cm) of that

facts.text: Seven or eight out of every ten sounds a male makes are borrowed from other birds. He is not really singing his own song. He is playing back the forest.
facts.more: He does not stitch them into mush, either. He runs one species cleanly, stops, and starts another. Kookaburra, whipbird, rosella, currawong. Each one is held long enough to be recognized, then dropped for the next.

facts.text: At the moment of mating the male makes a sound no single bird should be able to make. It is the panicked racket of a whole flock mobbing a predator. Several species at once, out of one throat.
facts.more: Researchers recorded it and lined it up against real mobbing flocks. It matches closely enough to fool the ear. Males produced it at two moments only — when a female tried to leave the display, and during mating itself.

facts.text: Songbird is a real scientific group, and this is one of its giants. Most songbirds fit in your palm. This one is chicken-sized, and the tail doubles it again.
The lyre-shaped tail is sixteen feathers. Two curved outer ones look like the arms of a harp. Twelve fine silvery filaments sit between them. Two thin ribbons run down the middle.
facts.more: The whole thing can reach 28 in (70 cm) — longer than the bird's own body. Females have a tail too, but plainer and shorter. Only the male grows the full instrument, and he sheds it and grows it again.

facts.text: During the display he throws the entire tail forward over his head. He vanishes under a shimmering silver canopy, and only the sound comes out.
Each male scrapes together a low mound of bare earth on the forest floor, climbs on top of it, and sings from there. He built the stage himself, and he comes back to it.
In midwinter, when most of the forest has gone quiet, a male may sing for four hours a day — nearly half the daylight there is.
He rakes the forest floor with his feet all day long. On a patch of forest the size of two football fields, lyrebirds turn over as much as 220 tons (200 tonnes) of soil and leaf litter in a year.
facts.more: That is the weight of roughly thirty elephants, shifted by birds using nothing but their feet. The scratching mixes dead leaves down into the soil and clears away the loose dry litter that lets a bushfire run.

facts.text: Worms, grubs, beetles, spiders, centipedes. He hooks them out from under the leaf litter with long strong claws, which is exactly why he does all that raking.
One egg. Just one, once a year. The female builds the domed nest, sits on it for up to seven weeks — a very long wait for a songbird — and raises the chick entirely alone.
Females copy too, which people missed for years. They use borrowed calls while foraging, and again when driving a predator away from the nest.
It barely flies. It runs, hops, and scrambles up branch by branch to roost at night, then launches off in the morning and glides down like a paper plane.

wonder: One throat given every voice in the forest, and one foot that turns the whole forest floor over while it sings.

name: Indian peafowl
blurb: The blue-and-green bird of India whose male grows a fan of shimmering eyespots taller than a doorway.
size: With the train trailing behind him, a male runs 79-91 in (200-230 cm) (6.5-7.5 ft) — longer than a doorway is tall

facts.text: That fan is not his tail. It is a cape of hugely overgrown feathers that grow above the tail. The real tail is short, stiff and plain brown. It hides behind the fan and props the whole thing upright.
facts.more: The train feathers are called upper tail coverts. On most birds, coverts are the small tidy feathers covering the base of the tail. On a peacock they have run away with themselves, and the actual tail is left doing the shoving.

facts.text: There is no blue or green dye anywhere in that train. The color is built, not painted: stacked microscopic rods inside each barbule bounce back only certain wavelengths of light.
facts.more: It is the trick of a soap bubble, or an oil slick on a puddle. Crush a train feather and the color dies with it. What is left is brown. The color lived in the shape, and you have just destroyed the shape.

facts.text: When he shivers the train it rattles about 25 times a second. High-speed film shows the eyespots holding almost still while every loose barb around them blurs.
facts.more: Each eyespot sits on its own shaft, its barbules hooked tightly together into one stiff disc. The looser feathery barbs surrounding it swing much further. The result is a field of steady eyes floating on a shaking sea of color.

facts.text: Cameras that track where a peahen actually looks found she mostly ignores the top of the fan. Close up she watches the bottom edge; only from a distance does she take in the whole thing.
Guides tracking tigers in India listen for peafowl. A peacock that has spotted a big cat screams from its perch, and every animal within earshot learns where the tiger is.
He drops the entire train every year after the monsoon and grows a whole new one by spring. For a few months, the most spectacular bird in India looks like a plain blue chicken.
facts.more: Growing that much feather takes real food and real time. The train is not fully grown until he is about four, so a young male spends his first seasons displaying with a stubby, unimpressive version of it.

facts.text: Yes, he can fly. Dragging all of that, he still hauls himself up into a tall tree every evening to sleep — slow, deliberate wingbeats, no gliding.
Grain, seeds, flower buds, berries, insects — and small reptiles. A peafowl will take a lizard without hesitating. That elegant bird is a hunter when it wants to be.
That famous scream, a harsh may-awe, is only one of his sounds. Researchers listening carefully sorted out about seven different calls, plus six more used only for alarm.
Three to eight eggs in a scrape on the ground, sat on for twenty-eight to thirty days. The chicks can walk and follow their mother within hours of hatching.
facts.more: Birds that hatch ready to run are called nidifugous — nest-fleeing. It is a very different childhood from a parrot's, where chicks sit blind in a tree hole for weeks. Peachicks are up and after their mother almost immediately.

facts.text: Wild peafowl belong to India and Sri Lanka: dry forest, farmland edges, riverbanks. India chose it as the national bird. In many villages it simply walks about among people.
Engineers study those feathers on purpose. Color made from structure never fades the way dye does, so labs build peacock-style nanostructures for inks and paints meant to keep their color for good.

wonder: Not one drop of dye in the whole train. The color is written into the shape of the feather itself.

name: Greater flamingo
blurb: A tall pink wading bird that eats with its head held upside down in water too salty for almost anything else.
size: Up to 5 ft (150 cm) tall — taller than you are — yet no heavier than a house cat

facts.text: It feeds with its head upside down. The bill is a strainer. The bird sweeps it through the water and the fat tongue pumps like a piston. Comb-like ridges called lamellae hold back the shrimp and algae.
facts.more: In almost every animal, the lower jaw is the one that moves. A flamingo's upper jaw swings instead — which is why the bill looks like it was put on backwards. Turned upside down in the water, it is exactly the right way up.

facts.text: The pink is eaten, not born. Brine shrimp and algae carry orange pigments called carotenoids; the flamingo digests them and lays the color into growing feathers. Fed the wrong food, a flamingo goes white.
facts.more: They are the same family of pigments that make carrots orange. Before nesting, a flamingo goes further. It rubs oil from a gland near its tail all through its feathers, pigment and all. It is brightening itself on purpose, like putting on make-up.

facts.text: Both parents make milk. Not from a chest — from glands lining the throat and gullet, and it pours out bright red. It is loaded with fat and protein.
facts.more: Making it drains the parents' own color straight out of their feathers. So a flamingo raising a chick fades to pale while the chick gets the pigment. Fathers produce it just as mothers do, and both feed the chick.

facts.text: Standing on one leg costs a flamingo almost nothing. The body settles and locks over the joint. A flamingo that has died can be balanced on one leg and it will stay standing on its own.
facts.more: Scientists tested exactly that, then measured living birds too — and found they sway less on one leg than on two. So the strange pose is the restful one. It is standing on both legs that takes the effort.

facts.text: That backwards-bending knee is not a knee. It is the ankle. The real knee is tucked up under the feathers against the body. A flamingo is standing on its toes, on very long feet.
Chicks hatch gray, with a straight bill. The famous downward kink only develops over the following weeks, and until it does they cannot filter-feed for themselves at all.
At about two weeks old the chicks leave the nest and gather in a crèche. That nursery mob can swell to thousands of gray chicks. A handful of adults watch over the lot.
facts.more: A parent returning with food has to find one chick in that crowd. It does it by voice: calling, listening, answering back, until the right chick pushes its way through. Both learn each other's call in the first days after hatching.

facts.text: A flamingo cannot simply jump into the air. It runs — several long splashing strides across the surface with wings already beating — before it finally lifts off.

It lives in salt pans and briny coastal lagoons that most animals cannot drink from, let alone live in. The tiny creatures it eats swarm there, and the best read is that they manage it precisely because so little else can.
Before nesting, a whole colony performs together. Hundreds of birds pack shoulder to shoulder, snap their heads side to side in time, and flash their black-and-red wings open on cue.
The nest is a chimney of mud, built up with the bill until it stands clear of the water, with a hollow scooped in the top. One chalky white egg goes in it. Just one.
Thirty to forty years is normal in the wild. One greater flamingo at a zoo in Australia reached at least 83 — older than almost any bird ever recorded.

wonder: A bill that works upside down, a leg that rests while standing, and a color it feeds to its chick. Nothing here is spare.

name: Toco toucan
blurb: A crow-sized South American fruit-eater. Its huge orange bill takes up a third of its whole length.
size: About as long as your arm — and a third of that is bill

facts.text: The bill runs about 8 in (20 cm) — close to a third of the whole bird. Only one bird beats that for proportion: the sword-billed hummingbird, whose bill is longer than the rest of it.
Pick it up and it weighs almost nothing. Under a thin shell of keratin — the stuff of your fingernails — the bill is a foam of bony struts and air pockets.
facts.more: That is a very good way to build something big and light: a stiff skin outside doing the hard work, a spongy honeycomb inside stopping it from crumpling. The whole bill is mostly empty space.

facts.text: The bill is a radiator. It is packed with blood vessels. The toucan opens them wide to dump heat, or shuts them down to hold it. Infrared cameras catch the bill glowing hot, then going cold.
facts.more: Between a third and a half of the bird's entire skin surface is bill. Sitting in still air it sheds only a quarter of the heat the resting bird makes; in a breeze it can shed four times that heat. No sweating — birds cannot sweat at all.

facts.text: Going to sleep, it swings its head right round. It lays the bill down its back, under the wing feathers. Then it flips its tail up over the top. The result is a ball of feathers with no bill in sight.
facts.more: Its tail bones have a joint that lets the tail fold forward almost flat onto its own back. Tucking the bill away is not just tidiness: it shuts the radiator down, and the bill cools within minutes of the bird settling.

facts.text: The tongue is nearly as long as the bill, flat, and frayed along both edges like a narrow feather. The toucan plucks a berry at the tip, then flicks its head back to throw it down its throat.

Perched on a branch strong enough to hold its weight, a toucan can still stretch out and take fruit from twigs far too thin to stand on. Nobody can ask the bird what the bill is for — but that reach is the strongest argument on offer.
Mostly fruit, swallowed whole. But also insects, lizards, and the eggs and nestlings of other birds — that cheerful-looking bill is a long-reach tool for raiding nests.
Two toes forward, two toes back: zygodactyl feet, made for gripping a branch rather than walking along it. Toucans hop sideways down a branch. They do not stroll.
It is a poor flier. Watch one cross a clearing — a burst of heavy flapping, then a glide, then more flapping — a bobbing, up-and-down line, and it will not go far.
Two to four white eggs in a hollow tree trunk. Both parents sit, for seventeen or eighteen days, and the chicks hatch naked, blind, and with no bill worth the name.
facts.more: There is no lining in the hole, just bare wood and old seeds. So toucan chicks come equipped with thick pads of skin on their heels, studded with small spines. They can squat on that rough floor for weeks without being rubbed raw.

facts.text: For the biggest toucan there is, the voice is a let-down. It is a dry, croaking grunt. It is repeated over and over for minutes at a time from the top of a tree.
It likes edges — the seam where forest meets open ground, palm groves, riverbanks, savanna with scattered trees. It is not a bird of the deep unbroken jungle.

wonder: One bill doing three jobs at once: picking fruit, reaching what the feet cannot, and cooling the whole bird down.

name: Great white shark
blurb: A huge, warm-bodied hunting shark that patrols cool coastal seas and takes seals with a single strike from below.
size: Longer than a car — up to 19.8 ft (6 m)

facts.text: A big female is longer than a car. The longest one anyone has properly measured was 19.8 ft (6 m), and the heaviest weighed 5,580 lb (2,530 kg) — more than most cars.
facts.more: Much bigger numbers get thrown around, but they come from lengths guessed over the side of a boat, not from a tape measure. When scientists went back through the catch records and checked, those were the largest anyone could actually prove. Females run larger than males.

facts.text: It cruises at barely walking pace, then sprints at about 15 mph (24 km/h) for the last few seconds of an attack.
facts.more: Speed costs energy, so a white shark spends almost its whole life idling. The sprint is saved for the final rush, usually straight up from below, where a seal at the surface cannot pick out a dark shark against dark water.

facts.text: A great white runs warm. Its stomach can sit at 25°C (77°F) while the sea around it is only 14°C (57°F). Warm muscle hits harder and faster.
facts.more: Bundles of blood vessels run side by side, called the rete mirabile, the wonderful net. Blood heading out to the cold gills warms the blood coming back in. The heat is trapped inside the body instead of leaking away. Most fish are exactly as cold as the water they swim in.

facts.text: Hundreds of jelly-filled pores sit under its snout. They are called ampullae of Lorenzini. They read the faint electricity leaking from every beating heart and twitching muscle nearby.
facts.more: Every living animal gives off a weak electric field simply by being alive. A shark that has lost sight of its prey can close the final stretch on that signal alone. It is also why a great white will sometimes bite a metal cage. Metal in seawater makes an electric buzz.

facts.text: One white shark tagged off South Africa swam to Australia and back — about 12,000 miles (20,000 km) — in under nine months.
facts.more: That is roughly halfway around the world and back, across open ocean with nothing to steer by. Researchers recognize the sharks on their return by the dorsal fin. The ragged notches along its edge are as individual as a signature.

facts.text: Seals, sea lions, dolphins and other sharks. Young great whites eat fish and squid, and only switch to seals once they pass about 10 ft (3 m) long.
facts.more: Their teeth change shape as they grow: narrow and spiky for gripping a slippery fish, then broad and saw-edged for cutting through blubber. You can tell a young white shark from a full-grown one by its teeth alone.

facts.text: Off South Africa, great whites hunting seals launch completely clear of the water. The whole shark goes up to 10 ft (3 m) into the air.
facts.more: It begins the run about 66 ft (20 m) down, points itself almost straight up, and arrives carrying so much speed that it cannot stop at the surface. Photographers call it a breach. The seal usually never sees it coming.

facts.text: Its teeth sit in rows on a conveyor belt. When a front tooth snaps off, the one behind rolls forward to replace it. About 300 in the mouth at once.
Pups grow inside their mother for about a year. They are born already 3.3 to 5.2 ft (1 to 1.6 m) (3 to 5 ft) long, about as tall as you are. Then they swim off alone.
facts.more: There is no nursing and no parental care at all. A litter is small, usually two to ten. Before they are born the pups feed on unfertilised eggs inside the mother, which is why they arrive so large and so completely ready.

facts.text: Dark gray on top, white underneath. From above it vanishes into the deep; from below it disappears into the bright surface. This is called countershading.
Two separate nostrils let it work out which side a scent reached first, and steer toward it. It cannot smell blood from miles away, though — that claim is stretched.
Cool coastal water is where you usually find it. But it also drops past 3,300 ft (1,000 m) into open ocean. That is far below any sunlight.

wonder: A hunter given warm blood for cold water, and a set of teeth that never runs out of edge.

name: Whale shark
blurb: The biggest fish in the world. This spotted, slow-moving giant swims with its mouth open. It eats some of the smallest food in the sea.
size: Up to 61.7 ft (18.8 m) long

facts.text: The largest fish alive. The biggest one ever properly measured was 61.7 ft (18.8 m) from nose to tail.
facts.more: You will see larger numbers repeated online, but those come from lengths eyeballed off the side of a boat. When scientists reviewed all the reports, 62 ft (18.8 m) was the one they judged reliable. Even an ordinary adult whale shark is longer than most living rooms.

facts.text: It has around 3,000 teeth, none bigger than a grain of rice, and never uses a single one for eating. It eats plankton — creatures mostly too small to see.
facts.more: Food is caught on 20 spongy filter pads behind the mouth while the water carries straight on out through the gills. A whale shark can push over 1,585 gallons (6,000 liters) of seawater through those pads every hour — about forty bathtubs' worth.

facts.text: Its eyeballs are covered in teeth. About 2,900 tiny tooth-shaped scales, called denticles, armor the surface of each eye.
facts.more: Shark skin is covered in these hard little scales, but the whale shark is the only animal known to grow them on the eye itself. Each one is shaped like an oak leaf. If something still comes too close, the shark yanks its eye halfway back into its head in under a second.

facts.text: Its mouth sits at the very front of its head, not tucked underneath like most sharks. It opens about 5 ft (1.5 m) wide. That is wide enough to swallow a doorway.
Every whale shark's spot pattern is unique. Researchers tell individuals apart with software first written to match patterns of stars in Hubble Space Telescope photographs.
facts.more: An astronomer adapted the star-matching math for shark flanks. Now anyone who photographs a whale shark can upload it to a shared library. The software says whether that exact animal has been logged before. Sometimes it was logged years earlier, an ocean away.

facts.text: A pregnant female nicknamed Rio Lady was tracked 4,829 miles (7,772 km) from Mexico. Her route ran out toward the middle of the Atlantic. She dived to 5,249 ft (1,600 m) over and over the whole way.
facts.more: That is most of the way across an ocean, alone, while carrying pups. Nobody knows for certain where whale sharks go to give birth. Following pregnant females like her is one of the main ways researchers are trying to find out.

facts.text: It dives deep. The deepest recorded was 6,325 ft (1,928 m) — well over a mile down, far below where any sunlight reaches.
One pregnant whale shark was found carrying around 300 pups, all at different stages of development. It is the largest litter known from any shark.
facts.more: The pups hatch from eggs inside the mother and are born 15.7 to 24 in (40 to 60 cm) (16 to 24 in) long — about as long as your arm. Newborn whale sharks are almost never seen in the wild. Where they spend their first years is one of the genuine mysteries left in ocean science.

facts.text: Its skin is up to 6 in (15 cm) thick — about as deep as your hand is long — and hard and rough to touch. Very little in the ocean can bite through it.
Warm water, above about 21°C (70°F). They gather at the same places at the same time each year, wherever the plankton blooms.
facts.more: Ningaloo Reef in Australia and the coast of Mexico's Yucatán are two of the reliable ones. In one year, more than 400 whale sharks turned up off the Yucatán at once. They fed on plankton swarms and clouds of fish eggs. Then they scattered back out into open ocean.

facts.text: Sometimes it stops swimming altogether. It hangs upright in the water like a huge column. Then it gulps downward at a swarm of food above its mouth.

wonder: The biggest mouth in the ocean, fitted out to catch the smallest food in it.

name: Great hammerhead
blurb: The largest of the hammerhead sharks, and a stingray specialist. Its head is wide, flat and shaped like a blade. Its dorsal fin is taller than your arm is long.
size: Up to 20 ft (6.1 m) long

facts.text: The biggest hammerhead there is. A large one reaches 20 ft (6.1 m). The heaviest ever put on scales came in at 1,280 lb (580 kg).
facts.more: That record-holder was a 14.4 ft (4.4 m) female caught off Florida. She was carrying 55 pups at the time. That is a good part of why she weighed what she did. Length is the fairer way to measure a big hammerhead.

facts.text: That head has a proper name: the cephalofoil. Flattened like a wing, it sweeps side to side across the sea floor as the shark hunts.
facts.more: Watch one and it looks exactly like someone working a metal detector along a beach. The wide head does give some lift as the shark swims, but its bigger job is searching — spreading the shark's sensors over as much ground as possible.

facts.text: Hundreds of pores are spread across the underside of that head. They read electricity. A stingray buried in sand holds perfectly still. It gives itself away anyway, with every heartbeat.
facts.more: The pores are called ampullae of Lorenzini. Every shark has them, but the hammerhead has spread its set across a much wider surface — the same trick as building a bigger antenna. It finds prey it cannot see, smell or hear.

facts.text: Eyes at the far ends of the hammer give it a full 360° view in the vertical. It can see above itself and below itself at the same moment.
facts.more: It also gets better depth perception than a pointed-nose shark. Those wide-set eyes overlap more out in front than you would expect. Researchers shone light into hammerhead eyes from many different angles. They recorded which angles the eye answered.

facts.text: Stingrays, above almost anything else. Also bony fish, squid, crabs and other sharks — including, when food runs short, smaller hammerheads.
It hunts stingrays by slamming the ray down into the sea floor with the flat of its head, pinning it there, and eating the wings first.
facts.more: One great hammerhead caught off Florida had 96 stingray spines stuck in and around its mouth. The venom does not appear to trouble them in the slightest. They simply keep hunting rays.

facts.text: It swims tilted on its side, sometimes rolled almost halfway over. Not a wobble — the tilt is held on purpose, and worked out on paper it cuts drag by around 10%.
facts.more: Scientists strapped small motion sensors to wild great hammerheads and found they spend as much as 90% of their swimming time rolled onto one side. That huge dorsal fin then acts like a wing, giving lift, so the shark burns less energy holding itself up.

facts.text: The first dorsal fin is enormous — tall, sharply pointed and curved back like a scythe. On a full-grown adult it stands taller than your whole arm is long.
Pups grow inside their mother for about eleven months and are born live, 20 to 40 at a time, each already 19.7-28 in (50-70 cm) (20-28 in) long.
facts.more: A female only does this once every two years. That slow pace is exactly why hammerhead numbers drop quickly when too many are caught, and climb back very, very slowly afterwards.

facts.text: Warm coastal seas all around the world. They work the shallows over sand and reef, and move toward the poles in summer before heading back.
Those famous photographs of hammerheads schooling by the hundred show a different species. It is the scalloped hammerhead. The great hammerhead is a loner.
The great hammerhead is listed as Critically Endangered. That is the highest warning level there is before an animal is gone from the wild.
facts.more: The main cause is fishing for their fins. Hammerheads also fare badly on a line. They are unusually likely to die from the stress of being caught, even when they are let go. Catch-and-release is far less forgiving for them than for other sharks.

wonder: A head shaped to find what is hidden — every square inch of it listening.

name: Greenland shark
blurb: A huge, slow, nearly blind shark of the freezing Arctic deep. It is the longest-lived animal with a backbone that anyone has ever measured.
size: Longer than a car — up to 21 ft (6.4 m) and over a tonne

facts.text: This is the longest-living animal with a backbone anyone has ever measured. The oldest one studied had been swimming for something close to four hundred years.
facts.more: Scientists worked it out by reading the very center of the eye lens. That tissue forms before the shark is born and then never changes again, so whatever is locked inside it is a record of the very beginning. The measurement is rough at the edges, but it put the whole species comfortably past 250 years.

facts.text: It is the slowest-swimming fish for its size ever recorded. Cruising speed is about 0.8 mph (1.2 km/h) — slower than you walk to the kitchen.
facts.more: One full sweep of its tail takes around seven seconds. At that pace it ought to have no hope of catching a seal, and yet seal remains keep turning up in Greenland shark stomachs. How they manage it is still argued over.

facts.text: Length is the part anyone can measure: a female Greenland shark is about 14 ft (4.2 m) long before her first pups. Put beside the eye-lens ages, that works out at somewhere around 150 years old.
facts.more: That is older than almost any other animal ever gets, period. It also means a shark pulled up in a net today may never have had a single pup. That is why the species recovers so terribly slowly from any losses.

facts.text: Most Greenland sharks swim around with a worm-like parasite dangling off each eyeball, chewing at the surface. It leaves the shark nearly blind.
facts.more: The parasite is a copepod called Ommatokoita elongata. It is a few centimeters long and hangs from the cornea like a luggage tag. It scars the eye badly. The shark hunts perfectly well without sight, using smell and the vibrations it feels in the water. So it seems to lose almost nothing.

facts.text: Its flesh is poisonous to eat fresh. It is loaded with a chemical called trimethylamine oxide, and anyone who eats it is left staggering as though drunk.
facts.more: Sled dogs fed fresh Greenland shark have been seen unable to stand up. In Iceland the meat is buried, fermented for weeks and hung to dry for months until it is safe — a dish called hákarl. The chemical is not there to poison anyone: it helps the shark's body cope with the pressure and cold of the deep.

facts.text: It lives in water between about -1°C and 7°C (30-45°F). That is cold enough that the sea is close to freezing. It goes down to around 3,900 ft (1,200 m).
facts.more: Far north it will come almost to the surface, because up there the surface is already as cold as the deep. Further south it stays down where the cold is. Either way it is choosing the same thing — water only a degree or two above freezing.

facts.text: Fish of every kind, seals, and a great deal of whatever it finds already dead on the sea floor. Reindeer, moose, horse and even polar bear remains have come out of their stomachs.
facts.more: Anything that drowns or dies at sea eventually sinks, and the Greenland shark is the animal waiting where it lands. One was found with an entire reindeer carcass inside it. Being unhurried is no handicap when most of your dinner is not going anywhere.

facts.text: Up to 21 ft (6.4 m) long and over 2,200 lb (1,000 kg). It is blunt-nosed and heavy-bodied. It cruises at about 0.8 mph (1.3 km/h).

Its top and bottom teeth do completely different jobs. The upper teeth are thin spikes that grip; the lower ones interlock into a broad, square cutting edge. It anchors with the top and saws with the bottom by rolling its head.
In the pitch dark of the deep it navigates by smell. A Greenland shark will find bait from a long way off, tracking the scent trail with eyes that barely work at all.
Its scientific name, Somniosus, comes from the Latin word for sleep. Anyone who has watched one drift past a camera would tell you the name is fair.

wonder: Slow, half-blind, and centuries old — flourishing in water that almost nothing else can survive.

name: Giant oceanic manta ray
blurb: The largest ray in the ocean. It is a huge, flat, completely harmless plankton-eater. It swims by flapping its fins like a pair of wings.
size: Wider than a giraffe is tall — up to 23 ft (7 m) wingtip to wingtip

facts.text: The biggest ray in the ocean. Wingtip to wingtip a giant manta reaches about 23 ft (7 m) — wider than a giraffe is tall — and the heaviest weigh over 4,400 lb (2,000 kg).
Those two paddles either side of its mouth are cephalic fins. It unrolls them to funnel water in while feeding, and curls them into tight spirals to swim clean and fast.
facts.more: They are forward extensions of the huge pectoral wings, reaching around the front of the head. Rolled up they look like a pair of horns, which is where the old sailors' name for mantas — devil rays — came from. Unrolled, they are simply a funnel.

facts.text: It eats plankton, straining it out of seawater. To do that it swims along with its mouth held open like a wide doorway and lets the ocean pour through.
facts.more: It never swallows the water. A mouthful goes in the front and straight out through the gill slits underneath, and the food is left behind on filter plates on the way past. A big manta processes an astonishing volume of sea in a day.

facts.text: Its filter should clog within minutes and never does. Water hits the filter plates and ricochets off at an angle, carrying plankton along the surface instead of jamming into it.
facts.more: Researchers who studied manta gill plates found the particles bounce rather than sieve. That is why nothing ever blocks. They named it ricochet separation. Filters built the same way could strain water without ever needing to be scrubbed clean. Engineers have taken very close notice.

facts.text: When it finds a thick patch of plankton, it does backward somersaults through it. It rolls over and over. That keeps it inside the cloud instead of swimming out the far side.
facts.more: It is called barrel rolling and it looks exactly like play. It is not. A straight line through a plankton patch is over in seconds, but a loop keeps the manta inside the food indefinitely. Several will sometimes line up nose to tail and cycle through together.

facts.text: For a fish, its brain is enormous. It runs up to 7 oz (200 g), the largest brain of any fish. That is five to ten times the size of a whale shark's.
facts.more: Parts of that brain are wrapped in a fine mesh of blood vessels called the rete mirabile. It keeps the brain warm while the manta is hunting down in cold water. A brain that stays warm carries on working properly when the rest of the body is chilled through.

facts.text: It has no sting. Stingrays carry a barb on the tail; the manta has only a small knob where one would sit, and nothing to defend itself with but size.
A manta has one pup at a time, after carrying it for about a year, and only every two or three years. The pup is born rolled up and unfurls as it swims away.
facts.more: It arrives already 4.6 ft (1.4 m) (4 ft 7 in) across and weighing about 20 lb (9 kg). That is bigger than a large dog. It gets no help from its mother afterwards. One pup at a time is why manta populations climb back so slowly once they fall.

facts.text: It dives past 3,300 ft (1,000 m) into cold black water. Nobody has watched it feed down there. The chemistry of its tissue is the argument. It points to roughly three-quarters of its food coming from the deep rather than the sunlit surface.
facts.more: For a long time people assumed mantas fed only at the top, because that is where we see them. Then chemical tests on manta tissue showed most of their food was coming from the deep. The surface feeding everyone photographs is the smaller part of the story.

facts.text: It returns to the same spots on the reef again and again to be cleaned. Small fish swim right into its gills and mouth, picking off parasites.
facts.more: Mantas remember these cleaning stations and come back to the exact same ones over many years. One will hover almost motionless above the reef, wings barely moving. It holds position while the little fish work. Then it moves off perfectly calmly.

facts.text: Every manta has a different pattern of dark blotches on its white belly. It works like a fingerprint. Researchers photograph bellies to keep track of who is who.
Giant mantas throw themselves clear out of the water and land flat with a crack you can hear a long way off. Nobody is certain why they do it.

wonder: The largest brain in all the fish, and a net of blood vessels to keep it warm in the cold and the dark.

name: Kiwi
blurb: A flightless, chicken-sized bird from New Zealand that hunts at night by smell, poking a long beak into the ground like a probe.
size: Stands roughly 16 in (40 cm) tall, and weighs about 6 lb (2.7 kg)
wonder: Not every bird was given wings that work. This one was given a nose instead — and it is enough.

facts.text: The kiwi is the only bird on Earth with its nostrils at the very tip of its beak. It sniffs the ground, then drives that beak straight down after a worm.
facts.more: Most birds have their nostrils up by the face, where the beak meets the head. The kiwi's sit at the far end, right where the digging happens — and when soil clogs them, the kiwi sneezes it out with a snuffly little blast.

facts.text: Most birds have hollow bones full of air. A kiwi's are heavy and packed with marrow, like yours — one reason it will never leave the ground.
facts.more: Flight costs weight, so a flying bird keeps its skeleton light and airy. The kiwi is built the opposite way: dense bones, thick muscular legs, and a whole body arranged for walking, digging and probing instead of the air.

facts.text: A kiwi egg can weigh up to a fifth of the mother's entire body. Imagine carrying a fifth of your own weight inside you.
facts.more: A brown kiwi egg can reach 1 lb (450 g), about six times a chicken's. By the last few days it fills so much of her that there is no room left for her stomach. She has to stop eating for two or three days.

facts.text: In brown kiwi the father does the sitting — seventy-five to ninety days on the egg, close to three months. Most garden birds are finished in two weeks.
facts.more: The egg carries nearly twice the yolk of most bird eggs its size. That is the chick's packed lunch. It hatches fully feathered, a miniature of its parents, and can live off the yolk still in its belly for well over a week.

facts.text: No kiwi chick is ever fed by its parents. About five days after hatching it walks out of the burrow and starts finding its own dinner.
For its body size, the kiwi has the smallest eyes of any bird. It hardly needs them — it works the night shift entirely by nose, ear and whisker.
facts.more: Stiff whisker-like feathers ring the base of the beak and feel the way ahead in the dark. Its ear openings are large and open, and a kiwi will cock its head toward a sound just as you do. Wild kiwi that are completely blind have been found living perfectly well.

facts.text: Kiwi feathers are long, loose and shaggy. They are far closer to coarse hair than to the sleek, zipped-together feathers of a bird that flies.
Somewhere under all that shag is a wing about 1 in (3 cm) long — shorter than your thumb — with a small cat-like claw on the end.
A kiwi runs cooler than most birds — about 38°C (100°F), close to your own temperature. Most birds idle nearer 40°C (104°F).
It feeds by tapping slowly along the ground. Then it punches its whole beak down into the leaf litter. It is after earthworms, beetle grubs, centipedes and big crickets called wētā.
A kiwi carries a strong, musty, mushroomy smell. Trained conservation dogs use it to find them in the bush. Unfortunately, so do introduced predators.
facts.more: Kiwi also mark their patch with pungent droppings. Conservation teams now work with certified kiwi dogs. The dogs locate birds by scent without ever touching them. Chicks can then be found, checked and protected.

facts.text: The name matches the noise. A male gives a shrill rising whistle, repeated fifteen to twenty-five times through the dark; the female answers slower, lower and throatier.

name: Bee hummingbird
blurb: The smallest bird in the world — a Cuban hummingbird so tiny that people who see one often think a large bee has just gone past.
size: Thumb-length, and lighter than a US penny
wonder: Two grams. And inside those two grams, every single thing a bird needs — nothing left out, nothing forgotten.

facts.text: No bird in the world is smaller. A male weighs about 1.95 grams — less than a US penny — and measures 2 in (5.5 cm) from beak tip to tail tip.
facts.more: Females are a little bigger, around 2.6 grams and 2.4 in (6.1 cm). Most of that length is beak and tail; the actual body is roughly the size of the end of your thumb. Bees have been mistaken for these birds, and these birds for bees.

facts.text: The nest is about 1 in (2.5 cm) across — a cup that would sit on a coin. The eggs inside are the size of coffee beans.
facts.more: She weaves it from cobwebs, bark and lichen up in a tree, and lays one or two eggs. They hatch after about twenty-one days, and the chicks are flying eighteen days after that.

facts.text: A bee hummingbird may visit around 1,500 flowers in a single day, and eat up to half its own body weight.
facts.more: An engine that small is expensive to run. Nectar is nearly pure sugar — instant fuel — and the bird tops up with tiny insects and spiders for protein. Pollen sticks to its head at every flower and rides to the next one, so it is planting as it feeds.

facts.text: Its wings beat about eighty times a second — far too fast for your eye to separate. In a courtship display a male drives them past two hundred.
facts.more: That hum is where the whole family gets its name, and it is not a voice at all — it is the sound of air being hammered by wings. A camera has to shoot in slow motion before the wing looks like a wing.

facts.text: The wing pivots right at the shoulder and traces a figure-eight, pushing air down on the forward stroke and the backward one. That is how it hangs still in midair.
facts.more: Almost every other bird gets lift only on the downstroke. A hummingbird's shoulder swivels so the wing flips over and works both ways — which also lets it fly backwards, straight up, and briefly upside down.

facts.text: The male's flaring pink-red head is not colored with pigment. The feathers are built in microscopic layers that split light, so the color blazes and vanishes as he turns.
facts.more: Tilt a soap bubble in sunlight and you see the same trick. There is no pink dye in those feathers at all, only structure. That is why a head that looks like fire from one angle can look flat black from two steps sideways.

facts.text: For something lighter than a penny it really moves. Ordinary level flight runs around 25-30 mph (40-48 km/h).
On a cold night it powers down. Its body cools, its heart slows to a small fraction of its daytime rate, and it burns almost nothing until dawn.
facts.more: This is called torpor, and metabolism can fall to roughly a fifteenth of normal. A bird in torpor is cold and stiff and takes several minutes of shivering to restart. Without it, an engine this small would run dry overnight.

facts.text: The entire species lives on Cuba and one island beside it, and nowhere else on the planet. That is the only place on Earth to see the smallest bird.
Small is not the same as timid. A male claims a patch of flowers and chases off intruders, including hummingbirds considerably larger than himself.
Its feet are almost useless for walking. It can grip a twig and shuffle sideways along it, but it cannot stride — everything else, it flies to.
The father takes no part. The female builds, incubates and feeds entirely alone, and about eighteen days after hatching the chicks fly out of that coin-sized cup.

name: Ruby-throated hummingbird
blurb: The little green hummingbird of eastern North America. It is the one that hangs at a garden feeder. It is also the only hummingbird that nests right across that half of the continent.
size: Not much longer than your thumb, and lighter than a five-cent coin
wonder: Nobody teaches a young ruby-throat the way south. It hatches already knowing.

facts.text: Nobody has followed a three-gram bird out over the Gulf of Mexico. The radar and the arrival dates say many cross in one go. That is about 500 miles (800 km) of open water. No land, no rest, roughly twenty hours of flying.
facts.more: There is nothing to land on for the entire crossing, and no plan B if the weather turns. Not every bird takes the sea route; plenty go the long way round the Texas coast. But the ones that go straight across do it non-stop, weighing three grams.

facts.text: Before it goes, it eats and eats. Weighed at banding stations, a ruby-throat can roughly double the fat it carries — and that works out to just about exactly what one flight over water would cost.
facts.more: Fat is the densest fuel a body can carry. It is the only way a three-gram bird can afford twenty hours over the sea. It arrives on the far shore thin and exhausted. Then it immediately starts looking for flowers.

facts.text: Its wings beat more than fifty times every second while it hovers. Your eye cannot follow that at all — it registers only a blur and a low hum.
The tongue is forked, and it does not suck. It flicks into the nectar, splits open, then snaps shut around the liquid and hauls it back — a pump, not a straw.
facts.more: People long assumed nectar simply wicked up the tongue the way water climbs a paper towel. High-speed film showed something better: the two halves of the tongue spring apart inside the liquid and clamp closed as they leave it, trapping nectar in the grooves. It happens many times a second.

facts.text: The male's throat is not painted red. It is a stack of microscopic layers that fling red light back at you — and from the wrong angle it goes flat black.
facts.more: This is iridescence: structure rather than pigment, the same reason a soap bubble has colors. He can aim it. During a courtship dive he angles that throat squarely at the female so it detonates into scarlet at the right instant. Females and young males have plain pale throats.

facts.text: The nest is thimble-sized, made of plant down and lichen and bound with spider silk. The cup stretches as the chicks grow instead of splitting, and the elastic silk is the best explanation for how.
facts.more: Spider silk is the trick, because it is elastic. A cup that starts barely wide enough for two pea-sized eggs can expand around two fast-growing chicks without ever being rebuilt. The lichen glued to the outside makes the whole thing look like a knot on the branch.

facts.text: It is not living on sugar alone. Ruby-throats hunt small insects and spiders, and will even pick prey out of spider webs. That is where the protein comes from.
On a cold night it shuts down completely. Body temperature falls, the heart slows enormously, and the bird hangs on its twig cold and unresponsive until morning warms it.
facts.more: This is torpor. A ruby-throat's heart can run past 1,200 beats a minute by day. In torpor it drops to a small fraction of that, and metabolism to roughly a fifteenth of normal. Waking takes several minutes of shivering before it can fly.

facts.text: A ruby-throat weighs about three grams. Put eight of them on a scale together and you would only just match one AA battery.
It is one of very few birds on Earth that can fly properly backwards — and hold a dead-still hover in a breeze while it drinks.
There are no flocks and no guides. Adults leave weeks before the young birds do, so a young ruby-throat that has never made the journey must be finding Central America without being shown.
facts.more: The route is not taught. Adults leave weeks before the young birds do. So the first migration is made by a bird a few months old, traveling solo. It navigates by something it was born already carrying.

facts.text: Ruby-throats come back to the same gardens year after year. Often it is the very same feeder. They arrive within a few days of the same date.

name: Kea
blurb: A big olive-green parrot that lives in New Zealand's snowy mountains. It is the world's only alpine parrot. It is also one of the cleverest and most destructive birds alive.
size: Crow-sized but heavier — about 19 in (48 cm) long and roughly a kilogram (2 lb)
wonder: A parrot given snow instead of jungle — and a mind restless enough to enjoy it.

facts.text: Almost every parrot on Earth lives somewhere warm. The kea breeds in New Zealand's Southern Alps at 5,200 ft (1,600 m) and higher — about a mile up, in snow.
facts.more: Picture a parrot: bright, tropical, sitting in a palm. Now picture that same bird walking across a snowfield in a mountain blizzard, digging through ice for roots. That is a kea, and no other parrot lives this way.

facts.text: Heavier than it looks. A big male runs to about 2 lb (1 kg) and roughly 19 in (48 cm) from beak to tail.

Kea take cars apart. They pick the rubber seals out of windscreens, strip wiper blades and unzip backpacks in ski-field car parks. There is no food in any of it, which is the strongest argument that they do it purely to find out what happens.
facts.more: This is genuine curiosity and it is relentless. Hand a kea an object it has never met and it will bite it, lever at it, pull it apart and flip it over. That same instinct is exactly why kea are so good at solving problems.

facts.text: Hidden cameras in a South Island valley caught kea breaking into baited stoat traps. More than three-quarters of the traps in that area had been set off.
facts.more: The traps are steel and spring-loaded, built so a stoat cannot beat them. The kea worked out how to reach the bait anyway. Conservation staff had to redesign the trap boxes to keep the birds out and the stoats catchable.

facts.text: A kea named Bruce lost the top half of his beak. At the wildlife park where he lives he learned to wedge a pebble against his tongue and comb his feathers with it.
facts.more: Without an upper beak, preening should be impossible. Keepers and researchers watched him pick pebbles of a particular size. He held them in place and used them. When he dropped one, he went after it to carry on. He appears to have worked the trick out entirely on his own.

facts.text: A kea eats more than forty kinds of plant, digs fat beetle grubs out of rotting wood, and will strip flesh and marrow off a dead animal. Very little is off the menu.
Kea have been filmed landing on live sheep and using that hooked beak to cut through the wool and feed on the fat underneath.
facts.more: It is rare, and most kea never do it, but it is real — farmers argued about it for generations before video settled the question. Kea were shot under a government bounty because of it. They are fully protected now, and only three to seven thousand remain.

facts.text: The upper beak is long, narrow and heavily hooked — closer to a crowbar than a nutcracker. It works as chisel, lever, and a third foot for climbing.
Kea nest underground, in rock crevices and tunnels under tree roots. Some of those tunnels run six meters (20 ft) back into the mountainside — longer than a car.
Play a recording of the kea's warbling call to wild birds. They break off what they are doing and start to play. They chase, tumble and throw things about.
facts.more: Researchers left the recording running for several minutes. Birds that heard it went off and played, often alone rather than with each other, and kept going after the sound stopped. Young kea, who roam in loose gangs of up to thirteen, play hardest of all.

facts.text: A kea will sit and wait as long as 160 seconds — nearly three minutes — for a better reward rather than take a worse one immediately. Very few animals hold out that long.
On the ground a kea is drab olive-green and easy to miss against rock and scrub. Then it opens its wings and the undersides flash brilliant orange.

name: New Caledonian crow
blurb: A glossy black crow from one Pacific island. It makes hooked tools out of twigs. Very few animals besides people manufacture a hook.
size: About as long as your forearm — roughly 16 in (40 cm) beak to tail
wonder: A mind that can look at a plain forked twig and see a hook that isn't there yet.

facts.text: This crow snips a forked twig off a branch, strips the leaves, and carves the fork down into a neat little hook. Then it goes fishing with it.
facts.more: Making a hook is a serious business. It means the bird is not just picking up a handy stick — it is reshaping an object for a job it has not started yet. Outside of humans, almost nothing on Earth manufactures a hook.

facts.text: What it is fishing for is a fat beetle grub jammed deep inside rotting wood. The crow pokes the hook in, annoys the grub until it bites the stick, then pulls it out still holding on.
facts.more: The grub's own jaws do half the work. A crow will spend a long time on a single hole, jiggling, twisting, listening. One big grub is worth a great deal of energy, so the patience pays.

facts.text: The pandanus plant has tough, saw-edged leaves. From them a crow cuts long barbed strips. It cuts in steps, wide at the base and narrow at the tip, so the tool tapers.
facts.more: The strip is torn out so precisely that it leaves a matching hole behind in the leaf. Researchers can walk the forest reading those holes like signatures. They count how many tools were made and what shape each one was, without ever seeing a bird.

facts.text: Young crows are hopeless at first. They watch their parents, steal their parents' tools, and fumble with twigs for the better part of a year before they can make a good one.
facts.more: Even a young crow raised without ever seeing an adult will start poking sticks into holes. The urge comes built in. But skill takes practice, and tool designs differ across the island. Crows in one district cut one pattern and crows in another cut a different one. Each youngster grows up copying the local shape.

facts.text: Most birds have eyes on the sides of the head and a curved beak. This crow has an unusually straight bill and unusually forward-facing eyes. Nobody can ask it why; the shape is the argument, and it lines the tool tip up right where both eyes can watch it.
facts.more: Hold a pencil in your fist and look down at the point — you need both eyes to judge exactly where it is. The crow's straight bill lines the tool up along its line of sight, and its wide overlapping field of view lets it aim the tip into a hole.

facts.text: A crow that has made a good tool does not drop it. It tucks it under a foot or wedges it into a hole while it eats, then takes it to the next log.
facts.more: Good tools take real time to make, and one dropped from high in a tree is gone. Crows are noticeably more careful about stowing a tool when they are working up in the canopy than when they are down on the ground.

facts.text: A captive crow named Betty was given a straight piece of wire. Food sat in a bucket at the bottom of a tube. She bent the wire into a hook and lifted the bucket out.
facts.more: Wire is not something a crow meets in a forest. She jammed one end against something solid and pulled the other into shape. Researchers later found wild crows bending twigs into hooks too — so she was not inventing hooks from nothing, but she applied the idea to a brand-new material.

facts.text: Show one a tube of water with a floating treat out of reach, and a pile of stones. It drops stones in until the water carries the treat up to it.
facts.more: On this puzzle the crows scored about level with a five- to seven-year-old child. They also sorted which objects sink and which float, and preferred a narrow tube to a wide one because the water rises faster. Some versions still beat them — but the core idea is clearly there.

facts.text: Some puzzles need three moves in order: use a short stick to reach a longer stick, then use the long stick to reach the food. Crows have solved these on the first attempt.
facts.more: The first move earns no reward at all — only a better tool. To make it, the bird has to hold the whole sequence in mind before it starts. Six of seven birds in one test got it right the very first time, with nobody training them through the steps.

facts.text: In one experiment crows were given short hollow rods and thin sticks, none long enough alone. Several slotted the pieces together into a pole long enough to reach the food.
It is not a big bird — forearm-length, about 10 oz (300 g), lighter than a can of soup. Every tool it makes, it makes with a beak and two feet.
The whole species lives on New Caledonia, a group of islands in the South Pacific, mostly in old undisturbed forest. There is nowhere else on Earth to find one.

name: Sockeye salmon
blurb: A Pacific salmon that lives silver in the open sea. It comes home fire-red to the exact river it hatched in.
size: About 2.5 ft (76 cm) long and around 8 lb (3.6 kg)

facts.text: At sea a sockeye is plain silver-blue, about 2.5 ft (76 cm) long. Nothing about it hints at the color that is coming.
facts.more: Most weigh 5 to 15 lb (2.3 to 7 kg) (5 to 15 lb). They run from 24 to 33 in (60 to 84 cm) long. Youngsters spend a year or two in a lake. Then they spend two or three more out in the open Pacific, feeding and growing. After that the journey home begins.

facts.text: Then it changes. The body turns fire-engine red, the head turns bottle-green, and the male grows a humped back and a hooked jaw called a kype.
facts.more: The red comes from a pigment called astaxanthin, which the salmon collects by eating krill and other tiny shrimp-like animals at sea. Out there the pigment sits in the muscle, which is why salmon flesh is pink. For spawning, it moves into the skin.

facts.text: A sockeye finds the one stream it hatched in — after years in the open ocean, past hundreds of wrong turns — by smell.
facts.more: As a young fish it memorises the exact chemical scent of its home water. The returning adult follows that scent upriver to the same gravel bed. Fish that end up in the wrong stream are few enough that biologists can count them.

facts.text: Some sockeye swim over 870 miles (1,400 km) (900 mi) up the Columbia and Snake Rivers. They finish at Redfish Lake in Idaho. They climb 6,500 ft (2,000 m) uphill doing it.
The moment it enters fresh water to spawn, a sockeye stops eating. Everything after that — the swimming, the climbing, the fighting — runs on its own body.
facts.more: Its digestive system shuts down and its stomach shrinks. The whole journey is powered by fat and muscle stored at sea. By the time it reaches the spawning gravel, a sockeye has burned through most of itself.

facts.text: Rapids and small falls do not stop them. A salmon uses the churn at the bottom of a drop to launch itself and leaps clear of the water.
facts.more: Bears know exactly where those spots are and stand in them, waiting. The fish that gets past the bear still has the current to fight, and it is doing it on an empty stomach.

facts.text: The female digs the nest herself, turning on her side and beating her tail against the riverbed until a pit opens in the gravel. It is called a redd.
facts.more: She lays her eggs in the pit and covers them with stones. Eggs hatch in six to nine weeks, and the hatchling still has its yolk attached in a sac under its belly. It hides down in the gravel and lives off it.

facts.text: Before a young salmon can leave for the sea, it rebuilds its own body chemistry. The change is called smoltification.
facts.more: Fresh water and salt water are opposite problems: one floods a fish with water, the other drains it. Special cells in the gills switch modes, the fish turns silvery, and it stops holding against the current and starts riding it downstream.

facts.text: Sockeye spawn once and then die. Every adult in that river is on a one-way trip.
facts.more: The bodies do not go to waste. Bears, eagles, gulls and beetles feed on them, and the rest rots into the streambed. Scientists can measure sea-borne nutrients from those salmon inside the trees growing along the bank — the ocean, feeding a forest.

facts.text: Some sockeye never see the sea at all. Landlocked in lakes, they live their whole lives in fresh water and stay small, rarely over 14 in (35 cm). They are called kokanee.

wonder: It leaves as a fingerling and comes back years later to the same handful of gravel, carrying a map it was given rather than taught.

name: Red-bellied piranha
blurb: A flat, deep-bodied South American river fish with a red belly. Its teeth are a single row of interlocking triangles.
size: About 10.8 in (27 cm) long, with a deep body flattened from side to side

facts.text: Usually 7.9 to 11.8 in (20 to 30 cm) (8 to 12 in) long, and deep from back to belly, so it looks like a plate swimming edge-on. Big ones reach 14 in (35 cm).
One row of teeth top and bottom, each a flat triangle with a razor edge, meeting like the blades of a pair of scissors.
facts.more: The upper and lower teeth mesh into each other instead of overlapping. So a piranha bite shears rather than grips. It takes a clean disc out of whatever it lands on, then lets go. That is why a bitten fish usually swims away.

facts.text: A piranha does not lose teeth one at a time. It sheds a whole half-jaw of them at once and replaces the lot in one go.
facts.more: That is why a wild piranha's mouth is never gappy. One side is always fully armed while the other side regrows. Researchers found this by scanning the jaws. A complete spare set was already waiting in the bone underneath.

facts.text: Mostly it eats insects, worms, snails, small fish, and fruit and seeds that drop into the river. A great deal of its food is already dead when it finds it.
Piranhas shoal, and the reason worked out from the experiments is fear, not hunting. Watch a shoal and you are watching frightened fish, not a pack.
facts.more: In experiments, piranhas kept in bigger shoals calmed down faster than those kept in pairs — their gill-beat rate, which rises with stress, dropped sooner. No study has ever shown piranhas hunting cooperatively. They are prey too: caimans, river dolphins and big birds all eat them.

facts.text: Piranhas bark. They make three different sounds, and you can hear them clearly when one is lifted out of the water.
facts.more: A low harmonic bark goes with a face-to-face stare-down. A shorter, deeper thud goes with squabbling over food. A sharp single pulse goes with chasing and biting. The barks come from muscles drumming against the swim bladder, which amplifies them the way a guitar body does.

facts.text: Both parents build a nest in flooded plants and both guard the eggs. A piranha on nest duty will charge things many times its own size.
Young red-bellies eat the fins of other fish — a quick bite, then away. The victim usually survives and grows the fin back.
In the dry season the rivers shrink into pools. Hundreds of piranhas end up trapped together with nothing to eat. That is the situation behind almost every dramatic story.
facts.more: In the wet season the Amazon spreads out into flooded forest. Food is everywhere, so piranhas scatter and ignore anything large. People swim, wash and fish in piranha rivers every day. Injuries do happen. They are almost always a single nip on a toe or a finger, in shallow, shrinking water.

facts.text: Its bigger cousin, the black piranha, has been measured biting at about 320 newtons. Picture a 70 lb (32 kg) weight pressing down through those teeth.
facts.more: Researchers caught wild black piranhas in the Amazon and let them bite a padded force meter. For its body size, that is one of the hardest bites ever measured in a fish. You would never guess it from looking.

wonder: Those blades are a river-cleaner's tools, not a monster's — exactly the equipment its actual job requires.

name: Lungfish
blurb: A freshwater fish that breathes air with real lungs and can survive months sealed inside a cocoon of dried mud.
size: Around a meter — an arm-span — and the largest African kind is longer than a bed

facts.text: A lungfish has lungs. Real ones, joined to the throat, and it swims to the surface and gulps air with them, the same way you breathe.
facts.more: Most lungfish have a pair of lungs; the Australian lungfish has just one. Roughly nine-tenths of an African lungfish's oxygen comes from the air it swallows, and only a tenth from its gills and skin.

facts.text: Hold an adult African lungfish underwater and it will drown. Its gills have shrunk so far that they can no longer keep it alive on their own.
When the river dries up, it burrows into the mud, wraps itself in a cocoon of its own hardened slime, and waits. Months later, rain wakes it.
facts.more: The cocoon leaves one narrow tube open to the air at the mouth. Inside, the fish's whole body slows to about one-sixtieth of its normal rate — a heartbeat you would have to be patient to count. The waiting is called aestivation.

facts.text: Sealed in mud, it cannot flush anything out. So it converts its own waste into urea and stores the lot inside its body until the water comes back.
It walks. Its fins are thin threads rather than paddles, and it pushes off the bottom with them and steps along the mud instead of swimming.
A lungfish packs more DNA into one cell than any other animal with a backbone. The marbled lungfish carries roughly 130 billion letters of code. You carry about 3 billion.
facts.more: That is more than forty times the amount inside one of your cells, in a fish. Extra length does not mean extra instructions, though — huge stretches of it are the same short sequences repeated over and over. A much bigger book telling a story of ordinary size.

facts.text: Instead of rows of small teeth it has two hard fan-shaped plates in its mouth, and it crushes snails, crayfish and clams between them.
The male digs the nest burrow, then stays with it. He guards the eggs and the hatchlings and beats his tail to fan fresh water over them.
facts.more: Newly hatched lungfish look startlingly like tadpoles. They even have feathery external gills sticking out behind the head. Those shrink away as the lungs take over. The young fish starts coming up for air like its father.

facts.text: The largest African lungfish reach about 6.6 ft (2 m) (6 ft 6 in) — longer than most beds — and look more like a thick eel than a fish.
It lives in swamps and floodplains that disappear every dry season. Water that vanishes is not a disaster for a lungfish; it is simply the schedule it lives by.
facts.more: People have cut a hardened block of mud out of a dried-up riverbed and carried it a long way. Then they put it in water and watched a live fish work its way out. The fish had been in there the whole trip, sealed and waiting.

wonder: Lungs and a mud cocoon: everything a fish needs to outlast a river that comes and goes.

name: Honeybee
blurb: A small furry insect that lives in a colony of tens of thousands. It turns flower nectar into honey.
size: Small enough to crawl inside a flower

facts.text: A bee that finds flowers comes home and dances. The angle of her waggle tells the others which way to fly. The length of it tells them how far.
facts.more: She runs a figure of eight on the vertical comb, shaking her body through the straight middle part. Straight up means fly toward the sun. Forty degrees left of straight up means forty degrees left of the sun. Other bees follow her, then leave and find the flowers.

facts.text: Bees cannot see red — it looks like black to them. But they can see ultraviolet, and plenty of flowers wear ultraviolet stripes and bullseyes pointing straight at the nectar.
facts.more: To a bee, a plain yellow flower can carry a dark landing target. Your own eyes will never see it. Photographers can capture it with ultraviolet filters. The flower suddenly has a runway painted down the middle of it.

facts.text: On a cloudy day she can still find the sun. A bee's eyes read the pattern of polarised light across the sky and work out where the sun must be behind the cloud.
The comb is made of wax the bees produce in their own bodies. Glands on the underside of the abdomen squeeze out flakes. The bees chew those soft and press them into shape.
facts.more: The hexagons are not decoration. Of all the shapes that tile a surface with no gaps, the hexagon holds the most space for the least wall — the most honey for the least wax. Mathematicians puzzled over that for a very long time before one of them finally proved it.

facts.text: The hive is heated. Bees hold the nursery at about 35°C (95°F) all year, close to your own body temperature. They shiver their flight muscles to warm it. They fan their wings to cool it.
One worker makes about a twelfth of a teaspoon of honey in her whole life. The jar in your cupboard is the finished work of thousands of lives.
facts.more: To fill a 1 lb (450 g) jar, the colony's foragers visit roughly two million flowers. Nectar arrives thin and watery. The bees fan it inside the comb until enough water has gone. Then it will keep without spoiling.

facts.text: A worker's sting is barbed like a fish hook. In skin it holds fast, and pulling away tears it out of her. She can only ever use it once.
facts.more: The queen's sting is smooth and she can use hers again and again. Worker stings work fine against other insects — the barbs only catch in the stretchy skin of animals like us. A sting left behind keeps pumping for about a minute, so flick it out fast.

facts.text: Japanese honeybees kill giant hornets by piling onto one and shivering. The ball of bees hits about 46°C (115°F) — hot enough to kill the hornet, just survivable for the bees.
facts.more: A hornet can bite a bee in half, so fighting it head-on fails. Instead several hundred workers smother it and vibrate. The heat and the carbon dioxide they pump out work together: the bees can take about 50°C, and the hornet cannot. The whole trick lives inside that narrow gap.

facts.text: At the height of summer a queen lays over 2,000 eggs a day. That is more than her own body weight in eggs, every day. Each one goes into a cleaned cell, one at a time.
Male bees, called drones, have no sting and do no work at all. They exist to mate — and a drone that succeeds dies in the act.
Some workers are undertakers. They find dead bees inside the hive, pick the bodies up, and fly them well clear of the entrance before letting go.
facts.more: A hive is warm, damp and crowded. That is exactly the sort of place disease loves. Removing the dead is one of several cleaning jobs. Beekeepers actively breed for colonies that are good at it, because those colonies stay healthier.

facts.text: Honey does not go moldy. Fanned down until it is thick and slightly acidic, it is a place where almost nothing can grow — nectar, preserved by wings.

wonder: Tens of thousands of bees, not one of them in charge, and what comes out of it is a warm, ordered, hexagon-perfect city.

name: Leafcutter ant
blurb: A tropical American ant that cuts leaves and carries them underground. It does not eat them. It feeds them to a fungus it farms.
size: From smaller than a grain of rice to about the width of your fingernail

facts.text: Leafcutter ants cut leaves they do not eat. The leaves go underground to feed a fungus, and it is the fungus the ants live on.
facts.more: Down in the nest the leaves are chewed into mash and planted with the fungus, which grows through it in spongy gray gardens. The fungus grows swollen, food-packed tips, and the ants harvest those and feed them to the young. Adults also drink sap from the leaves they cut.

facts.text: Workers come in sizes for different jobs. Tiny ones tend the young. Medium ones cut and carry. The largest soldiers have jaws that will cut through leather.
A carrier cuts a piece of leaf several times heavier than she is. She hoists it over her head like a green sail. Then she jogs home holding it up the whole way.

Look closely at a carried leaf and there is often a much smaller ant riding on it. Nobody has asked her what she is doing up there, but she snaps at the flies that come near — a bodyguard, watching the sky.
facts.more: Phorid flies hover above the trails and try to lay an egg on a carrier's head while her jaws are full and she cannot fight back. The rider snaps at them. The colony has essentially put a gunner on every truck.

facts.text: The ants grow bacteria on their own bodies. Those bacteria produce antibiotics. The ants use them to keep a weed-mold out of the fungus gardens.
facts.more: The mold is called Escovopsis, and it attacks nothing in the world except the fungus gardens of farming ants. The helper bacteria grow in whitish patches on the ants' outer shell, fed by the ants' own glands. They are farmers carrying their own pesticide.

facts.text: When a young queen flies off to start a colony, she carries a pellet of the old fungus garden in a pocket inside her mouth. The entire farm travels in her cheek.
One excavated nest ran deeper than a house is tall. It held more than a thousand chambers. Digging it had taken tonnes of soil out of the ground.
facts.more: Every grain of that soil came up in an ant's jaws. Big colonies hold millions of ants, with separate chambers for fungus gardens, for young, and for trash, all connected by tunnels wide enough for two-way traffic.

facts.text: The nest breathes. Warm stale air drifts up and out of the central turrets while fresh air is drawn down the outer tunnels, so the gardens far below never suffocate.
The colony has a trash dump and a crew that works it. Those ants do not go back into the main nest, and the other ants will not let them.
facts.more: Waste from the fungus gardens is dumped in its own chamber, where it rots and grows mold. The ants handling it are the oldest workers, given the most dangerous job last. It keeps the rot away from the gardens and the young.

facts.text: While she cuts, a worker vibrates her jaws about a thousand times a second. The buzz passes into the leaf and helps the blade slice cleanly.
facts.more: You can feel a version of it in a kitchen: a floppy sheet is hard to cut, a taut one is easy. The vibration also travels through the leaf and into the ground, so nearby ants know that cutting is happening here.

facts.text: Their trails are real roads, swept clear of pebbles and litter, running tens of meters from the nest and busy in both directions.
facts.more: A large colony can strip a small tree bare in a single night. The column heads out empty and comes back green, hour after hour, and the same road gets used again the following night.

facts.text: If something digs into the nest, the big soldiers come up out of the ground. They clamp down with those leather-cutting jaws. Then they simply do not let go.

wonder: An insect that plants, weeds, fertilises and composts — farming perfectly well without ever having been taught how.

name: Bombardier beetle
blurb: A small ground beetle that defends itself by firing a boiling-hot chemical spray out of its back end.
size: Small enough to balance on your thumbnail.

facts.text: Poke a bombardier beetle and it fires back. The spray leaves its body at about 100°C (212°F) — the temperature of boiling water.
