facts.more: Two liquids, hydrogen peroxide and hydroquinones, sit quietly in a storage sac. When the beetle is threatened it squeezes them into a tiny reaction chamber lined with enzymes. The reaction is instant and violent, and the boiling liquid blasts out of a nozzle at the tail.

facts.text: The spray does not come out in one smooth squirt. It fires in pulses — around 500 every second — which is why you hear a sharp pop.
facts.more: A single blast runs to about 70 pulses and is over in a fraction of a second. High-speed X-ray films show the chamber filling, firing and refilling faster than an eye can follow. The pulsing is what keeps the beetle from cooking itself: cool liquid refills the chamber between shots.

facts.text: The tip of its abdomen swivels. The beetle can aim over its own back, out to either side, and even forward past its own head.
facts.more: Some species skip aiming altogether. They fire against a small shield-shaped plate near the leg. That splashes the spray sideways, in whatever direction the attack came from. Between swiveling and deflecting, there is almost no angle from which you could safely grab one.

facts.text: Toads that swallow a bombardier beetle sometimes vomit it back up — alive, walking, unbothered. In one case the beetle came back out more than an hour later.
facts.more: In experiments, swallowed beetles fired their spray inside the toad's stomach. A good number of toads gave up and spat them out. Some beetles had been made to empty their spray beforehand. Those were far less likely to come back out at all.

facts.text: Adults are night hunters. They run down caterpillars, maggots and other soft-bodied insects on the ground — a bombardier beetle is a sprinter, not a stalker.
In many bombardier beetles the larva is not a hunter at all. A newly hatched grub goes looking for the buried pupa of a water beetle, latches on, and eats it slowly.
facts.more: It only ever needs that one meal. Once settled, the larva changes into a fat, legless grub that never leaves the spot. Different bombardier species specialize in different victims. Some take whirligig beetle pupae, others take water scavenger beetles.

facts.text: About a centimeter of beetle — less than half an inch. The reservoir, the mixing chamber, the valve and the swivelling nozzle are all packed into the back end of that.
No other animal is known to fire boiling liquid at an attacker. More than 500 bombardier beetle species do it. They live on every continent except Antarctica.
Engineers have studied that pulsing blast while designing fuel injectors and fire extinguishers. A nozzle that fires in bursts throws liquid further than one that simply streams.
facts.more: The beetle solves a problem engineers care about. It pushes a fine spray a long way out of a very small opening, without a pump. Working prototypes based on the beetle's fill-fire-refill cycle have been built and tested.

facts.text: Look under stones, logs and damp leaf litter, often close to water. Turn a rock over gently — most bombardier beetles would far rather run than fire.
The spray is not just hot. It carries benzoquinones, chemicals that stain skin brown and burn the eyes and mouth of anything trying to eat the beetle.

wonder: God fitted a mixing chamber, a valve and a swiveling nozzle inside a tiny beetle.

name: Hercules beetle
blurb: The longest beetle in the world — a rainforest giant whose males carry a horn longer than the rest of their body.
size: As long as your whole hand, wrist to fingertip — up to about 6.7 in (17 cm), horn included.

facts.text: A big male stretches about 6.7 in (17 cm) — long enough to hang over both edges of your palm. More than half of that length is horn.
facts.more: The horn is really two pieces: a long one curving down from the thorax and a shorter one curving up from the head. Together they work like a pair of pincers. Females have no horn at all and are noticeably shorter.

facts.text: The two horns close like a nutcracker. A male grips a rival between them, prises him off the branch, lifts him into the air, and drops him.
facts.more: Fights break out over sap runs on tree trunks and the females feeding there. The beetles rarely injure each other — most contests end the moment the loser loses his grip. Falling out of a tree is no great problem when you are this armored.

facts.text: Its wing cases change color. In dry air they are olive-yellow. Let the air turn humid and they darken to black — then pale again as it dries out.
facts.more: The color is not pigment. The outer layer of the wing case is a sponge-like lattice of microscopic channels that scatters yellow light back at you. When moisture soaks in and fills those channels the scattering stops, and you see the dark layer underneath.

facts.text: The Hercules belongs to a group called the rhinoceros beetles. They were tested carrying loads in the lab. They walked around under thirty times their own body weight. They barely worked harder for it.
facts.more: You will often hear that these beetles lift 850 times their weight. That number gets repeated everywhere, but it does not come from a careful measurement. The thirty-times figure does. Researchers strapped weights to rhinoceros beetles and measured the oxygen they burned while walking.

facts.text: The grub is as long as your hand and as thick as your thumb. It can top 3.5 oz (100 g) (a quarter of a pound). That is heavier than the adult beetle it will become.
facts.more: Hercules grubs are white, C-shaped and enormous. They spend up to two years chewing through rotten logs on the forest floor, and everything they break down goes back into the soil. When the grub finally pupates, the whole horn is folded up inside the case, waiting.

facts.text: For all that armor, the adult is a fruit-eater. It drinks tree sap and mashes soft, rotting fruit. It has no interest whatsoever in biting you.
Pick one up and it hisses at you. The beetle rasps its abdomen against the underside of its wing cases to make the sound — a warning, not a voice.
It flies. A beetle this heavy gets airborne with a low droning buzz you can hear right across a forest clearing, horn and all.
Its antennae end in a stack of flat plates that open out like a tiny paper fan. That fan is its nose — it can smell fermenting fruit from a long way off.
facts.more: Spreading the plates apart hugely increases the surface carrying smell receptors. Then the beetle folds them shut again for protection. All scarab beetles share this design. It is one of the quickest ways to recognize the family.

facts.text: No sting, no venom, no bite worth worrying about. Nothing much eats one, and the best read is that it is simply too large, too hard and too awkward to swallow.
They live in the rainforests of Central and South America and the Caribbean islands. The range runs from southern Mexico down to Bolivia. They stay mostly high up in the trees.
Only well-fed males grow the giant horns. A grub that finds a rich, rotting log becomes a monster; a grub on poor wood becomes a small male with a stubby one.
facts.more: The horn is built during the pupal stage. It comes out of whatever the grub managed to store while eating. Two brothers from the same batch of eggs can end up looking like different animals entirely. The only difference is the logs they landed in.

wonder: Everything about it is oversized — and God still folded that whole horn away inside a grub in a rotten log.

name: Firefly
blurb: A beetle that makes its own light in its abdomen. It uses that light to talk, flashing a coded signal on summer nights.
size: Even the biggest fireflies are under an inch (25 mm) long. Most are smaller.

facts.text: A firefly is not a fly. It is a beetle, small enough to sit on your fingernail — watch one land and you will see the hard wing cases fold down over its back.
The lamp is on the underside of the last segments of its abdomen. A chemical called luciferin meets oxygen and an enzyme called luciferase. The reaction gives off light.
facts.more: This is bioluminescence — living light. The firefly controls the flash by controlling oxygen: it opens microscopic air tubes to let oxygen reach the reacting cells, then shuts them off to stop the glow. A gas called nitric oxide works the switch.

facts.text: It is cold light. A bulb turns most of its energy into heat, but a firefly's lamp gives off so little you cannot feel it at all through your closed hand.
Every species has its own flash pattern — a length, a rhythm, a number of pulses. A male signals as he flies; a female answers from the grass if he got the code right.
facts.more: Some males flash one long dash. Some draw a quick J-shaped swoop of light. Some fire a burst of five or six. She replies after a precise pause, measured in fractions of a second. Get the pause wrong and nobody answers.

facts.text: Firefly larvae are ferocious. They hunt snails and slugs in the leaf litter, inject them to turn their insides to soup, and drink the result.
facts.more: Most of a firefly's life is spent down there as a glowing larva, sometimes for a year or two. The adult flashing over your lawn in July may have only a few weeks left, and in some kinds the adult barely eats at all.

facts.text: Females of one group, the Photuris fireflies, copy the flash codes of other species. She answers a male who is not her own kind, he flies down to her, and she eats him.
facts.more: She is not only hungry. The males she eats carry bitter defensive chemicals called lucibufagins, which she cannot make herself. After the meal those chemicals are in her body and in her eggs — and a jumping spider that grabs her is likely to let her go again.

facts.text: Firefly blood tastes appalling. A bird that grabs one usually drops it fast, and fireflies are genuinely poisonous to some lizards, so never feed one to a pet.
In a few valleys of the Great Smoky Mountains, thousands of fireflies flash at the same instant. Dark, dark, dark — then the whole hillside lights up together.
facts.more: The synchronous firefly fires four to eight flashes in a row, then the entire group falls dark for eight to twelve seconds before the next wave rolls through. So many people want to sit in those woods and watch that the park hands out places by lottery.

facts.text: Firefly luciferase is used in laboratories all over the world. Swab a kitchen surface, add the chemical, and anything living on it glows. That is how food factories check a bench is truly clean.
facts.more: The reaction needs ATP, the fuel molecule every living cell runs on. No ATP, no glow. Researchers also put the firefly's gene into other cells to make them light up, so they can follow exactly where those cells travel inside a living body.

facts.text: Not every firefly flashes. Plenty of day-flying kinds have no working lamp at all as adults and find each other by smell instead.
A male firefly has far bigger eyes than the female. The best read is the job those eyes do: picking a half-second flash out of a dark field full of waving grass, with one chance at it.

wonder: God put a lantern in a beetle under an inch (25 mm) long — and then gave it a language to speak with it.

name: Dragonfly
blurb: A long-bodied hunting insect with four glassy wings. It can flap them one at a time. That makes it one of the finest fliers alive.
size: Body about as long as your finger; the biggest spread about 6 in (16 cm) of wing — wider than your hand.

facts.text: Four wings, four separate controls. A dragonfly can beat each wing on its own, which is how it hovers, flies backwards, and stops dead in mid-air.
facts.more: Most insects flap both wings on a side together. A dragonfly's muscles attach straight onto each wing, so it can twist one, hold another still, and pivot around a single point in the air. It can even fly upside down for short stretches.

facts.text: In laboratory tests, hunting dragonflies caught up to 95 out of every 100 flies they went after. No lion or shark comes anywhere near that strike rate.
facts.more: It does not chase. It calculates. The dragonfly reads its target's speed and direction and works out where that target is going to be. Then it flies to the empty patch of air to meet it. It arrives from below and behind, where a fly cannot see.

facts.text: Almost the whole head is eye. A big dragonfly's compound eyes hold more than 20,000 separate lenses and see nearly all the way around it at once.
facts.more: Each tiny lens, an ommatidium, sends back a single dot of the picture — one hawker was counted at 22,650 of them. The lenses pointing forwards and upwards are the largest and sharpest, because that is the patch of sky it hunts in. Dragonflies also see ultraviolet, which we cannot.

facts.text: A young dragonfly lives underwater — for months, sometimes for years — before it ever sees the sky. Then it climbs a reed stem, splits its skin, and walks out with wings.
facts.more: The nymph breathes through gills inside its rectum, at the far end of its body. Squeeze that chamber hard and water shoots out the back, so a nymph can jet forward like a tiny squid when it needs to move in a hurry.

facts.text: The nymph's lower lip is a folded harpoon. It shoots out from under the face, grabs a tadpole or a young fish, and folds back — faster than your eye can follow.
facts.more: Biologists call it the labial mask. At rest it covers the nymph's face like a visor. It fires on hydraulic pressure. The nymph squeezes its abdomen, and the fluid inside shoots the lip out. That is how something that small moves that fast from a standing start.

facts.text: Nobody has followed one the whole way. The best read is that the globe skimmer crosses open ocean between India and Africa. That is about 1,900 miles (3,000 km) of water in one flight, with nowhere to land.
facts.more: The full round trip runs to roughly 11,000 miles (18,000 km), and no single dragonfly completes it. A chain of generations does. Each one lays eggs in temporary pools that appear after a storm and dry up weeks later. Globe skimmers ride high winds. One was recorded at 20,000 ft (6,200 m) over the Himalayas.

facts.text: A big hawker dragonfly can hit 22 mph (36 km/h) in a burst — quick enough to run down almost anything else flying at that size.
Its legs are a basket, not a walking kit. A dragonfly can barely walk at all; it holds those spiny legs forward and scoops prey out of the air with them.
Look near the tip of each wing for a small dark rectangle. It is called a pterostigma, and it is a weight — it steadies the wing and stops it fluttering at speed.
facts.more: Take the weight away and the wing tip starts to shudder as the dragonfly speeds up. That wastes energy and can tear a wing. The pterostigma pushes the shuddering back to higher speeds. Measurements put the gain at 10 to 25 percent.

facts.text: Find them at ponds, slow rivers and marshes. A male will patrol one stretch of bank all day, flying the same beat over and over and chasing off every rival that enters it.
Engineers building tiny flying robots study dragonfly wings closely. Nothing people have made yet matches that mix of hover, speed and instant turning in something so light.
The biggest dragonflies spread about 6 in (16 cm) of wing — wider than your hand — on a body you could balance on one finger. Damselflies are the slim cousins.
facts.more: Most damselflies fold their wings up along the body when they land; a dragonfly holds its wings out flat, always. That is the quickest way to tell the two apart, and it works even on a species you have never seen before.

wonder: Four wings, twenty thousand lenses, and the sense to aim at where you will be — all in something light enough to land on a reed.

name: Praying mantis
blurb: A long-necked ambush hunter. It sits perfectly still with its spined front legs folded. Then it grabs whatever walks past.
size: Most are about as long as your finger; the biggest are longer than your whole hand — over 6 in (15 cm).

facts.text: The strike is over in less than a tenth of a second. You cannot blink that fast — and the mantis can still change its aim halfway through.
facts.more: It holds its forelegs folded and cocked like a spring. Biologists call them raptorial legs, the same word used for a hawk's talons. When a fly comes within reach they snap out and shut again with the prey pinned between two rows of spines.

facts.text: Scientists glued tiny 3-D glasses onto mantises and showed them films of bugs. The mantis struck at the spot where the two images overlapped — it really does judge depth with two eyes.
facts.more: It is the only insect known to have stereo vision, but it works nothing like ours. A mantis does not compare the two pictures for detail, only for movement. A perfectly still object stays invisible to its depth sense, which is exactly why it waits for you to twitch.

facts.text: A mantis hears with a single ear, sunk in a groove down the middle of its chest between the back legs. It is tuned to a sound you cannot hear: the hunting calls of bats.
facts.more: There is one narrow chamber with a hearing membrane on each wall, which is why it works as one ear rather than two. When a flying mantis picks up bat ultrasound, it stops flapping, folds up and spirals toward the ground. In field tests, mantises that dived were caught far less often.

facts.text: It can turn its head almost halfway round — close to 180 degrees — and look straight back over its own shoulder. Almost no other insect manages that; a mantis has a real neck.
A mantis eats whatever it can hold: crickets, moths, wasps, other mantises. Some of the large ones have been photographed catching hummingbirds at garden feeders.
facts.more: Researchers gathered records from a dozen countries of mantises taking small birds, nearly always hummingbirds caught while hovering. The mantis simply waits on the feeder itself. It is rare, but it is well documented, and it is why feeders should be checked.

facts.text: The orchid mantis looks like a flower — and not in order to hide. Bees fly straight to it. In tests it pulled in more insects than the real blossoms growing around it.
facts.more: Its legs are widened into pale pink petal shapes. Researchers set real flowers beside orchid mantises and counted the visitors, and the mantis won. That makes it a lure, not just a hiding place — it does not even need to be sitting on a plant for it to work.

facts.text: Other mantises copy dead leaves, green stems, bark and lichen. They do it so precisely that you can stare straight at one for a minute. You still see nothing but a twig.
The female whips up a froth with her own body and lays her eggs inside it. It sets into a tough tan case called an ootheca, and in spring the hatchlings squeeze out all at once.
facts.more: One case holds anywhere from ten to four hundred eggs, depending on the species. The foam sets about as hard as styrofoam and shrugs off rain and frost all winter. The hatchlings come out on fine threads within minutes of each other and scatter fast — because the first thing a young mantis will eat is another young mantis.

facts.text: Females do sometimes eat the male after mating. But not always, and not in every species. Plenty of males simply walk away afterwards.
facts.more: Careful field studies found cannibalism in roughly a quarter of the matings they watched. When it does happen, researchers have traced the male's body directly into the eggs. A female who has eaten one lays eggs that are better supplied.

facts.text: Cornered, a mantis rears up, throws its wings wide and shows patches of color it normally keeps hidden. It suddenly looks twice its real size, and the best read is a bluff — one that usually works.

A newly hatched mantis is tiny. A typical adult runs about 3.6 in (9 cm), and the biggest are longer than your whole hand. Hatchling and adult hunt exactly the same way — by standing still until something walks past.
Look on shrubs, long grass and flower heads through the warm months. A mantis hardly moves at all, and when it does walk it rocks back and forth, the way a leaf moves in a breeze.

wonder: God gave the mantis two eyes that judge distance, one ear that hears bats, and a neck to turn and watch you back.

name: Lion's mane jellyfish
blurb: The largest jellyfish in the ocean. Its bell can reach 6.6 ft (2 m) across. A shaggy curtain of stinging tentacles hangs beneath it. It drifts in cold water.
size: The biggest bells reach about 6.6 ft (2 m) across; most are far smaller.

facts.text: The biggest ones measured had a bell over 7 ft (2 m) across. That is wider than a door is tall. The tentacles trailed more than 100 ft (30 m) behind.
facts.more: Most lion's manes you would actually meet are far smaller: a bell about 20 in (50 cm) across, roughly a bicycle wheel. The giants grow in the coldest water. Even in the record-holders nearly all of that length is tentacle — the body itself is a shallow bowl, and everything else just trails.

facts.text: Try to count the tentacles and you will give up. Around 1,200 of them hang in eight thick bunches, like eight separate mops under one umbrella.
Every tentacle is loaded with stinging cells called nematocysts. Brush one and it fires a coiled, barbed thread into your skin before you can pull away.
facts.more: A nematocyst is a capsule holding a barbed thread coiled under enormous pressure. Touch the trigger and the thread turns inside out and shoots. It is one of the fastest movements known in any animal, and a single tentacle carries them in their thousands.

facts.text: A tentacle torn loose still stings. A scrap of one washed up in the sand can fire into your foot long after the jellyfish itself is gone.
facts.more: This is why beach warnings mention broken-up jellyfish, not just whole ones. The stinging cells work on contact, not on command — no brain is involved anywhere in the process. A stranded fragment is still fully loaded.

facts.text: No brain. No heart. No bones. No blood. A lion's mane is a nerve net, a stomach, and an enormous amount of seawater.
facts.more: About 95% of a jellyfish is water. That is why a stranded one shrinks to a thin film on the sand as it dries — there was never much else there. Between its two thin layers of skin sits a jelly called mesoglea, doing the job your bones do.

facts.text: This is a cold-water animal. The giants live in the Arctic and the chilly northern Atlantic and Pacific. Farther south, lion's manes stay small.

Look inside the tentacle curtain and you may find small fish living there. They keep to the gaps, and nothing that hunts them will follow them in — so the best read is that the sting is the reason they stay.
facts.more: Young whiting and other small fish shelter among lion's mane tentacles. They thread carefully between the stingers. Predators that would happily eat them will not follow them in. It is a dangerous address with an excellent security system.

facts.text: It fishes by drifting. Anything that blunders into the curtain — small fish, shrimp, even other jellyfish — is stung, hauled up and swallowed.
It has nothing like your eyes. Eight little sensory clubs sit spaced around the rim of the bell. Each one holds light detectors and a balance stone. They are called rhopalia.
facts.more: Inside each rhopalium a tiny grain rolls with gravity. It presses against hairs and tells the jellyfish which way is up. Eight of them sit evenly around the bell. The animal senses in every direction at once, with no head to point anywhere.

facts.text: It pulses its bell to swim, but mostly it goes where the water goes. A big lion's mane is less a swimmer than a drifting net.
Something does eat it. Leatherback turtles swallow jellyfish whole, stingers and all, while seabirds and ocean sunfish mostly pick off the smaller ones.
facts.more: A leatherback turtle's throat is lined with backward-pointing spines. Slippery, half-liquid prey can go one direction only. Down. Around eastern Canada in summer, leatherbacks eat lion's manes and almost nothing else.

facts.text: It does not start as a jellyfish. It starts as a tiny polyp stuck to the seafloor, which stacks up like a pile of saucers and flicks them off one at a time.
facts.more: The polyp divides crossways into a stack of discs. The top disc pulses free as a swimming baby jellyfish. The process is called strobilation. One anchored polyp releases many babies, one after another, from the same spot.

wonder: No brain to plan with, no bones to stand on — and the largest jellyfish in the ocean still finds everything it needs in the drift.

name: Immortal jellyfish
blurb: A jellyfish smaller than your fingernail. When it is injured or starving, it rewinds itself back into a baby. Then it starts its life over.
size: Small enough to lose on your fingertip.

facts.text: A full-grown adult is about 0.18 in (4.5 mm) across. That is smaller than the nail on your little finger. It is see-through enough that you would miss it in a glass of seawater.
It is one of the very few animals known to go all the way back. Injure it, starve it, or chill the water, and instead of dying it sinks and turns into its own young stage.
facts.more: A student collecting jellyfish off the Italian coast noticed it first. The specimens simply refused to die. Kept in a dish, they shrank instead. Plenty of animals regrow lost parts. Almost nothing else rewinds the whole body after already growing up.

facts.text: The trick has a name: transdifferentiation. Cells that had already committed to being one thing — muscle, say — switch jobs and become something else entirely.
facts.more: In almost every animal, a cell that has become muscle stays muscle for life. In this one, cells reassign themselves, and the body takes itself apart and reassembles as an earlier version. Nothing new is added — it is rebuilt entirely out of itself.

facts.text: The shrunken blob settles on the seafloor and grows into a polyp, a tiny stalk. That polyp then buds off brand-new jellyfish, identical to the one that started over.
facts.more: One medusa that resets can become a polyp colony. That colony can bud off many new medusae. All of them carry the same instructions as the original. A single starving jellyfish can end up as a crowd of copies.

facts.text: It is see-through except for one thing: a bright red stomach glowing in the middle of the bell like a warning light.
A newly released one carries eight tentacles, evenly spaced. A grown one can carry eighty or ninety, fringing the whole rim of the bell like eyelashes.
It eats plankton, fish eggs and tiny molluscs, and it chases none of it. The tentacles hang in the water and wait for food to arrive.
It was first described in the Mediterranean and now turns up in harbors around the world. Big ships carry seawater for balance, and tiny drifters ride along inside.
facts.more: Large ships take on seawater to keep steady and pump it out again at the next port. Whatever was floating in that water goes with it. Turritopsis has since been found on both sides of the Atlantic and in the Pacific, far from where it was first named.

facts.text: Immortal is a nickname, not a promise. Out in the sea these jellyfish are eaten and struck down by disease constantly. The rewind only helps if nothing eats you first.
facts.more: Being able to reset is not the same as being safe. The reset needs time — the animal has to sink, settle and shrink, which takes days. Most never get that chance. What can go on and on in a laboratory dish usually does not, out in the open water.

facts.text: It has no brain and no speed. It cannot outswim anything that wants it. Its entire answer to serious trouble is to start again.

wonder: The smallest animal in this whole section carries the largest surprise: a body that knows how to begin again.

name: Sea star
blurb: A five-armed animal that walks on hundreds of tiny water-powered feet. It eats by pushing its stomach out through its own mouth.
size: Most would cover your open hand; the biggest spreads wider than a bicycle wheel.

facts.text: It is not a fish. No fins, no scales, no backbone — no bones at all. Sea stars are echinoderms, a word that means 'spiny skin'.
Turn one over. Those hundreds of wriggling stalks are tube feet, and they run on plumbing — a water vascular system that pumps seawater right through the animal.
facts.more: Seawater enters through a small pale sieve on the top surface called the madreporite and runs down canals into every arm. Squeeze water one way and a tube foot stretches out; squeeze it back and the foot pulls. Hundreds working together haul the whole animal along.

facts.text: It eats by turning its stomach inside out. The stomach slides out of the mouth, wraps around the meal, digests it outside the body, then folds back in.
facts.more: The stomach is thin and stretchy and pushes out through the mouth on the underside. Digestive juices go to work right where the food is, and the softened meal is drawn back in. This is how a sea star eats things far bigger than its own mouth.

facts.text: To open a mussel it grips with several arms and pulls — steadily, for hours, longer than the mussel can hold. It does not need much of a gap.
facts.more: The shell only has to part by a fraction of a millimeter. A sea star can slide its stomach through a crack thinner than a sheet of paper. Once it is inside, the mussel's shell is a lunchbox instead of a fortress.

facts.text: There is an eye at the tip of every arm. Each one is a cluster of up to 200 tiny light detectors. They cannot read print. They can make out the dark shape of a reef and steer for it.
facts.more: Each eyespot sits right at the arm's end, tucked under the tube feet. It is a patch of 80 to 200 pigmented light-detecting units. The picture it gives is blurry and coarse. It tells dark reef from open water, which is exactly enough to crawl home.

facts.text: No head anywhere on it, and no brain. A ring of nerve around the mouth and a cord down each arm run the whole animal, and no one arm is in charge.
facts.more: It does have a small heart, beating around six times a minute. A fluid circulates too. There is nothing like the red pigment in your blood. Most of the pushing and hauling is done by plain seawater in the tube-foot plumbing.

facts.text: Lose an arm and it grows back. A few kinds do the reverse as well: one dropped arm, drifting alone, can slowly rebuild an entire sea star around itself.
facts.more: For most sea stars a piece of the central disc has to come along with the arm. Linckia manages from the arm alone. The lone limb crawls off and sprouts four small new arms. For a while it looks like a comet with a tail. Divers call these comet forms.

facts.text: The sunflower star is the giant of the group. It grows up to a meter (3 ft) across. It can have as many as 24 arms and about 15,000 tube feet underneath.
Sea stars are slow, but they are not still. The quickest, the sunflower star, covers about a meter (3 ft) of seafloor in a minute — plenty, when your food cannot run.
The crown-of-thorns sea star eats living coral. A single one can strip up to 6 square meters (65 sq ft) of reef in a year, and its spines are loaded with toxin.
facts.more: The spines do not inject anything. They are wrapped in tissue full of a bitter chemical called saponin, and when a spine punctures skin that tissue tears off inside the wound. It makes for a nasty, long-lasting sting for anyone who kneels on one.

facts.text: Flip one upside down and it does not panic. It reaches out with the tube feet on one arm, takes a grip, and slowly rolls itself back the right way up.
Baby sea stars look nothing like sea stars. They are transparent drifting specks with waving bands of hair, floating in the plankton until they settle.
facts.more: The larva feeds and drifts for weeks. It is bilateral, with a left and a right, like you. When it settles on the seafloor it reorganizes completely into the five-part body. The swimming shape is gone for good.

wonder: No brain anywhere in it — and yet fifteen thousand tiny feet all decide to pull the same way.

name: Sea urchin
blurb: A living pincushion that walks on sticky tube feet. Underneath is a five-toothed jaw that scrapes at solid rock.
size: Body about 3.6 in (9 cm) across, ringed with spines as long as your fingers.

facts.text: Turn one over and there is a mouth in the middle with five teeth meeting in a point. The whole jaw has a name of its own: Aristotle's lantern.
The teeth never go blunt. As the tip wears away it breaks off along a set line, leaving a fresh edge behind — so the jaw sharpens itself by being used.
facts.more: Each tooth is built from layers of calcite. They are arranged so worn material snaps away cleanly instead of rounding off. Materials scientists have studied that arrangement closely. They want blades and drill bits that stay sharp as they wear down.

facts.text: In some places urchins chew hollows into soft rock and sit down in them. They grip with their tube feet while the surf tries to tear them out.
facts.more: They grind at the rock with the same jaw they eat with, and the pit deepens until the animal is sunk into the shoreline. On some coasts the rock is pocked with thousands of these hollows, each one occupied.

facts.text: Every spine sits in a ball-and-socket joint and swivels. Touch one side of an urchin and the whole pincushion turns its points toward your finger.
Between the spines sit pedicellariae — tiny jaws on stalks that snap shut on anything landing on the urchin. In the flower urchin, they carry venom.
facts.more: A pedicellaria is a stalk topped with three jaws, and thousands are scattered among the spines. Most simply grip and pick off settling larvae and debris. The flower urchin's are venomous, which makes a pretty pastel animal one of the worst things on a reef to pick up.

facts.text: A sea urchin has no eyes anywhere, yet it reacts to a shadow passing over. Light-sensing cells are spread across its body, so the whole animal works something like one big eye.
facts.more: Light-sensitive proteins have been found in the tube feet and skin. The spines shade some of that skin and leave the rest bare. A passing shadow falls unevenly across the animal. The unevenness itself tells the urchin which direction the shadow came from.

facts.text: The spines are not the feet. Long, sticky tube feet stretch out past the spines, take hold of the rock, and haul the urchin slowly along.
Urchins graze kelp. Where sea otters hunt urchins, the kelp forest stands tall; where the otters are gone, the urchins mow it down to bare rock.
facts.more: Divers call the bare version an urchin barren, and it is a startling sight — pink rock and spines where a forest full of fish used to be. Sea otters crack urchins open and eat them, and their hunting is what keeps the kelp standing.

facts.text: Red sea urchins are among the longest-lived animals in the sea. Nobody has watched one for a century. Tagging and the chemical traces locked in the shell do that work instead. They put the oldest at well past a hundred, still grazing the same rock.
facts.more: Their ages came from tagging and re-measuring wild urchins. Chemical traces locked into the shells filled in the rest. The oldest were well past a century. They were still feeding, still growing, still breeding.

facts.text: Hand an urchin a scrap of seaweed or a bit of broken shell. It holds the scrap overhead with its tube feet. It wears the thing like a hat while it grazes.
facts.more: It is called covering behavior. Urchins in bright shallow water pile on far more cover than urchins in the shade. Some kinds drop the whole load at night. They pick it up again in the morning.

facts.text: Under the spines is a shell called a test: chalky plates locked together in a five-part pattern. Find an empty one on a beach and you can trace all five with a finger.
A baby urchin is a see-through speck with long glassy arms, drifting in the plankton. Nothing about it hints at a pincushion until it settles and rebuilds itself.

wonder: A mouth that never goes blunt, in an animal with no hands to sharpen it.

name: Sea cucumber
blurb: A soft, leathery animal shaped like a fat sausage. It vacuums the seafloor clean. It can fire its own insides at anything that bothers it.
size: Most are forearm-length; the longest stretches taller than a grown-up.

facts.text: It looks nothing like a sea star, but it is built to the same plan: five rows of tube feet running nose to tail. It is a five-armed animal, lying on its side.
Squeeze one hard and it may fire its own guts out through its back end. The attacker gets a mouthful of stomach; the sea cucumber crawls off and grows a new one.
facts.more: The process is called evisceration. Depending on the species the organs go out the front or the back, and the animal is left nearly hollow. Over the following weeks it regrows what it lost. It is an expensive trick — but cheaper than being eaten.

facts.text: It breathes through its bottom. Water is drawn in through the anus and into branching tubes inside the body called respiratory trees, which pull the oxygen out of it.
facts.more: The respiratory trees are two feathery tubes that branch just inside the anus. They fill much of the body cavity. Water is pumped in and oxygen crosses into the body fluid. Then the water is pushed back out. It happens over and over, through the same opening everything else leaves by.

facts.text: Some species shoot sticky white threads, called Cuvierian tubules, out of that same opening. The threads swell in seawater and glue a crab's legs shut.
facts.more: The tubules are branches off the base of the respiratory tree. They are fired out through the animal's back end. On the way they stretch to many times their resting length. Seawater turns them intensely sticky. A crab that blunders into the mess can end up wrapped and unable to walk.

facts.text: It can go from firm to nearly liquid on purpose. Its skin is mutable collagenous tissue, which it can loosen at will and pour through a crack you would swear was too small.
facts.more: Mutable collagenous tissue is skin that changes stiffness under nerve control. A sea cucumber can go rigid and wedge itself immovably into a crevice. It can also slacken until it flows like thick soup. Then it pours into a gap far narrower than its own body.

facts.text: Some sea cucumbers have a lodger. The pearlfish reverses in through the anus, tail-first, and lives inside the body cavity, coming out at night to feed.
facts.more: The pearlfish is long and thin and tracks its host down by smell before backing in. Inside, it is safe from nearly everything in the sea. Some kinds slip out to hunt and return by morning; some simply eat their host's insides while they are in there.

facts.text: It eats sand. Feeding tentacles sweep grains into the mouth, the animal digests the film of dead matter coating them, and clean sand comes out the other end.
facts.more: A sea cucumber cleans sand by eating it. What it leaves behind is grain stripped of the bacteria and dead scraps that covered it. On a reef, thousands of them turn the sediment over the way earthworms turn a garden bed.

facts.text: Go past 29,000 ft (8,900 m) down, deeper than Everest is tall. Sea cucumbers make up around 90% of the animal weight living on that mud.
Not all of them crawl. Enypniastes swims above the seafloor, flapping a skirt of skin, and it is bioluminescent — its body glows blue in water where nothing else does.
facts.more: It has been filmed swimming in the deep sea, lit up and rippling. Its glowing tissue can rub off onto whatever touches it. An attacker swims away marked and shining in the dark. That is an awkward place to be, when everything down there hunts by light.

facts.text: Most are the length of your forearm. Synapta maculata is the stretch: over 10 ft (3 m) long, but no thicker than a garden hose.
Around the mouth is a ring of tentacles, ten to thirty of them. They are modified tube feet. They mop food off the seafloor. Each one gets wiped clean in the mouth, one at a time.
There is no brain in there at all. A ring of nerve around the mouth, with five nerve cords running the length of the body, handles everything it does.

wonder: The animal that cleans the seafloor is the one nobody notices — and the sand it leaves behind is cleaner than the sand it ate.

name: Water strider
blurb: A long-legged insect that spends its whole life standing on top of the water without ever sinking.
size: A tiny body, with legs that spread far wider than the body itself.

facts.text: It is not swimming. It is standing on the skin of the water, held up by surface tension, the invisible stretch across the top of a pond that behaves like a trampoline.
facts.more: Water molecules cling to each other harder at the surface than anywhere else, and that pull makes a thin elastic film. A strider is light enough and spread wide enough that its feet dent the film without ever breaking through. Look closely at a sunny pond and you can see the dimples its feet press into the water.

facts.text: Its legs are furred with hydrofuge hairs. More than a thousand are crammed into a single millimeter. They trap a layer of air, so water never actually touches the leg.
facts.more: Hydrofuge means water-repelling. Each hair is grooved, and the grooves hold air the way a wool sweater holds warmth. That is why a strider stays bone dry in the middle of a rainstorm, and why a drop of water rolls off its leg instead of soaking in.

facts.text: The middle legs are the oars. It rows across the surface at around 1 meter per second (2 mph), which is about a hundred of its own body lengths every single second.
Its legs are ears. When a fly falls in and struggles, the ripples spread outward, reach those legs, and the strider reads direction and distance from the wave alone.
facts.more: It does not need to see the fly at all. The front legs are the shortest pair and carry small claws set back from the tip, so they can grip prey without ever piercing the water film. Sensor and hook in one limb.

facts.text: Water striders talk in waves. A male drums the surface about 3 beats a second to court a female, 10 beats to threaten a rival, and 25 beats to tell one to clear off.
facts.more: Researchers measured these frequencies by filming striders and recording the ripples they made. The pond is basically a shared telephone line. Every message a strider sends spreads out in rings. Every other strider within range feels it arrive through its legs.

facts.text: It cannot chew. A curved mouthpart called a proboscis punches into a drowning insect, pumps in enzymes that turn the insides to soup, and then drinks it back out.
One group of water striders, called Halobates, lives out on the open ocean far from any shore. They are the only insects on Earth known to do this.
facts.more: Insects are everywhere on land and in fresh water. The open sea is almost entirely closed to them. Halobates is the exception. Five of its species live their whole lives skating on the swells, hundreds of miles from the nearest coastline. They stay in the warm band of ocean roughly between 40 degrees north and 40 degrees south.

facts.text: Ocean striders have no land to lay eggs on, so they glue them to whatever floats: feathers, drifting seeds, cuttlebones, and now plastic trash. A single scrap can come up carpeted in eggs.
facts.more: Cuttlebones are the chalky internal shells of cuttlefish, and they wash about the open sea in great numbers. Anything solid and drifting will do. Scientists sampling ocean plastic keep hauling up pieces with the surface hidden under layers of strider eggs.

facts.text: Push one under and it pops straight back up. The air trapped in its leg hairs makes the whole insect buoyant, so the pond simply spits it out again.
In one pond you can find striders with full wings, stubby wings, and none at all. When the water starts drying up, the winged ones fly off to find somewhere new.
facts.more: Which forms turn up depends on the water. Ponds that hold steady all year are usually full of short-winged and wingless striders. Puddles and ditches that vanish every summer are dominated by the long-winged kind, which simply leave when the water goes.

facts.text: Engineers have built small robots that copy those legs and that rowing stroke. The robots skim across water without ever needing a hull or a float.
Most are grain-of-rice small. One species in Southeast Asia is not. Gigantometra gigas has a body as long as your thumb. Single legs run over 4 in (10 cm), spanning wider than your open palm.

wonder: Six hairy feet and a film of water, matched so exactly that the pond holds the strider up without ever letting it in.

name: Goliath birdeater
blurb: The heaviest spider on Earth. It is a rainforest tarantula big enough to cover a dinner plate.
size: Legs spread right across a dinner plate; the furry body alone is longer than your palm.

facts.text: Set one on a dinner plate and its feet hang over the rim. Leg span reaches 12 in (30 cm), and weight reaches 6 oz (175 g), about the same as a large apple.
facts.more: The giant huntsman spider has longer legs, but it is a spindly thing that weighs a fraction of this. By sheer mass, nothing beats a Goliath. Picking one up feels less like holding a spider and more like holding a hamster with too many legs.

facts.text: It hardly ever eats birds. The real menu is earthworms, beetles, frogs, toads, lizards, and now and then a small snake, all ambushed at night on the forest floor.
So why 'birdeater'? An old engraving from South America showed a tarantula eating a hummingbird. That picture traveled the world, the name stuck, and the spider has been misnamed ever since.
Corner one and it turns its back on you. The hind legs scrape the abdomen and fling up a cloud of urticating hairs, which are barbed, nearly invisible, and agony in the eyes and nose.
facts.more: Urticating means stinging or itching. Each hair carries backward-pointing barbs, so once it works into skin it will not slide out. Curious animals that stick a nose down the burrow get a faceful and learn fast. The spider grows a bald patch where it has thrown too many.

facts.text: It hisses at you. Rubbing the stiff bristles on its legs and pedipalps against each other makes a dry rasping sound, a trick called stridulation, and it means back away.
facts.more: Crickets stridulate too, and so do grasshoppers, but they rub wings or legs to call for mates. The Goliath uses it purely as a warning. The hiss usually comes first, the hair-flinging second, and the fangs only if you have ignored both.

facts.text: The fangs swing straight down like two pickaxes, 0.8 in (2 cm) or more of curved black chitin. The venom will not seriously hurt you; the bite is more like a very deep splinter.
facts.more: Tarantulas and their relatives strike downward. So they hunt from above, or from a burrow mouth with the prey pinned beneath them. Garden spiders are built the other way. Their fangs pinch together sideways, like a pair of tongs.

facts.text: Eight eyes, and it still barely sees. It hunts by touch, reading the leaf litter through fine hairs called trichobothria that pick up the faintest stir in the air or ground.
The female spins a thick silk sac and packs 100 to 200 eggs inside it. She guards it in her burrow, turning it over and over, and will not leave it until they hatch.
Lose a leg and it grows back. Every time the spider moults, climbing out of its old skin like a hand out of a glove, a missing leg returns a little bigger than before.
facts.more: Molting is the most dangerous thing a tarantula does. It flips onto its back and splits the old shell along the edge. Then it drags itself out, soft and pale. It cannot run or bite for days, until the new skin hardens.

facts.text: It builds no web to catch food. It digs a deep burrow in swampy rainforest ground, lines the walls with silk, and lays threads at the doorway that tremble when something walks past.
It cannot chew either. It crushes prey between its fangs and floods it with digestive juice. Then it drinks the liquid. A dry knot of skin and bone gets tipped out at the burrow door.
Turn one over and you would see four pale patches on its belly. Those are book lungs, stacks of paper-thin tissue like the pages of a book, with air moving between the pages.

wonder: It cannot see the forest floor, and it never once gets lost on it. The whole spider is built to read the dark by touch.

name: Jumping spider
blurb: A small, bright-eyed spider that stalks prey on foot and pounces on it, instead of sitting in a web and waiting.
size: Most are smaller than your little fingernail; the largest has a body about as long as your thumb.

facts.text: There are more kinds of jumping spider than any other spider on Earth. Roughly 7,000 species have been named, which is about one in every eight spiders alive.
Look at that face. Two huge headlight eyes at the front and six smaller ones ranged around the sides give it the sharpest eyesight of any animal anywhere near its size.
facts.more: The two big front eyes are long tubes, with a lens at one end and a retina at the other. They are more like a pair of telephoto cameras than eyes. The side eyes are almost useless for detail but brilliant at catching motion. Anything that moves nearby gets the spider's head swung round instantly.

facts.text: Those big front eyes cannot move. So the retinas inside them do. Watch closely and you can see the dark spot behind each lens swivel and sweep, scanning the world like a searchlight.
It judges distance in a way nothing else does. Each big eye stacks several retinas at different depths, and the spider compares the sharp image with the blurred one to measure range.
facts.more: You use two eyes and compare the slightly different pictures to judge depth. A jumping spider does it with one eye, using image defocus. Green light focuses perfectly on the deepest layer of the retina. On the layer in front it is fuzzy. How fuzzy tells the spider how far off a fly is.

facts.text: It has no muscle for straightening its legs. Spiders push two of their leg joints open hydraulically, forcing haemolymph, which is spider blood, into the limb until it snaps out like a ram.
facts.more: You straighten your arm by pulling on a muscle at the back of it. A spider has no equivalent at those joints and uses fluid pressure instead. It is also why a dead spider curls up: the pressure is gone, and nothing is left to push the legs straight again.

facts.text: Before every leap it glues a silk thread to the spot it is standing on. Miss the target and it swings on that line, then climbs calmly back up.
facts.more: The dragline is more than a safety rope. Filming shows the spider paying out or braking the silk in mid-air to keep itself level and to control where it lands. It is a rope, a rudder and a parachute at once, and the spider never forgets to clip in.

facts.text: Most can clear several times their own body length from a standing start, with no run-up. They aim the whole jump before taking it. Those front eyes range the target first.
Portia hunts other spiders. It will walk away from its prey and take a long detour up a completely different plant. Then it drops in from above. It follows a route it cannot see the end of.
facts.more: In lab tests, Portia was shown a target. The only path through meant moving away from the prey first and losing sight of it entirely. It still got there. So it worked out the whole route before setting off. It held that route in mind the whole way.

facts.text: Almost every spider on Earth eats meat. One jumping spider, Bagheera kiplingi, mostly eats plants. It lives off nubs called Beltian bodies, which are rich in protein and fat. They grow on the leaf tips of acacia trees.
One jumping spider feeds her young milk. A female Toxeus magnus makes a nutritious fluid in her body, and her spiderlings drink it for the first forty days of their lives.
facts.more: She drips it onto the nest floor at first, then the spiderlings climb on and feed straight from her underside. If she is removed, they stop growing and die. Nothing else in the spider world does anything quite like this.

facts.text: Male peacock spiders dance. He raises a fan of brilliantly colored skin over his back. He waves his legs in a set pattern. Then he drums the leaf so hard she feels the beat through her feet.
facts.more: Some jumping spiders also carry markings that only show under ultraviolet light, which their eyes pick up and ours cannot. So a male showing off to a female may be wearing patterns you would need a UV lamp to see at all.

facts.text: They run from specks to giants. The smallest have bodies about a millimeter long, the size of this period, and Hyllus giganteus is twenty-five times that, roughly as long as your thumb.

wonder: A brain smaller than a grain of rice, running eyes that measure, aim and pounce. Small was never the same thing as simple.

name: Trapdoor spider
blurb: A stout, burrowing spider that spends its whole life in a silk-lined tunnel. The tunnel sits behind a hinged door it built itself.
size: About 1.2 in (3 cm) long, with a thick, solid body.

facts.text: The door is the whole trick. Soil, plant fiber and silk are packed into a thick bevelled plug that fits the burrow mouth exactly and drops shut behind her without a sound.
facts.more: Beveled means cut at a slant. So the door wedges into the rim like a cork in a bottle, instead of resting on top of it. The hinge is pure silk, laid down in layer after layer along one edge. It folds and folds again without tearing. She widens it as she grows.

facts.text: Walk right over one and you would never know. She finishes the outside of the door with the same moss, grit and dead leaf as the ground around it, so the burrow vanishes into the floor.
Many species lay a fan of silk lines or carefully placed twigs radiating out from the door. A beetle steps on one, the line tugs, and she knows exactly which way to strike.
facts.more: It turns a doorstep into a tripwire alarm covering a whole circle of ground. She sits underneath with her legs against the lid. She can tell a leaf landing from an insect walking. She can tell roughly how big it is, before she has seen anything at all.

facts.text: She never chases anything. The door flicks open and legs and fangs shoot out. The prey is hauled underground and the lid drops shut. All of it is over in a fraction of a second.
Beetles, crickets, moths, ants, millipedes: whatever walks over the door goes down through it. Her fangs swing straight down like two pickaxes, so she always strikes upward from beneath.
facts.more: Spiders built this way are called mygalomorphs. Their fangs stab downward. A garden spider's fangs pinch together sideways instead. Stabbing downward is exactly right for an animal that attacks from below, out of a hole in the ground.

facts.text: She is about 1.2 in (3 cm) long: squat body, short thick legs, nothing at all spent on running. The tunnel below her can run deeper than your forearm is long.
Try to lift the door and it fights you. She hooks her fangs and claws into the underside, braces all her legs against the burrow wall, and pulls down astonishingly hard for her size.
The oldest spider ever recorded lived in a hole in Western Australia. Known only as Number 16, she was checked in her burrow year after year for over forty years, and reached the age of 43.
facts.more: Number 16 was simply the label on that burrow, at a reserve near Tammin. The arachnologist who began the study went back to it season after season, and an assistant took the work over at the end. Number 16 did not die of old age, either. A wasp got her.

facts.text: She hatches, she digs, and she stays. A female trapdoor spider may live her entire life inside a tunnel just a few steps from the burrow she was born in.
The males are the only ones who ever leave. After his final moult he abandons his burrow for good and walks the ground on damp nights, looking for a door to knock on.
facts.more: This is when people meet them, plodding across a patio after rain. He has no home to go back to and only a season or so to find a female. She may live another thirty years underground after he is gone.

facts.text: Her worst enemy walks on six legs. A spider wasp finds the burrow, chews through the silk plug, stings her into paralysis, and lays a single egg on her. The larva eats her alive.
facts.more: The venom does not kill, it only freezes. That keeps the spider fresh while the grub feeds, and the grub eats in an order that keeps her alive as long as possible. This is exactly how Number 16's forty-three years ended.

facts.text: The spiderlings stay inside their mother's burrow for months after hatching. Then one damp night they slip out and start digging doors of their own, sometimes only a hand's width away.

wonder: A door, a hinge, a fan of trip lines, and the patience to sit behind them for forty years.

name: Diving bell spider
blurb: The only spider in the world that lives its entire life underwater. It stays inside a bubble of air it builds for itself.
size: About as long as your thumbnail.

facts.text: It builds a house out of air. First it spins a silk dome between underwater plants, then it ferries bubbles down from the surface one at a time until the dome inflates.
facts.more: The result looks like a small silver balloon anchored in the weed. The spider sits inside it perfectly dry. Everything happens in there: resting, eating, molting, mating, laying eggs, and waiting out the winter.

facts.text: That bubble is not just stored air. It works as a physical gill. Oxygen seeps in from the pond water through the surface of the bubble, and waste carbon dioxide seeps out.
facts.more: The silk is waterproof but gas passes straight through it, so the bell is not a tank slowly running down. It keeps drawing fresh oxygen from the pond. Nitrogen leaks the other way, though, which is why the bell gradually shrinks and has to be topped up.

facts.text: To fetch fresh air it swims up and pushes the tip of its abdomen through the surface. A silver bubble catches in the hairs on its belly. Then it rows back down carrying it.
It never actually gets wet. Dense water-repelling hairs cover its abdomen and hold a permanent skin of air, so even outside the bell the spider is wrapped in its own bubble.
facts.more: That trapped film is where the name comes from. Its scientific name, Argyroneta, means something close to 'silver spinner'. Underwater the air layer catches the light. The whole spider gleams like a drop of mercury.

facts.text: It hunts by feel. Silk threads run out from the bell through the weed, and when something blunders into one the spider feels the tug and shoots out to grab it.
Dinner is whatever swims past: mosquito larvae, water fleas, small crustaceans. It seizes them, hauls them back inside the bell, and eats sitting in the dry.
facts.more: Water fleas are the little jerky specks you see hanging in pond water, properly called Daphnia. A spider that worked its way through a pond's mosquito larvae would be doing you a considerable favor.

facts.text: She lays her eggs in air, underwater. The top of the bell is walled off into a nursery, and the spiderlings hatch out into a dry room sitting at the bottom of a pond.
In nearly every spider on Earth the female is the larger one. Here it is flipped. Males reach about 0.59 in (15 mm) and females about 0.47 in (12 mm), so the male is close to a third bigger.
facts.more: Bigger usually means more eggs, which is why the female is normally the larger spider. Underwater the pattern runs the other way round. Males swim far more than females do, crossing open water to find them, while a female may stay close to her bell for days at a time.

facts.text: It spends the winter down there too. It builds a tougher, sealed bell, stocks it with air, and waits out the cold months below the ice.
More than 50,000 kinds of spider have been named. Exactly one of them spends nearly its whole life under water, and this is it.

wonder: A pond is no place for a lung. This one was given silk that holds a bubble and hair that will not wet, and made the water home anyway.

name: Bullet ant
blurb: A giant rainforest ant, up to 1.2 in (3 cm) long. It carries the most painful sting ever measured in an insect.
size: Workers run 0.71–1.18 in (18–30 mm) long — among the biggest ants alive.

facts.text: An entomologist named Justin Schmidt let insects sting him on purpose and ranked the pain from 1 to 4. The bullet ant broke his own scale: 4.0+.
facts.more: Schmidt described it as walking over flaming charcoal with a three-inch nail embedded in your heel. In parts of South America the ant is called the veinticuatro, the twenty-four. The burning can roll on in waves for a full day.

facts.text: The venom carries a molecule called poneratoxin. It jams the sodium gates your nerve cells use to fire, so the pain signal never switches itself off.
facts.more: Nerve cells fire by flicking open tiny channels that let sodium rush in, then snapping them shut. Poneratoxin stops the shutting, so the nerve fires over and over. Muscles near the sting can shake on their own, and the pain arrives in waves for up to a day.

facts.text: Disturb one and it squeaks at you. It scrapes a ridged file on its abdomen against a ridge on its waist, and lets off a sharp alarm scent at the same time.
facts.more: The squeaking is called stridulation — the same trick a cricket uses. Nestmates pick it up as a vibration through the nest wall. It is a warning first. The sting only comes if you keep going.

facts.text: A worker can reach 1.2 in (3 cm) — bigger than a honeybee. Set one beside an ant from your backyard and they barely look like the same kind of creature.
For all that weaponry, the commonest thing a bullet ant carries home is sugar. It gathers nectar high in the canopy. Small insects and spiders come home too.
facts.more: A worker drinks nectar until her abdomen is stretched tight and hauls it home inside her own body. The sting is mostly for defending the nest, not for hunting. Very little bothers a bullet ant nest twice.

facts.text: The nest is a burrow dug in at the foot of a rainforest tree. Workers climb the trunk to the canopy to forage, then walk the whole trunk back down.
Among the Sateré-Mawé people of Brazil, a boy proves he is ready to be a man. He wears woven gloves packed with bullet ants, stingers turned inward.
facts.more: Around eighty ants go into a pair of gloves. He keeps them on for five to ten minutes, and must complete the ordeal twenty times over months or years. Afterwards his arms shake and go numb. It is one of the toughest initiation rites anyone has recorded.

facts.text: A bullet ant colony is small as ant cities go — several hundred workers, not millions. The best read is that the sting does the job other ants need numbers for.
A forager who finds a good nectar tree walks home dragging the tip of her abdomen along the ground. That lays a scent trail. Her sisters follow it straight back to the tree.
Chemists are testing the sting's poison as a crop insecticide. It is the exact molecule that makes the sting unbearable, pointed at pests instead.
facts.more: In one experiment a virus was engineered to deliver poneratoxin to fall armyworm caterpillars. As little as 10 nanograms was enough to paralyze them. That is far less than a grain of salt weighs. Taking a weapon apart to see how it works is a large part of venom research.

wonder: God gave the fiercest sting in the forest a squeak and a smell to warn you first — a fair chance to back away.

name: Army ant
blurb: A wandering ant that builds no permanent nest. The whole colony marches and hunts as one enormous swarm. It makes its shelter out of its own bodies.
size: Workers run from 0.12 to 0.47 in (3 to 12 mm) (0.1–0.5 in) — the smallest like a comma on this page, the biggest about the length of your smallest fingernail.

facts.text: At the end of a day's march the colony builds its shelter out of itself. The ants link legs into a hanging ball, bigger than a basketball, with the queen sealed inside.
facts.more: It is called a bivouac. The oldest, toughest workers form the outer shell; the young ones and the growing brood stay in the warm middle. The living wall even holds the inside at a steadier temperature than the air outside.

facts.text: When a gap opens in the trail, ants throw themselves across it and lock together into a living bridge. The column runs over their backs. Then the bridge gets up and follows.
facts.more: Others do road repair. A worker whose body is the right size flattens herself into a pothole. The traffic then runs smooth over the top of her. Researchers measured the bridges too. The ants take one apart as soon as holding it costs more bodies than the shortcut saves.

facts.text: A single Eciton burchellii colony holds 100,000 to 600,000 ants. One raid can send up to 200,000 of them out of the bivouac at once.
facts.more: The workers come in a range of sizes, from 0.12 in (3 mm) minims up to 0.47 in (12 mm) submajors, and the biggest of all are the soldiers. Every one of them is a sister, and every one of them came from the same single queen.

facts.text: A raiding colony hauls home around 3,000 prey items an hour — and almost every one is an insect, a spider or a scorpion. Their favorite target is other ants' nests.
facts.more: They do not eat cattle, and they do not eat people. That is film-making. What a swarm really does is flush the forest floor: everything that can run, runs — which is exactly why other animals have learned to follow along behind.

facts.text: Most workers are effectively blind. Each eye is reduced to a single lens, enough to tell light from dark and nothing more. They read the whole world by smell and touch.
facts.more: The trail is a chemical line laid down by the ants in front. Antennae sweep it constantly, left and right, like a blind person's cane. Rub out a stretch of the scent and the column stalls and casts about until it finds the line again.

facts.text: The queen has no wings and an abdomen swollen like a broad bean. In one burst each cycle she lays tens of thousands of eggs, and they all hatch together.
facts.more: She never leaves the middle of the colony. When a colony grows too large it splits in two. The old queen takes one half and a daughter queen takes the other. The two armies march away from each other and never meet again.

facts.text: They live on a 35-day clock. For about 15 nights the colony marches to a brand-new bivouac every single night. Then for about 20 days it stops and stays put.
facts.more: The brood runs the schedule. While the larvae are growing they are ravenous, so the colony hunts hard and moves nightly. One move takes six to eight hours. The moment the larvae spin up into pupae and stop eating, the colony settles and the queen begins laying.

facts.text: Researchers have recorded 557 kinds of animal traveling with this one species of army ant. Twenty-one species of antbird check the bivouac each morning to see whether the ants are raiding.
facts.more: The antbirds do not eat the ants. They eat the insects the ants panic out of the leaf litter. And certain butterflies follow the antbirds to drink from their droppings. One column of ants carries a whole traveling neighbourhood along with it.

facts.text: A raid front can spread 66 ft (20 m) across. That is about five cars parked bumper to bumper. A column trails 650 ft (200 m) behind it, the length of two football fields.
Soldiers grow sickle-shaped jaws so long and so curved that they cannot feed themselves. Other workers feed them. Their whole job is to stand at the edge of the column facing outward.
They have no nest. No tunnels, no chambers, no address — an army ant colony is a city that never stands still for more than about three weeks at a stretch.
Above 43°C (109°F) the ants abandon the trail entirely. On a hot day one sunlit patch of bare ground can shut a raid down until the shade comes back.
facts.more: Ants caught out on ground that hot need upwards of half an hour in the shade before they can work again. To a column that reads the world by touch and smell at ground level, bare sunlit soil is a wall as real as a river.

wonder: Not one of them can see the gap, and not one of them is giving orders — yet the bridge appears exactly where a bridge is needed.

name: Monarch butterfly
blurb: An orange-and-black butterfly that eats poison as a caterpillar. One single generation then flies most of the way across a continent.
size: Wings spread 3.5–3.9 in (9–10 cm) — about as wide as a grown-up's open palm.

facts.text: Some monarchs fly from Canada to central Mexico — up to 2,800 miles (4,500 km). Not one of them has ever been there before, and no butterfly alive remembers the way.
facts.more: They gather on the same mountainsides, in the same groves of oyamel fir, generation after generation. The butterflies that arrive are the great-grandchildren of the ones that left Mexico. That was the previous spring. Whatever they navigate by, it is not memory.

facts.text: A monarch steers by the sun. But the sun slides across the sky all day, so it needs a clock to correct for that — and the clock sits in its antennae.
facts.more: Researchers painted monarch antennae with black enamel and the butterflies lost their heading; clear paint changed nothing. The antennae hold a working daily clock that tells the brain what time it is, so the brain knows where the sun ought to be.

facts.text: Summer monarchs live two to five weeks. The generation that hatches in late summer lives seven or eight months — it flies south, waits out the winter, and starts back north in spring.
facts.more: Its body simply postpones growing up: no eggs, no mating, all fall. It coasts through the cold on a Mexican mountainside, and only the lengthening days of spring switch its reproduction back on.

facts.text: Monarch caterpillars eat milkweed and nothing else. Milkweed is loaded with cardenolides, which are heart poisons. The caterpillar stores them in its own body instead of breaking them down.
facts.more: A bird that eats a monarch usually throws up. Then it learns the orange-and-black pattern and leaves the next one alone. The wings carry roughly three times the dose the rest of the body does. So a bird that grabs a wingtip gets the warning and lets go.

facts.text: Milkweed fights back. Cut a leaf and it bleeds sticky latex that can glue a caterpillar's mouth shut. So the caterpillar bites a trench across the leaf first, drains the pressure, then eats past it.
facts.more: Look at a monarch caterpillar on a big leaf and you can usually spot the notch it cut. The latex pours out of the trench instead of into its jaws. It is a caterpillar solving a plumbing problem with its mouth.

facts.text: A monarch egg is barely bigger than a pinhead, about 0.05 in (1.2 mm) tall. In roughly two weeks the caterpillar that hatches out of it grows around two thousand times heavier.
facts.more: It eats almost without stopping and moults five times, shedding a skin it has already outgrown at every stage. The last skin it wriggles out of reveals the chrysalis waiting underneath.

facts.text: The chrysalis is jade green with a rim of gold dots, like something out of a jeweler's case. Inside it the caterpillar rebuilds itself completely. That takes about eleven or twelve days.
facts.more: Near the end the green wall turns clear, and you can see the folded orange and black wings pressed against the inside, finished and waiting. Warm weather speeds it up; cool weather can stretch it to a fortnight.

facts.text: A female monarch tastes with her feet. She drums her front legs on a leaf, and chemical sensors in her tarsi tell her whether it is milkweed before she will lay an egg.
They winter in a handful of mountain fir forests in Michoacán, Mexico. They pack onto the branches so thickly that the trees look wrong. It is bark made of butterflies.
facts.more: They need it cold but not freezing, and the fir canopy works as blanket and umbrella at once. When midday sun reaches the clusters, whole sections of the forest lift into the air together.

facts.text: The viceroy butterfly looks almost exactly like a monarch. People long assumed it was a harmless copycat. Then taste tests showed viceroys are foul too — both of them are telling the truth.
facts.more: When two nasty-tasting species share one warning pattern, it is called Müllerian mimicry. A bird that learns the lesson from either one then leaves both alone. The two species share the work of teaching the birds.

facts.text: A monarch cruises at about 6 mph (9 km/h) — slower than you can run. It crosses a continent by finding rising columns of warm air and gliding, saving its wingbeats.
facts.more: Glider pilots have spotted monarchs hundreds of meters up, riding thermals the way a hawk does. Flapping the whole way south would burn more fuel than a butterfly that light could possibly carry.

facts.text: Nobody knew where they went. Volunteers stuck numbered tags on butterfly wings and mailed in sightings. It took decades of that before the Mexican wintering forests were finally tracked down.

wonder: Half a gram of butterfly crossing a continent to a forest it has never seen — and arriving. Nobody taught it the way. It was given the map.

name: Atlas moth
blurb: One of the largest moths on earth. This hand-sized insect has snake heads drawn on its wingtips. As an adult it never eats a single meal.
size: Wings spread about 10 in (25 cm) — wider than a sheet of paper — and the largest females reach 12 in (30 cm).

facts.text: Hold your hand out flat and spread your fingers as wide as they go. An atlas moth's wings can be wider than that, tip to tip.
facts.more: Very few insects carry that much wing. Females are the big ones — noticeably larger and heavier than males — while the males have far broader, feathery antennae. The wings are huge in area as well as span, which is what makes one so startling up close.

facts.text: An adult atlas moth has no working mouth. It cannot eat or drink, not once, not ever. Everything it will spend was eaten by the caterpillar it used to be.
facts.more: The adult lives about a week or two on fat stored by the larva, and every hour of that goes to one job: finding a mate. It is essentially a flying reproductive stage with a fuel tank that never refills.

facts.text: Look at the tip of each forewing. There is a snake's head drawn there — dark eye, curved snout, mouth line — one on the left and one on the right.
facts.more: In Hong Kong it is called the snake's head moth. Markings that startle a predator rather than hide from it are called deimatic — a bluff rather than camouflage. Whether birds truly see a snake here is not settled, but the resemblance is hard to miss.

facts.text: The male's antennae are wide feathery combs. They pick up a female's scent from kilometers downwind — a few molecules of pheromone drifting in a whole night's worth of air.
facts.more: Each branch of the comb is furred with receptor hairs tuned to that one chemical and nothing else. He flies zig-zags across the wind, turns back whenever the scent drops out, and rides that invisible thread all the way in.

facts.text: The caterpillar reaches 4.5 in (11.5 cm) long and 1 in (2.5 cm) thick. That is longer than your hand is wide and thicker than your thumb. It is pale green under a dusting of white wax.
It spins a papery brown cocoon 2.8–3.1 in (7–8 cm) long. The cocoon is slung inside a dead leaf. The whole thing hangs off a twig looking like ordinary forest litter.
facts.more: The silk is called fagara. It is coarser, browner and tougher than the smooth white silk of the domestic silkworm. In parts of India people gather the cocoons and weave with it. Often they collect them after the moth has already flown.

facts.text: Each wing carries a triangular window with no scales on it at all, clear as cellophane. Hold a spread atlas moth up to the light and you can see straight through in four places.
It belongs to the warm forests of South, East and Southeast Asia, from India across to Borneo, and it flies at night.
Which moth is 'biggest' depends entirely on how you measure. The atlas moth is near the top for wing area and near the top for wingspan — but it is not top of either.
facts.more: The white witch of Central and South America stretches further from wingtip to wingtip. The Hercules moth of Australia and New Guinea carries more wing area. All three are enormous in a way that photographs never quite convey.

facts.text: For all that wing, it flies slowly and heavily. Most of the day it simply rests with its wings held flat and open, and the best read is that the pattern does the work of a bodyguard.
The female barely travels at all. She waits near the cocoon she came out of, releases her scent into the dark, and lets the males do the flying.

wonder: A creature that will never once eat, given a week to live and wings worth stopping everything to look at.

name: Dung beetle
blurb: A beetle that finds fresh animal droppings and carves out a piece. It shapes the piece into a ball and rolls it away. Then it raises its family inside it.
size: Most are between a grain of rice and your thumb in length — 0.2 in (5 mm) to 1.2 in (3 cm) (0.2–1.2 in) — though a few tropical giants get much bigger.

facts.text: A male Onthophagus taurus was measured pulling 1,141 times its own body weight. Scaled up to you, that is like towing 1,141 kids your size at once.
facts.more: The pull happens underground. Two males meet head to head in a narrow tunnel and shove, horns locked, until one of them gives up and backs out. Almost everything about that beetle's body is built around winning that one contest.

facts.text: A dung beetle rolls its ball in a dead straight line. On moonless nights the African species Scarabaeus satyrus holds that line by reading the pale band of the Milky Way.
facts.more: Researchers fitted beetles with tiny caps and tested them inside a planetarium. Under a full starfield they rolled straight. Under a blank ceiling, or wearing a cap, they wandered in circles. They are not reading individual stars — they steer by the whole bright smear of the galaxy.

facts.text: Before it sets off, the beetle climbs on top of its ball and turns a full circle. That little dance is how it takes a snapshot of the sky and locks in a heading.
facts.more: It dances again every time something knocks it off course. Straight-line rolling matters because the dung pile behind it is crawling with thieves. Any direction will do, as long as it is away, and as long as it never curves back.

facts.text: Adults of many species do not chew dung at all. They squeeze it and drink the liquid, straining out microscopic particles, because the fluid is where the nutrition actually is.
facts.more: Their mouthparts are soft and brushy rather than hard and biting. The larva is the one that handles solid food, eating its way through a sealed ball its mother built and packed for it in advance.

facts.text: The mother buries a ball, lays one single egg inside it, and seals it shut. The larva hatches into the middle of its own food supply and eats its way outward.
facts.more: In some species she stays underground with it for weeks, patching cracks in the ball and scraping off mold. That is unusually careful parenting for an insect, and the grubs she tends survive far better than the ones left alone.

facts.text: There are three ways to make a living here. Rollers cut a ball and drive it away. Tunnellers dig straight down beneath the pile and drag dung under. Dwellers just move in and live in it.
