One beetle can bury 250 times its own mass of dung in a single night. Drop a 2 lb (1 kg) pile of elephant dung on African ground after dark and 13,700 beetles turn up to work it.
facts.more: Beetles land within seconds of dung hitting the ground. With that many at work a pile can be shredded and buried within hours, which is why the savanna is not knee-deep in dung. One elephant's daily output can feed two million beetles.

facts.text: Midday desert sand gets hot enough to cook a beetle's feet. So it climbs on top of its own dung ball to cool down, then hops off and keeps rolling.
facts.more: The moist ball is genuinely cooler than the sand. Researchers filmed it and measured it: on hot ground the beetles climbed far more often, and beetles fitted with tiny silicone boots climbed much less. The ball is a portable patch of shade.

facts.text: Australia's imported cattle dropped wet pats that the native beetles would not touch, so twenty-three kinds of dung beetle were brought in from overseas. Bush fly numbers fell by around 90%.
facts.more: Native Australian dung beetles are built for small dry marsupial pellets, not for big soggy cow pats. The pats simply sat there, killing the grass underneath and breeding flies by the million. Import the right beetle and the problem buries itself.

facts.text: One relative gave up dung altogether. It is called Deltochilum valgum. In the Peruvian rainforest it hunts live millipedes. It wrestles them down and decapitates them.
Male horns come in two settings. Large males grow long horns and fight at the tunnel mouth. Small males grow no horns at all and dig a side tunnel to sneak past the fight.
facts.more: Which one a male becomes is decided by how much dung he managed to eat as a larva. Same species, same parents. Two completely different body plans, and two completely different strategies for the same goal.

facts.text: The Egyptians carved this beetle in stone by the thousand. They had watched it push a ball across the ground, and made it their emblem for the sun being pushed across the sky.

wonder: The dirtiest job in the world, handed to a beetle that steers by the galaxy.

name: Golden orb-weaver
blurb: A big tropical spider that spins a wheel-shaped web out of silk the color of real gold.
size: A big female's body is as long as your thumb; with her legs out she covers your palm.

facts.text: The gold is real color, not a trick of the light. Her silk carries a yellow pigment called xanthurenic acid, laid down as she spins.
facts.more: It works two ways, depending on where the web hangs. In a sunlit gap the gold glows and insects fly at it the way they fly at a flower. Against dark forest shade the same threads read as nothing at all.

facts.text: Find the tiny spider loitering at the edge of the web. That's the male. Her body can be about 1.2 in (3 cm) long; his is many times smaller.
facts.more: Hers is the web, the food and the decisions. He spends his life on the rim, waiting for a safe moment to approach, and he often times it for when she is busy eating something else.

facts.text: Her web can be wider than you are tall — up to about 5 ft (1.5 m) across — slung from support lines strung meters between two trees.
facts.more: The guy-lines are the giveaway. Walk into one across a forest path and it doesn't snap and drape over you like an ordinary cobweb. It pushes back, and you feel it stop you.

facts.text: Weight for weight, her dragline silk is stronger than steel. It also soaks up more energy before snapping than Kevlar, the fiber used in bulletproof vests.
facts.more: Strength alone isn't the trick. The silk stretches roughly a third of its length again before it breaks, and strong-plus-stretchy is what engineers call toughness. A fly hits the web at speed and the silk absorbs the whole punch instead of pinging apart.

facts.text: Small birds and bats have been found tangled in golden orb webs. The silk really is that strong — though a bird is a disaster, not a dinner.
facts.more: Researchers who gathered reports of birds caught in spider webs from around the world found this group of spiders turning up again and again. She isn't hunting them. A thrashing bird wrecks a web that took her hours.

facts.text: People have woven cloth from this silk. One golden cape took silk from over a million wild orb-weavers, each gathered, milked and then released.
facts.more: In Madagascar, teams collected spiders each morning, held each one gently while a few meters of silk were drawn from her, then let her go. The work took years. The finished textile is gold with no dye in it anywhere, and it now sits in a museum case.

facts.text: Before machines could match it, spider silk was strung inside telescopes and gun sights as crosshairs. It was fine and dead straight. It was also tough enough to survive the recoil.
facts.more: Nothing manufactured came close. A drawn wire that thin would sag or snap; silk holds its line, holds tension, and is nearly invisible against whatever you are aiming at. Instrument makers kept spiders on hand and drew fresh line whenever a new reticle was needed.

facts.text: She has eight eyes and barely uses them. The web is her real sense organ: a fly, a falling leaf and a courting male each arrive as a different vibration.
facts.more: Spiders read those vibrations through slit sensilla — narrow stress-detecting cracks in their leg joints. She keeps the web under tension so signals travel cleanly. A male approaching has to tap out a rhythm that is unmistakably not prey.

facts.text: She walks across her own sticky web without getting caught. Almost nothing of her actually touches the glue.
facts.more: Filmed close up, spider feet do three things at once. Dense hairs cut the contact area down to almost nothing. A non-stick coating sits on those hairs. And she lifts each leg in a peeling motion rather than a straight pull. Glue cannot get a grip on any of it.

facts.text: Look at the edge of her web for tiny silver spiders that are not her babies. They're dewdrop spiders — freeloaders that steal food off her table.
facts.more: They tiptoe along her lines. Some snip out a wrapped parcel of prey and carry it off. Others feed at the same carcass while she is busy at the other end. A large web can carry dozens of them.

facts.text: She can bite, but for a human the venom is weak — closer to a bee sting. Her first move is almost always to drop out of the web and hide.
facts.more: An animal that has invested hours in a web does not want a fight it could lose. Dropping on a dragline costs nothing, and she can climb straight back up the same thread once whatever alarmed her has gone.

facts.text: She wraps her eggs in a fluffy silk purse and carries it off the web. She hides it in leaf litter or against bark. A layer of camouflage silk goes over the top.

wonder: A fiber tougher than anything in our factories, spun in the dark by an animal the size of your thumb.

name: Emperor scorpion
blurb: One of the largest scorpions in the world. It is a glossy black, heavy-clawed burrower from West Africa.
size: Up to about 8 in (20 cm) long, and wide enough to cover an adult's palm.

facts.text: Shine ultraviolet light on one at night and it glows an eerie blue-green. The glow comes from substances built into the clear outer layer of its shell.
facts.more: A scorpion that has just moulted barely glows at all — the glow strengthens as the new shell hardens. What the glow is actually for is still an open question; the scorpion itself gives no sign of using it.

facts.text: One of the biggest scorpions there is. It runs about 8 in (20 cm) long. Around 1 oz (30 g), it is heavy enough to feel sitting in your palm.
facts.more: Big does not mean deadly here. Some of the largest scorpions are among the mildest, and this one is calm enough that it is a common first scorpion for people who keep invertebrates.

facts.text: The rough rule with scorpions is: fat claws, mild venom — skinny claws, nasty venom. The emperor has enormous claws, and its sting is roughly a bee sting.
facts.more: It crushes most of what it catches outright and hardly bothers to sting at all. The scorpions that are genuinely dangerous to people are slim-clawed ones, which have no way to stop prey except chemistry.

facts.text: Turn one over and you'll find two combs on its belly. It drags them along the ground as it walks, tasting and feeling the dirt.
facts.more: They're called pectines and they're studded with thousands of tiny sensors. A male reads a female's chemical trail with them; both sexes use them to judge whether the ground is right for digging. Nothing else in the animal kingdom has this organ.

facts.text: She doesn't lay eggs. She gives birth to live young — pale, soft and helpless — and they climb straight onto her back and ride there.
facts.more: A litter can be a dozen or more. For the first week or two they are white and soft-shelled. They ride stacked on the one place nothing can reach them. She carries the whole heap with her wherever she goes.

facts.text: Emperor scorpions put up with each other. Family groups share a burrow, and a mother will let her grown young stay on — unusual for a scorpion.
facts.more: Most scorpions treat every other scorpion as either a rival or a meal. These live in loose colonies, and young ones have been seen feeding on prey their mother caught rather than being driven off.

facts.text: It digs. A burrow can run as deep as an adult is tall. It will also happily move into a termite mound. The air there stays damp and the food walks in.
facts.more: Underground is where the water is. Above ground in West Africa a scorpion dries out. Down in the burrow the humidity stays high and the temperature stays steady. Termites keep blundering past the front door.

facts.text: Termites make up much of what it eats. An adult usually just grabs and crushes — stinging is a last resort, because venom costs the body real effort to make.
facts.more: Venom is expensive chemistry, rebuilt slowly once it is spent, so a scorpion that stings everything runs empty. Watch a big adult with a small insect and the claws do all the work while the tail stays folded.

facts.text: It can make a rasping sound, scraping a rough patch on its pincer arm against its jaws. Up close it's like a fingernail dragged over sandpaper.
facts.more: The signal is aimed at animals too big to fight. A scorpion that would rather not be trodden on can rattle out a warning before it ever has to raise its tail.

facts.text: There's a pair of eyes on top of its head and more along the front edge, and it still can't see much detail. What those top eyes do is catch light — almost any light.
facts.more: They are among the most light-sensitive eyes measured in any animal. They are tuned for a starlit night rather than for shapes. The scorpion reads brightness and direction, not pictures. It does the rest of the work by touch.

facts.text: Its body runs slow. A well-fed adult can go months between meals without coming to harm — sit still, spend nothing, and let dinner walk past the burrow.
facts.more: Some scorpions can last close to a year without eating. That low idle is why they survive where food arrives unpredictably. It is not laziness. It is an engine deliberately turned right down.

facts.text: Chemists found germ-killing molecules in this scorpion's venom and named them pandinins after it. Venom turns out to be a whole chemistry set, not one single poison.
facts.more: A single scorpion's venom can hold dozens of different peptides, each doing a different job. Some jam nerves and some kill bacteria. Researchers now comb through them looking for medicines.

wonder: An animal armed with venom that mostly chooses not to use it, walking about with a heap of white babies on its back.

name: Horseshoe crab
blurb: A helmet-shaped sea animal with a spike for a tail and bright blue blood — and despite the name, it is not a crab.
size: About 2 ft (60 cm) from front to tail tip; the tail spike is nearly half of that.

facts.text: It isn't a crab. Look at the mouthparts and it lines up with spiders and scorpions instead — a chelicerate, named for the small pincers beside its mouth.
facts.more: A true crab has antennae and jaws. A horseshoe crab has neither. What it has is a pair of chelicerae, the same feeding pincers a spider uses. That is why zoologists file it with the arachnids, not with anything else in a rock pool.

facts.text: A big female is a broad shell with a spike behind it. She runs about 2 ft (60 cm) front to tail-tip. Males run smaller.
facts.more: Almost none of that is her body. Most of what you are lifting is armor — one curved plate over the front, a hinged plate behind it, and the tail. Underneath, the animal itself is surprisingly small and soft.

facts.text: Its blood is blue. Ours carries oxygen using iron; a horseshoe crab uses copper, in a protein called haemocyanin, and copper turns blue when it grabs oxygen.
facts.more: The color only shows once the blood meets air. Inside the animal, before it picks up its oxygen, the blood runs almost colorless — so the famous blue is really the moment of loading, caught on camera.

facts.text: That blue blood matters to hospitals. It clots instantly around bacterial poison. That reaction is used to check that vaccines and injectable medicines are clean.
facts.more: Cells in the blood called amebocytes turn liquid to gel at the faintest trace of bacterial endotoxin. Hundreds of thousands of crabs are collected and bled each year and most are returned to the sea, though not all survive it. Synthetic replacements are now taking over some of the work.

facts.text: Its two big side eyes are built from about a thousand separate units. Studying them won a scientist a Nobel Prize, because they revealed how any eye sharpens an edge.
facts.more: Each unit quietens its neighbors when it fires. That is called lateral inhibition, and it is why edges look crisper to you than they physically are. This eye was simply big and orderly enough to wire up and measure — and what it taught applies to yours.

facts.text: Two big eyes on top are only the start. There are simpler eyes dotted over the shell, and light sensors on the tail spike itself.
facts.more: A buried animal with a tail sticking out can still tell day from night. Much of that scattered light-sensing seems to be about tides and moonlight rather than about seeing objects at all.

facts.text: The tail spike doesn't sting and cannot hurt you. It's a lever. When a wave flips the animal upside down, it uses the tail to arch, push and roll back over.
facts.more: A stranded horseshoe crab that cannot right itself dies in the sun. If you find one flipped on a beach, lift it by both sides of the shell. Set it down the right way up. Never carry it by the tail, which can snap off.

facts.text: On the biggest spring tides, whole beaches fill with them. Females dig into wet sand and lay thousands of pale green eggs the size of pinheads, batch after batch.
facts.more: Delaware Bay is the great gathering place. The tides that count are the highest ones, around the new and full moon. Those bury the eggs high up the beach. Ordinary waves will not dig them back out.

facts.text: Those eggs feed a bird. Red knots arrive exhausted from South America, land on the same beaches in the same few weeks, and eat almost nothing else.
facts.more: A red knot can put on close to its own body weight again on horseshoe crab eggs before flying north to the Arctic. The timing has to line up exactly, which is why limits on collecting the crabs are partly about protecting the birds.

facts.text: Under the shell are five pairs of gills stacked like the pages of a book. The animal flaps them to breathe, and young ones flap them to swim — upside down.
facts.more: Book gills is the actual name. The pages are thin flaps stacked in the hundreds. That packs a huge surface into a small space. A juvenile paddles along upside down just under the surface, which is a genuinely odd thing to watch.

facts.text: It grows by climbing out of itself. The old shell splits open at the front rim, the animal walks out, and what's left behind is a perfect hollow copy — legs and all.
facts.more: People find these on the tideline and assume they have found a dead crab. Pick one up: it weighs almost nothing, and there is a clean split seam around the front edge. A horseshoe crab does this about seventeen times before it is full-grown.

facts.text: It has no jaws. It grinds its food between the bristly bases of its own legs as it walks, then pushes the mash into a mouth sitting in the middle of them.
facts.more: So a horseshoe crab has to keep moving in order to chew. Stop walking and the mill stops. Those leg bases are called gnathobases, and they are lined with stiff spines that do the work teeth would.

wonder: Blue blood that keeps hospital medicine safe, and eyes that taught us how seeing works — from an animal most people step over on a beach.

name: Giant Pacific octopus
blurb: The largest octopus in the world. It is a soft, boneless, color-shifting hunter of the cold North Pacific.
size: Arms spread, about as wide across as a car is long.

facts.text: A big adult spans about 14 ft (4.3 m) from arm tip to arm tip. It weighs around 33 lb (15 kg) — with not a single bone in its body.
facts.more: There is no skeleton anywhere in it. That whole mass is muscle and skin, which is why an octopus this size can flow into a shape you would swear it could not fit. Exceptional ones grow several times heavier.

facts.text: Its only truly hard part is a beak, like a parrot's. Anything the beak fits through, the rest of it can follow — a whole heavy adult through a gap not much wider than two fingers.
facts.more: Aquarium keepers bolt lids down and screen off pipes, because an octopus will patiently find the one gap in an enclosure and pour itself through. The beak sits right where the eight arms meet, and it sets the only limit.

facts.text: About 280 suckers run down each arm — roughly 2,000 in all. Every one of them grips and tastes at the same time, so this animal can taste whatever it touches.
facts.more: The suckers are packed with chemical sensors. Reaching blind into a dark crevice tells it not just the shape of what is in there but the flavor. One big sucker alone can hold up 35 lb (16 kg).

facts.text: It has three hearts. Two push blood through the gills and one drives it round the body — and that third heart stops beating every time the octopus swims.
facts.more: Which is exactly why it would rather walk. Jetting through open water tires an octopus out because the heart supplying its body quits while it does. Given any choice, a giant Pacific octopus crawls along the bottom on its arms.

facts.text: About two-thirds of its nerve cells are not in its head. They are in its arms, and each arm can feel, taste and work out a small problem largely by itself.
facts.more: Around half a billion nerve cells in total, most of them strung down the eight arms. The central brain seems to hand down a general instruction — go into that hole — and the arm sorts out the details on its own.

facts.text: It repaints itself in under a second, squeezing thousands of tiny pigment sacs open and shut. And as far as anyone can measure, it is colorblind.
facts.more: Octopus eyes carry just one light-sensitive pigment. That normally means seeing the world in a single color. Yet the skin matches red rock and brown kelp closely. It changes texture too, raising bumps called papillae to fake weed, gravel or bare stone.

facts.text: It hunts crabs, clams and fish. When a clam refuses to open, the octopus drills a neat round hole through the shell and squirts in saliva that loosens the muscle holding it shut.
facts.more: The drill is a rasping tongue called a radula. Those little bored holes are a giveaway: divers looking for an octopus den hunt for the trash heap of empty shells piled outside the front door.

facts.text: She lays tens of thousands of tiny eggs. She hangs them in long plaited strands from the roof of her den.
facts.more: Then she stops eating. For around six months she blows fresh water over them and cleans them one by one, and never leaves. They hatch, and she dies. It is the only brood she will ever raise.

facts.text: A hatchling weighs about 0 oz (0.03 g) — you could lose it in a teaspoon. To reach adult size it has to grow roughly half a million times heavier.
facts.more: It drifts off as plankton first, tiny and see-through, riding currents with no control at all. Only a handful out of tens of thousands ever settle to the bottom and start becoming the animal you would recognize.

facts.text: In one study, giant Pacific octopuses learned to tell two people apart. One fed them. The other prodded them with a bristly stick. The octopuses treated each of them differently.
facts.more: Same uniform, same time of day, so the only difference was the person. The octopuses aimed water jets at the one who had bothered them. They moved toward the one who brought food. They had it worked out within a couple of weeks.

facts.text: Its ink is more than a smokescreen. It carries chemicals that blunt a hunter's sense of smell, so the octopus doesn't just vanish from view — it becomes hard to track at all.
facts.more: And if something gets a grip anyway, the octopus can shed the arm. It grows back, suckers and all. Losing a limb is a survivable inconvenience rather than a permanent injury.

facts.text: It lives in cold water, from the shallows down past 6,600 ft (2,000 m). It does best between about 8 and 12°C (46-54°F). That is the chilly rim of the North Pacific.

wonder: Three hearts, blue blood, and a mind spread out along eight arms — built on a plan nothing like ours, and still curious about us.

name: Mimic octopus
blurb: A small octopus that lives out on bare open sand. It survives there by pretending to be other animals.
size: Stretched out, about as long as your arm — but the arms themselves are no thicker than a pencil.

facts.text: It lives where nothing can hide: flat open sand and silt at shallow river mouths, mostly shallower than 50 ft (15 m). No reef, no crevice, no weed.
facts.more: Most octopuses answer danger by backing into a hole. Out here there are no holes. This one meets danger in the open, in full view, and deals with it by being mistaken for something else.

facts.text: Watch it cross open sand and it doesn't look like an octopus. It flattens, sweeps all its arms back into a leaf shape, and glides along the bottom like a flatfish.
facts.more: It copies the movement as well as the outline — that low, wobbling skim a few centimeters above the sand, held all the way across. Reef hunters leave soles alone: bony, awkward to swallow, not worth the chase.

facts.text: Threatened, it hangs in the water and fans all eight arms out around itself. The stripes come up bold brown and white. The shape is a lionfish, an animal bristling with venomous spines.
facts.more: The pose does the work. Arms held out stiff and evenly spaced turn a soft round body into a spiky wheel, and fish in these waters already know to leave that silhouette alone.

facts.text: Attacked by a small damselfish, it buries six arms and waves the other two in opposite directions, banded black and white. From a fish's eye level, that is a sea snake.
facts.more: Sea snakes eat damselfish. The octopus appears to bring this one out mainly when damselfish are the problem. It is the right lie told to the right audience. And it comes from an animal with no bones to build a snake out of.

facts.text: Laid out flat it is about as long as your arm, but there is almost nothing to it. The arms are pencil-thin and the body is smaller than your fist.
facts.more: That thinness is what makes the impersonations work. Thick, muscular arms could never pass for a sea snake or fold flat into a fish shape. Everything this animal does depends on being long, thin and boneless.

facts.text: It hunts by touch, pushing a long arm down burrows in the sand to flush out small fish, crabs and worms that thought they were safe.
facts.more: The arm goes in on its own and works blind, feeling and tasting the inside of a hole the octopus cannot see into. Whatever bolts out the far end meets the rest of the octopus waiting.

facts.text: Most octopuses hunt at night. This one is out in daylight, on open ground, in plain sight. The best read is that it can only afford that because of everything else it can do.
facts.more: Daylight is when the impersonations pay. Color and pattern are useless in the dark. An octopus that can look like something dangerous can afford those hours. Everything else with eight arms stays hidden then.

facts.text: Its skin does the whole trick. Thousands of tiny pigment sacs open and shut under the surface, so a pattern can switch from sandy beige to hard black-and-white bands in a second.
facts.more: Nothing is painted on and nothing is fixed. The same square of skin that was blank sand a moment ago becomes a warning stripe. Then it goes blank again. Muscle controls it directly, which is why it happens so fast.

facts.text: When a display does not work, it drops into a burrow in the sand and is simply gone. One moment there is an animal the length of your arm. The next there is a small hole.
facts.more: The whole body funnels into an opening you would not think it could use. There is no skull, no shell and no bones anywhere. Nothing can catch on the way in.

facts.text: Under the act it is an ordinary octopus. Eight arms, a parrot-like beak, blue blood. It also has ink it can fire if all the impersonations fail.
facts.more: Every octopus can ink. What is unusual here is how much this one gets done with shape and pattern before it ever needs to. Ink buys a second or two of confusion; a costume can work for as long as the other animal keeps believing it.

wonder: No bones, no shell, no armor — staying alive on an empty plain by being the shape of something else.

name: Pufferfish
blurb: A slow, round, big-eyed fish that swells into a spiky ball when something tries to eat it. It also carries one of the deadliest poisons in the ocean.
size: From smaller than your thumb to longer than your forearm, depending on the species

facts.text: Underwater, a puffer doesn't blow up with air. It gulps seawater into a stomach that stretches like a balloon, until it's a spiky ball too wide for a predator's mouth.
facts.more: It has no ribs and no pelvic bones in the way, so nothing stops the stomach expanding. Those spines are its scales, stiffened into spikes. They lie flat against the body and stand up only when the fish inflates.

facts.text: Many puffers carry tetrodotoxin. It is a poison with no antidote. It plugs the tiny gates that let nerves fire, so the muscles simply stop answering.
facts.more: Nerves send signals by letting sodium rush through openings called sodium channels. Tetrodotoxin blocks them shut. The chilling part is what it does not do. A poisoned person can be completely paralyzed and still wide awake, thinking clearly the whole time.

facts.text: Puffers don't make the poison themselves. It comes from bacteria in what they eat, which is why a puffer raised on clean food ends up completely harmless.
facts.more: Feed a toxin-free puffer a diet containing tetrodotoxin, and the poison builds back up in its liver. The fish is borrowing a weapon from the bacteria in its food. It stores that weapon in its own body. Its own nerves are unbothered by it.

facts.text: Its family name means four teeth, and four teeth is all it has. Two are fused above and two below. Together they form a beak that cracks crab shell and snail.
facts.more: Those teeth keep growing all through its life, so a puffer has to eat hard-shelled food to wear them down. In aquariums, a puffer fed only soft food grows a beak so overgrown that it can no longer close its mouth.

facts.text: A male puffer small enough to sit in your palm plows a ridged circle into the seabed. The circle measures 6.6 ft (2 m) across. The whole job is to attract a female.
facts.more: He digs it with his fins and body, then keeps the ridges and valleys sharp while females come and inspect. She lays in the fine sand at the center. He never reuses a circle: every batch of eggs gets one dug from scratch.

facts.text: Watch one swim and you'll wonder how it survives anything. It sculls with small fins, slow as a drifting leaf, but it can hover, reverse, and turn on the spot.
Each eye swivels independently. One can track a crab off to the left while the other keeps watch on open water to the right.
In Japan puffer is eaten as fugu, and only licensed chefs may prepare it. The poison sits in specific organs that have to be cut away perfectly.
facts.more: The training takes years and ends in an exam. Poisonings still happen, most often when someone prepares a puffer at home instead of buying it from a licensed kitchen. There is no antidote, so treatment is life support until the body clears it.

facts.text: The very same poison turns up in the blue-ringed octopus and in the rough-skinned newt. Three animals that look nothing alike carry one identical chemical.
Not every puffer lives in the sea. About 35 species spend their whole lives in African, Asian and South American rivers. They crack snails off the riverbed.
Puffers run from smaller than your thumb up to the mbu of Africa's Congo rivers. The mbu is the biggest freshwater puffer. It passes 20 in (50 cm), longer than your forearm.

wonder: No ribs so the stomach can stretch, and spines that lie flat until the moment they're needed. A defense thought through from the bones outward.

name: Flying fish
blurb: A slim silver ocean fish with pectoral fins as long as wings. It launches clear of the sea and glides above the waves. That is how it escapes whatever is chasing it.
size: Between a pencil and a school ruler long, about 5.9-11.8 in (15-30 cm) (6-12 in)

facts.text: It doesn't flap. Once it's airborne the fins lock out stiff and it glides, like a paper plane with a fish inside.
facts.more: Real flight means beating wings to make lift, and a flying fish never does that. All the energy comes from the launch underwater, plus rising air off the front of a wave, which is why the longest flights happen along the wave crests.

facts.text: It builds its speed underwater first, then breaks the surface at over 43 mph (70 km/h) with its tail still beating behind it.
The longest flight ever filmed lasted 45 seconds. A television crew off southern Japan recorded it. That fish stayed up longer than most people can hold their breath.
facts.more: To keep going that long, a flying fish drops the tip of its tail back into the water and beats it hard. It never fully lands. It launches straight into a fresh glide before the first one has run out.

facts.text: A normal flight covers about 160 ft (50 m), the length of an Olympic pool. Riding the rising air off wave crests, one can string glides together for 1,300 ft (400 m).
The bottom half of its tail is far longer than the top. That long lower blade stays in the water and beats while the rest of the fish is already flying.
facts.more: It works like a tiny outboard motor. The fish is in the air but still being pushed, so it can build speed for another glide without properly landing. Everything that powers the flight happens in the water. The air is only where it ends up.

facts.text: Some species have two pairs of wings. The long pectoral fins go out front, with enlarged pelvic fins behind. The result is a fish-shaped biplane.
Almost everything eats flying fish. Tuna, marlin, dolphins, squid, mackerel. Flight is the only answer they have, and it works right up until a frigatebird is waiting overhead.
facts.more: Frigatebirds learn to patrol above hunting tuna. Tuna are what push flying fish into the air in the first place. The fish escapes one predator by launching itself straight into the reach of another.

facts.text: They live in the open ocean, in warm water near the surface. It's the emptiest place on Earth, with nothing to hide behind — and that emptiness is the best explanation anyone has for why they fly.
Their eggs come with sticky threads. Adults wind them around drifting seaweed, feathers, even floating trash, so the eggs have something to hold onto instead of sinking.
facts.more: Out in open water there is nothing to lay eggs on. No rock, no reef, no plant rooted to anything. A raft of drifting weed is the only nursery available, and a good one can end up carrying clumps of eggs from many different fish at once.

facts.text: They feed mainly on plankton, the tiny drifting animals near the surface. The fish that flies to avoid being eaten spends its day hunting things you'd barely be able to see.
Barbados is nicknamed the land of the flying fish, and flying fish served with cou-cou is the national dish. A whole country named itself after a glide.

wonder: Wings for the air, fins for the sea, and a tail that works in both at once. One small fish given two worlds to move through.

name: Mudskipper
blurb: A fish that walks. It spends most of its life out of the water on tropical mudflats. It props itself up on its front fins, with its eyes bulging off the top of its head.
size: Most are shorter than a pencil; the largest reach about 12 in (30 cm), roughly your forearm

facts.text: Its front fins are jointed and set far forward, underneath the body. It plants them and hauls itself along, a movement called crutching, because that's exactly what it looks like.
A mudskipper breathes through its skin. As long as it stays damp, oxygen soaks straight in through the skin and through the lining of its mouth and throat.
facts.more: This is cutaneous respiration: breathing through skin. It only works wet, which is why a mudskipper that has been out a while flops back into a puddle and rolls in it. Let one dry out completely and it suffocates in open air.

facts.text: Both eyes sit on top of its head and swivel like periscopes. It lowers them into their sockets while a fold of skin called the dermal cup rises over them. That's a fish blinking.
facts.more: The blink isn't about dust. It's a wipe. The eye dips into a pocket of water inside the head and comes back up wet. Most fish never blink because they are already underwater and never need to. A mudskipper is not underwater.

facts.text: It carries its own air supply. Before heading out it packs the enlarged chambers around its gills with air and seals them shut, built-in cheeks that keep the gills damp ashore.
A giant mudskipper takes mouthfuls of air down into its flooded burrow. It releases them in the dark, trip after trip. That gives its eggs oxygen to develop in.
facts.more: Deep mangrove mud holds almost no oxygen at all, and the water in the burrow would smother the eggs. So the father surfaces, fills his mouth, dives back down and lets the bubble go, building an air pocket up in the burrow's ceiling.

facts.text: Startled, it flexes its whole body sideways and flings itself up to 24 in (61 cm) in one hop. Two school rulers, cleared by a fish shorter than one of them.
It lives where the river meets the sea, in mangrove mud that's underwater half the day and bare the other half. Mudskippers spend up to three quarters of their lives on land.
Males argue in sign language. The body arches, the posture changes, the dorsal fin flicks up like a flag. On an open mudflat everyone can see everyone. So disputes get settled by display.
It climbs. Using those same front fins, a mudskipper hauls itself up mangrove roots and out onto low branches, well clear of the water it came from.
It hunts on land: crabs, insects, worms. Some species carry a mouthful of water, push it out over their food, then suck it back in, using water as a tongue.
facts.more: A fish has no tongue that works in air, and dry food won't slide into a fish's mouth the way it does underwater. So the mudskipper brings the water with it. The bulge of water flows out over the prey and draws it back in.

facts.text: The burrow is home, nursery and panic room all at once. A frightened mudskipper skips across the mud and drops straight down a hole it dug itself and knows by heart.

wonder: Most fish were given one world to live in. This one was given the shoreline, and everything it needs to work on both sides of the tideline.

name: Sailfish
blurb: A long blue open-ocean hunter with a spear for a nose. The fin on its back opens like a sail. Up it goes when the sailfish closes in on a school of small fish.
size: About 10 ft (3 m) from bill tip to tail: lay two nine-year-olds head to toe and add a bit

facts.text: You'll read everywhere that a sailfish hits 68 mph (110 km/h). It doesn't. Careful measurements put its real ceiling nearer 20-35 mph (35-55 km/h).
facts.more: The famous number came from an old fishing test, not a laboratory. Researchers later measured how fast sailfish muscle can actually contract, and filmed real sailfish attacking real sardines: bursts around 15 mph (25 km/h), never past 20 mph (35 km/h). Still one of the fastest fish alive.

facts.text: The sail is a dorsal fin that can stand taller than the fish is deep. It folds down flat into a groove along the back when the sailfish is just swimming.

Raise the sail and the head stops swinging side to side. Nobody can ask a sardine what it saw. But a steadier bill slides through the water almost still. That is the argument for why the sail goes up.
facts.more: Researchers filming attacks found the sail does more than look impressive. With it up, the hunting sailfish's head oscillates less as it closes in, so the bill slides through the water almost still and the school reacts late.

facts.text: Sailfish gather in loose groups around a school of sardines, but they don't all rush in together. They attack one or two at a time, taking turns at the ball of fish.
facts.more: Filming shows the turn-taking clearly. Only one or two sailfish press the attack at any moment while the rest hold off. Fewer bills swinging at once means fewer collisions, and the sardine ball stays packed instead of scattering in every direction.

facts.text: The bill isn't a spear. The sailfish swipes it sideways through the packed sardines, tap, slash, tap, then comes back for the ones too stunned or too cut to swim straight.
facts.more: The bill is covered in tiny rough teeth, so a slash doesn't just knock a sardine sideways, it scrapes it. Watch one attack from beginning to end and the count of injured sardines in the ball climbs steadily. That climb is the strategy working.

facts.text: A hunting sailfish lights up. Bright blue bars flicker along its flanks and fade within seconds, while the other sailfish in the hunt do the same thing.
facts.more: The color comes from cells in the skin that the fish controls directly, the way an octopus does. In a crowded attack, with several bills swinging in a small space, the flashing appears to keep the hunters from hitting each other. It stops when the hunt does.

facts.text: A sailfish hatches as a speck of a larva and reaches 3.9-4.9 ft (1.2-1.5 m) (4-5 ft) inside its first year. Taller than you are, in twelve months.
facts.more: The bill grows in along the way. A young sailfish's snout starts short. It stretches out as the rest of the body lengthens underneath it. So a half-grown sailfish looks oddly stubby-nosed next to a full-sized adult.

facts.text: Everything on a sailfish folds flat. The pelvic fins tuck into grooves, the gill covers seal down, the sail drops away. Nothing sticks out to drag through the water.
A big one runs 10 ft (3 m) bill to tail. They rarely top 200 lb (90 kg), about what a full-size fridge weighs.
It lives in the warm surface layer of the open ocean. Mostly it stays above the thermocline. That is the sharp boundary where sun-warmed water sits on top of cold water below.
Sailfish do not hold territory. They are travelers, following warm water and bait fish across whole ocean basins. They turn up enormous distances from where they were tagged.

wonder: A fin that hides the bill, steadies the head, and folds into a groove until it's wanted. Nothing on this fish does only one job.

name: Ocean sunfish
blurb: A huge flat gray fish shaped like a head with two fins and no proper tail. It drifts through the open ocean. It eats almost anything small enough to swallow.
size: Up to 10.8 ft (3.3 m) (nearly 11 ft) long and even taller fin tip to fin tip: bigger than a doorway in both directions

facts.text: A grown sunfish weighs 551-2,205 lb (250-1,000 kg). The heaviest one ever measured came in at 5,100 lb (2,300 kg).
facts.more: Measured fin tip to fin tip it can be taller than it is long, so a big one is roughly a square of fish standing on edge. Another sunfish, the bump-head, holds the record for the heaviest bony fish ever weighed: 6,049 lb (2,744 kg).

facts.text: It hatches 0.1 in (2.5 mm) long, covered in spines. Three of them would sit side by side across your little fingernail. A survivor ends up 60 million times heavier.
facts.more: Nothing else with a backbone changes size like that. A human grows about twenty times heavier from birth to adult. And the larva looks nothing like the parent: a spiky little star, far closer to a pufferfish than to the giant it becomes.

facts.text: One female was estimated to be carrying 300 million eggs at once. That is more than any other known backboned animal on Earth.
It has no tail. Where a tail should be there's a stiff lumpy rudder called a clavus, and the fish flaps its top and bottom fins like wings instead.
facts.more: Most fish sweep a tail from side to side to move. The sunfish hasn't got one to sweep. Its dorsal fin and anal fin beat up and down together, in time, the way a penguin flies underwater, and the clavus does the steering at the back.

facts.text: It looks lazy and isn't. Tagged sunfish cruise at about 2 mph (3.2 km/h) and cover 16 miles (26 km) in a day, steering the whole way.
It was long described as a jellyfish eater. When researchers checked what was actually inside them, jellyfish and salps came to only about 15%. The rest was small fish, squid and prey off the seabed.
You'll find one lying flat on its side at the surface, looking like something has gone badly wrong. Nothing has. It's rewarming after a dive into cold deep water.
facts.more: Adults hunt below 660 ft (200 m), where the water is dark and cold enough to slow a big body right down. Back at the top it turns broadside to the sun and lets its enormous flat side soak up heat. Researchers call it thermally recharging.

facts.text: More than 40 kinds of parasite live on and in a sunfish. Getting rid of them takes up a serious part of its day.
facts.more: It queues at cleaning stations where small reef fish pick parasites off its skin. At the surface it lies sideways and lets seabirds do the same job from above. And it breaches, throwing its whole body about 10 ft (3 m) clear of the water and landing flat.

facts.text: Under that gray surface its skin runs up to 2.9 in (7.3 cm) (nearly 3 in) thick. It is tough rubbery collagen you could not push a thumb into. The whole thing is coated in slime.
Its teeth are fused into a single beak and its mouth doesn't fully close. It sits permanently ajar, giving every sunfish a look of mild, lasting surprise.
Mola is Latin for millstone, the big round gray stone used for grinding grain. In German the fish is called Schwimmender Kopf: the swimming head.

wonder: From a spiky speck you could balance on a fingernail to a ton of fish, and it is the same creature the whole way through.

name: Giant clam
blurb: A shellfish up to 3.3 ft (1 m) wide that sits on a coral reef and farms its own food inside its own body.
size: About 3.3 ft (1 m) across and up to 441 lb (200 kg)
wonder: It plants a garden in its own skin, bends the light to reach it, and never has to leave home to eat.

facts.text: The longest giant clam ever measured was 54 in (137 cm) across. It weighed 510 lb (230 kg).
facts.more: That is the record for any shelled mollusc alive. Most stop growing somewhere near a meter, which is still wide enough that you could not get your arms around one. They keep growing their whole lives, and can pass a hundred years.

facts.text: A giant clam grows its own lunch. Millions of tiny algae live inside its flesh, catching sunlight and handing over sugar — about two-thirds of everything the clam eats.
facts.more: The algae are called zooxanthellae. The clam farms them the way you would tend a garden. Every morning it spreads its brilliant mantle out into the light. It pulls the mantle back in when a shadow crosses. It still filters plankton from the water for the rest of its meals.

facts.text: That electric blue-and-green skin is not paint. Cells called iridocytes bend sunlight and scatter it deep down into the clam's flesh. The best read is that this feeds the algae growing in the shade.
facts.more: Without those cells only the top layer of algae would ever get light. The iridocytes work like a hall of mirrors, spreading the sun evenly through the tissue so the whole crop can work at once. Different clams scatter the light in different colors, which is why no two look the same.

facts.text: One adult can release more than 500 million eggs in a single spawning. That is more eggs, from one animal, than there are people in the United States.
facts.more: Giant clams are hermaphrodites. Every adult makes both eggs and sperm. None of them fertilize themselves. A whole reef spawns at once, filling the water like smoke. Only a handful of those eggs will ever become a clam.

facts.text: A grown giant clam of the biggest kind cannot shut its shell all the way. It is the only giant clam that can't — there is simply too much clam for the box.
facts.more: Look along the gap and you will see the mantle bulging out, too swollen with light-catching tissue to be tucked away. Smaller kinds close up fine. This one outgrows its own door.

facts.text: There is no head anywhere on a giant clam. Instead the mantle is dotted with hundreds of pinhole eyespots, each about half a millimeter wide, watching for shadows.
facts.more: They cannot see shapes. What they read is a change in light — a shadow sliding across, the way a hand passes over a flashlight. That is enough. The clam starts closing before whatever cast the shadow arrives.

facts.text: No shellfish on Earth wears a bigger shell. Giant clams are the largest shelled molluscs alive, and they build every gram of that shell out of plain seawater.
It only settles once. After about a week drifting as a speck of plankton, a young clam picks a patch of reef, glues itself down, and never moves again.
facts.more: That one choice is the last big move it ever makes. Land somewhere too dark and the algae starve. Land somewhere too deep and the same. Everything after that is just growing — slowly, in the light, in one spot, for a very long time.

facts.text: The old story about giant clams trapping divers by the ankle is not true. A giant clam closes far too slowly, and has to shove a tub of water out of the way as it goes.
facts.more: Sailors' charts once carried warnings about man-killing clams. Watch one shut and the story falls apart: the closing muscle works at a lazy pace, and the shell has to push all that water aside first. You could pull your foot out and go and get lunch.

facts.text: Giant clams need clear, shallow, sunlit water, usually no deeper than 66 ft (20 m). Any deeper and the algae inside them cannot catch enough light to pay the rent.
A young giant clam holds on with byssal threads — tough strands it spins to anchor itself to rock. The biggest kind lets go as it grows and relies on being too heavy to shift.
facts.more: By then, a storm big enough to move a giant clam is a storm big enough to break the reef underneath it. Weight is the entire defense. There is no running, no hiding and no fighting back — just a couple of hundred kilograms of clam, staying put.

name: Cone snail
blurb: A beautiful sea snail that hunts fish with a venom-loaded harpoon it fires out of its own mouth.
size: Most fit in your palm; the biggest runs about 8.5 in (21.6 cm)
wonder: One drop of something built to stop a fish turned out to be the thing that lets a person in pain finally sleep.

facts.text: A cone snail hunts with a harpoon. One tooth in its mouth is hollow, barbed and loaded with venom, and it fires that tooth into a fish on the end of a stretchy tube.
facts.more: The tube is called a proboscis. The snail creeps up, extends it like a slow gray finger, and then a muscle fires. The tooth stays attached, so the snail can reel its catch straight back in. A fishing rod, a spear and a syringe, all in one.

facts.text: The harpoon is disposable. After a meal the snail spits out the used tooth along with the fish's scales, and a fresh one is already waiting in the tube behind it.
facts.more: The teeth are grown in a row inside a pouch called the radular sac, each one hollowed and barbed before it is ever needed. Fire, discard, reload. There is always another loaded tooth ready to go.

facts.text: The strike is one of the fastest movements ever measured in an animal. In the cat cone the harpoon leaves the mouth at 56 mph (90 km/h) — from a snail.
facts.more: It goes from still to full speed at about 40,000 times the tug you feel standing still. A rollercoaster manages four. The whole strike is over before a fish can flinch, and the animal doing it moves at a snail's pace the rest of the day.

facts.text: A cone snail hunts by smell. It waves a snorkel-like tube called a siphon in the current, reads the water, then buries itself in the sand with only that tube showing.
facts.more: It never has to chase anything, which is just as well. Some cone snails eat worms, some eat other snails, and a few hunt fish — a strange job for an animal that cannot run anything down. The fish comes to the snail.

facts.text: The geography cone stuns fish with insulin. It floods the water with the same chemical your body uses to handle sugar, and the fish's blood sugar crashes so hard they go limp.
facts.more: The fish drift into the snail's waiting mouth in a daze, already too weak to swim off. Cone snails are the only animals known to use insulin as a weapon, and only a few kinds of cone snail do it.

facts.text: Do not pick up a cone shell. A few species carry venom strong enough to kill a person, and the snail can drive its tooth straight through a glove.
facts.more: About 27 human deaths have been confidently traced to cone snails, and nearly all of them were people who picked up a pretty shell. Most of the 800-odd species are no threat to us at all. The rule on the beach is simply look, don't touch.

facts.text: One cone snail's venom became a medicine. A single ingredient from the magician's cone is now a painkiller for people whose pain morphine cannot reach.
facts.more: It is called ziconotide. It blocks the channels that carry a pain signal up into the spinal cord. Morphine uses a completely different trick. That is exactly why ziconotide works for people morphine has stopped helping. The body does not become addicted to it.

facts.text: Every species mixes its own venom. A single cone snail's venom can hold as many as 200 different active ingredients, and no two species make the same recipe.
facts.more: Across the whole family that adds up to tens of thousands of separate compounds called conotoxins. Each one is a tiny key shaped to fit one particular lock in a nervous system. It is why chemists keep coming back to these snails.

facts.text: The smallest cone snails are about 0.5 in (1.3 cm) long; the biggest reach 8.5 in (21.6 cm).
The shell is the disguise. Those brown-and-white patterns look like nothing much on a sandy reef, and the snail spends most of the day buried anyway, with only its siphon showing.
A cone snail glues its eggs to rock in tough capsules. What hatches out is not a snail at all but a swimming speck called a veliger, which drifts before settling down.
facts.more: The veliger has a tiny shell and a pair of beating flaps to swim with. It lives up in the plankton with everything else too small to see. Only when it finds the right patch of seabed does it drop down. Then it changes shape and starts being a snail.

name: Coral
blurb: Not a rock and not a plant. Coral is a colony of tiny soft animals. They build a stone city and then live inside it.
size: One coral animal is smaller than a pea; together they build reefs you can see from space
wonder: Animals smaller than a pea, working without ever meeting, raised the largest structure any living thing has built.

facts.text: Coral is an animal. Each polyp is a soft sac, usually a few millimeters across. A ring of stinging tentacles sits on top. It builds itself a limestone cup to live in.
facts.more: The polyp pulls calcium and carbonate straight out of the seawater. It lays them down underneath itself, cup by cup. A reef is mostly stonework left behind by polyps that lived there before. Only a thin skin of living coral covers the outside.

facts.text: The Great Barrier Reef runs more than 1,243 miles (2,000 km) (1,250 mi) along the coast of Australia. It is the largest structure on Earth built by living creatures, and you can see it from space.
facts.more: It is not one reef but around 2,900 of them, plus some 900 islands, all of it made by animals small enough that several would sit on your thumbnail. Nothing else alive has ever built anything on that scale.

facts.text: A coral polyp is a farmer and a hunter at once. Algae living inside its body hand over sugar made from sunlight — as much as nine-tenths of the coral's food.
facts.more: The algae are zooxanthellae, the same partners giant clams keep, and they are also where the color comes from. At night the polyp changes job: out come the tentacles, and it catches plankton drifting past in the dark.

facts.text: The color you see in coral mostly isn't the coral. It's the algae in its skin. When water gets too warm the coral throws them out and turns bone white — that's bleaching.
facts.more: A bleached coral is not dead yet. It is starving. If the water cools soon enough the algae move back in and the color returns. If it stays hot, the polyps die and the stone city is left empty. A rise of only 1–2 °C can do it.

facts.text: Whole reefs spawn on the same night. Millions of corals release their eggs together a few nights after a full moon, and the sea turns into a slow pink snowstorm.
facts.more: Nobody signals them. Corals track water temperature, day length and moonlight, and they all arrive at the same answer. Releasing everything at once means the water is so thick with eggs that no predator could possibly eat them all.

facts.text: Corals fight each other. Neighbors growing too close send out long sweeper tentacles at night to sting. Some push their stomach lining out onto a rival and digest it where it stands.
facts.more: The prize is space — a patch of sunlit rock. These battles run for weeks and the winner is usually whichever colony can reach furthest. Look closely at a crowded reef and you can spot the no-man's-land gaps between colonies that have fought to a standstill.

facts.text: Coral reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor. Nobody has counted every creature in the sea, but the best estimate puts about a quarter of all the kinds on reefs.
facts.more: It is the most crowded address in the ocean. Fish, crabs, octopuses, eels, snails, sponges and worms all pack into the cracks and branches of the stonework, the way a hedge fills up with birds.

facts.text: A boulder coral grows about a centimeter taller in a year — the width of your little fingernail. Fast branching kinds can manage ten times that, but the city is still stacked in slow motion.
Coral polyps are cousins of jellyfish and sea anemones. Same group, same stinging cells — nematocysts — but a coral is the one that built a stone cup and stayed in it.
facts.more: Brush a coral and you are being stung. You simply cannot feel most of them through your skin. Each nematocyst is a coiled harpoon held under pressure. Touch the trigger hair and it fires in less than a thousandth of a second.

facts.text: Not all coral needs sunlight. There are coral gardens far below where any light reaches, in cold black water. Those polyps have no algae at all. They catch every scrap of their food from the dark.
facts.more: Reef-building corals hug warm, clear, shallow water because their algae need the sun. The deep ones have no such partner and no color to lose. They spread their tentacles into the current and wait, in the cold, for whatever drifts by.

name: Sea slug
blurb: A sea snail with no shell, soft and ludicrously colorful. It is also a thief. It takes weapons, poison and even sunlight from the things it eats.
size: Most are shorter than your thumb; the biggest is as long as your whole arm
wonder: Armor, poison, even a way to eat sunlight — it borrows every one of them, and wears the whole borrowed kit in color.

facts.text: Nudibranch means "naked gills". Look at the feathery plume standing up on a sea slug's back — that is the gill, worn on the outside, with nothing covering it at all.
facts.more: Most snails do their breathing tucked inside a shell. A nudibranch starts life as a swimming speck with a tiny coiled shell and sheds it when it changes into its adult shape, so everything ends up exposed. Which raises the obvious question — how does anything that soft survive on a reef?

facts.text: The bright colors look like a warning label. Nobody can ask a fish what it makes of them. The best read is that a slug blazing orange and purple is advertising that it tastes foul, or worse. Predators learn that lesson fast.
facts.more: Some brew their own bad chemicals. Others take them straight from dinner. A slug that eats a poisonous sponge stores the sponge's poison in its own skin. It wears the sponge's colors while it does it.

facts.text: Some sea slugs steal weapons. They eat stinging hydroids and swallow the sting cells without setting them off. The cells get moved up into the frilly tips on their back. Then the slug fires them at anything that bothers it.
facts.more: The stolen cells are called kleptocnidae — literally "stolen stingers". They travel through the slug's gut untriggered and end up stored point-outwards in little sacs at the ends of the frills, which are called cerata. The slug never has to build a weapon of its own.

facts.text: The blue dragon eats Portuguese man o' war and keeps the stings. It packs them in tighter than they started, so a sting from this thumb-sized slug can be worse than one from the animal it ate.
facts.more: It floats upside down at the surface, holding a bubble of gas in its stomach to stay up, riding wind and current. Blue side up toward the sky, silver-gray side down into the water — hard to spot from above and hard to spot from below.

facts.text: Some sea slugs steal solar panels. They eat algae, keep the chloroplasts alive inside their own gut lining, and turn leaf-green while those stolen parts go on catching sunlight for months.
facts.more: The trick is called kleptoplasty. Elysia chlorotica is the famous one — leaf-green, leaf-shaped, and so packed with working chloroplasts that at a glance you would file it under plant rather than animal. No other group of animals does this the way sea slugs do.

facts.text: One sea slug can throw away its entire body. The head crawls off on its own, wound and all, and grows a new heart, gut and everything else back.
facts.more: Researchers watched Elysia marginata do it. The head takes hours to work free at a groove just behind it. It is crawling and feeding again the same day. It has a complete new body in about three weeks. Only young ones manage it. The cast-off body moves for days but never grows a head.

facts.text: Those two horns on its head are noses. Rhinophores pull scent out of the water and steer the slug toward food, and many species can pull them down into a pocket if danger gets close.
facts.more: Its eyes are almost useless — two dots about a quarter of a millimeter across that tell light from dark and little else. A sea slug lives in a world of smell and touch, feeling its way across a reef it has never really seen.

facts.text: Every sea slug is male and female at the same time — and still needs a partner. Two line up side by side, and both crawl away able to lay eggs.
facts.more: The eggs go down in a coiled ribbon, often bright white or pink, stuck to a rock or sometimes to the very animal the parent was eating. Some ribbons hold tens of thousands of eggs. The parents do not stay around for any of it.

facts.text: Nudibranchs run from 0.16 in (4 mm) — smaller than a grain of rice — up to 2 ft (60 cm). The big one is the Spanish dancer, which swims by flapping its whole body like a red skirt.
facts.more: For all that color and machinery, the show is short. Most sea slugs are gone inside a year, and some last only a few weeks.

facts.text: Others go the opposite way and disappear. A slug that lives on one particular sponge grows the exact color and bumpiness of that sponge — you can stare straight at it and miss it.
Sea slugs live in every ocean on Earth. Tide pools you could stand in. Tropical reefs. Water more than 2,300 ft (700 m) down. The cold dark underneath polar ice.

name: Mantis shrimp
blurb: Not actually a shrimp. It is a reef crustacean called a stomatopod. It has the fastest punch in the ocean and the strangest eyes on Earth.
size: About as long as your hand; the biggest is the length of your forearm
wonder: A spring, a latch, three-way eyes and armor that engineers are still trying to copy, all packed into something the length of your hand.

facts.text: The punch travels at 23 m/s (51 mph), about the speed of a car on a main road. It starts from a dead stop, inside a body the length of your hand.
facts.more: The arm goes from still to full speed in around two ten-thousandths of a second, pulling more than 10,000 times the tug of gravity you feel standing still. You never see it happen. You only see the result.

facts.text: Muscle alone is far too slow for that. The mantis shrimp cocks its arm against a saddle-shaped spring in its shell, latches it, and lets go. That is a crossbow, not an arm.
facts.more: The spring is a curved plate of stiff and stretchy layers that squashes flat as the muscle slowly pulls it down. A latch holds everything in place. When the latch slips, all that stored energy dumps out at once. Slow to load, impossible to dodge.

facts.text: It lands about 1,500 newtons of force. That is more than a thousand times its own body weight. It cracks open the shell of a crab, a snail or a clam like a nut.

The punch is so fast the water cannot keep up. The arm tears open a bubble of vapor behind it. A heartbeat later the bubble collapses with a bang and a burst of heat. That is a second hit on the same spot.
facts.more: The effect is called cavitation. It means a mantis shrimp can damage a snail it technically missed. Aquarium keepers know the sound. It is a dry crack from somewhere inside the tank, like someone tapping the glass with a coin.

facts.text: People keep mantis shrimp in aquariums, and people keep replacing the glass. If one decides it does not like the wall of its tank, it will punch the wall, and glass has lost before.
Your eye has three kinds of color cell. A mantis shrimp's has twelve to sixteen, reaching from deep ultraviolet all the way past red into light you will never see.
facts.more: You would assume that means richer color than we get. It doesn't — tested carefully, a mantis shrimp is actually worse than you at telling similar shades apart. It seems to sweep its eyes across a scene and read color in one pass instead of comparing. Cruder, but far faster.

facts.text: Each eye works on its own. It sits on a stalk, swivels wherever it likes, and is split into three strips — so one eye by itself can judge how far away something is.
facts.more: You need both of your eyes to judge distance. A mantis shrimp needs one, and has a spare aimed somewhere else entirely. For an animal whose whole plan is a single perfectly aimed strike, knowing the exact range matters more than almost anything.

facts.text: Mantis shrimp see a kind of light no other animal is known to see. Light can spiral as it travels — circular polarisation — and they read it, and reflect it off their own bodies.
facts.more: It amounts to a private channel. Almost nothing else in the sea can pick up that spiralling light, so a signal sent in it is invisible to a predator swimming right past. Only a handful of mantis shrimp species are known to do it.

facts.text: There are two kinds of mantis shrimp: smashers and spearers. Smashers carry a club and break shells open. Spearers carry a spiny arm and stab soft, fast things like fish.
facts.more: A spearer sits in a burrow with just its eyes out. It waits for a fish to swim within reach. Then it snaps the barbed arm out and drags the fish in. A smasher goes shopping instead. It crawls the reef, turning over crabs and snails and hammering them apart.

facts.text: Engineers are copying the club. The smasher's hammer takes thousands of hits without shattering, because inside it the fibers are stacked in a slow twisting spiral that stops cracks running.
facts.more: A crack tries to travel straight. In a spiral stack there is no straight line to follow, so the crack bends, splits and runs out of energy. Materials scientists have built the same twisting pattern into test panels and body armor, chasing something light that simply refuses to break.

facts.text: Some mantis shrimp pair up for life. A male and female zebra mantis shrimp share one burrow, and the same pair turns up in the same hole year after year. Nobody has followed a couple the whole way; twenty years together is the best read.
facts.more: They take turns. One guards the mouth of the burrow while the other hunts, and the pair keep the tunnel dug out and clear between them. For an animal famous for hitting things, it is a surprisingly settled home life.

facts.text: Most mantis shrimp are about 4 in (10 cm) long — the width of your hand. The zebra mantis shrimp reaches 15 in (38 cm), roughly the length of your forearm.

name: Pistol shrimp
blurb: A thumb-sized shrimp with one oversized claw that kills by snapping a bubble at things.
size: About as long as your thumb — and one claw is nearly half of that
wonder: God put one of the ocean's loudest sounds inside a claw smaller than your thumb.

facts.text: Its weapon isn't the claw — it's the bubble. The claw shuts so fast the water tears open into a vapor pocket called cavitation, and the pocket's collapse is the punch.
facts.more: Snap the claw and a jet of water shoots out at about 56 mph (90 km/h) — highway speed. Water cannot follow that fast, so it splits, leaving an empty bubble behind. Less than a thousandth of a second later the bubble caves in, and that collapse is the shockwave.

facts.text: It never has to touch its dinner. A small fish or worm passing the burrow gets hit by the shockwave and stops moving. The shrimp strolls out and collects it.
facts.more: That is why the claw is shaped the way it is. There is no cutting edge and no crushing surface — just a plunger and a socket, built to slam and make a bubble. A shrimp that misses simply resets and waits.

facts.text: Point a microphone at a coral reef and the crackle you hear — like bacon frying — is thousands of these shrimp snapping. It is one of the loudest sounds in the sea.
facts.more: Snapping shrimp compete with sperm whales and belugas for loudest animal in the ocean. In the Second World War, submarine crews learned to hide inside shrimp beds. The racket swamped enemy sonar completely. A steel submarine full of people simply vanished into the noise.

facts.text: When the bubble collapses, it flashes. Real light, made by a shrimp — far too faint for your eye, but cameras in dark tanks have caught it.
facts.more: The name for it is shrimpoluminescence. The collapse squeezes that speck of gas violently. It passes 5,000 degrees, about the temperature of the sun's surface. That lasts a few billionths of a second, then it goes dark. The shrimp itself is completely unbothered.

facts.text: Some share a home with a fish. The shrimp digs and repairs the burrow; the goby stands guard at the doorway and signals when danger comes.
facts.more: The shrimp sees very poorly, so it keeps one antenna resting on the goby's body the whole time it works. A flick of the fish's tail sends the shrimp straight back down the hole. Neither animal could hold that patch of seabed alone.

facts.text: One kind lives inside a sponge in a colony of over three hundred, with a single egg-laying queen and big-clawed defenders at the door. Eusocial — the same word used for ants.
facts.more: Everyone in the sponge is family. The defenders do not breed; they patrol the tunnels and snap at any shrimp that is not kin. This was the first animal ever found living an ant's kind of life underwater.

facts.text: The claws don't match — one huge, one ordinary. Lose the big one and the small claw grows into a snapper, while a new small claw sprouts where the big one was.
facts.more: Lose the snapping claw and the tool on the other side gets promoted. A replacement tool then grows in the empty socket. No other animal is known to do this.

facts.text: Most snapping shrimp are 1.2 to 2 in (3 to 5 cm) long (1 to 2 inches). That is small enough to sit in a tablespoon. It is also loud enough to rival a whale.
The snap is a warning as much as a weapon. Two shrimp arguing over a burrow will snap at each other until one backs down — no contact, just pressure and noise.
Most live in burrows they dig themselves under rubble and coral. In many species a male and female share one tunnel. They keep it in repair together.
It sees very poorly. Two pairs of antennae do nearly all the work, tasting the water and reading the current for anything that moves close by.

name: Coconut crab
blurb: The largest crab that walks on land — a hermit crab that outgrew every shell in the sea and climbs trees instead.
size: Leg tip to leg tip, about 1 meter (3 feet) — the width of a doorway
wonder: God gave one crab lungs, climbing claws, and armor tough enough to survive the fall.

facts.text: It is the largest arthropod that walks on land. Leg tip to leg tip a big one spans a meter (3 feet) and weighs about 9 lb (4 kg) — a large housecat.
Scientists measured the pinch. The strongest crab tested squeezed with 1,765 newtons — like balancing two adults on a single point, and it does not let go quickly.
facts.more: Researchers coaxed twenty-nine wild crabs into gripping a force sensor, and the biggest produced that figure. A strong adult's hand manages a few hundred newtons at most. The claw is not a threat display — it genuinely crushes.

facts.text: It is a hermit crab. As a youngster it lugs a borrowed snail shell around like any other, then outgrows every shell in the sea and hardens its own back instead.
facts.more: Young coconut crabs will even use a broken coconut shell when snail shells run short. Once the abdomen toughens up the crab gives up shells for good, and a full-grown one could never squeeze into one again.

facts.text: It cannot swim, and it cannot breathe underwater. Leave an adult in the sea for about an hour and it drowns, because it breathes air through a branchiostegal lung.
facts.more: The lung sits where a sea crab's gills would be, in a chamber under the shell. It only works while it is damp, so the crab dips its legs in a puddle and lets the water wick up into the chamber.

facts.text: It hunts by smell, and it is extremely good at it. The antennae pick up rotting meat, split fruit and coconut from a long way across an island.
facts.more: Its smelling organs work more like an insect's than a sea crab's. Scent drifting through air behaves nothing like scent dissolved in water. The equipment has to match. A dead animal on a beach pulls crabs in from well inland.

facts.text: Yes, it really does open coconuts. It hammers at the three soft eye-spots with its claw, sometimes over several days, then digs the flesh out with its smaller legs.
facts.more: It is slow, unglamorous work — hours of stripping husk fiber by fiber before the shell underneath is even exposed. Coconuts are not the main course either. These crabs eat fruit, seeds, dead animals, and sometimes each other.

facts.text: It is not only a scavenger. A researcher on a Pacific island watched one climb a tree at night, grip a sleeping seabird by the wing, and break it.
facts.more: The bird was a red-footed booby, which roosts up in the branches. Once it was down, more crabs arrived out of the dark to share it. That was the first clear record of a coconut crab hunting an animal with a backbone.

facts.text: It climbs. Adults go straight up coconut palms, hooking in with the sharp tips of their walking legs — and the quickest way down is to let go.
facts.more: A coconut crab can drop 4.5 meters (15 feet) onto hard ground — higher than a basketball hoop — and simply walk away, protected by its own armor. Up a trunk there is nothing on the island that can eat it.

facts.text: The mother carries her eggs down to the sea and shakes them loose at high tide. The larvae drift as plankton for three or four weeks before crawling ashore — where the adults can never follow.
It digs a burrow in sand or leaf litter and lines it with shredded coconut fiber, which holds moisture. A coconut crab in a dry burrow is a coconut crab in trouble.
It grows only by shedding. The whole armored shell splits and slides off, and the crab hides underground for weeks, soft as rubber, eating its old shell for the calcium.

It takes its time. A coconut crab can breed at about five years old, but reaching full size takes forty years or more. Nobody has followed one from hatching to that size; the growth rate is the argument, and it puts the biggest past sixty.
facts.more: That is the strange thing about a really large coconut crab. The animal in front of you has been walking that same patch of island since before you were born, growing a fraction wider at every shed.

name: Japanese spider crab
blurb: A deep-water crab whose legs stretch further than any other animal with a shell on the outside.
size: Claw tip to claw tip, up to 12 ft (3.7 m) — two grown adults lying head to toe
wonder: Twelve feet across, in water where almost no light reaches — made beautiful with nobody down there to see it.

facts.text: No animal with an exoskeleton reaches further. Claw tip to claw tip: 12 ft (3.7 m). Lie down beside one and its legs would stretch past your head and your feet.
The body is the surprise. Nearly all that span is leg — the shell itself, the carapace, is only about 15.7 in (40 cm) across.
For all that reach, it is not heavy. The biggest weigh about 42 lb (19 kg) — a five-year-old child, spread thin across twelve feet of leg.
It lives deep. Most are found 656 to 984 ft (200 to 300 m) down (650 to 1,000 ft) on sand and rock, in cold water where almost no daylight arrives.
facts.more: The full range runs from about 164 to 1,969 ft (50 to 600 m). That depth is why almost nobody meets one. They come up in traps and nets off the Pacific coast of Japan. A handful live in aquariums. In the wild they are a submarine's find, not a diver's.

facts.text: It decorates itself. The crab picks up sponges, anemones and scraps of seaweed and presses them onto its shell until it looks like a lump of seabed with legs.
facts.more: The passengers are called epibionts, and they keep growing where they are put. Some sponges taste foul, which makes an already well-hidden crab an unappetising one too. Decorator crabs will move their trimmings across to the fresh shell after a moult.

facts.text: Those legs come off on purpose. If something grabs one, the crab casts it away at a built-in break point — autotomy — and walks off on the other nine.
facts.more: Crabs pulled up in nets are often short two or three legs, and they get along perfectly well on what is left. A really big spider crab is almost never quite symmetrical.

facts.text: It is a scavenger with enormous patience. Dead fish, shellfish, algae, anything soft on the bottom — it prises shells apart and picks the seabed over slowly.
A female can carry up to 1.5 million eggs at once, glued in a mass under her body. They hatch in about ten days as specks of plankton, and hardly any survive.
facts.more: Almost all of that million and a half drift off and are eaten within days. A handful settle to the bottom and begin the long, slow climb to twelve feet across.

facts.text: It grows only by moulting. The old shell splits along the back and the crab drags all ten enormous legs out through the gap, like peeling off soaking wet gloves.
The males are the giants. A male's front claw-bearing legs, the chelipeds, grow far longer than the rest of him, while a female's stay shorter than her walking legs.
Once a year they come up. In winter and early spring they gather in shallower water, sometimes only 164 ft (50 m) down, to breed — the one season anyone finds them easily.
For all its size it is a mild animal. Keepers describe them as slow and gentle — though a claw on the end of a six-foot leg still has surprising reach.

name: Hermit crab
blurb: A crab with a soft, curled tail that borrows an empty snail shell to live in, and trades up as it grows.
size: Most are between a thumb and a fist in size, shell included
wonder: A creature born without armor — set down on a shore already scattered with exactly the right empty shells.

facts.text: Its back half is bare. Under the borrowed shell the abdomen is soft, pale and twisted into a spiral, curled to fit the inside of a snail shell exactly.
facts.more: That spiral is the whole reason for the shell. The front of a hermit crab is armored like any crab — claws, legs, hard head end. Everything behind it is naked, and would be a free meal in seconds.

facts.text: It doesn't just sit in the shell — it grips. Hooked rear legs and a muscular tail clamp onto the columella, the shell's inner pillar, and it will not let go while it lives.
facts.more: Pull at a hermit crab and it will let its own legs tear off before it comes out. If you want to see the crab, put a better empty shell nearby and wait. Never tug.

facts.text: They queue for houses. A crab that finds a shell too big waits beside it. As others arrive they line up largest to smallest. Then all of them swap at once, down the line.
facts.more: Biologists call it a vacancy chain, and a line can reach twenty crabs holding onto one another. The largest takes the new shell, the next takes the one it just left, and the smallest walks off in a shell nobody else wanted.

facts.text: When shells are scarce, they fight. One crab grabs another's shell and raps it hard against its own — knock, knock, knock — until the owner gives up and is evicted.
facts.more: The rapping is a test as much as an attack. A strong, well-fed occupant holds on far longer than a tired one. How hard and how fast the attacker knocks tends to decide who ends up in which shell.

facts.text: Not everything they live in is a shell. Hermit crabs have been found inside bottle caps, broken glass and burned-out light bulbs — anything hollow with a rim to grip.
facts.more: On some beaches this turns deadly. A crab can climb into slippery plastic and never climb out. One that dies inside gives off a scent that says empty shell going spare. That draws in more crabs. Hundreds have been found in a single container.
