facts.text: Some carry a bodyguard. A sea anemone rides on the shell, stinging anything that comes too close, and gets the crab's leftovers and a free ride in return.
facts.more: When the crab moves house it strokes the anemone until it releases its grip, then lifts it across to the new shell by hand. Neither animal is trapped. This is mutualism — two creatures, each getting something out of it.

facts.text: It shops carefully. Finding an empty shell, a crab will roll it over, run its claws around the opening, weigh it, and climb in and out before committing.
It starts life at sea. The eggs hatch into drifting plankton. A young crab eventually crawls ashore and goes looking for its first tiny shell.
To grow, it buries itself. Land hermit crabs dig down, shed the whole exoskeleton, and stay hidden for up to two months while the new one hardens — then eat the old one.
The biggest hermit crab gives up on shells altogether. The coconut crab starts out shell-carrying like the rest, then outgrows every shell in the ocean and hardens its own back.
A land hermit crab carries its own water supply. A little puddle of seawater sloshes in the back of the shell, keeping the gills damp — no water, no breathing.
facts.more: This is why land hermit crabs stay near the coast, and why a tank needs both fresh and salt water. Gills only work wet. Let that puddle dry out and the crab suffocates in open air.

facts.text: They last. The big land species live for decades, not seasons — and the oldest hermit crab ever kept as a pet reached forty-five, older than most people's parents.

name: Fiddler crab
blurb: A small mudflat crab. The male has one ordinary claw and one absurdly enormous one. He waves the big one like a flag.
size: About 1.2 in (3 cm) across, with a claw nearly as big as the rest of him
wonder: God set the rhythm of the tides ticking inside a crab about 1.2 in (3 cm) across.

facts.text: One claw is a spoon and the other is a wrecking ball. In a male fiddler crab that big claw — the major cheliped — can reach half his total weight.
facts.more: He carries it everywhere: in and out of a burrow, across open mud with birds overhead. It is heavy, it slows him down, and it is almost useless for eating. He waves it for hours anyway.

facts.text: He waves it. Every species has its own wave — a slow arc, a sharp snap, a circle — and females read the timing as carefully as the size.
facts.more: Put a hundred males on one mudflat and the whole surface flickers. A female walks through the display, stopping at burrow after burrow, and inspects the hole he dug as well as the crab waving beside it.

facts.text: Watch the mud and you can see the leftovers. A fiddler crab scoops up sediment, sifts out the algae and bacteria, and spits the cleaned grains back out as neat little balls.
facts.more: The mouthparts work like a stack of sorting sieves, floating the light organic bits upward and letting the heavy sand drop. One crab can leave hundreds of pellets around its burrow in a single low tide — a map of exactly where it walked.

facts.text: Females have two small claws and both work as spoons. A male can only feed with one — so the female beside him gets through her dinner at roughly twice his rate.
Lose the big claw and a new one grows at the next moult, about the same size but much weaker. From any distance it looks identical, so it still works as a bluff.
facts.more: A fight between two males is mostly a shoving match of interlocked claws. A regrown claw is lighter to carry and hopeless in a real contest. Most disputes are settled by waving, long before anyone tests it.

facts.text: Its eyes are on sticks. Two long stalks lift them clear of the mud for almost all-round vision — a fiddler crab can watch a bird behind it while walking forwards.
facts.more: The stalks fold flat into grooves on the shell when the crab reverses into its burrow. Above the eye's midline is sky; below it is ground. Anything appearing above that line gets treated as a bird, and the crab runs first and checks later.

facts.text: It digs a hole and shuts the door. At high tide the crab seals the top with a plug of mud, trapping a pocket of air to breathe until the water drains away again.
It knows the tide without seeing it. Keep a fiddler crab in a lab with no sea and no daylight, and it still turns active exactly when low tide would be.
facts.more: The rhythm runs on a roughly 12.4-hour cycle, matching the tides, and it keeps time for weeks with no cue at all. The color change runs on schedule too — dark by day, pale by night, inside a sealed box far from any shore.

facts.text: Some males build. Beside the burrow they raise a small pillar or hood of mud. Females walk toward the structures. So it looks like a landmark, pulling them in from further away than a waving claw can.
When a shadow crosses the flat, the whole colony vanishes. Hundreds of crabs drop into their burrows at the same instant, and the mud goes still and empty in under a second.
It drums as well as waves. At night, when no one can see a claw, the male raps it against the ground and the female feels the beat through the mud.
The female carries her eggs in a spongy orange mass under her body, then wades out at high tide and shakes them loose. The larvae go to sea and return weeks later as pinhead crabs.

name: Colossal squid
blurb: The heaviest animal on Earth without a backbone. It is a deep-water squid from the seas around Antarctica. It is built like a barrel and armed with hooks.
size: About 13.8 ft (4.2 m) long and up to about 1,091 lb (495 kg).
wonder: The finest eye in all the world, made for a place where almost nothing is there to see it.

facts.text: No animal without a backbone weighs more. One hauled up off Antarctica tipped the scales at 1,091 lb (495 kg).
facts.more: A New Zealand fishing crew brought it up from the Ross Sea, froze it whole, and shipped it to a museum. Scientists later thawed it in a bath of salt water so they could measure it properly. Its body alone was 8 ft (2.5 m) long.

facts.text: Its eye is the largest known on any animal — about 10.5 in (27 cm) across when measured, and probably wider still in life. A dinner plate, with a lens like a grapefruit.
facts.more: Below 2,000 ft (600 m) — deeper than two Eiffel Towers stacked — the only light is light that living things make. A huge eye gathers whatever faint glow reaches it. Sperm whales hunt in that same black water, and they are hunting for this.

facts.text: Look at the arm tips. Every one carries hooks that swivel round in their sockets — no other squid in its whole family has them.
facts.more: The two long tentacles end in clubs fitted with three-pointed hooks as well. Between the hooks and the suckers, the squid gets a grip that a thrashing fish cannot twist its way out of.

facts.text: The only hard part of a colossal squid is its beak. Everything else is muscle and water — and that beak is the biggest of any squid known.
facts.more: It works like a parrot's: two curved plates that shear instead of crush. Beaks do not break down quickly, so they collect in the stomachs of sperm whales. Counting them is one of the main ways we know these squid are down there at all.

facts.text: That record-breaking squid was caught mid-meal. It was still gripping a hooked Patagonian toothfish when the fishing line reached the surface.
Its flesh is soaked in ammonium, the sharp-smelling stuff in cleaning spray. That fluid is lighter than seawater, so the squid simply hangs in the dark without swimming.
facts.more: Floating for free is a clever way to live where food is scarce — no fins beating, no energy burned. The cost is flavor. Colossal squid meat is bitter and reeks of ammonia, which is why it never turns up on anybody's plate.

facts.text: It circles Antarctica in water barely above freezing. The young drift in the top 1,600 ft (500 m); the adults sink far below that, into permanent dark.
A deep-sea camera 1,969 ft (600 m) down has filmed a living colossal squid. It was the first time ever. The animal was a young one, see-through, about the length of your forearm.
facts.more: The juvenile was roughly 12 in (30 cm) long and almost completely transparent. Its arms trailed like glass threads. Adults are not transparent at all. Until that footage, every colossal squid anyone had ever examined was already dead.

facts.text: It is not the longest squid — the giant squid wins on tentacles. But the colossal squid is far heavier: thick and barrel-bodied where the giant squid is stretched thin.
Sperm whales dive after them. We know because whale stomachs are full of squid beaks, and in one Antarctic study one beak in every seven belonged to a colossal squid.
facts.more: A sperm whale can dive past 3,300 ft (1,000 m) and stay down for the better part of an hour. There is no light in that water at all. It hunts by echolocation. It finds its meal by listening to the echo of its own clicks.

facts.text: Nobody has ever seen a fully grown colossal squid alive. Everything we know about the adults comes from bodies in fishing nets, or beaks inside whales.

name: Vampire squid
blurb: A small, soft, red deep-sea animal that is neither a squid nor an octopus, and wears its eight arms like a hooded cloak.
size: About as long as your forearm, hand included.
wonder: Built for a layer of ocean almost nothing else can live in — and given a light of its own to carry there.

facts.text: Its scientific name means "vampire squid from hell." It drinks no blood, chases nothing, and eats mostly falling scraps. The name is about the cloak.
facts.more: The webbing between its eight arms pulls up over its whole body like a cape, and the skin is deep red to black. Under a ship's floodlight it looks sinister. Down where it actually lives, red light never reaches, so a red animal simply looks black — which is to say, invisible.

facts.text: It fishes with a thread. One long sticky filament drifts out into the dark, collects whatever is sinking past, and gets reeled slowly back in.
facts.more: What it collects is marine snow. That is crumbs of dead plankton, shed skin and waste, drifting down from the sunlit water far above. Tiny finger-like cirri wipe the filament clean. They mix the catch with mucus and roll it into a ball small enough to swallow.

facts.text: Eight arms, but it is no octopus. Two thin filaments, but they are not squid tentacles. It belongs to a group all of its own, and it is the only kind in it.
It lives in a layer of ocean with almost no oxygen in it — as little as three percent of what surface water holds. Almost nothing else can stay there.
facts.more: That band sits roughly 1,969 to 2,953 ft (600 to 900 m) (2,000 to 3,000 ft) down — call it a mile of black water overhead. Most hunters cannot follow it in. The vampire squid drifts through on a body that burns less fuel than any other deep-sea cephalopod ever measured.

facts.text: Threatened, it turns itself inside out. The cloak flips up over its head, and what was soft webbing becomes a ball of spines pointing outward in every direction.
facts.more: The spines are not really sharp — they are the soft cirri it feeds with, and they bend. But the shape is convincing. Remote submarine cameras have caught the animal holding this "pineapple" pose under a bright light, then flipping back the moment the light swings away.

facts.text: It has no ink at all. Instead it fires a cloud of sticky mucus packed with glowing blue orbs, and by the time that cloud fades — nearly ten minutes — it is long gone.
facts.more: Ink works in sunlit water, where a black cloud hides you against the blue. At 2,297 ft (700 m) there is nothing for a black cloud to hide against, because everything is already black. A cloud of light is the version that works down there.

facts.text: For its size, its eyes are the largest of any animal. Its soft body is only 6 in (15 cm) long, and its eyes are 1 in (2.5 cm) across — marbles, set in your palm.

Nearly every squid and octopus breeds once and then dies. Not this one. Nobody has followed a female through her whole life, but the bodies say she can spawn, rest, and spawn again — twenty times or more.
facts.more: Researchers found this by studying preserved females. Some carried the spent remains of an old batch of eggs. A fresh batch was getting ready alongside it. That shows a resting phase in between. In the slow, cold, low-oxygen deep, there is time to do it more than once.

facts.text: As a youngster it jets about. Grown up, it flaps two ear-like fins instead and cruises — far cheaper travel when meals are only crumbs.
Its skin is dotted with light organs it can switch on and off, and the tips of all eight arms can glow. A flash may last a blink or several minutes.
Its body is a jelly loaded with ammonium, weighing almost exactly what the seawater around it weighs. So it does not sink and does not float. It just hangs.
Full grown, it is about 12 in (30 cm) from arm tips to tail — and the soft body is only half of that. Smaller than the name makes you expect.

name: Common cuttlefish
blurb: A shallow-water relative of the squid and octopus. It can redraw the pattern on its own skin in less than a second.
size: About as long as your forearm — and the biggest have a body half a meter (19 in) long all by itself.
wonder: Skin that thinks — two hundred color sacs in a pinhead of it, every one wired straight to the brain and ready in a heartbeat.

facts.text: In one square millimeter of skin — a pinhead — there can be 200 color sacs. Each is a bag of pigment ringed with tiny muscles, wired straight to the brain.
facts.more: Pull the muscles and the sac stretches wide, showing its color. Let go and it shrinks to an invisible speck. Because nerves run to each one directly, with nothing in between, a whole pattern can sweep across the body in well under a second.

facts.text: Here is the strange part. A cuttlefish is colorblind. It has one single kind of light detector and sees the world in shades of gray — and still matches the colors of the seafloor.
Its pupil is a wavy W. And it focuses like a camera, sliding the whole lens forwards and backwards, instead of squashing the lens the way your eye does.
Eight arms are for holding. The other two are hidden weapons: they fire out of pockets under the eyes in about 30 thousandths of a second, several times faster than you can blink.
facts.more: There is no bone anywhere in a tentacle. Muscle alone stiffens it. Squeezing one set of muscles makes the tentacle longer instead of fatter. It shoots out most of its own length again. The shrimp has not registered anything at all.

facts.text: It can see the twist in light — polarisation — that your eyes cannot. Silvery fish scales and see-through shrimp show up in patterns completely invisible to you.
Watch one stalk a crab. Dark bands roll down its body, over and over, like cloud shadow crossing a field. Scientists call the display the passing cloud.
facts.more: It shows up mostly while the cuttlefish is closing in on crabs and shrimp. There is still real argument about what it does. One thing is certain. The crab is watching a moving pattern on the front of the animal when the tentacles arrive.

facts.text: Inside its back sits the cuttlebone: a stack of thin chambers holding gas and liquid, layered like the pages of a book. Shift the balance and the cuttlefish rises or sinks without moving a fin.
facts.more: A submarine does the same trick with ballast tanks. Here it is packed into a piece of shell lighter than a slice of bread. The chambers cannot take deep pressure. A cuttlebone crushes somewhere between 656 and 1,969 ft (200 and 600 m) (650 to 2,000 ft) down. That keeps cuttlefish in shallow water.

facts.text: Three hearts. Two push blood through the gills, one pushes it round the body. And the blood is not red but green-blue, because it carries oxygen on copper instead of iron.
Two males meeting go striped. Bold black-and-white zebra bars flare across both bodies. Usually one of them backs off before anybody actually touches anybody.
facts.more: Smaller males have been seen doing something sneakier. They drop into the soft mottled pattern of a female and tuck their arms in close. Then they drift straight past a much larger guarding male without ever being challenged.

facts.text: A cuttlefish starts learning before it hatches. Embryos that watched crabs through the clear wall of the egg chose to hunt crabs once they came out.
facts.more: The eggs are laid in dark bunches that look like grapes. They turn clear as the embryo grows inside. The eyes work well before hatching. In experiments, hatchlings shown crabs later picked crabs over shrimp. Shrimp is the usual favorite. That preference was set before the animal had eaten anything.

facts.text: Resting cuttlefish twitch. Their skin flickers through colors, their eyes roll, their arms jerk — a state that looks a great deal like the sleep in which people dream.
facts.more: It arrives in short bouts of a minute or two in an otherwise still animal, over and over. Whether a cuttlefish dreams, nobody can say. What the cameras record is a sleeping creature whose skin will not hold still.

facts.text: Its ink has a name you already use. Sepia — that warm red-brown in old photographs — was made from cuttlefish ink for hundreds of years.
facts.more: People borrowed the cuttlebone too. Caged birds gnaw it for calcium. Jewelers press a shape into a split cuttlebone and pour molten silver straight in. Those fine chambers hold the detail and survive the heat.

name: Chambered nautilus
blurb: A cephalopod that lives inside a coiled shell. About ninety small tentacles and two pinhole eyes peer out of it.
size: Shell about as wide across as a side plate; the biggest reach dinner-plate size.
wonder: Thirty sealed rooms, grown one at a time, each exactly the right size — built by an animal that cannot see clearly enough to admire what it made.

facts.text: Every other cephalopod alive — octopus, squid, cuttlefish — keeps its shell on the inside, or has none at all. The nautilus is the only one that lives inside one.
The shell is a spiral of sealed chambers, around thirty in a grown animal. The nautilus lives only in the outermost room. The rest are empty and full of gas.
facts.more: A living tube called the siphuncle threads through every wall. It pumps salt out of a chamber and the water follows the salt out, leaving gas behind. Pump more out and the nautilus rises; let water back in and it sinks. A ballast tank, made of shell.

facts.text: The world's first nuclear-powered submarine was named Nautilus, and the name fits. Machine and animal both change depth by moving water in and out of sealed chambers.
Its eye has no lens whatsoever. It is a pinhole, open to the sea, filling and draining with seawater — a working eye with a hole where the lens should be.
facts.more: Light comes through the tiny opening and lands on the retina, exactly the way a pinhole camera works. The picture is dim and blurry. A nautilus can make out shapes and shadows, but it does not read a reef the way an octopus reads one.

facts.text: Smell does most of the work instead. A nautilus tracks a dead crab through pitch-dark water by scent alone, and baited traps pull them in from a long way off.
Count the tentacles: about ninety of them. Not one has a sucker. They are grooved and coated in sticky mucus, and they hold prey firmly without a single sucker between them.
Pull back, and a thick leathery hood folds down over the shell opening like a door filling a doorway. Then there is simply nothing left to bite.
It has been described as eating anything that smells. Dead fish, crab scraps, shed shells — the nautilus is mostly a tidier-up of the reef slope.
facts.more: It even eats the old moulted shells that crabs and shrimp leave behind. It moves slowly, eats rarely, and can go a long stretch between meals — a completely different life from a squid, which hunts almost constantly.

facts.text: Every night it climbs. By day it hangs deep. The deepest one ever tracked was at 2,306 ft (703 m), two Eiffel Towers down. After dark it rises up the reef slope to feed.
facts.more: There is a floor it cannot cross. Go deep enough and the water pressure would crush the chambers and the shell would implode. The animal that carries its own ballast tank also carries its own depth limit.

facts.text: A single egg takes nine to fifteen months to hatch — a very long wait for a sea creature.
facts.more: There is no swimming baby stage at all. Most sea animals hatch as a speck of drifting larva. A nautilus stays shut inside the egg until it is a tiny finished nautilus — shell, chambers, tentacles and all — and then crawls out ready to go.

facts.text: Most cephalopods live a year or two and die. Nobody has followed a nautilus from hatching to death. The shell grows very slowly, and that is the clue. The best read is that a nautilus can pass twenty years. It does not breed until it is well into that long life.
facts.more: That slow schedule is why collecting nautiluses for their shells is risky. A population that takes so long to replace itself cannot bounce back quickly. International trade in nautilus shells is now restricted by treaty.

facts.text: Four gills, arranged in two pairs. Every other living cephalopod makes do with two. The nautilus is the only one that breathes through four.

name: Box jellyfish
blurb: A cube-shaped jellyfish with tentacles trailing from each corner. It swims after its prey instead of drifting. Its sting is one of the fiercest in the ocean.
size: The largest bells reach basketball size; most are smaller. Tentacles trail up to 9.8 ft (3 m). A big one weighs about 4 lb (1.8 kg).
wonder: Twenty-four eyes and not one brain behind them — and still it steers, hunts, and finds its way home.

facts.text: Twenty-four eyes. They sit in four clusters of six, one cluster on each flat side of the box, and two eyes in every cluster have a proper lens.
facts.more: That is more kinds of eye than you own. Most are simple pits that only register light and dark. The two lensed ones build a real image — a blurry one, but an image — in an animal with nothing you could call a face.

facts.text: Twenty-four eyes, and no brain at all. What it has instead is a ring of nerve running right round the rim of the bell, coordinating every pulse and every turn.
One box jellyfish in the Caribbean keeps an eye aimed permanently straight up. It watches the mangrove trees through the surface and steers by them, back to the lagoon edge where the food is.
facts.more: Researchers tested this by floating the jellyfish in a clear tank among the mangroves and then moving the tank around. The animals swam toward the tree canopy every time. Take the canopy out of view and they swam in no particular direction at all.

facts.text: This one hunts. Most jellyfish go wherever the water goes. A box jellyfish beats its bell instead. It reaches about 1.5 meters a second (5.4 km/h, 3.4 mph), a brisk walking pace. It turns a half-circle in a few pulses.
Every tentacle is carpeted in stinging cells, so tiny the tentacle still looks smooth. Each is a coiled harpoon held under pressure, and it fires in less than a thousandth of a second.
facts.more: They do not go off just because something brushed past. It takes touch plus a chemical signal — the kind of proteins found on fish skin, and on yours. Which is exactly why a smooth plastic bag, or a thin nylon stinger suit, slides by untouched.

facts.text: Vinegar is the standard first aid on Australian beaches. Poured over a fresh sting, it shuts down for good every stinging cell that has not fired yet.
facts.more: It does nothing about venom already in the skin. That needs a hospital, and there is an antivenom. Stopping the unfired cells still matters enormously. A tentacle stuck to the skin keeps firing for as long as it stays there.

facts.text: It is among the most venomous animals known. At least 64 deaths have been recorded in Australia in all the time anyone has kept count — serious, but genuinely rare.
facts.more: Roughly three meters (10 ft) of tentacle stuck to skin can be life-threatening. One study followed 225 stings. Only about one in twelve needed a hospital bed. Most stings hurt badly and then heal.

facts.text: Almost perfectly clear. In shallow tropical water a box jellyfish is very nearly invisible. Lifeguards net off the swimming areas instead of trying to spot them.
Prawns and small fish, mostly. The tentacles stay short and coiled while it cruises, then stretch out to three meters (10 ft) — basketball-hoop height — once it starts hunting.
It begins life in a river mouth. Tiny polyps sit in mangrove creeks and brackish water, and the swimming jellyfish only appear in the warm wet season.
facts.more: Which is why northern Australia has a stinger season rather than a stinger problem all year round. The swimming adults live a matter of months and then are gone; the polyps back in the creeks simply carry on.

facts.text: Sea turtles eat them. A green turtle's skin and throat are thick enough that the stingers cannot get through, so it swallows box jellyfish whole, tentacles and all.
Not every box jellyfish is big. The Irukandji is the size of your thumbnail, small enough to lose in a glass of water, and it still puts people in hospital.
facts.more: Its sting is barely felt at first. The trouble comes about half an hour later — a wave of pain, sweating and sickness that doctors call Irukandji syndrome. Two deaths in Australia have been linked to it.

name: Orchid mantis
blurb: A hunting insect from the rainforests of Southeast Asia. Its whole body is shaped and colored like a flower. The flower is the trap.
size: A grown female is about as long as your thumb. The male is less than half her size.

facts.text: Look at those legs. Each of the four walking legs is flattened into a wide curved lobe, the exact shape of a petal. The mantis is not sitting on a flower. It is the flower.
facts.more: Biologists call this aggressive mimicry: a predator dressed as something harmless or inviting. The mantis holds still, forelegs folded, and waits. A bee or a butterfly comes shopping for nectar that was never there.

facts.text: Researchers set orchid mantises out in the rainforest, beside real flowers. Then they counted the visitors. More pollinating insects flew to the mantis than to the flowers.
facts.more: That is the startling part. The lure works better than the real thing. Bees, flies and butterflies chose the fake over blossoms growing an arm's length away — exactly what a hunter wants, and exactly what a flower does not.

facts.text: Despite the name, it is not copying one particular orchid. Measured the way a bee's eye would see it, its color sits inside the range of the flowers blooming around it.
facts.more: Bees see color differently from you — they pick up ultraviolet light your eyes cannot. When scientists compared the mantis with nearby blossoms using bee vision, they could not tell it apart from a flower. A general disguise, not a portrait of one species.

facts.text: A grown female is about as long as your thumb. The male is less than half her length and far lighter — the two barely look like the same insect.
facts.more: He is slim and quick, and he flies well. She is broad, petalled and heavy, and mostly stays put. The famous flower-shaped photographs are nearly always females.

facts.text: A newly hatched orchid mantis is not pink at all. It is red and black, and it looks like an assassin bug — an insect that tastes foul and bites hard.
facts.more: So the smallest, softest stage of its life is spent pretending to be something dangerous. After its first moult the red and black go, the white and pink come in, and the flower disguise begins.

facts.text: Mantises see in 3D. Scientists fitted them with tiny glasses and showed them an insect cinema, and the mantises struck at prey that existed only in the depth of the image.
facts.more: That makes them the only insects known to have stereopsis — judging distance by comparing what the left eye sees with what the right eye sees. It is the same trick your own two eyes are running right now.

facts.text: Bees, flies, butterflies, small wasps. The strike comes out of those folded front legs and it is finished before you could blink.
Some mantises can swivel the head nearly halfway round without shifting the body. Almost no other insect can turn and look behind itself.
It can shift between pink and brown to match whatever it is sitting on. The change is slow — days, not seconds. Nothing about this insect is in a hurry.
Cornered, a mantis rears up, throws its front legs wide and shows every marking it has. It suddenly looks twice its size and nothing at all like a flower.

Warm, wet rainforest across Southeast Asia: Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, Vietnam. It waits on leaves and stems in bright places. Flowers are everywhere there, and so are the insects that visit them.

wonder: The disguise reaches all the way down to the shape of one leg joint — that much care, on an insect the size of your thumb.

name: Stick insect
blurb: A long, slow, leaf-eating insect. It is shaped exactly like the twig it is standing on. Your eye slides straight past it.
size: Most are about 3.6 in (9 cm) long, about the length of a finger. The record-holder stretched longer than two 12-in school rulers laid end to end.

facts.text: The longest insect ever measured is a stick insect. Front foot to back foot with its legs stretched out, it reached 24.6 in (62.4 cm) — two school rulers, end to end.
facts.more: Its body alone, legs not counted, was 14.2 in (36.1 cm). The record-holder was found in southern China and is kept in a museum in Chengdu. One of its offspring, raised in captivity, grew longer still — 25 in (64 cm).

facts.text: The disguise is not only the shape. It is the stillness. A stick insect can hold one position for hours, and a hunting bird's eye is built to catch movement.
When the wind blows, it sways. Rocking gently from side to side is exactly what a real twig does in a breeze — so moving makes it harder to spot, not easier.
facts.more: Stillness only works while everything around it is still. The moment the branch starts moving, a perfectly motionless twig is the odd one out. So it joins in, swaying along with the branch.

facts.text: Many stick insects need no male at all. A female on her own lays eggs that hatch into daughters, every one of them a copy of her. It is called parthenogenesis.
facts.more: In some species almost the entire population is female. Where males do exist they can be rare, and much smaller than the females. A female that has never met one will still fill a branch with young.

facts.text: The eggs look like seeds — hard-shelled, and capped with a fatty knob called a capitulum. Ants find them, carry them underground, eat the knob and leave the egg unharmed.
facts.more: The egg then sits inside an ant nest: dark, damp, and guarded by ants against the wasps and beetles that would eat it. When it finally hatches, the young stick insect walks out through the ants' own tunnels.

facts.text: Grabbed by a leg, a stick insect can simply let the leg go. The joint has a built-in break point. A young one grows the missing leg back over its next few moults.
facts.more: This is autotomy — shedding a body part to escape. The bird is left holding a twitching leg while the rest of the insect walks away. The replacement usually comes back a little smaller than the original.

facts.text: Some species fight back with chemistry. A pair of glands just behind the head fire a fine spray, and they aim it. If it reaches your eyes it burns badly.
Not all of them are thin. The Lord Howe Island stick insect grows up to 8 in (20 cm) and weighs about 0.8 oz (23 g) — the weight of a AA battery. Islanders called it the tree lobster.
facts.more: It has no wings at all — heavy, glossy black, and it runs rather than flies. It was thought gone from the world entirely, until scientists climbing a bare sea stack called Ball's Pyramid found twenty-four of them living under a single shrub.

facts.text: Tree lobsters pair up. Keepers watching them at night see the male resting with three of his legs draped over his female — behavior almost unheard of anywhere else among insects.
Leaves, and nothing else. Stick insects chew through foliage at night when birds are not hunting, and spend the daylight hours pretending to be part of the plant.
Over 3,500 species are known. Some are shaped like leaves rather than twigs — flat bodies with fake veins, dried-looking brown edges, and holes that look nibbled.

wonder: Nothing about a stick insect asks to be noticed. Every part of it was made to be looked straight past — and it works, all day, every day.

name: Periodical cicada
blurb: A big red-eyed insect that spends more than a decade underground, drinking from tree roots. Then it climbs out in millions all at once to sing.
size: About 1.2 in (3 cm) long, with clear wings that reach past the end of its body.

facts.text: A periodical cicada spends 13 or 17 years underground. Not asleep — feeding, the whole time, on xylem fluid pulled from tree roots in the dark.
facts.more: Xylem is the plumbing that carries water up a tree, roots to leaves. It is thin stuff, mostly water, so a nymph has to pump a great deal of it to grow. It usually stays within about 2 ft (60 cm) of the surface the whole time.

facts.text: Thirteen and seventeen. Both are prime numbers. Nothing divides into them evenly except one and themselves. Every periodical cicada runs on one of those two clocks. Never twelve, never sixteen.
When they come up, they come up together. More than 1.5 million cicadas per acre have been counted — around 370 in every single square meter of forest floor.
facts.more: That is five or six cicadas on every patch of ground the size of your hand. It runs for miles in every direction. Every bird, squirrel, fish and dog eats until it cannot manage another. Millions are still left over to sing.

facts.text: The chorus can reach 100 decibels — as loud as a chainsaw or a motorbike going past. It is not a noise you hear so much as a wall you stand inside.
facts.more: Only the males sing. Each has a pair of ribbed plates called tymbals on the sides of his body. Muscles buckle those plates in and out hundreds of times a second, and the mostly hollow abdomen behind them works like the body of a guitar.

facts.text: They do not use a calendar. The nymphs come up when the soil about 8 in (20 cm) down passes 18°C (64°F). They are reading the temperature, underground, in the dark.
facts.more: Then the whole neighborhood goes at once. They dig upward and climb the nearest vertical thing. That means a trunk, a fence post, or your leg if you stand still long enough. Then they grip on tight for the last molt of their lives.

facts.text: The nymph digs with front legs thickened into shovels. At the end its back splits open, a soft pale crumpled adult hauls itself out, and the empty shell stays clinging to the bark.
facts.more: For an hour or two the new adult is pale and helpless while its wings unfold and its shell hardens. Those brown hollow hook-footed cases get left by the thousand on tree trunks — the easiest insect skin in the world to find.

facts.text: A female cuts slits into pencil-thin twigs with a blade on her abdomen and packs about 20 eggs into each one. She will lay 600 or more before she dies.
facts.more: The cutting damages the twig ends and the leaves beyond them turn brown — foresters call it flagging. A grown tree shrugs it off. When the young hatch they drop to the ground, dig in, and the long wait starts over.

facts.text: Adults are 0.9 to 1.3 in (2.4 to 3.3 cm) (about an inch) long. The body is black and the wing veins are orange. Two enormous red eyes stand out from across a room.
No sting. No bite. No poison, no speed, no hiding. The best read is that the whole defense is arithmetic — arrive in numbers too vast to be finished off.
Adults sip a little sap through a straw-shaped mouth, but they are not really here to eat. Four to six weeks above ground, and one job: find a mate.
There are seven kinds of periodical cicada — three on the 17-year clock, four on the 13-year clock. Each sings a different song, and females answer their own with a flick of the wings.

wonder: Seventeen years in the dark for six weeks in the light — and a whole forest keeps the appointment on the same day.

name: Termite
blurb: A small, pale, blind insect that eats wood and lives in colonies of millions. Some colonies sit inside earth towers that rise higher than a house.
size: A worker is tiny. The queen of the same colony can reach 4 in (11 cm), longer than your index finger.

facts.text: A worker termite is tiny. The queen of the same colony can reach 4 in (11 cm), longer than your index finger — and she cannot walk.
facts.more: Her abdomen swells into a soft white sausage packed with eggs, far too heavy for her legs to lift. Workers bring food to her, groom her, and haul the eggs away as fast as she makes them. She never leaves the royal chamber again.

facts.text: A big queen can lay more than 20,000 eggs in a single day. That works out at roughly one egg every four seconds, all day and all night, for years on end.
facts.more: She can head the same colony for decades. Termite queens are among the longest-lived insects known. Every worker in the mound came out of her. So did every soldier, and every winged one that flies off to start a colony somewhere else.

facts.text: Termites eat wood. The tough stuff inside it is called cellulose, and very few animals can break it down. Termites cannot manage it on their own either.
facts.more: A termite's gut is a packed zoo of microbes that break the cellulose down and hand the sugars over. Without them a termite would starve on a full stomach. Partners like this are called symbionts: two living things doing one job between them.

facts.text: Every time a termite moults it sheds its gut lining and loses its microbes along with it. It has to be topped up by a nestmate — and often that food comes out the back end.
facts.more: Termites feed each other constantly, mouth to mouth and end to end. The word for it is trophallaxis. A newly hatched termite starts with no microbes at all and gets its starter culture the same way. The colony passes its digestion around like a recipe.

facts.text: Some African mounds stand more than 16 ft (5 m) high. Stack three of yourself on top of each other and you still would not reach the top — and the builders are blind.
facts.more: In most species workers and soldiers have no eyes at all. They build by touch, by smell, and by feeling vibration through the walls. Nobody is holding the plan. Each termite simply responds to what the termite before it did, and a tower comes out of it.

facts.text: The mound is not the nest. The colony lives below it and inside it, and air really does move through the tower standing above — the best read is that it works as a chimney.
facts.more: As the sun heats one side of the mound and the night cools it down again, air rises and sinks through the tunnels in a slow daily cycle. Stale air and carbon dioxide go out, fresh air comes in. The mound breathes on a 24-hour rhythm.

facts.text: Architects in Harare, Zimbabwe built a large office block to work the way a termite mound works. It stays cool through the African day without normal air conditioning.
facts.more: The Eastgate Center pulls cool night air in at the bottom. The concrete soaks up that cool. Chimneys at the top push the day's hot air out. Cooled that way, the building runs on about a tenth of the energy. A conventional air-conditioned building of the same size needs the other nine tenths.

facts.text: Some termites are farmers. They chew wood, pass it through their bodies, and build the result into combs where they grow a fungus called Termitomyces — then eat the fungus.
facts.more: The fungus finishes the job the termites started, breaking the last of the wood down into food they can actually use. The combs sit deep inside the mound at a steady temperature. Very few animals on earth farm anything at all — leafcutter ants do, some beetles do, and these termites do.

facts.text: Soldier termites in some species have heads drawn out into a nozzle. They cannot bite at all. Instead they spray a sticky, resinous liquid that gums an attacking ant's legs together.
Termites drum. A disturbed soldier bangs its head against the tunnel wall, and the vibration runs out through the wood and the soil to the rest of the colony.
In north-eastern Brazil there are around 200 million termite mounds, spread over an area larger than Great Britain. Each is about 8 ft (2.5 m) tall and 30 ft (9 m) across.
facts.more: They stand roughly 66 ft (20 m) apart, built by one species, Syntermes dirus, an insect a centimeter and a half long. The mounds are not nests — they are spoil heaps from an enormous network of tunnels running underneath. The spacing is so regular it shows up from the air.

facts.text: Termites are not ants. People call them white ants, but scientists classify them with the cockroaches — a completely separate group from ants, bees and wasps.

wonder: Blind builders, working by touch, raising a tower that breathes on its own — and not one of them can see what they made.

name: Flea
blurb: A tiny wingless insect that drinks blood and jumps further for its size than almost anything else alive.
size: Tiny, and squashed flat from side to side.

facts.text: A flea can jump 7 in (18 cm) straight up — about 60 times its own body length. At your size that would be clearing a 25-story building from a standing start.
facts.more: Do the sum yourself. Sixty times the height of a nine-year-old comes out at roughly 275 ft (84 m). Sideways it manages 13 in (33 cm), further still for its size. There is no run-up — just a push off something as unhelpful as a carpet fiber.

facts.text: The jump is not muscle. Muscle is far too slow. A flea squeezes energy into a pad of rubbery protein called resilin, latches it shut, then lets it go all at once.
facts.more: Resilin is one of the springiest materials known — press it and it gives back almost every scrap of the energy you put in. The flea loads it slowly over a long moment, then releases the catch. What went in over a second comes out in an instant.

facts.text: People argued for years about which part of the leg did the pushing. High-speed film settled it: a flea shoves off from the tibia and tarsus — its shin and foot — not from the joint above them.
A flea is 0.06 to 0.13 in (1.5 to 3.3 mm) long. Three of them nose to tail would sit across your thumbnail. Everything else on this list is done by an animal that size.
A flea is flattened side to side like a page in a book, so it slips between hairs. It is covered in backward-pointing bristles. It also carries hard combs called ctenidia.
facts.more: Those combs catch in hair like the teeth of a ratchet, so a scratching paw drags over the flea rather than out with it. Its shell is tough enough that squeezing one between two fingers often does not kill it.

facts.text: Blood, and nothing but blood. A flea's saliva carries an anticoagulant — a chemical that stops blood clotting — so the wound keeps flowing while it drinks.
facts.more: The itch is not the bite. It is your own body reacting to the flea's spit, which holds more than a dozen substances that can set off an allergy. Some animals barely notice fleas at all; others are driven frantic by a handful of them.

facts.text: A female lays 20 to 30 eggs a day, about one an hour, and the eggs are smooth and non-sticky. They roll straight off the animal and land wherever it sleeps.
facts.more: So the bed, the carpet and the back of the sofa become the nursery, not the pet. Over a lifetime one female can produce hundreds of eggs, sometimes thousands. This is why treating the animal on its own almost never clears an infestation.

facts.text: Flea larvae are blind, legless and pale, and they do not drink blood. They eat the dried blood the adults drop — the black specks in a pet's fur that people call flea dirt.
facts.more: In feeding trials, larvae given adult flea droppings did better than larvae given dried blood alone. The adults are, in effect, feeding their own young by leaving crumbs behind them everywhere they go.

facts.text: A flea can wait inside its cocoon, fully formed and doing nothing at all. It comes out when it feels warmth, vibration through the floor, or the carbon dioxide of something breathing nearby.
facts.more: That is why an empty house can seem flea-free for weeks and then, an hour after someone moves back in, be full of them. The pupae had not gone anywhere. They were lying there listening for footsteps.

facts.text: There are about 2,500 kinds of flea, and most stick to a favorite sort of host. The one you are most likely to meet is the cat flea — which is also the flea usually found on dogs.
The oriental rat flea carries a bacterium back and forth between rats and people. It is called Yersinia pestis. That bacterium causes plague, one of the most serious diseases in human history.
facts.more: A blocked flea is a dangerous flea. The bacteria multiply in its gut until food can no longer get through. The starving insect bites again and again. Each bite pushes some of the blockage into the fresh wound.

facts.text: Flea circuses were real. Showmen fitted fine wire harnesses to live fleas and had them pull miniature carts and chariots using nothing but the flea's own strength.

wonder: No wings, no size, nothing to look at — and folded into one leg, a spring that works perfectly every single time.

name: Planarian
blurb: A soft, flat little worm that glides along the underside of stones in a cold stream. It can rebuild its whole body from a scrap.
size: Small, and as flat as a scrap of wet ribbon.

facts.text: Cut a planarian in half and you get two planarians. Cut it into pieces and every single piece can rebuild what it is missing — head, brain, gut, eyes, all of it.
facts.more: A fragment as small as one two-hundred-and-seventy-ninth of the worm has regrown into a complete animal. That is a speck you could lose on your fingertip. It rebuilds an entire body, front, back and middle, in about a week.

facts.text: Roughly one in five cells in its body is a stem cell called a neoblast. A neoblast is a blank cell. It can turn into whatever part the worm needs next.
facts.more: Most animals keep a few stem cells tucked away in special places. A planarian carries them scattered right through its body. That is why a random scrap of it already contains everything needed to start over.

facts.text: Split the head down the middle, but only partway, and each half finishes itself. The worm grows two heads and gets on with life using both.
facts.more: Scientists do this deliberately to study how a body knows which end is which. Each cut half rebuilds a full head, eyespots included, and the two-headed worm crawls around perfectly well.

facts.text: Those two dark dots are eyespots called ocelli. They cannot make a picture — they only report how bright it is and roughly which direction the light is coming from.
facts.more: Each eyespot sits inside a cup of dark pigment that shades it from one side. By comparing the two, the worm works out where the light is and crawls the other way. The pigment cups are also what give planarians that permanently cross-eyed expression.

facts.text: Its mouth is halfway down its belly, not on its head. It is also the only opening for food and waste — everything that goes in must come back out the same way.
facts.more: The gut branches through the body like a tree with no back door. Whatever cannot be digested gets pushed out through the mouth again.

facts.text: To eat, it shoves a muscular tube called a pharynx out through its belly, presses it into its food, and sucks. Dinner is drunk, never chewed.
Mostly it glides. Millions of microscopic hairs called cilia row against a strip of slime the worm lays down, and it slides along like a tiny hovercraft.
facts.more: Watch one on glass and it looks like it is being towed by an invisible string. When it needs to hurry it adds waves of muscle to the rowing, and it can swim with the same rippling motion.

facts.text: Some planarians make more planarians by gripping the ground with the tail, crawling forward with the front, and tearing themselves in two. Each half then regrows what it lost.
facts.more: The split is called fission. The back end holds fast while the front end pulls, and the worm rips apart at the waist. Within a few days there are two whole worms where there was one.

facts.text: Starve a planarian and it does not just get thin. It shrinks — the entire animal gets smaller while staying in proportion, then grows back when food returns.
facts.more: It is closer to resizing a photograph than to losing weight. The worm reduces the actual number of cells in its body, and builds them back once there is something to eat.

facts.text: Turn over a stone in a cool, clean stream and check the wet underside. Planarians hate light, hide beneath rocks all day, and slide out to feed after dark.
facts.more: Two little flaps on the sides of the head, called auricles, feel the water and pick up chemicals drifting in it. That is how a planarian finds a dead insect from a distance in total darkness.

facts.text: It has a real brain — a small two-lobed knot of nerve cells behind the eyespots, with nerve cords running the length of the body. Remove the head, and the tail grows a new brain.

wonder: Every scrap of it carries the plan for all of it — nothing in that body is spare, and nothing is ever quite lost.

name: Velvet worm
blurb: A soft, stubby-legged night hunter of damp forest floors that catches its dinner by shooting glue at it.
size: About as long as your finger — the biggest are nearly as long as your forearm.

facts.text: It hunts with glue. Two nozzles either side of the mouth fire jets of sticky slime that stiffen in seconds, leaving the prey wrapped in a net it cannot break out of.
facts.more: The jets leave the nozzles at 3 to 5 meters per second (10 to 20 ft/s) — faster than you could snatch your hand back. Most shots are fired from about a centimeter away, though the longest squirts on record reach ten times that.

facts.text: The nozzles whip side to side 30 to 60 times a second — about as fast as a hummingbird beats its wings — crossing the two streams into a tangled mesh. No muscle does the whipping.
facts.more: The nozzles are floppy tubes, and fluid shoved through a floppy tube fast enough starts to oscillate all by itself. It is the same physics as a garden hose dropped on the lawn while the water is still running.

facts.text: Slime is expensive, so nothing is wasted. Once the meal is over, the velvet worm eats its own dried glue and recycles the protein.
facts.more: Refilling an emptied slime store takes about 24 days. A velvet worm that fires and misses has just lost most of a month's hunting equipment — which is exactly why it creeps so close before it shoots.

facts.text: Its legs have no joints at all. Each one is a baggy cone held stiff by the fluid pumped inside it — a walking water balloon, tipped with a pair of small hard claws.
facts.more: Onychophora, the group's name, means claw bearer. Depending on the species there are anywhere from 13 to 43 pairs of these legs. They move in smooth traveling waves. The animal seems to flow rather than step.

facts.text: The whole family runs from 0.04 to 8.7 in (1 millimeter to 22 centimeters). The largest is longer than your outstretched hand.
Its breathing holes cannot close. Air comes in through pores that are permanently open. So a velvet worm loses water forty times faster than a caterpillar. It dies quickly in dry air.
facts.more: That one fact explains everywhere it lives: rotting logs, leaf litter, termite tunnels, damp cave walls. It comes out only at night, when the air is wet, and is back underground by morning.

facts.text: Some velvet worms live in groups of up to fifteen, usually relatives, and hunt together. At the kill the order is strict: top female first, then other females, then males, then the young.
facts.more: The group is led by a dominant female who wins her place by fighting. Outsiders who try to join get chased off. That is a surprisingly organized social life for an animal with no jointed legs and two tiny eyes.

facts.text: Run a finger along one and it feels like dry velvet, not slime. The skin is covered in thousands of minute bumps called papillae, and water beads up and rolls off instead of soaking in.
facts.more: Each of those bumps is tipped with a sensory bristle. The surface that keeps the animal dry is also the surface it feels the world with. It reads the ground through the same skin that repels the rain.

facts.text: Many velvet worms give birth to live young instead of laying eggs. In some species the pregnancy runs up to 15 months. That is longer than a human one, in an animal that fits in your palm.
facts.more: There is no larva and no dramatic change of shape along the way. What comes out is simply a miniature velvet worm, legs and claws already in place.

facts.text: It is nearly blind. Two small simple eyes on top of the head tell light from dark and little else. So it hunts with its antennae, sweeping the ground ahead until something moves.
A velvet worm eats about once every one to four weeks. In between it does almost nothing at all — folded into a damp crack, waiting for the next warm, wet night.

wonder: Two soft nozzles, not a muscle between them, and the shape alone weaves the net.

name: Banana slug
blurb: A big, bright yellow slug that mops up the floor of the Pacific coast forests. It eats what has fallen and turns it back into soil.
size: As long as the banana it is named after — up to 9.8 in (25 cm).

facts.text: It is the second-largest land slug in the world. It grows up to 9.8 in (25 cm) long and about 4.1 oz (115 grams).
facts.more: Only one slug grows bigger, a European species called the ash-black slug, which reaches about 12 in (30 cm). Almost everything you can see of a banana slug is muscle, water and mucus.

facts.text: Top speed is about 17 centimeters (6.5 in) a minute. At that pace, crossing a football field would take it roughly nine hours of continuous, unbroken effort.
facts.more: It is not being lazy. A slug moves by rippling one huge muscular foot along a laid-down strip of slime, and that costs a great deal of energy for very little distance.

facts.text: Slime is the whole trick. Banana slug mucus can soak up a hundred times its own volume in water, so the slug travels inside a wet coat it manufactures and carries with it.
facts.more: The mucus is not quite a liquid and not quite a solid. It is stiff enough to hold its shape, but goes runny the moment the foot presses on it — which is what lets the slug both stick and slide.

facts.text: The slime is also a weapon. It carries a chemical that numbs the mouth of an animal that bites down, and it is sticky enough that the attacker often gives up mid-meal.
facts.more: Pick one up and you will meet the same problem. The slime is nearly impossible to rinse off with water. Rubbing your hands with dry soil works far better than the faucet.

facts.text: Four tentacles, all retractable. The upper two carry the eyes; the lower two smell and taste the ground. Lose one and the slug simply grows a new one.
facts.more: The eyes pull back inside the way you push a finger down into a glove. They cannot resolve shapes, only light, dark and movement. Almost everything a banana slug knows about the world arrives through the lower pair.

facts.text: It is the forest's cleanup crew. Dead leaves, moss, animal droppings and mushrooms all go in, and come out again as fertiliser spread across the forest floor.
facts.more: Banana slugs are especially keen on mushrooms, and they carry spores and seeds around the forest as they travel. A slug feeding in one damp hollow is quietly seeding the next one.

facts.text: It breathes through a hole in its right side. The opening is called a pneumostome, and if you watch closely you can see it slowly widen and close like a small round mouth.
facts.more: Behind that hole is a single simple lung. Everything else about a slug is soft and shifting and hard to find twice, but that one neat opening stays exactly where it should be.

facts.text: In a dry spell it burrows into the leaf litter. It seals itself inside a layer of mucus and shuts down completely. It waits there, sometimes for weeks, until the rain comes back.
Every banana slug is male and female at the same time. When two meet, both can go on to lay eggs — up to 75 of them, tucked into a damp log or a hollow under bark.
facts.more: Before mating they circle each other for hours, nipping as they go. The eggs are clear and pearly and are left entirely alone; no parent ever comes back to check on them.

facts.text: The yellow is not fixed. The same slug can turn green, brown, tan, white, or blotched with black. It depends on what it has eaten, how damp it is and how much light it has had.
facts.more: Among wet fallen leaves, a yellow slug speckled with black is much harder to pick out than you would expect. Walk a redwood trail after rain and you will step over several before you spot one.

facts.text: It lives where the fog lives: the damp coastal forests running from southeastern Alaska down the coast to central California. No fog, no banana slugs.
It has fans. The University of California, Santa Cruz sits in the middle of banana slug country. Students there made it the official school mascot, over far fiercer suggestions.

wonder: An animal made almost entirely of water and slime, and set down in a forest wet enough that it never has to dry out.

name: Garden snail
blurb: The common brown snail you find under a flowerpot after rain. It is a soft-bodied animal that carries its own house on its back.
size: Shell about 1 to 1.6 in (25 to 40 mm) across.

facts.text: Its tongue is a ribbon carrying well over ten thousand tiny teeth, called a radula. A snail does not bite a leaf. It rasps it, dragging the toothed belt across like sandpaper.
facts.more: Teeth at the front wear down and are replaced by fresh rows sliding forward from behind, over and over for the snail's whole life. In a very quiet room you can sometimes hear a big snail rasping away at a leaf.

facts.text: Snails have been timed while actually racing. Top speed is about 2 millimeters a second. Crossing a one-meter garden path takes roughly eight minutes of steady, unhurried work.
facts.more: You may see a much faster figure quoted — around 1.3 centimeters a second. Timed races do not back it up. A snail is even slower than its reputation, which is quite an achievement.

facts.text: The shell is not a house it found lying around. It grew there, it is attached to the body, and it gets bigger as the snail does — one new curl at a time.
facts.more: An adult shell has four or five whorls. It is built from calcium carbonate, the same mineral as chalk. If a snail's food is short on calcium, it will eat soil to get what the shell needs.

facts.text: When it gets too dry or too cold, the snail withdraws and seals the doorway with a lid of dried mucus called an epiphragm. Then it waits — sometimes for months.
facts.more: Sealed in like that, and with its blood chemistry changed for winter, a garden snail can survive down to about minus 5 degrees C (23 F). Rain drumming on the shell is the signal to break the seal and come back out.

facts.text: A garden snail has an address. It feeds at night and returns to the very same crack or stone to rest, finding its way back partly by following slime trails.
facts.more: Mark a few with a dot of nail polish and you will keep finding the same individuals in the same spot night after night. Good resting crevices get shared, so one crack may hold a dozen snails.

facts.text: The two long tentacles carry the eyes on their tips. Touch one and it collapses inwards like a sock pulled inside out, then slowly pushes back out again.
facts.more: Those eyes cannot form a sharp picture — only light and shadow. The short lower pair does the real work, smelling and tasting the ground just ahead of the snail's head.

facts.text: It moves on one enormous muscular foot. Put a snail on a sheet of glass and look up from underneath. Waves of muscle ripple forward along the sole. Each wave shoves the snail a little further.
facts.more: The mucus underneath is thixotropic — solid until the foot presses on it, briefly runny, then solid again. So the snail is gluing and un-gluing itself to the ground, wave after wave, the entire way.

facts.text: Startled, it snaps back into the shell. Then it blows out a froth of bubbly mucus around the opening. The froth is sticky, hard to grip, and thoroughly unpleasant to bite into.
Every garden snail is male and female at once. Two snails court for hours, then each fires a tiny chalky spike into the other — a love dart — before they mate.
facts.more: The dart is about 0.28 in (7 mm) long, and the snail cannot aim well: about a third of shots miss altogether or fail to go in. It is not a weapon. Its coating carries a substance that helps the sender's sperm survive inside the other snail.

facts.text: Its waste opening is not at the back. A snail's body is twisted around inside its shell, so the opening ends up near the front, just inside the shell's mouth — right above its own head.
One snail can lay around six batches of eggs in a single year, about fifty pearly white eggs a batch. That is why a single snail in a lettuce bed stops being a single snail rather quickly.
It comes from around the Mediterranean and now lives almost everywhere with a mild climate. People carried it around the world in soil and in plant pots, and on purpose, as food.

wonder: A house that grows with its owner, built out of chalk the snail gathers from the very ground it crawls across.

name: Tardigrade
blurb: A microscopic eight-legged animal. It is small enough to live in a film of water on a scrap of moss. It can survive being dried to dust and brought back.
size: About 0.02 in (0.5 mm) long — roughly the size of a period at the end of a sentence.

facts.text: Half a millimeter long, and yet a complete working animal: eight legs, claws, muscles, a gut, a brain. The whole thing is built from only about a thousand cells.
facts.more: Your body holds trillions of cells. A tardigrade runs a mouth, a gut, a brain and eight legs on roughly a thousand — a number you could sit down and count in an afternoon.

facts.text: Dried out, a tardigrade pulls in its legs, folds into a barrel shape called a tun, and stops. No feeding, no moving, almost no chemistry happening at all.
facts.more: The state is called cryptobiosis, meaning hidden life. A lump of Antarctic moss sat in a freezer at minus 20 C (minus 4 F) for more than thirty years. Then it was thawed and watered. Two tardigrades and one egg came back to life.

facts.text: As it dries, it fills its own cells with special proteins. Those proteins set into a glass-like solid. Every fragile part is held exactly in place until water comes back.
facts.more: Cells losing their water normally tear themselves apart, because everything inside collapses together and sticks. Nothing inside a tun can move at all, so nothing can break. The animal becomes, for a while, a piece of living glass.

facts.text: In the tun state, tardigrades have survived being chilled to minus 272 C (minus 458 F) — one degree above the coldest temperature there can possibly be. Short spells only.
facts.more: Heat is the opposite story. Warmth is the one thing a tardigrade is genuinely bad at. A hot afternoon on a dry wall is far more dangerous to it than a freezer ever was.

facts.text: A dose of radiation that would kill a person many times over barely troubles a tardigrade. They have come through roughly a thousand times what a human body can take.
facts.more: Part of the answer is a protein found in tardigrades and nowhere else. It is nicknamed Dsup, short for damage suppressor. It wraps around the animal's DNA like packing material. Far fewer strands snap when radiation goes through.

facts.text: A batch of dried tardigrades was carried into orbit and the container opened for ten days. Exposed to the raw vacuum of space, most of them came home alive.
facts.more: Adding the Sun's full ultraviolet, though, killed nearly all of them. That detail matters. Tardigrades are not indestructible. They are extraordinarily good at one specific thing, surviving without water. Ultraviolet light is a different problem entirely.

facts.text: Tardigrades have been fired out of a gas gun. They survived hitting a target at about 900 meters per second (2,000 mph). That is roughly the speed of a rifle bullet.
facts.more: That impact squeezes them at something like ten times the crushing pressure at the bottom of the deepest ocean trench. Fired any faster and they do not survive. So this is a limit, not a superpower.

facts.text: Here is the surprise. They do not live in extreme places on purpose. Most tardigrades live in a film of water on moss, lichen or leaf litter — including your own garden wall.
facts.more: Their real enemy is a sunny afternoon. When the moss dries out the water film vanishes and the tardigrade must shut down or die. The same shutdown that carries it through a dry Tuesday is what carries it through the cold and the vacuum.

facts.text: It eats by stabbing. Two needle-sharp stylets punch through the wall of a moss cell, an algal cell, or another tiny animal, and the tardigrade sucks the contents out.
facts.more: The stylets are built from aragonite, the same mineral that makes seashells and pearls. They are not permanent either. Every time a tardigrade sheds its skin it loses the stylets too. It must grow a fresh pair before it can eat again.

facts.text: Its name means slow stepper, and it earns it. Filmed under a microscope, a tardigrade plods along using the same ordered leg pattern insects use, rather than moving its legs at random.
facts.more: It even adjusts. On a soft surface it slows down and takes short steps. On a hard surface it speeds up and lengthens its stride. A far larger animal makes the same choices crossing sand or stone.

facts.text: Scoop up a handful of damp soil and you may be holding hundreds. Soil can hold 300,000 tardigrades in a square meter — and a square meter of moss over two million.
facts.more: That is more animals in one patch of moss than there are people in most cities. They turn up from Himalayan mountaintops to deep-sea mud to Antarctic ice, and on the wall outside your window.

facts.text: Some tardigrade species lay their eggs inside the skin they have just shed, leaving them in a tidy little bag. Others lay eggs covered in spikes, cones and crowns, like microscopic sea mines.

wonder: Something so small it lives in a drop of water on a wall, and built to wait out anything that drop can do.

name: American lobster
blurb: A heavily armored sea-floor crawler with two mismatched claws. It walks the cold Atlantic seabed hunting anything it can crack open.
size: A common one is about as long as your forearm. The big old ones reach the length of your whole arm.

facts.text: Look at the claws — they don't match. One is a fat crusher with blunt knobs for smashing shells. The other is a thin ripper with a jagged edge, like a steak knife.
facts.more: Which side gets which claw isn't fixed. A lobster can be right-crushered or left-crushered, the way you are right- or left-handed. Lose a claw to a fight or a predator and a young lobster can grow a new one back over several moults.

facts.text: A lobster chews with its stomach. Just behind the mouth sits a gastric mill — three hard teeth that grind up food after it has already been swallowed.
facts.more: The mill is a set of calcium-hardened plates worked by muscle. Food goes down barely broken, gets ground there, and only then passes on. When the lobster moults it sheds the lining of that stomach too, and grows a fresh set of teeth with the new shell.

facts.text: Lobsters argue by weeing at each other. Two nozzles beneath the antennae fire a plume of urine one to two meters (3-6 ft) straight at a rival's face.
facts.more: The chemicals in that stream carry a message: how big I am, how ready I am to fight, whether we have met before. Two lobsters square up, exchange squirts, and often one simply backs down without a claw ever landing. The loser remembers the winner's smell for days.

facts.text: A lobster tastes with its feet. Chemical sensors cover its legs and the little antennules on its head, so crossing the seabed is like licking every step.
The heaviest lobster ever recorded weighed 44.4 lb (20.1 kg). It was hauled up off Nova Scotia.
facts.more: Lobsters never stop growing; they simply have to keep swapping shells to do it. A lobster that heavy has climbed out of its own shell and rebuilt it dozens of times, and its claws alone would fill both of your hands.

facts.text: It escapes backwards. One hard flick of the tail fan shoots the lobster away from a predator, tail-first, faster than you could clap your hands.
facts.more: The flick runs on a giant nerve fiber — a single nerve cell so thick it carries the signal almost instantly. The lobster is already moving before there is time to decide anything. It is the same trick a crayfish uses when you reach into the bucket.

facts.text: Lobster blood runs clear, then turns blue in air. It carries oxygen with copper instead of iron, using a molecule called haemocyanin.
facts.more: Your blood is red because haemoglobin holds oxygen with iron. Haemocyanin holds it with copper, and copper goes blue when it grabs on. Copper works well in cold water with little oxygen in it — which is exactly where a lobster lives.

facts.text: Lobsters walk the cold rocky floor of the north Atlantic. They usually stay between 13.1 and 164 ft (4 and 50 m) (13-164 ft) down. By day they wedge into crevices. After dark they come out hunting.
A mother lobster glues her eggs under her own tail. She carries them there for ten or eleven months. She fans them with her swimmerets until they hatch.
facts.more: She may carry tens of thousands at once. The hatchlings look nothing like lobsters — they are transparent specks that drift near the surface, moulting as they go. Only about one in a thousand survives long enough to sink down and start life on the seabed.

facts.text: Lobsters eat crabs, clams, sea urchins, worms and fish, and they are not above scavenging. They also eat their own shed shell, to win back the calcium for the next one.
To grow, a lobster climbs out of itself. The shell splits at the back and the whole animal drags free — legs, antennae, claws, eye coverings and all.
facts.more: The escape takes about fifteen minutes. It is the riskiest thing a lobster does. The new shell underneath is soft as wet paper. The lobster swallows water to swell into a bigger size. Then it hides for days or weeks until the shell hardens.

wonder: Claws, legs, eyes, even the teeth inside its stomach — all shed and rebuilt again and again, and the lobster steps out whole every time.

name: Barnacle
blurb: A crustacean, and a cousin of crabs and shrimp. When young it glues its own head to a rock. It spends the rest of its life inside a little limestone cone.
size: Most are smaller than your thumbnail.

facts.text: A barnacle is lying on its back in there, head cemented down, legs waving out of the top. Every time it feeds, it kicks food into its own mouth.
facts.more: Those feathery legs are called cirri. They sweep out through the opening, curl shut around whatever plankton they catch, and haul it back inside. Watch a barnacle in a tide pool and you will see the little fan flick out and in, out and in.

facts.text: A barnacle gets one decision in its whole life: where to land. The swimming larva, called a cyprid, crawls over a rock testing it, then cements its forehead down for good.
facts.more: The cyprid checks the surface texture, the chemistry, how well it wets, and whether other barnacles already live there — company proves the spot works. Once it commits it glues itself head-first and rebuilds its entire body inside a shell. It will never move again.

facts.text: Cemented in place, a barnacle cannot go looking for a mate. So it reaches — stretching a long flexible tube across to a neighbor. The best read is that this is why barnacles nearly always settle in crowds.
Barnacle glue sets underwater, on a wet, dirty, moving surface — exactly what human glues fail at. Engineers copied it to make a paste that seals a bleeding wound in about fifteen seconds.
facts.more: Nothing manufactured sticks to a wet surface the way barnacle cement does. A team at MIT built a barnacle-inspired paste for surgeons. Shipbuilders chase the same glue from the opposite direction. They want a hull coating that barnacles cannot grip at all.

facts.text: When the tide goes out, a barnacle shuts its front door. Plates on top slide together and seal it in, with a drop of seawater trapped inside.
facts.more: An acorn barnacle's cone is six limestone plates it builds around itself, with a four-plate lid on top — ten in all. Sealed up, it survives hours of baking sun and drying wind. That is why a barnacle rock is silent at low tide and quietly clicking when the sea comes back.

facts.text: It eats by filtering. Plankton, larvae, and scraps far too small to see get combed out of the water by six pairs of feathery legs, over and over and over.
Some barnacles ride whales. They settle on a humpback's skin and cross entire oceans with it, filter-feeding wherever the whale happens to go.
facts.more: Whale barnacles grow rooted prongs of shell down into the skin and lock on there. A single humpback can carry a heavy crust of them. The pattern of markings and scars on its tail is unique. Researchers use it to tell individual whales apart.

facts.text: Barnacles take the worst spot on the coast on purpose: the splash zone, where the waves hit hardest. Also harbor walls, pier legs, ship hulls and turtle shells.
One barnacle weighs almost nothing. A ship's hull crusted with them drags so badly it burns far more fuel, which is why hulls get scraped clean in dry dock.
An adult barnacle has no proper eyes — just three simple light detectors. That is enough to notice a shadow sweep overhead and snap its legs back inside.

wonder: It picks one spot, once, and never moves again — and is still fed twice a day by a tide it does not control.

name: Antarctic krill
blurb: A small, almost see-through, shrimp-like animal of the freezing Southern Ocean. It swarms in numbers vast enough to feed nearly everything else down there.
size: About as long as your little finger.

facts.text: A full-grown krill is about 2.4 in (6 cm) long and weighs 0.1 oz (2 g) — roughly two paperclips. It is so nearly transparent you can see its green gut straight through the shell.
Nobody can count them. The best estimate puts all the Antarctic krill in the ocean together at hundreds of millions of tons. That is one of the greatest weights of any wild animal on earth.
facts.more: Nobody counts them one by one. Ships tow nets and bounce sound off the swarms to work out how much is down there. The swarms stretch for kilometers and pack so tightly that from above they stain the sea a rusty pink-red.

facts.text: Krill swarm. At their thickest, 10,000 to 30,000 of them pack into one cubic meter of water — a box you could just about curl up inside.
facts.more: Predators do not hunt individual krill; they swim straight into the swarm with their mouths wide open. Whales, crabeater seals, penguins, squid and fish all take their share. The swarm survives because there is so much of it that no single mouth makes a dent.

facts.text: A starving krill shrinks. Most animals just get thin — a krill moults into a smaller body and waits for the food to come back.
facts.more: It sheds its shell every 13 to 20 days, all its life. Normally the new one is bigger. Through the dark Antarctic winter there is little to eat. A krill can come out of a molt smaller than it went in. It goes backwards on purpose, then grows again when the light returns.

facts.text: Krill are bioluminescent — they make their own light. Organs beneath the eyestalks and along the underside glow yellow-green for two or three seconds at a time.
facts.more: The light organs are called photophores, and a krill can rotate them to aim the glow. A swarm flickering in black water is one of the strangest sights in the Southern Ocean. What the flashing is for is still unsettled — keeping the swarm together in the dark is the leading idea.

facts.text: Krill farm the underside of the sea ice. They hang upside down beneath it and scrape algae off the frozen ceiling with brush-tipped legs.
facts.more: Through the long, dark winter the ice is the pantry. A krill works along the rough underside of it like a shopper going down a shelf. Its front legs make a basket of bristles. It combs loose algae into the basket and swallows the lot.

facts.text: Every single day krill ride an elevator. They drop to about 330 ft (100 m) in daylight, where it is dark and safer, then climb back up at night to feed.
facts.more: This is called diel vertical migration. Across all the world's oceans it is the largest daily movement of animals on the planet. It happens everywhere at once, every night. Antarctic krill make the trip one to three times a day.

facts.text: Grabbed by a predator, a krill can throw off its own shell in a heartbeat and shoot backwards. Nobody has watched what the predator does next; the empty moult left hanging in the water reads as a decoy.
A female releases thousands of eggs at a time and they sink. They fall for about ten days into the cold and the dark. Then they hatch.
facts.more: The larvae hatch far below and then have to swim all the way back up. The climb takes days and they eat nothing on the way; there is no food until they reach the sunlit surface layer where the algae grow. Getting there in time is the hardest thing a krill ever has to do.

facts.text: Krill live in the Southern Ocean, the ring of freezing water that circles Antarctica. It is some of the coldest, roughest, darkest sea anywhere on the planet.

wonder: Something the length of your finger holds up a whole ocean — the smallest link carrying the heaviest load.

name: Earthworm
blurb: A soft, ringed, boneless animal that eats its way through soil. It swallows dirt at one end and leaves it richer at the other.
size: A big garden nightcrawler is about 9.6 in (24 cm) long.

facts.text: An earthworm has no lungs at all. It breathes straight through its skin, which is why it has to stay damp — a dried-out worm suffocates.
facts.more: Oxygen dissolves into the film of moisture on the skin. Hemoglobin floating loose in the worm's blood picks it up. That is the same oxygen-carrying molecule that makes your blood red. It is exactly why a worm's blood is red too.

facts.text: Five pairs of thick muscular tubes wrap around a worm's gut and squeeze blood along them. They are called aortic arches, and most people just say a worm has hearts.
A bird can rip off a worm's tail and the worm may still survive. But cut one in half and you do not get two worms — the back end dies.
facts.more: The brain, the mouth and nearly all the vital organs sit in the front section, so the back half has nothing to rebuild with. Some composting worms regrow a lost tail well. The common nightcrawler in a garden often cannot regrow one at all.
