facts.text: A worm eats soil. It swallows dirt, digests the dead leaves and microbes mixed into it, and pushes the rest out the back end as a casting.
facts.more: Castings come out richer than the soil went in. They are packed with nitrogen and phosphorus in forms a plant can actually use. In leaf-rich ground one worm can make over 10 lb (4.5 kg) of castings a year.

facts.text: No bones, no legs. A worm moves by squeezing fluid around inside a sealed body and gripping the tunnel wall with tiny stiff bristles called setae.
facts.more: Run a worm gently backwards between your fingers and it feels like sandpaper — those are the setae. It anchors its back half, stretches the front forward, anchors the front, then hauls the back up. Squeeze, grip, stretch, repeat. That grip is why a robin has to pull so hard.

facts.text: A worm has no eyes, but its skin can tell light from dark. Cells scattered over the body, thickest at the head end, make it flinch away from a flashlight beam.
facts.more: Light means the surface, and the surface means birds and drying out — so bright light sends a worm diving back down its burrow. Red light barely registers, which is how people watch nightcrawlers at night without sending them all underground.

facts.text: Worm charmers drive a stake into the ground and rattle it, and worms come up out of the soil. The vibrations feel like a digging mole — the one thing a worm flees upward from.
facts.more: Moles hunt worms by tunneling. A worm's escape is to bolt for the surface, where moles rarely follow. People have used the trick for generations to collect fishing bait. They are not the only ones. Wood turtles stamp their feet to do it, and gulls patter theirs on wet grass.

facts.text: Worms do not come out in the rain because they are drowning. They can survive underwater for a long time. The best read is simpler: wet ground lets them travel over the surface without drying out.
facts.more: Damp air is a worm's chance to move house, find a mate, or leave a flooded burrow — journeys that would kill it on a dry day. Rain drumming on the soil may also sound enough like a digging mole to send some of them straight up.

facts.text: Every earthworm is male and female at once. Two of them line up head-to-tail, swap sperm, and both go away able to make eggs.
facts.more: The pale saddle around a worm's body is the clitellum. After mating it oozes a slimy ring. The ring slides forward off the worm, collecting eggs and sperm on the way. Then it seals shut into a lemon-shaped cocoon no bigger than a grain of rice. A few tiny worms hatch out fully formed.

facts.text: Most garden worms fit across your palm. But one kind along the Mekong River in Southeast Asia stretches to 10 ft (3 m) — longer than you are tall, lying down.
Some worms live in the top few centimeters of leaf litter. Others dig permanent vertical shafts more than a meter straight down and drag dead leaves in after them.
Worms rebuild the ground beneath your feet. Given time, they pass the whole top layer of soil through their bodies — mixing it, draining it, burying dead leaves inside it.

wonder: The soil your food grows in was partly made by animals that never see it, working in the dark, one mouthful at a time.

name: Medicinal leech
blurb: A soft, muscular freshwater worm with a sucker at each end. It feeds on blood. Hospitals still keep them in tanks today.
size: About as long as your hand, though it stretches and shortens constantly.

facts.text: A leech has a sucker at each end. The back one is a clamp for holding on. The front one has the mouth right in the middle of it.
Inside that front sucker are three jaws arranged in a Y, each lined with rows of tiny teeth. The bite leaves a mark shaped like a three-pointed star.
facts.more: The jaws saw rather than stab, rocking back and forth to open a small clean wound. There are around a hundred cutting edges in there, each finer than a pin point. The Y-shaped mark is distinctive enough that a doctor can spot a leech bite on sight.

facts.text: A leech drinks until it looks like a fat sausage. A big one takes up to ten times its own body weight in one meal, then may not eat again for a whole year.
facts.more: The blood goes into pouches called crops that branch off the gut. Bacteria living inside the leech break it down slowly over months. A freshly fed leech is several times its normal size and can barely move. So it lets go, drops off, and hides.

facts.text: Ten little eyes in five pairs run along the top of its head, and not one of them makes a picture. They read light and shadow — enough to notice something entering the water.
facts.more: The leech also feels vibration through the water and tastes chemicals dissolved in it. Warmth, sweat, and the ripples of a wading animal all pull it in. Step into the right pond and leeches will start swimming toward you within a minute.

facts.text: Where you have one brain, a leech has a chain of nerve clusters. They are called ganglia. There is one to a segment, running the whole length of the body, all wired together.
facts.more: There are 21 of them down the middle, plus fused clusters at the head and the tail. Each ganglion drives the swimming of its own segment while staying in step with the rest. The cells are big enough to study one at a time, which has taught people a great deal about how any nervous system times a movement.

facts.text: Leech saliva contains hirudin — an anticoagulant, a chemical that stops blood clotting. It is why a leech bite keeps bleeding for hours after the leech has let go.
facts.more: A leech makes about sixty different proteins in its spit at once. Hirudin stops the blood clotting. Others widen the blood vessels and keep the wound open. Drug companies have copied hirudin to make medicines. Those keep human blood flowing during surgery.

facts.text: The leech is officially medical equipment. In 2004 the American medical regulator classified the medicinal leech as a medical device. That is the same legal category as a scalpel.
facts.more: A surgeon reattaching a finger or an ear can usually reconnect the arteries bringing blood in, but the tiny veins carrying it out are far harder. Blood pools, the tissue turns purple and starts to die. A leech set on that spot drains the pooled blood and keeps it moving until the body grows new veins of its own.

facts.text: On land a leech walks like an inchworm — front sucker down, body arched, back sucker up. In water it swims by rippling its flattened body like a ribbon.
A leech is both male and female at once. After mating, the band around its body makes a foamy cocoon that it leaves tucked in damp soil at the water's edge.
Medicinal leeches live in shallow weedy ponds and marshes. Their range runs across Europe and into western Asia. They have become genuinely rare, partly from being collected for medicine.
A leech has no fixed length. Three layers of muscle — running long, running around, running diagonally — let it be a squat blob one second and a thin thread the next.
You usually feel nothing. A leech bite is painless, so the first sign is the blood rather than the pain — and by then it has already been drinking for a while.

wonder: The creature most people flinch from carries, in its spit, exactly what a surgeon needs — and nobody had to invent it.

name: Bdelloid rotifer
blurb: A complete animal with a brain, gut, jaws and muscles. All of it is built into a body far too small to see without a microscope.
size: About the size of the dot on the letter i
wonder: God built a whole animal — brain, jaws, muscles and all — into a body you would need a microscope to find.

facts.text: You need a microscope to find one. It is still a real animal. It has a mouth, a gut, a bladder, a brain and muscles. All of that is packed into less than a millimeter.
facts.more: Most things this small are single cells. A bdelloid is not. It is built from about a thousand cells, and here is the strange part — that number is fixed. It never grows new ones. The cells it hatches with are the cells it dies with; they only get bigger.

facts.text: Its head ends in two rings of beating hairs called the corona. Under a lens they look exactly like two spinning wheels — but nothing is actually turning.
facts.more: The hairs, called cilia, beat one after another in a traveling ripple, the way a stadium crowd does a wave. Your eye reads the ripple as rotation. The wheels drag a current of water — and any bacteria floating in it — straight down into the mouth.

facts.text: Dry one out completely and it does not die. It shrivels into a speck of dust, waits, and swells back to life when water returns. This is called anhydrobiosis.
facts.more: Rotifers have been brought back after nine years dried out. As they dry, their DNA snaps into pieces — and on rewetting they stitch it back together again. Add a drop of water to a pinch of dry moss and you can watch them uncurl and swim away.

facts.text: A bdelloid shrugs off radiation doses more than a hundred times what would kill a person. The best read is that this is the same trick that lets it survive drying out.
facts.more: Drying shatters DNA. So does radiation. An animal that can already glue its own broken genome back together barely notices the difference. It is one of the toughest creatures ever tested in a laboratory, and it is smaller than a grain of salt.

facts.text: Nobody has ever found a male bdelloid rotifer. Every single one ever caught, anywhere in the world, is female, and each lays her eggs on her own.
facts.more: That is not for lack of looking. Bdelloids have been collected from ponds, gutters, roof moss and desert crusts on every continent, and the count of males still stands at zero. Each mother's eggs hatch into daughters that are copies of her.

facts.text: Behind its mouth sits a mastax. That is a muscular grinder holding hard jaws called trophi. The jaws chew bacteria and algae into paste before swallowing.
Up to a tenth of a bdelloid's genes match bacteria, fungi and plants rather than anything animal. Nobody has watched one take a gene in; the match in the DNA is the argument.
facts.more: This is called horizontal gene transfer. Bdelloids carry more borrowed genes than almost any other animal. Some of them are working genes, too. They are recipes for enzymes no other animal has, switched on and running inside a rotifer.

facts.text: A dried rotifer is basically dust, and the best read of how they turn up everywhere is that the wind carries them. A speck that lands in a rain puddle on your driveway can uncurl and be feeding again within hours.
Look in the green moss on a wall, a roof gutter, or the damp grit in a plant pot. Squeeze the moss into a drop of water and they are there.
facts.more: Moss is a rotifer city. It holds water after rain, bakes dry in the sun, then wets again — a rhythm that would kill most animals and suits a bdelloid perfectly. A single pinch of roof moss can hold dozens of them.

facts.text: Bdelloid means leech-like, and that is how they usually travel: gripping with the head, arching the body, reaching forward again, exactly like an inchworm. They can swim too, using the corona.
Many bdelloids carry a pair of red eyespots on the snout. They cannot form a picture — they only tell light from dark, which is enough to know whether you are out in the open.

name: Amoeba
blurb: A single living cell with no fixed shape at all — it simply flows into whatever shape it needs next.
size: A big one is about half a millimeter — just barely a visible speck
wonder: One cell, and God left nothing out of it: it hunts, builds, bails out water and makes more of itself, without a single organ.

facts.text: An amoeba has no front, no back and no fixed shape. It pushes out a bulge of itself called a pseudopod, pours its insides into it, and that is how it travels.
facts.more: The name comes from a Greek word meaning change. Its insides are part stiff jelly and part runny liquid, and it switches between the two on demand — stiffening to make a wall, softening to flow. Watch one for a minute and it is never the same shape twice.

facts.text: It has no mouth. It simply flows around its dinner until the dinner is inside it, two arms of cell meeting on the far side and sealing shut. This is phagocytosis.
facts.more: The trapped meal ends up in a bubble called a food vacuole. Enzymes take it apart in there. Amoebae eat algae, bacteria and other single cells. A captured paramecium can go on thrashing inside that bubble for a minute or two before it stops.

facts.text: Fresh water leaks into an amoeba non-stop, by osmosis. If it did nothing it would swell and burst — so it bails, filling a bubble with the extra water and squirting it out.
facts.more: That bubble is the contractile vacuole. Under a microscope you can time it: swelling slowly, then collapsing in an instant, over and over, for the whole life of the cell. It is a pump that never once gets to stop.

facts.text: A relative called Chaos can reach 0.2 in (5 mm). That is a single cell you can spot on the pond floor with no microscope at all.
facts.more: Most are smaller, between one and three millimeters. And Chaos does not have one nucleus the way most cells do. It has hundreds, sometimes as many as a thousand, scattered all through it — one single cell running on a whole crowd of control centers.

facts.text: The water dries up, or the food runs out. Many kinds of amoeba then roll into a ball and build a tough wall around the outside. They wait inside this cyst until things improve.
An amoeba does not have babies. It becomes two. The cell pinches in at the middle, pulls apart, and where there was one amoeba there are now two, each a complete one.
facts.more: This is called binary fission. The nucleus copies itself first, so both halves get a full set of instructions. The two halves stay joined by a thinning thread of cytoplasm that stretches and stretches until it finally snaps.

facts.text: Some amoebae build houses. They glue sand grains, or tiny plates they make themselves, into a shell with a single doorway, then stick their arms out through it.
facts.more: These are called testate amoebae. Difflugia picks sand grains out of the mud and cements them into a neat flask — and it is fussy about grain size. A single cell, with no eyes and no hands, sorting building material.

facts.text: It has no eyes, no nose and no nerves, but it still finds food. It senses the chemicals leaking out of its prey and grows its pseudopods toward the strongest trace.
An amoeba drinks as well as eating solid food. It puckers tiny channels inward and swallows droplets of water whole. The habit is called pinocytosis, which means cell-drinking.
Scoop the brown gunk off the bottom of a pond, not the clear water above it. Amoebae live down in the ooze among rotting leaves, where the bacteria they hunt are thickest.
Amoebae are in no hurry. A big one crosses a few millimeters in an hour, which makes the width of your fingernail most of a morning's travel.

name: Paramecium
blurb: A single cell shaped like a slipper that swims by rowing with thousands of tiny beating hairs.
size: About the size of the dot on a letter i
wonder: No brain, no nerves, no eyes — and it still backs up, turns, and tries again. God fitted the whole instruction set inside one cell.

facts.text: It is covered in thousands of hairs called cilia, and they all row together. A paramecium crosses about a millimeter every second. That is four of its own body lengths.
facts.more: Four body lengths a second is a serious sprint. For you, that would be four of your own body lengths every second. The cilia never all beat at once; they beat in traveling waves, so the cell is always being pushed and never coasting.

facts.text: For a single cell it is a giant. Line up a hundred of the bacteria it eats and you have the length of one paramecium. Hold a jar to the light and it shows as a white speck.
It does not swim in a straight line. It spirals, turning slowly around its own long axis the entire way, like a rifle bullet or a well-thrown football.
Bump a paramecium into an obstacle and it does something clever: every hair reverses, it backs up, turns slightly, and tries forward again. It repeats this until it gets past.
facts.more: This is called the avoidance reaction, and it is the whole of a paramecium's problem-solving. It has no brain and no nerves. The bump changes the electricity across its skin, the cilia flip direction, and back it goes — a reflex built into one single cell.

facts.text: Under its skin sit hundreds of loaded darts called trichocysts. Threaten it and they fire at once, shooting out long threads that swell into a spiky halo around the cell.
facts.more: The threads are not poisonous. They work by shoving — a predator gets a face full of them and the paramecium jets away through the gap. Fire them and they are gone; the cell has to build a fresh set from scratch.

facts.text: A groove runs down one side, lined with more cilia that sweep bacteria into it like a conveyor belt. At the bottom the food is wrapped in a bubble and digested.
facts.more: Those bubbles are food vacuoles, and each one takes a tour. It is carried along a set path around the inside of the cell. Enzymes work on it as it goes. The leftovers are dumped out through one fixed spot in the skin, a permanent back door.

facts.text: A paramecium keeps two kinds of nucleus. The big one, the macronucleus, runs the daily work. The small one is held in reserve and used only when two cells meet.
facts.more: The macronucleus holds many copies of the instructions — it is the working, dog-eared reference book. The micronucleus is the pristine master copy, locked in a drawer. Damage the working copy and the cell can print a fresh one from the master.

facts.text: Two paramecia can stick together side by side. They open a channel between them. They swap the contents of their small nucleus. Then they part and carry on separately.
facts.more: This is called conjugation, and it is not how they make new cells — they do that by simply splitting in two. Conjugation makes no babies at all. Two cells go in and two cells come out, each carrying a mixed set of instructions it did not have before.

facts.text: Fresh water floods in constantly. A paramecium runs two pumps, each with canals spreading out like the spokes of a star, collecting the extra water and firing it back outside.
facts.more: You can watch a star fill and vanish, fill and vanish, several times a minute. Move the same cell into saltier water and the pumping slows right down — less water is pushing in, so there is less to throw back out.

facts.text: Look in still water that has turned cloudy and smells faintly bad. A jar of pond water with a few dead leaves in it will be swarming within about a week.
facts.more: The leaves rot, the bacteria bloom, and the paramecia arrive to eat the bacteria. This is the classic way to grow them on purpose. Hay in water works just as well, which is why the mixture has its own name: a hay infusion.

facts.text: One kind, Paramecium bursaria, is bright green. Hundreds of tiny algae live inside it, making sugar from sunlight and handing it over. The best read is that the algae get a safe ride in return.
facts.more: It is a straight trade. The algae get shelter and a supply of carbon dioxide; the paramecium gets fed even when there are no bacteria about. Keep one in the dark long enough, though, and it loses its green.

facts.text: Paramecia get hunted too. A barrel-shaped cell called Didinium rams into one and harpoons it. Then it swallows a paramecium bigger than itself, stretching open like a snake.
facts.more: Didinium fires out barbed threads to grip its prey, then opens a mouth that expands far beyond its normal size. Swallowing can take several minutes. It is one of the classic sights in a drop of pond water: one single cell eating another whole.

name: Diatom
blurb: A single-celled drifter that makes food from sunlight and lives inside a shell made of real glass.
size: Far too small to see without a microscope
wonder: Twelve thousand kinds named so far, and God gave every one of them a different pattern in the glass.

facts.text: A diatom lives inside a shell it makes out of silica — the same mineral as sand and window glass. It is called a frustule, and it is a glass house of the cell's own making.
facts.more: The cell pulls dissolved silicon out of the water and lays it down in a shell so finely patterned that no two kinds look alike. Ribs, pores, spikes, stars, triangles, spirals. Microscopists arrange them on glass slides like jewels, and people still do it today.

facts.text: The shell comes in two halves that fit together like a box with its lid. The top piece overlaps the bottom piece exactly the way a shoebox does.
Here is the odd part. When a diatom divides, each new cell keeps one old half and builds the new half inside it. So the next one is slightly smaller. And the next.
facts.more: A line of diatoms shrinks a little with every single split, until they reach a lower limit. Then one cell escapes its shell completely, swells back to full size as a bare cell called an auxospore, and builds a brand-new large shell. Then the shrinking starts over.

facts.text: Diatoms make oxygen from sunlight, the way a leaf does. There are so many of them in the sea that, on the best estimate, roughly one breath in every five you take was made by a diatom.
facts.more: They are not plants and they are not seaweed — they are single cells drifting near the surface. When conditions are right they multiply into blooms so vast that the ocean changes color, and the swirling pattern can be photographed from space.

facts.text: Long boat-shaped diatoms can move. A slit called a raphe runs down the shell, and the cell squeezes a sticky ribbon out through it, gripping the ground and hauling itself along.
facts.more: You can find their tracks. On wet mud at low tide, diatoms glide up toward the light during the day. They slide back down into the mud before the water returns. Faint trails are left behind them in the surface film.

facts.text: Some diatoms live inside sea ice, in the salty channels running through it. So many pack in that the underside of the ice turns brown.
facts.more: That brown layer feeds the whole polar food chain. Krill scrape it off the ice from below to graze on it, and whales eat the krill. When the ice melts in spring, the released diatoms bloom in open water and the whole system switches on at once.

facts.text: Chalky white diatomaceous earth is nothing but heaped-up diatom shells. It goes into swimming pool filters, cat litter, and is used as a gentle scrubbing powder.
facts.more: Alfred Nobel used it too. Nitroglycerine is dangerously twitchy on its own. Soak it into diatomaceous earth and it becomes a stable paste you can carry around safely. That paste is dynamite, held together by microscopic glass shells.

facts.text: A glass box sounds fragile. It is not. Diatom shells resist crushing so well that engineers study them, hunting for ways to build strong things that are almost entirely empty space.
Most diatoms are about the width of a hair. The largest reach a millimeter or two. That is a single cell you could actually pick out with your own eye.
More than twelve thousand kinds have been named, and each is told apart by its shell pattern alone. Circles, needles, boats, chains, stars, fans, crescents — all of them in glass.
A diatom needs three things: sunlight, carbon dioxide, and dissolved silicon for its shell. Run the silicon out and a bloom stops dead, however much light and food is left.
Many diatoms link into chains, ribbons and zigzags, cell joined to cell at the corners. The best read is that a long chain is far harder for a small grazer to fit into its mouth.

name: Dust mite
blurb: A tiny eight-legged cousin of spiders that lives in your mattress and eats the flakes of dead skin you shed.
size: Smaller than the period at the end of this sentence
wonder: Even the skin you shed and never think about is somebody's daily bread. In God's world nothing is left over.

facts.text: Right now there are dust mites in your mattress, your pillow, your carpet and your sofa. Not because your house is dirty — they are in almost every house that has people in it.
facts.more: They want three things: warmth, damp air, and dead skin. A bed supplies all three, every night. This is not a sign that anything is wrong. Homes scrubbed absolutely spotless still have them, because the thing they are eating is you.

facts.text: You shed dead skin constantly without ever noticing, and it settles into your bedding. That is the dust mite's entire diet. Your bed is its dinner table.
facts.more: It struggles with a fresh dry flake. Dust mites do better on skin that mold has already softened up, so they favor the damper corners of a mattress. In effect, the mold does the cooking and the mite eats the meal.

facts.text: Here is the good news. A dust mite cannot bite you and has no interest in your blood. It has no idea you exist. It only wants the flakes you leave behind.
facts.more: This matters, because dust mites get blamed for bites they are physically unable to make. Their mouthparts are built for scraping and chewing dry crumbs, not for piercing skin. If something bit you in bed, it was not a dust mite.

facts.text: Dust mites do not make people ill by touching them. It is their droppings. One mite makes about two thousand of them in a ten-week life, each smaller than the width of a hair.
facts.more: Every pellet is coated in digestive enzymes. Those proteins are called allergens, and some people's bodies react to them. Thump a pillow and the pellets lift into the air. Breathe them in and they set off sneezing, itching or asthma.

facts.text: A dust mite never drinks. It cannot. It pulls water vapor straight out of the air using a salty fluid it secretes near its front legs, which soaks up damp like a sponge.
facts.more: That is why they need humid air. Dry a room out and the mites dry out with it and die — no amount of skin flakes can save them. It is also why they are scarce in deserts and rare in houses high up in the mountains.

facts.text: It is about a quarter of a millimeter long, smaller than a printed period. You could line up eighty of them across the width of your thumbnail.
Count the legs and it gives itself away: eight. A dust mite is not an insect at all. It is an arachnid, a cousin of spiders, scorpions and ticks.
facts.more: It also has no eyes and no antennae. The body is a single see-through bag with legs on it — you can look straight through the shell at the gut inside. It navigates entirely by touch and by chemicals, feeling its way through the dust.

facts.text: A female lives about ten weeks and lays sixty to a hundred eggs. The young hatch with only six legs, and grow the last pair when they moult.
facts.more: Sixty eggs is a modest number by insect standards, but it is plenty. Ten weeks is long enough for generations to overlap. Inside a mattress the temperature barely shifts and the air stays damp. Fresh food arrives every single night.

facts.text: A single gram of mattress dust — about a pinch — commonly holds a hundred mites or more. Allergy doctors use roughly that level as the mark where a house starts causing trouble.
Sprays do very little. Heat and dryness are what work: a wash hotter than about 55°C (130°F) kills them, and so does a spell in a hot tumble dryer.
Dust mites cannot fly or jump, and they mostly stay put. Nobody has tracked one moving house — the best read is that they ride along on clothes, bedding and second-hand furniture.
